  That is `mask_mode`'s rule and the reason the panel **dims** the fields an alignment does not read
  rather than hiding them.
- **Two guards, and "does it fit" is not "how many are there"** (§15 D488). `tracks` refuses a grid
  whose *numbers* do not fit — a zero count, a non-finite field, margins and gutters leaving no room —
  and every clause of that test is denominated in units of the frame's extent, where a count is a
  number of **allocations**. Under `Stretch` a track is `extent / n`, positive and finite for every
  `n`, so the fit guard is structurally unable to fire however large the count is: `u32::MAX` on a
  400×200 frame passes it and asks the paint path for 137 GB, where `handle_alloc_error` **aborts**.
  `count` is bounded by nothing in the model, the save format or the loader — only the panel clamps,
  to 1000, which is a guard on the keyboard and not on the document — so `tracks` clamps to
  `MAX_TRACKS`. ⚠️ **Clamped rather than refused**, which is `count`'s own bargain and
  `geometry::MAX_SIDES`' rule: a number dragged past sense is not an error. The cap is deliberately
  well above the panel's, so a file written by some future build with a wider field is drawn rather
  than truncated.
- **The arithmetic is a free function and the clip is not.** `tracks` reports what the grid *says*,
  including a fixed run longer than the frame; `canvas::draw_layout_grids` intersects each band with
  the frame's own box, in local space so a rotated frame's bands turn with it. ⚠️ **Both of the
  frame's own numbers are read through the preview** — the size off `Session::display_node` and the
  world transform off `Session::preview_world_transform` — so the bands follow a move, a rotation or
  a skew that has not committed exactly as they follow a resize. Taking either of the two off the
  committed resolve is §15 D391, where the frame slid out from under its own grid and the two met
  again only on release. Drawn over the pixel
  grid and under the frame labels. ⚠️ **Present mode is not a switch over it** (§15 D750): the grids
  used to return early under it, on the premise that present mode *"already
  hides every other overlay"* — measured false, and then overruled, present mode hiding the app's
  chrome while the canvas goes on working, so a designer editing with the panels out of the way still
  sees the grid they are aligning to. D385 declined a global *Show layout grid* toggle **because** of
  that premise, so falsifying it reopened the question rather than answering it — and **the maintainer
  answered it on 2026-09-15** (§15 D755): *View ▸ Show layout grid*, `OndinApp::show_layout_grids`, read here
  as an early `return`. 🚨 **It is the outermost of three gates and it is not a write.** A band draws
  only while its own grid's eye is on (`LayoutGrid::visible`, document state, saved) and only on a
  frame `shown_visible` admits; this one sits above both and deliberately leaves the eyes alone, so
  turning it back on restores exactly what they said. Clearing `LayoutGrid::visible` across the
  document instead would spend the per-grid state the Layout grid card exists to keep, and would land
  in the undo history as an edit to the artwork.
- Authored in the inspector's **Layout grid** card, the third panel a frame gets and directly under
  *Frame templates* — and the third a multi-selection gets too, in the same order and by the same
  calls: both cards ask the selection what they are acting on rather than being handed a node
  (`frame_subjects`, one rule for the two of them), so each acts on every selected **frame** at once
  and draws nothing where there is no frame in the selection (§9.4, §15 D387, D389, D390).
  ⚠️ Its numeric fields are hand-wound rather than valved, exactly as the export panel's JPEG quality
  is and for the same reason — there is nothing to preview through `RenderOverrides` — with the
  in-flight value in `app::InFlight::grid_scrub` (§15 D785), which names **every frame the drag is being written to**
  and which the **canvas** reads too, so the bands move under the hand on all of them rather than on
  the anchor alone while the release commits to five. `cancel_gesture` drops it by name.
- **A grid's colour is `PaintSlot::Grid(i)`** — the sixth slot naming something that is not a fill, so
  the chip, the hex field and the detached picker are the app's own rather than a second colour panel,
  and the percentage beside the hex **is** the alpha, exactly as a shadow's opacity is (§15 D333,
  D387). The write goes to **every selected frame**, not to the slot's anchor node alone, which is safe
  for the one reason the card's rows are drawn at all — the frames agree, so the anchor's list is every
  subject's list (§15 D389). ⚠️ **So the picker over that anchor has to close when the agreement goes,
  and it did not until §15 D553**: `PaintSlot::Grid(i)` fell into `picker_ui`'s catch-all
  `!selection.contains(node)`, and the anchor stays contained through a Shift-click, so a hex typed
  after the card had stopped drawing rows recoloured the *other* frame's grid. Its arm asks
  `shared_grids(&frame_subjects())` — the **frames**, not the selection, or a Shift-clicked rectangle
  would close a picker whose row is still on screen. ⚠️ It is the only slot whose paint is chrome, so it owes a **second preview
  path**: `RenderOverrides` absorbs the operation, and `OndinApp::preview_grid` fills `grid_paint` beside
  `preview_guide`'s `guide_previews` — **gathering** the transaction's one op per frame into a single
  buffer naming them all, since a buffer holding only the last would preview the drag on one frame and
  commit it to five. That is deliberately a *second* buffer over the same grid rather
  than `grid_scrub` — a colour landing in the fields' buffer would be read on the next frame as a
  finished field edit and committed once a frame — so the canvas applies it **after** the scrub, and
  `remap_grid_slots` walks an open picker down when a grid above it is removed.
- **The colour a new grid *starts* at steps** (§15 D388). `next_grid_color` hands back the first entry
  of `GRID_COLORS` nobody on the frame is using — not the entry at the new grid's index, which hands
  back a duplicate the moment a grid is deleted and another added. The six are `DEFAULT_GRID_COLOR`
  rotated by multiples of 60° at its own saturation, value and alpha, entry 0 being that constant bit
  for bit. ⚠️ **Their order is not the wheel's**: thirds first (red, green, blue), halfway points after
  (olive, cyan, magenta), so that *two* grids — the ordinary case, a column grid beside a row grid —
  are 120° apart rather than 60. Past six it repeats, stepping by the list's length. Only the panel's
  `+` steps: `LayoutGrid::new` carries the plain default, which is what a loaded file or a fixture
  should get.

### 5.4 Text node

**Three scopes, two of them spannable** (`typography.rs`). A character attribute may vary over a byte
range, so it lives in the node's defaults *plus* a set of per-range overrides. **Seven paragraph
attributes now do the same** — the spacing, the first-line indent, `hanging`, the two block indents, the
list marker and its nesting level — while every block attribute, and the rest of the paragraph scope, may
not vary within a node and is a plain field. One list serves both: `Spans<A>` is generic over a `SpanAttr`, implemented by `CharAttr`
over `TextStyle` and by `ParaAttr` over `ParagraphStyle`, so the invariants, the boundary rule and the
byte-stable sort exist once rather than twice. Scope is still a type-level fact, and the sentence it buys
is unchanged: nothing can write a per-range alignment, because no span type carries one (§15 D77, D163).

```rust
NodeKind::Text {
    content: String,
    style: Box<TextStyle>,     // character defaults — boxed, see D77
    spans: CharSpans,          // per-attribute character overrides; empty on uniform text
    para_spans: ParaSpans,     // per-paragraph overrides, byte-keyed like `spans` — D163
    paragraph: ParagraphStyle, // paragraph defaults: align, indents, wrapping, direction, spacing
    block: BlockStyle,         // node-wide: vertical align, box trim, overflow, max lines
    sizing: TextSizing,
}

/// One length type for line height, letter/word spacing, paragraph spacing,
/// indent, baseline shift and decoration thickness/offset.
pub enum Length { Px(f64), Em(f64) }   // Em is a FRACTION of the font size, not a CSS percentage

pub enum TextSizing {
    Auto,                      // no wrapping; the box grows both ways
    AutoHeight(f64),           // wraps at this width; the box grows downwards
    Fixed(kurbo::Size),        // wraps at width; the box is exactly this, per BlockStyle::overflow
}
```

- **One span carries one attribute** (`Spans<A>` holds `Span<A> { start, end, attr: A }`).
  Two adjacent runs differing only in weight share every other attribute rather than duplicating a
  whole style struct — which is also the shape parley resolves styles in, so the layout call is a
  translation rather than a reconciliation. Invariants, all established by `Spans::normalize` and
  therefore the same in both scopes: no empty span; no two spans of one kind overlapping; no span equal
  to the node default; sorted by `(attribute, start)` for byte-stable saves (invariant 9).
  ⚠️ **"Attribute" there is the *declaration order* of `CharAttrKind` and `ParaAttrKind`, so that
  order is part of the file format** (§15 D598, amending D154's reason). The rule it imposes is that
  **an existing variant never moves** — a kind exchanged with its neighbour re-sorts the spans of every
  document on disk *that holds both*, and each one then churns a diff on its next save while saying
  nothing, which is the wording the test's own failure message uses for the same reason. A
  kind that merely *arrives* is harmless at any index: the ones already there keep their relative
  order, and `CharAttr` serializes under its variant name rather than its position. Appending is still
  the convention, because it is the one edit that cannot move a variant. `CharAttrKind::ALL` and
  `ParaAttrKind::ALL` are the written-out lists, and asserting them strictly ascending is what makes a
  move visible — D154 named a test for this that could not see one.
  ⚠️ **"No two overlapping" is a postcondition, and until 2026-09-09 nothing said what an overlap
  *becomes*** (§15 D643). **It is resolved by painting**: spans of one kind are laid down in sorted
  order, each byte takes the value of the last one covering it, and a span painted over keeps whatever
  lies outside the shared bytes on **both** sides. The old rule was a truncation whose own comment was
  false in both clauses — it claimed the *later* span won as *"the one a caller set most recently"*,
  where the list has just been sorted, so "later" meant "starts further right" and a tie was decided by
  the order the file's array happened to be in; and emptying a span popped its **whole** range,
  including bytes nothing overlapped. `std::cmp::Reverse(end)` joins the sort key to break that tie
  widest-first, which is the only reason two spans sharing a start have a defined winner — it changes
  which *input* survives and not how the survivors are written, so the `(attribute, start)` save order
  above is untouched. Two spans with an **identical** range and different values are still decided by
  array order, which is stated rather than guarded: nothing here compares values, and this crate
  cannot produce the case. Reachable from a file only — `set`, `edited`, `clamped`, `restated` and
  `scaled` cannot make a containment — which is why it is the loader's normalize (§5.11) that meets it.
- **`Length` is canonicalized on write** — rounded to four places — so span coalescing can use exact
  equality. Without it a drag producing `0.020000000000000004` never merges with a typed `0.02`: the
  span list fragments, the file grows, and every diff churns. ⚠️ **"On write" did not include the way
  in until 2026-09-07** (§15 D443): `TextStyle` and `Spans<A>` are plain `#[derive(Deserialize)]`, so
  serde builds them field by field and never calls a constructor, and a hand-edited value survived the
  load exactly as written. `Spans::clamped` now puts every span's attribute through `canonical_attr`,
  which round-trips it through `SpanAttr::set_on` into a clone of the defaults and reads it back —
  the only way to canonicalize without a per-variant list, since `set_on` *is* the scope's own setter.
  The **defaults themselves** are still not canonicalized on load, which is stated rather than assumed:
  closing that needs the enumeration this shape exists to avoid. ⚠️ **The rounding must not manufacture an
  infinity out of a finite number, and it did** (§15 D424): the obvious `(v × 10⁴).round() / 10⁴`
  overflows for any `|v| > f64::MAX / 10⁴`, and the `is_finite` guard above it is asked of the *input*
  — so the sanitizer was the thing producing the value that makes a document never open again.
  `round_to_places` returns such a magnitude unchanged, which is exact rather than approximate: at that
  size the gap between representable neighbours is astronomically larger than `1e-4`. `Length::scaled` is also the whole of
  the photographic scale tool's rule for text ("multiply the `Px`, leave the `Em`"), replacing the
  per-field list §5.6's `scale_scalars` had to remember. **All three scopes publish that rule from
  core** — `CharAttr::scaled_by` for the spans, `ParagraphStyle::scaled` for the paragraph defaults
  and `TextStyle::scaled` for the node defaults — so the app calls rather than restates. ⚠️ **The
  node one was missing until 2026-09-09** (§15 D664) and `tools::scaled_text_scopes` had re-stated
  all six of its decisions in a literal, above a byte-identical private twin of `scale_decoration`,
  with `ParagraphStyle::scaled` called one line below the copy. ⚠️ **It is a field literal rather than
  a loop through `TextStyle::set`, deliberately**: `set` canonicalizes and `Spans::scaled` does not,
  so a canonicalized default compared against an un-canonicalized span is a different comparison from
  the one `normalize` makes — which would change *which spans are stored*, not what any of them says.
  The two are held together by a test asked over `CharAttrKind::ALL`, not by the type system.
  ⚠️ **A `Length`'s unit is data even where its number is zero, and the save threw it away** (§15
  D537). All seven optional lengths — `letter_spacing`, `word_spacing`, `baseline_shift`, and
  `spacing`, `indent`, `indent_start`, `indent_end` — elided on `Length::is_zero`, which is true of
  `Em(0.0)` as readily as of `Px(0.0)`; `Length::default()` is `Px(0.0)`, so a field set to `%` and
  left at 0 was absent from the file and came back `px`. **Zero is the only value this can go wrong
  at**, because `resolve` gives `0.0` for both and nothing rendered ever disagrees — the unit is
  unobservable in the drawing and still observable in the panel. `Length::is_default_zero` asks about
  the *default* variant rather than about the number, which is what a `skip_serializing_if` on a
  non-scalar type has to do; `is_zero` survives for `svg.rs`, which asks a different question. No
  schema bump: it only adds a key an older reader already understands (§5.11).
  ⚠️ **The panel half of that is the reader's, and it is a comparison on the *resolved* value** (§15
  D799). Keeping the two distinct is what made `Spans::shared_in` — which compares structurally, and
  must — report *Mixed* over text whose spacing is zero throughout, so the Type panel's `shared` and
  `para_shared` fall through to `agreed_zero` for all seven lengths: every value a zero length means
  one value, whatever units they are in, and it hands back the **first** one so the unit chip keeps
  the suffix the user chose. **It stops at zero on purpose** — that is the only amount at which the
  unit says nothing about the ink, and a general resolved comparison would flip a field between a
  number and a dash as the text was resized.
- **The boundary rule, stated once**: typing at the edge of a span inherits from the character to the
  left, unless the caret was explicitly restyled while empty (`TextEdit::pending`). Every rich-text
  bug in every editor lives in this question; `Spans::edited` is the single implementation, for the
  paragraph list as much as the character one — a paragraph reads the value in force at its **first
  byte**, so one character typed before it moves that byte out from under an override.
- **A paragraph-scoped write acts on the selection snapped outward to hard breaks**
  (`text::paragraph_bounds`, `pub` so the panel and `TextEdit::paragraph_range` share one statement of
  it — the hard-break set is parley's and nothing outside `text.rs` restates it). Two edges in it are
  not what the obvious formula gives: a selection ending exactly *on* a boundary does not reach the
  paragraph after it, where a bare caret in that same position does; and a paragraph with no bytes of
  its own — the one a trailing newline makes — reaches back over its own break, an empty range being
  one `Spans::set` would silently no-op on (§15 D164).
- **`Option<Length>` where `None` means "the font decides"** — a decoration's thickness and offset, and
  line height's Auto (`MetricsRelative(1.0)`, CSS `normal`). The same "absence is a state" pattern as
  `Option<Pivot>`, and what keeps the value correct across a font swap. The offset is positive **up**,
  which is why its field is prefixed with an arrow that points rather than one that spans (§15 D151).
  **The two differ in sign and only one of them says so**: the offset is signed and the thickness is
  **floored at zero** in `canonical_decoration`, in both units, because a negative thickness has no
  meaning and rendered three different ways — nothing on the canvas, `-5px` in the exported file, and
  the face's own weight on re-import (§15 D546). ⚠️ **`Some(0.0)` and `None` are different answers**
  and neither collapses into the other: no line, against the font's own.
- **Three things move text after parley is done with it** — paragraph spacing, box trim and vertical
  alignment — and all three are folded into one `text::YMap`, the single statement of how far each line
  moved, read at **both** boundaries: the scene walk that draws, and the hit test that asks parley where
  a point landed. One statement of the amount is what keeps the caret under the pointer (D79). **A shift
  belongs to a line, not to a y**, and the readers therefore differ: `YMap::to_local` decides from the
  coordinate and is right only for a *baseline*, while a caret or highlight rectangle's edges are **ink**
  coordinates that fall outside their own line box, so those go through `to_local_on_line` with the line
  named. Deciding a rectangle's spacing from its own y drew the caret one whole gap too high in every
  paragraph after the first (§15 D166). **The way back is not a subtraction**: a paragraph gap is space
  that exists in local y and not in layout y at all, so `Shaped::layout_y` resolves which line's box the
  point is in or nearest to — the boxes tile — and only then asks for that line's shift. Doing it
  arithmetically put a click in the gap on a line up to a whole paragraph away (§15 D166). **Spacing is
  space-*before***, and `y_map` reads it off the paragraph *below* each hard break:
  that reproduces the node-level meaning exactly — a gap at every break, none over the opening line —
  while leaving one paragraph free to ask for its own.
- **Every line's baseline is stored, because it cannot be recovered afterwards.** `TextLayout::baselines`
  is one text-local y per line, top to bottom, filled in `extract`'s existing line walk from the same
  `YMap::to_local(line.metrics().baseline)` the list-marker collection already asks for — one level
  finer, not a second walk. It has to be stored: `Glyph::y` sits on the baseline only for a run with no
  `baseline_shift`, and a shift is a *draw offset* rather than a metric, so a superscript's glyphs are
  deliberately off their line's baseline and collecting distinct glyph `y`s invents one baseline per
  superscript (§15 D355). `text::export_lines` reports the same number honestly and is the wrong door
  on the render path — it takes a `TextRef`, re-shapes through parley and allocates a `Vec<ExportLine>`
  per call. The app reads this for baseline snapping and the baseline overlay (§9.4).
- **Box trim never moves the ink.** `TextLayout::origin` is the offset from the node's local origin to
  the top-left of its box; trimming shifts *that* and shrinks the box, so the glyphs keep their
  coordinates and `TextSizing::Fixed(size)` goes on meaning exactly the box the user typed (D78).
  **New text is trimmed to `CapToBaseline`, and the app is what authors that** — `BoxTrim::None` is
  still the type's `#[default]`, because that is what an absent field in every saved file means (D78,
  D199). So a text node has two boxes: `TextLayout::bounds()`, the trimmed one everything *measures*
  with, and `untrimmed_bounds()`, the full line box, which exists only to be **drawn** (§9.4) and is
  equal to `bounds()` exactly when trim changed nothing — including every `Fixed` node, where trim
  moves only the vertical-alignment datum. Consumers test that equality rather than asking what the
  trim setting is.
- **Type on a path is a pass over the finished flat layout, and it maps the plane rather than the
  line** (§15 D405). `NodeKind::Text::on_path` is a `BezPath` rail in the node's own space — the path
  belongs to the text node, is not referenced from it, and is consumed from the layer it came from by
  `build::text_on_path`, with `build::detach_text_path` the way back. `text::bend` runs **last**, after
  `decoration_ink` and `skip_ink`, so bands and their skip-ink gaps are still computed as plain
  intervals in flat space; it then maps flat `x` to distance *along* the rail and flat `y` to distance
  *across* it. Because it maps the whole plane, a second line, a marker, a superscript and a descender
  all land where the same arithmetic puts them, with no case of their own. **Glyphs are carried
  rigidly and continuous geometry is warped**: `Glyph::rot` rotates each glyph about its own origin —
  a *bent* letter would be a font bug — while `TextLayout::warp` is what a decoration ribbon follows,
  and is the only thing that reads it. ⚠️ **Each glyph is placed by its own midpoint**, SVG's rule,
  because rotating about the left edge fans wide glyphs outward on a tight curve; a midpoint needs an
  **advance**, and `GlyphRun` carries positions and no advances, so one is read off the next glyph
  **on the same line, across run boundaries** — the runs sharing one flat coordinate space, which
  makes it a measurement rather than an estimate — and only a glyph with no successor at all borrows
  its predecessor's. Scanning each run separately gave a run of *one* glyph — one styled character,
  or one glyph of font fallback — an advance of zero and so placed it by its left edge, 8.56° out of
  line on a 120-radius circle (§15 D489). The same-line test is load-bearing and is **not** a
  comparison of `x`: under a right or centre alignment the next line's first glyph can sit further
  right than this line's last. **On a rail the box is inert**: the rail's length is the
  measure, so `TextSizing` neither wraps nor sizes and `ParagraphStyle::align` becomes an offset along
  the rail — which is why **every resize door has to edit the rail instead**: its own handle
  (`tools::resize_to_handle`, §15 D405), and, since 2026-09-07, the group, selection and skew doors
  that come through `tools::scale_geometry` (§15 D472). A door without that arm writes a patch the
  layout ignores, so the layer stands still while the gesture reports a box it never reached (§5.6).
  The node's box is the ribbon the **whole rail** sweeps, not the stretch the glyphs occupy
  — the latter moves the box as the string is typed, which is the instability the "don't use ink
  bounds" rule below is about. Text that outruns the rail is **dropped rather than clamped**, and says
  so through `TextLayout::truncated`. **The flip is one bool** (`on_path_flip`, §15 D406): traversing
  the rail backwards negates the tangent, and the normal is the tangent turned a quarter, so the type
  reverses *and* changes sides from one sign. It is a field **beside** the rail rather than inside the
  `Option`, so detaching and re-attaching does not silently discard it — the same argument
  `Node::mask_mode` makes beside `Node::mask`.
  **`PathWarp` maps ordinary text-local coordinates in both directions** (§15 D407): `place` carries
  the first line's baseline itself, so a glyph, a decoration band and a caret rectangle are all handed
  to it in the space they are already in, and `nearest` is its inverse — which is what every pointer
  question on a railed node goes through. ⚠️ **A live `TextEdit` bends its box and nothing else on its
  own**: caret and selection geometry come from parley's flat layout, so the session carries a warp of
  its own (built by the same `warp_for` the layout uses) and answers with `caret_quads` /
  `selection_quads` rather than rectangles. **The Text tool's click on an outline** makes a railed node
  outright (`query::outline_at`, `build::text_on_new_path`, §15 D408) — **the only way type gets onto a
  curve**, the context-menu verb having been deleted as redundant (§15 D409) — and a railed node's rail
  is drawn as chrome while it is selected or edited, outline only, and **once however both come to be
  true at the same time** (§15 D690): a session's node is put in the selection by `begin_edit_text` the
  line before the session is installed, so the union's two halves agree at the moment they are both
  read, and an unfiltered chain stroked the working rail at a weight no other rail had. **A boolean's operand is neither
  offered as a rail nor accepted as one** (§15 D453): a boolean's children are operands rather than
  artwork, so the pick skips anything with a `Boolean` ancestor and the builder refuses it — consuming
  one deleted a member of the boolean and hid the new text inside it, where nothing paints it.
  **Nor is a mask, nor ink a mask has clipped away** (§15 D456): `outline_at` asks `masked_away`, the
  third of `hit_test`'s three questions and the one it was not asking, and the builder refuses a node
  whose `mask` flag is set — consuming a mask deleted it without the flag travelling to the `Text`
  that replaced it, so the artwork it was hiding came fully into view. ⚠️ **Three roles in a row have
  reached this builder as ordinary kinds** — operand, frame, mask — and each is answered by a guard of
  its own: the property that governs is a node's **role**, and the rule is still written as kinds.
  **`on_path_offset` is where along
  the rail the type starts**, as a fraction of its length so it survives the rail being scaled: the
  click writes it, `ParagraphStyle::align` composes with it, and the SVG writer adds it to
  `startOffset`'s percentage. ⚠️ **A closed rail wraps and an open one runs out** — `PathWarp::fits`
  asks a different question of each, and without the wrap an offset near the seam of a circle would
  truncate the type to nothing. The caret wraps with it: `PathWarp::shortest_way_round` moves a
  pointer's arc length by whole laps into the half-turn nearest the text's own start, where
  `PathWarp::nearest` deliberately does not (§15 D409), and **that arm is pinned only since 2026-09-07**
  (§15 D496) — every rail fixture in the workspace was an *open* one, on which the function is `x`, so
  deleting it outright left 374 tests green while re-arming D407's reported bug. A closed-rail test
  needs a **non-zero `on_path_offset`** or the wrap point sits at the seam, before the first letter. **A filled dot on the rail, where the type starts, drags it along**
  (`Drag::RailOffset`, §15 D410) — round and filled where every transform handle is square and hollow,
  because it slides rather than resizes. ⚠️ **The gesture carries only the node**: a preview writes
  `RenderOverrides` and leaves `Resolved` alone, so the committed offset stands still for the whole
  drag and is read each frame rather than carried, and the new value is
  `committed + nearest / length`.
- **The indents are the mirror image and go in *before* the break.** They change how wide a line may be,
  so `text::break_lines` sets parley's per-line `line_x` and `line_max_advance` from the paragraph the
  next line falls in (`text::line_geometry`) rather than folding anything in afterwards — which is what
  makes an indent vary by paragraph on a single `Layout`, and the hit test, the highlight and the ink
  need nothing for it, because those two values *are* the line's
  `inline_min_coord`/`inline_max_coord`, which `Selection::from_point` and the selection geometry
  already read. **The caret is the one exception and `TextEdit` corrects it itself**, parley's caret
  geometry measuring in a frame that omits the line's start edge (§15 D165).
  `Layout::set_text_indent` is deliberately never called: it is
  a second mechanism on the same edge and using both double-counts (§15 D163).
- Layout is computed by `parley` in `text.rs` and cached in `Resolved` (derived state, never
  serialized). Shaping is the most expensive thing in the pipeline and *three* consumers need it —
  bounds, hit-testing, and the scene walk — so nothing outside `Resolved` may call `text::layout` in a
  hot path. The brush parley carries is our own **run index**, which is how the decoration walk
  recovers the two things parley cannot hold (a line style, a decoration colour) from a `GlyphRun` it
  is handed rather than guessing from the geometry.
- **Font metadata is read off the face, never from a table of ours**: `text::family_axes`,
  `family_named_instances`, `family_variants` and `family_features` go through `skrifa`/`read-fonts`,
  both of which were already in core's dependency closure via parley. The Character tab's lower half
  builds itself from those, so a family that ships no small caps offers no small-caps switch.
  ⚠️ **Read off the face, but not *trusted* off it** (§15 D435). Nothing validates `fvar` on the way
  in — `skrifa` hands back the raw `AxisRecord` values and fontique's parse is not a filter — so an
  axis whose `minValue` exceeds its `maxValue` registered cleanly and then panicked the next layout of
  *any* text node, `f64::clamp` being an `assert!` that fires in release. `FontAxis::from_fvar` is the
  **one** place a `FontAxis` is built from a file (there were two, differing only in where the name
  came from): it orders the ends, replaces a non-finite end with the other, and pulls the `default`
  inside the range, `fvar` promising none of the three. `FontAxis::clamp` is what every reader asks,
  the fields being `pub`.
  **Which face is asked differs by question, on purpose.** The *variant list* asks every face in the
  family (`with_family_fonts`), because a variable family usually keeps its italics in a second file and
  those cuts are the list's whole subject — reading one face left italic Inter with no control anywhere
  in the app (§15 D149). The *axis rows* and the *feature switches* ask the default face only: an axis
  or a feature the shaping face does not have would be a control that does nothing when used.
  **And the *shaper* asks the family it will actually shape in**, which for a family the machine does
  not have is the bundled fallback (§15 D711): `text::shape` gathers the fallback's axes beside every
  family the runs name, so an unknown family's `opsz` tracks the font size exactly as `"Inter"` spelled
  by name does. It answered *no axes* until 2026-09-09 — the face fell back and the metrics did not,
  and the same string measured 8.4% wider at 96pt under a name nobody had installed. ⚠️ **Unknown means
  `fontique` cannot find the family, not that its axis list came back empty**: a family that *is* there
  and declares no axes must keep its empty list, or the fallback's `opsz` is asked of a static face
  that has no such axis.
  **A feature tag is the one place this rule has a second half**, because a tag's *meaning* is not the
  face's to decide: the OpenType registry fixes it, so `family_features` returns a `FaceFeature`
  carrying only what the font may legitimately say — the `ssXX`/`cvXX` label, tooltip and the *names*
  of a `cvXX`'s values out of `FeatureParams`, one per value in value order — and the name, the
  description and whether the feature is a user's choice at all come from a static table beside the
  panel that shows them (§15 D157). Every generic fallback is the panel's too, down to "Alternate 2"
  for a value the font declared and left unnamed.

- In-canvas editing uses `text::TextEdit`, a caret/selection model over the parley layout
  (`Cursor`/`Selection`): cluster-correct deletion, word motion, vertical motion, click and
  drag-select. It lives in core because everything it needs is parley's, and the app owns only
  when a session starts and ends. **Two things in it are ours rather than parley's, and both for one
  reason**: the caret *rectangle* and *vertical* motion, because parley measures a caret in a frame
  that omits the line's start edge where its own hit test reads that edge — so `move_up`/`move_down`
  are no longer wrappers over `Selection::previous_line`/`next_line` and `TextEdit` keeps its own
  sticky column (§15 D165).
- Glyph fills come from the node's `Paint`, and so do its **strokes**. Each visible fill is one pass
  over the *same* shaped runs; the strokes then go on the outline of those glyphs
  (`text::outline`), through the construction a shape's strokes use, which is what makes
  `StrokeAlign::Outside` on text mean outlined type (§6.3, §15 D145). **That same outline is what
  *Convert to path* replaces the layer with** — `build::outline_text`, §9.4 — so the glyph contours
  have one statement and the menu row was wiring rather than the feature it was scored as (§15 D260).
  A text node with **no ink at
  all** draws in black rather than not at all — no fill *and no stroke*, because outlined type is a
  stroke with no fill and a black stand-in would fill every hollow letter.
- Bounds and hit-testing come from the parley layout (through `TextLayout::bounds`, which is the one
  place the trim offset is applied — so every consumer gets it for free).
- **Decoration ink is reported by `Resolved` and drawn at the render boundary.** parley says where an
  underline or strikethrough goes and how thick it is; the four line styles (solid, dashed, dotted,
  wavy) are ours, and are built in the scene walk for the same reason a stroke's dash pattern is
  (§6.3) — the band and its length are both to hand there, where baked-in numbers would go stale the
  moment the type size was scrubbed.
- **Skip-ink is the exception to that split, and it is an interval rather than a path** (§15 D356).
  An underline breaks around the glyph ink it crosses — CSS's `text-decoration-skip-ink: auto`, which
  is what every browser draws — and `DecorationInk::gaps` says where, computed in `text::skip_ink`
  from the glyph outlines as part of the relayout that shaped the node. **Underlines only**: a
  `line-through` is meant to cross the letters (css-text-decor-4), so a strikethrough's gaps are
  always empty. The reason it can be geometry rather than drawing is that a *span along the band* is
  true whatever pattern is chosen afterwards, so the phase of a dash run and the crests of a ribbon
  are still the scene walk's to build — where a path subtracted from the band would have had to be
  cut after the pattern was baked, on the frame path, with a boolean nothing else runs uncached.
- **And it is a setting, per underline** (§15 D357). `Decoration::skip_ink` defaults to on, which is
  CSS's initial value, and the Typography popup carries one icon button for it beside the line style —
  lit while skipping is on, and offered on an underline only, since a strikethrough's flag is read by
  nothing. It is applied by **not listing the band** among the indices `text::skip_ink` is handed, the
  same list that keeps strikethroughs out, so a run that opts out keeps the empty `gaps` it was built
  with and the outlining pass is skipped along with it. The SVG writer says **nothing** about skip-ink
  for an ordinary underline — CSS's initial value is the behaviour, so the silence that used to be a lie
  (§15 D281) is the accurate statement — and writes `text-decoration-skip-ink="none"` for exactly the
  runs that asked for a continuous bar, off the underline alone rather than the two decorations' agreed
  value. Of the two, `none` is the one that exports *exactly*; two `auto` implementations agree in kind
  and gap within a fraction of a letter of each other.
- **`gaps` is the *final* answer about where a band is interrupted, cosmetics included**, which is why
  the scene walk's side of it is a plain complement with no judgement of its own. **The structure is
  settled before any air is given, and that order is the design**: the band breaks where glyph ink
  crosses it with no clearance at all, fragments that are not rules are closed (a hole inside one
  letter's ink, or anything under half a thickness), and only then does each gap grow by up to a
  thickness a side — taking just what the bar beside it can spare above a floor of one thickness. So
  air narrows a bar and can never remove one, which is what keeps an underlined `g` showing two marks
  and a lone `j` one, at every type size. Widening first and choosing after is what makes a drawing
  *pop*: a bar's width is then `bearing − clearance`, and every minimum has a size where a bar crosses
  it (§15 D356). It is stated here rather than at the render boundary because a rule that straddled it
  would be one rule written down in two crates.
- **Text case is a display transform, never a rewrite of `content`** — applied to the string handed to
  the shaper, so switching back to "as typed" recovers the original exactly and an export reads the
  real text. Restricted to characters whose cased form is the same number of UTF-8 bytes (D80).
- **A list marker is ink without bytes.** `ParagraphStyle::marker` is a spannable `Option<ListMarker>`,
  and the marker it names is **never in `content`** — byte indices are the currency of the span lists,
  the caret, the hit test and the case transform, so a marker in the string would need every one of them
  to know it was not text. Nor is it a parley **inline box**: `OutOfFlow` is the only kind that reserves
  no space in the line, and parley honours the kind when it draws while ignoring it in
  `Cluster::visual_offset`, `Cluster::from_point` and `Selection::geometry` (§15 D169). The gutter is the
  paragraph's own `indent_start` — which every line already honours, so *that is the hanging measure* —
  and the marker is right-aligned on it, which is what keeps `1.` and `10.` putting their text in one
  column. Numbering has no markup to read, so a list is a run of consecutive paragraphs asking for the
  **same** marker; anything else ends it and the next run counts from one.
- **Nesting is `ParagraphStyle::level`, a `u8` of its own, and one gutter per level.**
  `ParagraphStyle::start_edge` is `indent_start × (level + 1)` and is the **only** place that
  multiplication happens: the lines read it through parley's `line_x` and the marker reads it for its
  right edge, and two derivations of one edge is how a marker ends up on a gutter its own text is not
  using. It is a field rather than a reading of `indent_start`, which is a `Length` a user drags.
  `ListMarkers::ordinals` keeps one counter per open level, so a sublist counts from one while its parent
  counts through it, and the numbering rule generalises to the same marker **at the same level** (§15
  D172). A level with no marker still indents, which is how a continuation paragraph sits under its item
  — but it does not stay *inside* the list, because a paragraph with no marker still ends every open run.
  **`Tab` and `Shift`+`Tab` are the keyboard route** (`TextEdit::step_list_level`, §15 D173), and they are
  relative and per paragraph where the panel's field is one absolute value over the range: a parent and
  its sublist keep their shape instead of levelling. Only paragraphs with a **marker** move, the panel's
  own field being reachable only through an item.
- **An ellipsis is ink without bytes too, and it is set in the type it *follows*** (§15 D490).
  `BlockStyle::overflow`'s `Ellipsis` shapes a `…` on its own rather than appending it to `content`,
  so it never enters the byte space the caret and the spans live in — the same argument the list
  marker makes. Whose type it is set in is the question that has a wrong answer available: the style
  at the end of the *string* is, on a truncated node, precisely the text that is not drawn, so the
  style is resolved at the **last visible byte** — `line.text_range().end` of the last drawn line,
  never a run's range, a parley run spanning every line it was broken over. The lookup is the last
  span *starting* before that byte rather than one containing it, because the byte can fall in a gap
  between spans and what the reader last saw is the run that began before it. ⚠️ **`extract_flat`
  returns no colour on purpose** — its third caller is the font picker's family list, which draws in
  the chrome's own text colour — so both of its other callers, `marker_run` and `ellipsis_run`, owe
  the run colour a line of their own; only one of them was paying it, and an ellipsis after a red run
  came out in the node's fill. **The export walk appends one too** (§15 D506): `text::export_lines` is
  a second walk of the same shaped layout and had no ellipsis logic at all, so a truncated node
  exported as the clipped text with nothing saying it was clipped — the same class of node-level ink
  `ListMarkers` exists to keep the two walks agreeing about, and the one that got no such treatment.
  It is **appended to the last line's runs rather than placed**, `<tspan>`s flowing, so this walk
  computes no `x` and needs no counterpart to the shift below — flow cannot overshoot a measure it is
  not laying out against. ⚠️ **Room for it is made by moving the line, not by moving the ellipsis**
  (§15 D610). `extract` used to clamp the glyph's own x to `w − advance`, which keeps it inside the
  box — the stated aim — and says nothing about the **ink**: under `Center` and `End` the last line's
  right edge reaches the box edge by construction, so the clamp always bit and drew the `…` back over
  the characters it was ending. The last line's runs and decoration bands are shifted left by the
  overlap instead, never past the line's own left edge, and `ellipsis_run` is handed the position
  rather than deciding it. **The visible string is still not shortened**, which is the trade taken
  deliberately: no document already using `BlockStyle::overflow == Ellipsis` loses a character, and a
  uniform translation is the answer a **bidi** line can take, where dropping "the trailing clusters"
  would eat its beginning. ⚠️ **Still wrong at the same call site**: the ellipsis goes at the line's
  *right* edge whatever the direction, and an RTL line's logical end is its left.
- **Rich text is built** (this section), and so are per-paragraph attributes and the node-level block
  indents (§15 D163), the Paragraph tab's controls for them (§15 D164), lists (§15 D169) and their
  nesting (§15 D172). What is still deferred: the deferrals `roadmap.md` carries.
### 5.4a Fonts

Designers expect local fonts **plus the entire Google Fonts library** — this is table stakes
(Figma-parity). Three sources, in resolution order:

1. **System fonts** — enumerated at runtime via `fontdb`, on a background thread.
2. **Google Fonts** — on-demand, **and the one source the user can switch off** (*Settings › Web
   fonts › Load web fonts*, `prefs::Prefs::web_fonts`, default on; see the bullet on the switch
   below). A catalog of family metadata is fetched from the Fontsource API,
   cached on disk (`%LOCALAPPDATA%\ondin\catalog.json`) and read from there first on every later
   launch (§15 D83), with the network asked again only once that copy is older than
   `CATALOG_MAX_AGE` — seven days, and the freshness of the copy that could actually be *read*
   (§15 D111). The font picker lists the full catalog, and selecting an uninstalled family
   downloads the font files into a per-user disk cache (`%LOCALAPPDATA%\ondin\fonts` /
   `$XDG_CACHE_HOME/ondin/fonts`). Cached fonts are registered into the `fontique` collection and
   behave exactly like system fonts thereafter — including offline. (Google Fonts are
   open-licensed — OFL/Apache — so caching and redistribution are fine; the library is far too large
   to bundle, so download-on-demand is the only sane model.)
3. **Bundled fallback** — one open-licensed font (e.g. Inter or Noto Sans) compiled in, so tests and
   headless export are deterministic on every machine.

**A family's *variable* file is preferred over its static cuts.** Fontsource publishes both, and one
variable file carries every weight where the statics are one file each — nine downloads become one,
and the Character tab's axis rows and the variant list are then reading a face that actually has the
axes (both are built from `fvar`, §9.2). The cost is that variable files are woff2 only, so `ondin-app`
decodes them to sfnt (`woff2-patched`) before handing them to core, which knows sfnt alone; a family
whose file the **decoder** cannot read falls back to the static cuts automatically. ⚠️ **That fallback was
true of an `Err` and false of a *panic*, which is what a malformed woff2 actually produces** (§15
D450): 53 bytes take `push_simple_table_record` out of range, the unwind left the worker's `while let`
loop, and the family sat at *loading* for the rest of the session with no fallback ever attempted. The
decode is wrapped now, so "cannot read" means one thing. ⚠️ **And *decoder* is the load-bearing word,
which the code did not read that way until 2026-09-08** (§15 D585): `FontMsg::Failed` carried no
reason, so a **503** on the variable file downgraded the family exactly as a bad file would, and one
transient fetch failure made Roboto a static family for the rest of the session — no axes, the static
cuts in place of the nine named instances, and no way to recover short of a restart, `entry.cut`'s
only other writer being `fetch_catalog`. `FaceFailure` splits `Fetch` from `Decode` and only `Decode`
falls back; a caught unwind counts as `Decode`, the bytes being in hand by the time a decoder can
panic. Which file to ask for
is derived from the axes the API reports, and the three names Fontsource uses are not
interchangeable — see `fonts::variable_cut`, whose rule was probed against the CDN rather than
guessed.

**A web face is a *subset* of the face the foundry shipped**, and the only place that shows is the
Character tab. The CDN path names the subset, and the one asked for is the family's own `defSubset`
from the list API — `latin` for every Latin family, and the only subset name the parsed catalog entry
carries. Subsetting drops glyphs, and a feature whose glyphs are gone goes with it, so an OpenType
list read off a web face is not the font's: Andika through the picker offers four features where the
installed 654 KB file declares 43 `cvXX` alone (§15 D192). *Anything about a face's tables has to be
checked against an installed copy.*

Architectural consequences:

- **Core does no network I/O — ever.** `ondin-core` resolves fonts only through the `fontique`
  collection it is handed. Acquisition (catalog, downloads, cache) lives in a `FontService` in
  `ondin-app` (shared by GUI and `serve`), which registers acquired fonts into that collection.
  A document that references an unavailable font must still load, lay out (fallback font), render,
  and export — with a warning; fetching is an *enhancement* that may resolve the warning, never a
  prerequisite.
- Documents record family **names** (plus weight/style), never font file paths or embedded font
  data (v1). When a missing family is a Google family, `FontService` fetches it automatically on
  document open — **and again whenever the family list changes**, because `ensure_loaded` can only
  queue a family it can already resolve, and both things it resolves against (the system scan, the web
  catalog) land on a later frame than the open that asked for them. Genuinely unknown families fall
  back with a warning, **in the MCP snapshot and — since 2026-08-19 — in the Type panel too**
  (§15 D227). ⚠️ **The fallback is a fallback for the *metrics* too, which it was not until 2026-09-09**
  (§15 D711): the face resolved to the bundled family and the axes did not, so the same text measured
  8.4% wider at 96pt under a name the machine did not have and snapped back the moment an install or a
  download made that family real — a reflow of a document nobody edited. The warning is meant to be the
  only difference the user sees. It was a gap rather than a decision for as long as it was one, and the reason is worth
  keeping: "not here yet" and "never coming" are the same answer to `text::is_family_available`, which
  is what `snapshot.rs` derives its per-node warning from, so a panel warning built on it would have
  accused a font that was still downloading. **The third state is `fonts::FamilyStatus`** — `Ready` /
  `Pending` / `Missing`, where `Pending` folds together the three reasons that all mean *wait* (a face
  in flight, a source that could still list the family not landed, nothing having asked) and `Missing`
  means every source has landed and none of them has it. Two facts the service was not keeping had to
  be added for it: a count of faces that came back unusable — which `poll` received as
  `FontMsg::Failed` and read only for the variable-file retry — and whether the catalog thread has
  finished, read off its channel *closing* rather than from a message, because that covers the failed
  fetch as well as the two successful paths. The panel says it in the vocabulary that already existed:
  `theme::color::WARN` on the family row's own glyph, the way a layer row whose picture cannot be drawn
  says it (§9.2, §15 D179), with the family's *name* left full strength because that is the identity
  the row reports. **The two warnings are not yet the same question asked twice**: `ondin-export` has
  no `FontService`, so the snapshot still asks core directly — which is honest for a headless run that
  never fetches anything. Text layouts in `Resolved` are invalidated when a
  better font arrives mid-session (treat font arrival as dirtying all Text nodes using that family).
- **Only *font data* invalidates the text cache, and only data for a family the document names.**
  `FontService::poll` reports the family list growing and font bytes being registered as two separate
  facts, because the catalog landing changes what the picker offers and nothing about how a single
  node shapes. Re-shaping the document on it was work for no change (§5.9's cache is the reason that
  is worth a sentence). ⚠️ **The second half was missing until 2026-09-08** (§15 D591): the picker
  fetches preview faces for as long as it is scrolled — the `preview` lane, backlog 48 — and every
  one that landed re-shaped every text node in the document, ~23 ms on a twenty-block one, in the
  interaction the row list was virtualized for. `FontPoll` carries the registered family names now
  and `FontPoll::touches` asks the question, which is what the bullet above already promised by
  saying *"using that family"*. ⚠️ **The retry is deliberately not narrowed with it** — a picker miss
  is a family whose preview strip could not be drawn, and an arriving preview face is exactly what it
  was waiting for. ⚠️ **The set of families is the node's default *unioned with its spans***: a
  family applied to a *selection* is a `CharAttr::Family` span and appears in no
  `TextStyle::font_family` anywhere, so reading the defaults alone left exactly those runs in the
  fallback face until something else touched the node — a hole the coarse flag had covered by
  accident, and the narrowing is what made it reachable. Both callers read the one walk, so the gate
  and `ensure_document_fonts` cannot disagree about which families a document has.
- **Font *acquisition* never happens on the UI thread; registration and rasterization do.** The
  sentence used to say "nothing font-shaped happens on the UI thread except registration", which read
  as covering more than it meant. Registration has to be there: the `fontique` collection is
  thread-local (§5.9). Everything else about *getting* a face — the `fontdb` scan, reading a local
  file, fetching the catalog, downloading and decoding — is on a worker, dispatched through a
  bounded pool with three priority lanes (`fonts/queue.rs`): urgent FIFO for a face something is
  waiting on, preview LIFO and capped at `PREVIEW_BACKLOG` for a picker row that may scroll away
  first, and prefetch FIFO, uncapped and served last, for the popular set below. **A job the preview
  cap pushes out has to be given back to the bookkeeping**: it never reports, so its claim and its
  family's outstanding count would otherwise stand for the session, and `ensure` filtering on
  `claimed` would make that family's face unrequestable for good (§15 D354). One `ureq::Agent` is
  shared by all of it, because `ureq`'s free functions build a *use-once* agent and a family's four faces then cost four
  TLS handshakes, serially. **Every request on it is bounded** — a connect, response, body and global
  deadline, `ureq`'s own defaults being `None` for all eight — because a peer that accepts and then
  stops sending would otherwise hold a worker for the life of the process (§15 D441). **And every job
  is unwind-guarded, which is the same loss by a second road** (§15 D450): the loop is
  `while let Some(job) = queue.pop()`, so a panic anywhere inside one — `woff2-patched` on a malformed
  file, measured — ends the thread *and* skips the `FontMsg::Failed` that clears `claimed` and
  `outstanding`, leaving that family reading as *loading* for ever and unrequestable. `load_one_face`
  guards the whole job and `sfnt_from` guards the decoder known to panic today; both rest on
  `panic = "unwind"`, which is enforced by the build rather than hoped for (§15 D445). **Every one of those threads holds an `egui::Context` and repaints after
  each successful send**, `FontService::new`'s only argument: this eframe is reactive, so a message
  nobody wakes up for is a font that arrives on the next mouse move (§15 D110).
  **A picker row's preview strip is the exception, and it is not movable**: it goes through core's
  thread-local shaping engine, so a worker would build a second font collection rather than share the
  registered one. It is bounded in time instead — 2 ms of a frame, past which a row draws its name in
  the UI font and asks for another frame (§15 D160).
- **The picker registers font data for families the user is merely scrolling past** (§9.2, the
  preview rows), so the service can also un-register: `text::unregister_family` plus an LRU over the
  preview-only families, **budgeted in bytes** — a Latin subset is tens of KB and a CJK face is
  megabytes, so a count of families bounds nothing (§15 D160). A family anything asked for *in full* —
  a document's font, a user's pick — is exempt for good, so eviction can never pull a face out from
  under the canvas. `fontique` keeps a family's *name* after its last face is removed, which is why
  `text::is_family_available` asks about faces; asking about the name reports a family that can no
  longer draw anything as available.
- **The disk cache is bounded in the same unit, and swept once at startup.** Every family a picker row
  previews leaves a file in `%LOCALAPPDATA%\ondin\fonts`, and until 2026-08-19 nothing ever removed one.
  `fonts::trim_font_cache` deletes least-recently-used faces until the directory is back under
  `FONT_CACHE_BYTES` — 256 MB, so the whole Latin catalog browsed end to end (~85 MB) is never touched,
  and what the budget is *for* is the browse through CJK families. What makes "least recently used" true
  is that a cache **hit** touches the file, so its mtime means last wanted rather than first downloaded.
  The sweep is spawned on its own thread by `FontService::new`, off the startup path, and it runs
  **once**: a single session can still go over the budget, but nothing stays there permanently
  (§15 D237). There is no
  floor here, unlike the preview LRU above, and D237 has why that difference is deliberate.
- **And its size is visible, with a verb beside it** (§15 D330). *Settings › Web fonts* carries
  `180 MB of web font cache · Clear`: `fonts::dir_bytes` on a background thread when the modal opens
  — a `read_dir` per frame for as long as a dialog is open is a directory scan sixty times a second
  for a number that changes when one button is pressed — and `FontService::clear_cache`, which is
  synchronous because it answers a button and the status line reports how much went. **Three states,
  not two**: a scan that has not landed says *counting* rather than `0 MB`, or a directory holding
  two hundred megabytes would read as clear for however many frames the scan took. Clearing
  un-registers nothing, so the document on screen does not repaint; the cache is derived data and the
  cost is one re-download apiece. This is the row §14 carried as *"the cache's size is not visible
  anywhere"* and the roadmap carried as blocked on a surface that did not exist.
- **The whole source is switchable, and off means no request.** With `prefs::Prefs::web_fonts` off,
  the picker lists the machine's installed families plus the bundled Inter and nothing else, no
  catalog is fetched — `FontService::new` does not spawn the catalog thread at all, so its receiver
  is disconnected from the first `poll` and the service reports *no catalog, finally* rather than
  *not yet* — and no face is downloaded. It is a real state and not a degraded one: neither setting
  hides a family the other shows, which is what a curated middle tier would have done and is why the
  three-way `Off | Popular | All` was rejected (§15 D330, which carries all three reasons). **Two
  doors have to close, and the second is the one that is easy to miss**: `rebuild_families` leaves
  the web names out of the picker's list, and `faces_of` refuses to dispatch a web face — because a
  family name reaches `ensure` from a *document* saved on a machine where the switch was on, which
  never goes near the picker. `FontService::set_web_fonts` moves it inside a session, and turning it
  back on is a rebuild rather than a re-fetch whenever the catalog is still in memory.
  ⚠️ **A third door, and the one neither of those two can see: the fetch that is already out** (§15
  D720). Both doors above decide whether a *new* request starts, so a user who turned the switch off
  while `spawn_catalog` was inside `fetch_catalog` still had two calls reach `api.fontsource.org`,
  `catalog.json` written to their disk, and the entries merged. `FontService::catalog_live` is a
  cancel flag **per spawned thread**, read immediately before the fetch and again before the write —
  the second being the half that matters, since the fetch blocks and that is the whole window. Off
  cancels; on either spawns with a **fresh** flag or spawns nothing, because storing the switch's
  value back into the existing flag un-cancels the thread still holding it. It cannot interrupt a
  call in flight — nothing here can — so what it guarantees is that the result is dropped rather than
  written or merged, and one already-open socket is the residual.
- **And the popular set is prefetched, which is what the rejected middle tier was reaching for**
  (§15 D352). `fonts::POPULAR` is fifty families — an editorial list, because the catalog carries no
  rank, count or trend and its order is alphabetical — warmed at `Want::Preview`, once per session,
  from `poll` on the frame `catalog_done` turns true. It goes down the **prefetch** lane, which is
  the whole design decision: the picker's own lane is LIFO and bounded, so routing speculation
  through it would reverse the editorial order, drop two of the fifty before a worker woke and evict
  the rest on the first scroll. That is also why `Lane` is separate from `Want` — how much of a
  family to fetch is not how badly it is wanted — and why `FamilyState::lane` is stored, so a
  variable-file retry goes back down the lane it came from. Families this machine already has are
  skipped, `faces_of` resolving them to a local file; and the `web_fonts` guard rather than the
  timing is what refuses when the switch is off, since `catalog_done` is true from the first frame
  of a session launched that way. ⚠️ Turning the switch off mid-session does **not** cancel warms
  already queued — up to fifty requests can still go out. **The rule, rather than the count** (§15
  D720): what the switch cannot stop is a request *already queued or already in flight* when it is
  turned off, and since the catalog fetch learnt to cancel this warm is the only one of those left.
  It read *"the one bounded hole"* while the catalog thread was a second and larger one, which is why
  it is written as a rule — anything new that reaches the network must either be startable only while
  the switch is on, or hold a cancel flag as `spawn_catalog` does.
- Font embedding in `.ondin` files (for portability of non-Google local fonts) is deferred — parked
  in §14.

### 5.5 Document

```rust
pub struct Document {
    schema_version: u32,
    nodes: FxHashMap<NodeId, Node>,
    root: NodeId,
    canvas_background: peniko::Color,   // the ground behind and around the frames
    guides: Vec<Guide>,                 // ruler guides; unordered
}
impl Document {
    pub fn new(root_id: NodeId) -> Self;
    pub fn get(&self, id: NodeId) -> Option<&Node>;
    pub fn root(&self) -> NodeId;
    pub fn canvas_background(&self) -> peniko::Color;
    pub fn guides(&self) -> &[Guide];
    pub fn guide(&self, id: GuideId) -> Option<&Guide>;
    pub fn guides_owned_by(&self, owner: NodeId) -> impl Iterator<Item = &Guide>;
    pub fn apply(&mut self, tx: &Transaction) -> Result<ApplyOutcome, OpError>;
    // NO public mutable access to nodes or the tree.
}

pub struct Guide {                 // guide.rs
    pub id: GuideId,
    pub axis: GuideAxis,           // Horizontal | Vertical — the direction of the line itself
    pub position: f64,             // y for a horizontal guide, x for a vertical one — read in
                                   //   owner's LOCAL space when it has one, world when it does not
    pub color: Option<peniko::Color>,   // None = follow DEFAULT_GUIDE_COLOR
    pub owner: Option<NodeId>,     // the frame it is scoped to; None = the whole canvas
}
```

- **Two pieces of document state are not nodes**: `canvas_background` and `guides`. Both are
  reclassifications with the same narrow reason — people set them for the artwork, not for the
  sitting — and neither loosens the line the rest of the document draws between document and view
  data (§9.2/§9.3).
- `canvas_background` is the ground the artwork sits on, opaque by construction (there is nothing
  behind the canvas to be transparent against), it defaults to `DEFAULT_CANVAS_BACKGROUND`, and it
  is changed through `SetCanvasBackground` like everything else — no second mutation path
  (invariant 2). It lived on `EditorSession` as a view preference until it turned out people set it
  per document; §15 D28 has the reversal and what it cost.
- `guides` are the lines a designer pulls out of the rulers (§9.4). They are saved with the file for
  the same reason the ground is: a guide down the middle of a layout is part of how that layout was
  built, and losing it on reopen makes it worthless. `color: None` means *follow*
  `DEFAULT_GUIDE_COLOR` (the design's dark red `#a3332d`), not "a copy of today's default", so
  retuning the default carries every guide that was never recoloured with it.
- **A guide is deliberately not a `Node`.** It has no parent, no transform, no paint and no bounds;
  it never renders into the scene, never hit-tests as artwork, and must never appear in the layers
  tree or be swept up by Select All. Each of those would need special-casing away if it were a node,
  which is a longer list than the five operations it takes to keep them apart.
- The list is **unordered**: guides have no z, nothing stacks against them, and no operation names
  one by position. `apply` therefore appends, and IO sorts by id on save so the bytes stay stable
  whatever order they were drawn in (invariant 9).
- **A guide is either global or scoped to one frame**, and `owner` is the whole of that distinction:
  `None` means the guide runs the full canvas and its `position` is a world coordinate, `Some(frame)`
  means it is drawn only within that frame and its `position` is read in the frame's **local** space.
  Which one you get is decided by where the pointer is when the drag ends (§9.4), and a guide can be
  dragged from either mode to the other. Stored as an owner on the one flat list rather than as a
  `Vec<Guide>` per node, deliberately: `guides()`, `remove_all_guides` and the id-sorted save all stay
  exactly as they were, so a one-guide edit is still a one-line diff — and changing scope becomes a
  **field edit** rather than a move between two collections, which is what makes it one undoable
  operation (`SetGuideScope`, §5.7).
- **The owner must be a live `Artboard`**, enforced by `Document::check_guide_owner` on both `AddGuide`
  and `SetGuideScope` (`OpError::BadGuideOwner`), and by the loader (§5.11). Not a shape, not a group
  and not the root: a scope is a *box* to clip the line to and to measure the offset from, and none of
  the other three has one — a guide on the canvas is spelled `None`, which is the state this is
  distinguishing itself from. **Deleting a frame therefore has to take its guides with it**, in the
  same transaction; `build::guides_of` (§5.7a) collects them, nested frames inside the doomed subtree
  included.
  ⚠️ **And that is now enforced rather than merely owed** (§15 D491): the two operations above name an
  owner, and removing the frame breaks the same rule without naming anything, so `apply` re-checks
  every guide's owner once at the end of the transaction (invariant 8, §5.7). Until 2026-09-07 a
  `DeleteNode` on a guide-owning frame was accepted and the document it produced never opened again —
  the loader's refusal is deliberate and permanent, so the file was lost while the session that could
  still undo it was the only copy. `guides_of` is not made redundant by the check: it is still what
  makes the Delete verb *succeed*, and the check is what turns a caller that has never heard of it
  into a refused edit rather than an unopenable file.
- **A scoped guide is stored frame-local, so it rotates with its frame and stays clipped to it** —
  better than Figma, which *deletes* a rotated frame's guides. Nothing is destroyed; what degrades is
  the snapping rather than the data, because a leaning guide has no single world x or y to offer
  (§9.4). A frame resize leaves the offset where it is and the Scale tool multiplies it, which is
  §5.6's split inherited rather than a new rule, and an offset that outgrows a shrunk frame is kept
  rather than clamped — `guide_span` lets the clip hide the line, so re-growing the frame brings it
  back.

### 5.5a Images (`image.rs`)

Scoped in `images.md`, which was the source for the *feature* until its build list closed: that file was
folded into this document and **deleted on 2026-08-16**, so §5.5a and §15 D176–D191 are now the whole
record — D191 being the out-of-v1 list it carried, which is the half of it that has no other home. An
old session's notes pointing at `images.md` are pointing at nothing.
**Built so far: the table, the reference, the brush, the decode cache, placing — framing, so an
image draws across its shape rather than at one unit per source pixel in the corner, the
crop gesture that authors the rectangle and the mode strip that overrides it — both now inside
**image editing** (`Tool::ImageEdit`, §9.4, §15 D181, D268, which replaced the crop tool and moved
the strip off the paint row) — and its card's other half: orientation, the tile scale and *reset
crop* (§9.4, §15 D182), *original size* having moved to the context menu alone on 2026-08-23 (§15
D305), and the other two ways in —
drag-and-drop and paste (§9.4, §15 D183), with the drag's own announcement over the window (§15 D184),
and SVG export, where an image fill becomes a `<pattern>` over the encoded original (§7.1, §15 D185),
written once per picture however many shapes show it (§15 D595),
and the missing-image placeholder with the *Replace…* that repairs it and the layers-row mark beside it
(§6.3, §7.1, §9.2, §9.4, §15 D179), and the seven per-pixel adjustments, in all three writers and in a
card of their own (§6.3, §7.1, §9.4, §15 D186), and the thumbnails the layers tree and the paint
row's chip draw, which close `images.md`'s build list (§9.2, §9.4, §15 D189). The row's one card has
since become two — Framing and Adjustments, behind two buttons (§9.4, §15 D190).**
What is not: fetching a linked image. `ImageStore::prepare` walks the table and **skips a linked entry
outright**, because reading a file is not `ondin-render`'s job — whoever has the bytes calls
`ImageStore::insert` with them — so a link behaves exactly as a picture that is missing until something
loads it, which is one code path and one drawing with a link whose file has moved (§15 D179).

- **An image is a fill, not a `NodeKind`.** Any shape, path or boolean can carry one, so "image in a
  circle" works without masks existing — which is why they could wait, and did until 2026-08-21
  (§5.3, §15 D191, D282). **`Paint::image_fill` is the one spelling of "is this layer a picture"** —
  the index of the first *visible* image fill — and it is in core rather than in the app because the
  model came to ask it too: `build::mask_target` has to know which member of a selection is the
  photograph and which is the shape (§9.4, §15 D287). `tools::croppable_fill` is one line onto it, so
  its sixteen call sites keep the name that reads right there and there is still one rule. The
  *interaction* is still layer-shaped (placing makes a Rect sized to the image, with a thumbnail in the
  layers panel, and the word "fill" never appears), which is Figma's model and for Figma's reason.
- **The document owns a table of images, keyed by an opaque `ImageId`**, and a `Fill` holds an
  `ImageRef` into it. Two layers showing the same photograph store it once; a geometry edit produces a
  diff nowhere near the bytes. The id is a **content hash of the encoded bytes**, computed by whatever
  puts the bytes in — core neither computes nor verifies one, because hashing is a dependency core's
  rules do not permit (§3) and the app is holding the bytes anyway. Dedup is therefore the *caller's*
  question, asked as `Document::has_image` before adding.
- **The stored bytes are the encoded original, never a decoded buffer.** A 2000×1500 photo is 12 MB as
  RGBA and ~300 KB as its JPEG, and the file is text. Decoding belongs to the app, once, into a cache
  keyed by the same id. `ImageEntry::href` is how a document that is not ours refers to the picture —
  `data:<mime>;base64,<encoded original>` for an embedded image, the stored path exactly as written for
  a linked one — and it is **here rather than in the SVG writer** because base64 and the save format are
  core's already, and one encoder is what keeps a document and its export saying the same thing about
  the same file. The encoded original goes out, never a re-encode: it is what the content hash names
  (§7.1, §15 D185).
- **Four accepted encodings — PNG, JPEG, WebP and GIF** (`ImageFormat`, which also owns the MIME type
  the data URI needs; the extension it can spell is **read by nothing** since *Export original…* was
  removed on 2026-08-23, and `ImageFormat::extension` is `pub` in a library, so nothing warns — §15
  D305). Named as a closed list so that "why
  not TIFF" has an answer that is a *decision* rather than an omission: TIFF and AVIF are a decoder
  each and neither is worth it. **The closed list stands on the decode side**, which is where the
  decision is taken rather than merely declared: `ondin-render`'s `images::signature_is_accepted`
  reads the magic number with `image::guess_format` and refuses any format it *recognises* and the
  four do not include, before it can become a placement — so the enum is what the app will *accept*,
  not a list of things a filename can end in. **A GIF is its first frame**; animation and video are
  out (§15 D191).
  🚨 **That sentence read "which is where it always did the work", and it did not** (§15 D600,
  `[S22-L2-02]`). Two doors got past the sniff. `app::image_format_of` sniffs first but falls through
  to the **file extension** for anything it recognises and v1 does not accept, so a BMP named `.png`
  reached `decode` hinted as a PNG; and `svg_in::data_uri` maps a foreign file's declared MIME type
  straight through with no sniff at all. `decode` then called `image::load_from_memory`, which places
  the bytes with **whatever decoders cargo compiled** — and the manifest's four are what this
  workspace *asks* for, not what it gets, because feature unification lets `arboard` add `bmp` under
  `cfg(windows)` and `tiff` under `cfg(target_os = "macos")`. So one document drew the picture on
  Windows and the missing-image placeholder on Linux, with no report on either. `guess_format` is a
  fixed table of magic bytes and is **not** gated on the compiled decoders, which is the whole reason
  the guard is written on it: it answers the same thing on every platform and under either cargo
  spelling. Bytes `image` cannot place at all are still handed to the hinted decoder exactly as
  before — the guard is about a format we can name and do not accept, not about tightening what
  reaches the decoder.
  ⚠️ **The cost argument above has quietly stopped applying to TIFF on one platform**: its decoder is
  already compiled on macOS whatever we ask for. That is a reason to stop calling the exclusion free
  there, not a reason to admit the format — the list is a decision about what a document may contain,
  and it now says so in one place that every platform reads the same way.
- **Embedded by default, linked as a per-image escape hatch** (`ImageSource`) — Illustrator's split: a
  file that breaks when you send it to someone is a worse failure than a large one. A link stores the
  path *as a string*, because a document is portable and a path is not.
- **The intrinsic size is stored on the entry**, so placing a layer, laying out its box and drawing a
  layers row never wait on a decode — and a document with a dead link still knows how big the picture
  was.
- **Nothing garbage-collects the table.** `AddImage`/`RemoveImage` are explicit operations and
  `AddImage` carries the whole entry, which is what makes undo whole: deleting the only layer showing an
  image and undoing must bring the *bytes* back, and an inverse naming only the key would restore a
  reference to nothing. The cost — a document can carry an image nothing shows — is what a *Purge
  unused* command is for.
- **A dangling reference is a state, not an error.** A fill naming an id the table does not carry loads
  and saves with the reference intact, so a relink has something to repair: it is the same condition as
  a linked file that has moved, which v1 has to survive anyway, so refusing it at load would turn a
  repairable picture into an unopenable document. The rule is that it is **never silently dropped and
  never a silent blank**: the fill draws the missing-image placeholder — grey and a cross, one drawing
  described by `image::missing_placeholder` and painted by the walk, the CPU export and the SVG writer
  alike — the layers row tints its kind glyph, and *Replace…* in the image row's popover is the repair
  (§6.3, §7.1, §9.2, §9.4, §15 D179). What *is* rejected is a malformed
  table — bad base64, a zero intrinsic size. **That drawing has a second user now**: a boolean whose
  arithmetic was abandoned draws the identical placeholder over its operands' box, and tints the same row
  glyph, because it is the same fact about a layer (§9.2 "Booleans", §15 D298–D299).

**The model's brush is peniko's, over a reference instead of pixels** —
`peniko::Brush<ImageBrush<ImageRef>, GradientBrush>`, aliased as `ondin_core::Brush`. `images.md` expected
this to need a brush enum of our own; it does not, and the reasoning is in §15 D176. **Both of peniko's
payload parameters are substituted, and the second arrived long after the first**: `GradientBrush` is a
`peniko::Gradient` plus the affine that carries it from the space it was authored in onto the shape's own,
which is the identity for every gradient this app makes and a squash for the elliptical radial gradient
`peniko::RadialGradientPosition`'s two circles cannot say (§15 D412). Three things follow, and they are why:

- **The save format did not move.** `Solid` and `Gradient` are the same variants of the same enum
  carrying the same types, so every document written before images loads byte-for-byte unchanged, with
  no schema bump and no migration. ⚠️ **`Gradient`'s payload stopped being the same *type* on
  2026-09-03 and the property still holds**, by `#[serde(flatten)]` plus a `skip_serializing_if` on the
  transform: a gradient written before the field existed loads unchanged, and one at the identity
  writes no key, so nothing rewrites on its next save (invariant 9, §15 D412).
- **`alpha` and `extend` are not restated**, because `ImageBrush` already carries an `ImageSampler`
  holding both, plus quality.
- **The render boundary is the one place that changed**, which is where the seam was already waiting:
  `ondin_render::color::brush_to_backend` returns `Option<(peniko::Brush, Affine)>` and is the single
  point where a reference becomes pixels, resolving one through the decode cache
  (`ondin_render::images::ImageStore`) by `images.pixels` — **not `images.get`**, which answers the
  decode rather than what the fill shows, and the second half of the pair is the buffer's own grid,
  which a reduced preview makes not the source's (§15 D186). `None` means only that this reference cannot
  be resolved *yet* — a dangling id, a link nothing has read off disk, bytes that will not decode —
  which are all states a document is allowed to be in, so it is never treated as an error: a **fill**
  is diverted to the placeholder before it reaches here, and a stroke or a text run draws nothing
  (§6.3, §15 D179). **Each backend resolves for itself**, not through one shared conversion:
  `vello_cpu` paints through `vello_cpu::ImageSource`, a handle it registers itself, so there is no
  peniko image that satisfies it and `cpu.rs` takes the image arm off the *model's* brush — the id
  **and the adjustment's bits** are what its per-render memo is keyed on, and the backend brush has
  dropped both.

**A gradient's stop offsets ascend, and a descending one is not a wrong picture but no picture at all**
(`image::make_stops_monotonic`, §15 D455). Each offset is clamped up to the running maximum — SVG's own
rule, *"equal to or greater than the previous"*, and the rule here because a `.ondin` ramp is most often
an SVG ramp. Stored descending, `[0, 0.8, 0.2, 1]` drew a **flat fill of the first stop's colour**, and a
