descent of one part in ten million was enough. **It is asked at four doors, and no one of them covers
another**: `svg_in::Gradients::collect`, so the model says what the file means and a re-export
round-trips; `ondin_render::color::brush_to_backend` (§6.2), so a hand-edited file draws correctly;
`ondin_export::svg::gradient_def` (§7), on a copy, so an **export** of a document that predates the other
two says what the app just drew; and the app's gradient **chips** (`ui::paint_ramp`, §9.4), which read
the stop list straight off the brush and are the one door that draws *chrome* rather than artwork —
missed when the other three were done, so a descending ramp painted the swatch **mirrored** beside a
canvas that had clamped it, and one document was drawn two ways in one frame (§15 D564). The chip
shares the rule rather than restating it: `image::monotonic_offset` is the single step, and
`make_stops_monotonic` is a loop over it. ⚠️ **It is a clamp, not a sort**: `[0, 0.8, 0.2, 1]` clamps to
`[0, 0.8, 0.8, 1]` and sorts to `[0, 0.2, 0.8, 1]`, two
different pictures, and `panels::paint::with_stops` keeps its sort because dragging a handle past its
neighbour means *"put it there"* where a file is to be read. ⚠️ **Nothing clamps on load**, so a document
written before this still holds its stored list — which now costs only the *editor*: touching one colour
of such a gradient puts it through `with_stops`' sort and commits the third picture.
⚠️ **A stop's *alpha* has the same shape and a shorter list of doors** (§15 D692). Nothing in the model
states a `0..=1` rule for it — invariant 8 weighs a stop's colour for finiteness, which 5.0 passes
without comment — so an out-of-spec `stop-opacity` used to survive import, save and load, and reach a
`0..=100` opacity field as 500. Two sites clamp: `svg_in::stop_of` on the way in, beside the `offset`
clamp two lines below it, and `panels::paint::alpha_of` on the way out. As with the offsets,
**nothing clamps on load**: a document already carrying such a stop keeps it.

🚨 **A ramp's opacity is a field on `GradientBrush` and not a rewrite of its stops** (§15 D767), which
is what makes the paragraph above about the *readout* alone. `panels::paint::with_alpha` used to scale
every stop by `alpha / peak`, so `alpha_of` was the producer for that division as well as for the
field — one bare click at 100% divided the ramp by an unclamped 5.0 and took a second stop from 25% to
5%. **It is not invertible through zero**: at 0% the peak is zero and the only fallback is one flat
alpha across the ramp, so `[1.0, 0.0]` — the shape every gradient this app authors starts as — came
back `[1.0, 1.0]`, opaque with the fade destroyed. The field is a multiplier beside the stops, which is
the shape `peniko::ImageSampler::alpha` has always had on the image arm, and the stops are now left
exactly alone. ⚠️ **So a rogue stop can no longer reach the opacity control by any route, and the
accidental normalisation D692 got for free is gone with the division** — `stop-opacity="5"` stays 5.0
in the document, harmless because the raster clamps it, and that is a stop-validation gap rather than
an opacity one. ⚠️ **The field is `#[serde(default)]`, so the loader is not its guard**:
`build::brush_is_finite` asks `valid_opacity` rather than `is_finite`, because a non-finite value dies
at serde and what has to be refused is the **finite out-of-range** one.
🚨 **The chips were the door this multiplier had not reached, which is D564's paragraph above
happening again** (§15 D767, fixed by **D773**). It is folded in at `color::brush_to_backend` for both
backends and written as `fill-opacity` by `svg::paint_attr`, and `picker::ramp` folded nothing, so a
gradient at 30% drew its swatch opaque beside a canvas that drew it faint. **It was right for free
while the opacity *was* the stops** — *a derived value that becomes a stored one turns every reader of
the old derivation into a bug*, with nothing in the workspace able to see it. `ramp` folds the
multiplier in now and the **stop bar** asks `picker::stop_colours`, the named exception: it is the
editing surface for the stops and sits directly under the opacity slider, so fading it would dim the
handles being dragged. **The common case is the default and the exception opts out by name**, which is
what makes a chip written later right by doing nothing. **The image arm is closed too, on the
maintainer's ruling** (§15 D185, D773, **D784**): `ImageSampler::alpha` is folded in by neither of
those two functions and does not need to be, because a picture's chips read
`panels::paint::image_brush_alpha` instead — the single clamp, with `image_alpha` as the arm that
answers the identity for a brush that is not a picture, two entry points because the inspector holds a
`&Brush` and a layers row an `&ImageBrush`. That gap was older and wider than the gradient one, having
stood since an image brush had an alpha at all, and **it closed because D773 wrote down the half it
was not doing** rather than leaving it implicit. ⚠️ **It was two surfaces and D773 named one**: beside
`Swatch::Picture`, `panels::layers` draws the same picture on every image layer's row, through a
`picture_of` that returned `&ImageRef` and dropped the sampler on the floor — *a helper that returns
half of a brush is how the other half gets forgotten by every caller at once.*

**How a picture sits in its frame is a fit, not a matrix** — `ImageFit` on `ImageRef`, resolved by
`ImageRef::framing(frame, width, height)` into a `Framing` of a brush transform, a `peniko::Extend`
and an optional clip. One function, so both backends and the SVG writer cannot answer differently:

- **Four modes: `Fill` (cover — the default, and Figma's), `Fit` (contain), `Crop` and `Tile`**, and
  none of them resamples the picture. The same decoded blob is drawn under a different brush
  transform, so switching mode costs nothing and scrubbing a crop costs nothing.
- **`ImageFit` is a bare four-variant enum and the parameters sit beside it on `ImageRef`** — `crop`
  and `tile_scale` as fields, not as variant payloads. Fill and Fit read neither: cover and contain
  are re-derived against whatever the frame currently is, so resizing the shape re-frames the picture,
  and a mode that stored a baked-in affine would come apart on the first resize, which is the whole
  reason this is an enum of *intents*. Crop and Tile each read exactly one of the two, because each
  needs something the frame cannot re-derive — *this rectangle of the source, not that one*; *that*
  repetition scale. **The parameters persist while their mode is not selected**, which is what makes a
  mode switch a change of view rather than a reset (§15 D178); the isolation the variant payloads used
  to give for free is asserted instead, by `a_mode_ignores_the_parameters_it_does_not_use`.
- **A mirror and a quarter turn sit *before* the four modes** — `ImageOrient { quarters, mirrored }`
  on `ImageRef`, read by all four where `crop` and `tile_scale` are each read by one, because turning a
  picture turns it whether it is filling, fitting, cropped or tiled. `framing` composes
  `orient.affine` under the mode's own transform and runs the mode's arithmetic against
  `orient.oriented_size`, so Fill covers with the turned aspect, Fit letterboxes on the other axis and
  Tile turns each tile. **Eight states, spelled canonically as mirror-then-turn** rather than as
  `flip_x`/`flip_y`/`turns`, which would spell the rectangle's eight symmetries sixteen ways and let a
  file carry one the buttons can never produce; and the ops are `OrientOp::{FlipH, FlipV, Turn}`
  *composed* onto whatever the picture is already in, never flags set, because once a quarter turn is
  involved "is it flipped horizontally?" has no answer (§15 D182). **The popover offers the two
  mirrors only, and nothing writes `Turn`** — a decision rather than an oversight, said on the variant
  itself, which leaves four of the eight states reachable. The turn count is live regardless, because
  `applying` resolves `FlipV` to `quarters: 2`, and the eight-state algebra is what makes the two
  mirrors correct (§15 D182).
- **A crop rectangle is normalized to the picture *as oriented* (`0..1`), never in pixels**, so
  *replace image* keeps the framing across a differently sized picture, which is what makes the
  popover's *Replace…* a repair rather than a fresh placement (§9.4, §15 D179).
  Oriented rather than raw because that is the space the crop gesture drags in, which is what
  keeps `crop_panned` and `crop_reframed` innocent of orientation entirely; the price is that a flip or a
  turn has to carry the rectangle with it, which `OrientOp::crop_carried` does and
  `ImageRef::reoriented` is the only way to reach (§15 D182).
  `image::whole_crop()` is the whole of it, and it is a **sentinel meaning "never cropped"** rather
  than a picture anybody chose: mapped onto a frame of a different aspect it stretches. It is what
  *reset crop* restores (§9.4), and the next entry into cropping seeds cover from it again (§15 D181).
  The rectangle maps onto the frame **exactly**, so aspect is the frame's business: cropping to a
  square and then stretching the shape stretches the picture, which is what having chosen a region
  means.
- **Everything that enters cropping replaces the sentinel with `ImageRef::cover_crop` — the rectangle
  Fill is already showing** — so picking the mode changes nothing on screen for a `Fill` picture and the
  gesture starts from the picture the user is looking at, rather than from the whole source stretched
  onto the frame. ⚠️ **For a `Fit` picture it does move, and no seed exists that would not** (§15 D561):
  a `Crop` framing maps its rectangle onto the *whole* frame, so reproducing a letterbox needs a
  rectangle larger than the source, and `crop_clamped` shrinks any such rectangle back about its own
  centre before it can be stored. Cover is therefore the closest rectangle a crop can *name* rather
  than a convenience, which is a stronger claim and an asserted one — `crop_clamped` of the exact
  `Fit` rectangle **is** `cover_crop`, at all eight orientations
  (`a_fit_pictures_exact_crop_leaves_the_source_and_clamps_to_the_cover_one`). Both
  entries do it: the canvas gesture, and the inspector's mode strip through `panels::paint::with_fit`,
  which is handed the frame or `None` and changes the mode without a seed rather than with a guessed
  one. `None` covers a slot spanning a **selection** as well as an unknowable frame — there is no one
  frame to compute a seed for when a single brush is written to every node in scope, so those pictures
  keep the sentinel and do jump (§15 D181). Cover is also the widest rectangle the gesture can reach:
  anything larger leaves the source, where `Extend::Pad` smears the edge row — which since §15 D268 is
  enforced by the *frame* being clamped to `ImageRef::picture_box` rather than by the rectangle being
  clamped after the fact, the two being the same wall approached from opposite sides. The pure
  functions image editing is made of — `cover_crop`, `cover_scale`, `picture_box`, `crop_scale`,
  `crop_panned`, `crop_reframed`, `crop_scaled`, `crop_clamped` — are all in `image.rs`, and the four
  that take the intrinsic size are exactly the four that have to know how many pixels a unit is: a pan
  divides the pointer's travel by the frame, a reframe re-reads a normalized mapping and a scale
  multiplies one, so the source's dimensions cancel out of those three (§15 D181, D271). The
  **methods** are the four that must see `orient`: cover and its scale are computed against the turned
  aspect, `picture_box` is read off `framing`, and `crop_scale` divides by the turned width (§15 D182,
  D268, D271). `crop_reframed` is deliberately **not** clamped — a crop that left the source would be a
  frame that had grown past the picture, and the caller is the one holding the frame to stop that with;
  `crop_scaled` **is** clamped, because there the frame is standing still and the rectangle is the only
  thing that can run out of room.
- **A tile is anchored at the frame's top-left**, at `scale` times the intrinsic pixel size (`1.0` is
  one document unit per source pixel). Anchored rather than centred, because a repeat has no centre
  and a tiling that shifted when the shape was resized from the far edge would read as the pattern
  sliding.
- **The frame is the shape's bounding box in its own local space** — the same space the path is in,
  which is §6.2's rule for gradients, so the transform composes under the node's transform on both
  backends. It is the shape's box and not the *ink's*, so widening a border does not re-frame the
  picture underneath it.
- **Fit is the one mode that costs a layer**, because peniko has no transparent extend and the
  letterbox would otherwise be a smear of the picture's edge row. The clip is emitted only where the
  aspects genuinely differ, so a click-placed image — whose shape carries the picture's own aspect —
  pays nothing. §15 D178 is the whole of that finding.
- **Nothing degenerate produces a singular brush transform.** A zero-sized source, an empty frame and
  a zero-area crop resolve to `Framing::identity`, and a tile scale that is not finite and positive
  draws at 1:1: a frame with no area has no drawing to get right, and what a backend does with a
  singular affine is a question with no good answer. **Degenerate means *unusable*, not merely
  zero** — a span is judged by `image::usable_span`, which is `> 0.0 && is_finite()` — so a crop of
  `-1e308..1e308`, whose four coordinates are perfectly finite and whose width overflows to `inf`, is
  refused alongside the empty one. Every span test in the module asks that one predicate, because the
  guards that asked `<= 0.0` went on to divide `inf / inf` and hand a `NaN` rectangle to the file
  (§15 D452). ⚠️ **The rule is not fully honoured yet**: a span is weighed and a crop's *origin* is
  not, so `Crop`'s `-r.x0 * iw` can overflow while the span is perfectly usable and produce a
  transform with an infinite translation. D452 carries the *Fix*.
- **All four framing fields are `#[serde(default, skip_serializing_if)]`** (§5.11) — `fit` against
  `Fill`, `crop` against the whole picture, `tile_scale` against 1.0, `orient` against the identity —
  so every image placed before framing or orientation existed keeps its byte-for-byte line in the file
  and no saved document moved. A predicate each rather than one is what lets an image that has been
  cropped and set back to Fill still write its rectangle: it is still the user's.
  `only_the_parameters_that_were_changed_are_written` pins both halves and
  `only_an_orientation_that_was_set_is_written` pins the fourth field.

**What is done to a picture's colours is the fill's, not the image's** — `ImageAdjust` on `ImageRef`:
seven `f32`s, all `0.0` at rest and all held in `-1.0..=1.0` (exposure, contrast, saturation,
temperature, tint, highlights, shadows):

- **Per fill, not per entry.** The bytes are shared and deduplicated by content hash; what is done to
  them is not, so two layers showing one photograph adjust independently. It is the **one field on
  `ImageRef` that is not geometry**, and the difference is what it costs: the other four are answered
  by a brush transform over the buffer the whole document shares, where this one produces a *second
  buffer*.
- **`ImageAdjust::pipeline()` is the resolution, and it is `ImageRef::framing`'s counterpart** — one
  description all three writers read, so a per-pixel function cannot mean one thing on the canvas and
  another in an export. `None` for the neutral value, so an untouched picture costs nothing anywhere,
  and `None` for a value that is not finite **or is outside `-1..=1`**, which is what a hand-edited
  file can carry. ⚠️ **The range half was missing until 2026-09-08 and it is the half that mattered**
  (§15 D538): finiteness alone let `"exposure": 1000.0` through, `2f32.powf(1000.0)` is `inf` and
  `inf * 0.0` makes all twenty matrix coefficients `NaN`, so the photograph rendered as a solid black
  rectangle from `|exposure| >= 128` up; `"shadows": 2.0` made the tone curve double back at 12 of
  its 32 steps, inverting the dark end, the bound being the file's own algebra — the derivative of
  `v + 0.4s(1−v)²` at `v = 0` is `1 − 0.8s`, non-monotonic above `1.25`. **And it is a backend
  divergence**, which is worse than a wrong picture: both pixel backends quantise `NaN` to zero and
  agree on black, while the SVG writer emits `<feColorMatrix values="NaN NaN …">`, which a viewer
  rejects outright. **Refused, not clamped** — `is_default` already reports such a value as
  non-neutral, so clamping would make the file draw something it does not say.
- **`AdjustPipeline`'s shape is dictated by the writer that cannot invent arithmetic.** Two optional
  stages — a 4×5 colour matrix and a per-channel transfer table of `TONE_STEPS = 33` samples — because
  those are exactly `feColorMatrix type="matrix"` and `feComponentTransfer type="table"`, the only two
  SVG primitives that can say this. The pixel backends evaluate the very same numbers, with
  `ondin_core::transfer` spelling out SVG's own table interpolation rule, so the export is the same
  description read by a different reader rather than an approximation (§7.1, §15 D186).
- **Which slider lands in which stage is forced, not chosen.** Exposure, contrast, saturation,
  temperature and tint are linear in the channels and collapse into one matrix; highlights and shadows
  are a tone curve and cannot. Saturation uses SVG's own luminance coefficients (0.213/0.715/0.072) so
  the emitted numbers are recognisable, contrast pivots on mid-grey through the matrix's fifth column,
  and **the matrix runs before the curve** — set the exposure, then pull the highlights back — which
  `the_matrix_runs_before_the_tone_curve` pins on a pixel the matrix pushes past white. The tone
  curve's ±0.4 strength is the largest that keeps it monotonic at both ends; more inverts one end of
  the picture at a strong setting.
- **`Adjustment` is the list and everything reads it** — the panel's rows, the cache key and the
  snapshot all come off `Adjustment::ALL`, so a slider cannot exist that one of them does not know
  about. There are two doors and they differ: `Adjustment::set` is what the panel and *reset* write
  through and it clamps to `-1..=1`, mapping a non-finite value to zero, while `pipeline` is what a
  hand-edited file reaches and refuses one outright — **asking the same range question since §15
  D538**, where it had asked only about finiteness and `set`'s own doc had stated the reason all
  along (*"a range the model does not enforce is a range a hand-edited file ignores"*). The
  *operation* is a third door and shuts against a different half: `op_set_fills` weighs all seven
  sliders through `build::image_ref_is_finite` (§3, §15 D452), so what still reaches `pipeline` is
  always finite and the range is the only thing left to ask.
- **`adjust` is `#[serde(default, skip_serializing_if)]` as the four framing fields are** (§5.11), so
  adding it bumped no schema and needed no migration, and each of the seven carries its own predicate
  as well — only the sliders that moved reach the file (`"adjust":{"exposure":0.25}`).

**The decode cache** (`ondin_render::images::ImageStore`) is the other half, and it is what makes an
image draw:

- **It lives in `ondin-render`** because two crates need decoded pixels — the app's canvas and
  `ondin-export`'s PNG — and both already depend on it. Core cannot hold it: core does no decoding and
  has no image dependency (§3).
- **It holds the shared form**, `peniko::ImageData` (straight-alpha RGBA8 in an `Arc`-backed blob). The
  GPU takes that inline, so resolving a fill is an `Arc` clone. The CPU takes a `vello_cpu::ImageSource`,
  which **premultiplies a whole buffer** — so `cpu.rs` memoizes it per render, keyed on the image id,
  and takes the image arm off the model's brush to have that id to key on.
- **`prepare(doc)` decodes what the table carries, and the canvas calls it every frame.** Once the
  decoding is done it is one hash lookup per entry, against a scene walk that touches every visible node
  — so driving it off a change signal would save nothing measurable and would eventually miss one.
- **The budget bounds bytes, and it bounds *waste* rather than the working set.** Eviction only ever
  drops an image the document has stopped carrying, oldest-first. Evicting something a fill still refers
  to would either take the picture off screen mid-frame or re-decode it on the next one — the thrash
  `PREVIEW_FLOOR` exists to prevent in the font cache (§15 D160). A hard bound on a document larger than
  the budget needs decode-on-demand with a resident set, which is a different design.
- **A decode that refuses is remembered**, so corrupt bytes are not re-attempted every frame, and an
  image wider or taller than 65535 is refused at the decode rather than asserting inside `vello_cpu`.
  ⚠️ **It also refuses on the one unit none of the three caps was in** (§15 D449): `MAX_DECODED_BYTES`
  weighs `width × height × 4` *before* `into_rgba8` runs, because `image`'s own `max_alloc` bounds the
  decoder's buffer in the decoder's format, `MAX_EDGE` bounds edges, and the budget below bounds only
  stale entries — so a 76 KB grayscale PNG expanded to 256 MB with nothing consulted, and a larger one
  to an allocation failure, which is an abort rather than an `Err`. `TooMuchPixelData` is a separate
  variant from `TooLarge` because a caller explaining itself wants to say which. **It does not make a
  large document cheap**, only bounded: the cap is `DECODED_BYTES` itself, and it has to be, a 50 MP
  camera file being 240 MB of RGBA.
- **Every failure ends at the same place**: a dangling reference, an unread link and undecodable bytes
  are one state, and it is the state the placeholder draws — grey and a cross, on both backends and in
  the SVG writer, for a *fill*. Not black, and never nothing, which is the blank that gets exported
  into a deliverable unnoticed. A stroke or a text run with the same brush is still skipped (§6.3, §15
  D179).
- **It holds derived pixels beside decoded ones**, keyed by `(ImageId, AdjustKey)` — the seven values'
  bit patterns, an `f32` struct being neither `Eq` nor `Hash`, and safe bitwise only because the
  neutral value resolves to no pipeline and so never reaches a key. They live behind a `Mutex` because
  they are filled **where they are read, not where the table is prepared**: an adjustment belongs to a
  *fill*, and only the scene walk knows the fills — including a previewed one a walk of the document
  would never see. So `ImageStore::pixels(&ImageRef)` is what a backend paints with; `get(&ImageId)`
  is still the decode and still the right question for `ScenePainter::has_image`, an adjustment being
  able to fail at nothing (§15 D179's placeholder path is untouched).
- **A fresh adjustment is previewed while scrubbing and promoted on stillness, never on commit.** A
  miss is answered with the picture reduced by a whole factor towards `PREVIEW_EDGE = 1024`, which is
  a **floor** and not a ceiling — the reduced long edge lands in `[1024, 2048)` and a picture under
  twice it is not reduced at all (§15 D186) — box-averaged in premultiplied
  space, one integer factor, one reduced copy per picture shared by every adjustment of it — and
  rebuilt at full resolution once the same value has been asked for on `SETTLED_FRAMES = 2`
  consecutive frames, which is what a released slider looks like and what a moving one never does. One
  frame is not enough: it spends a full-resolution pass on every value a drag passes through, one
  frame late and thrown away. *On commit* was rejected because the cache has no way to know when a
  commit happened, and being told would be a signal to keep in step by hand (§15 D186).
- **`Pixels` carries `to_source`**, the map from the answered buffer's pixel grid onto the source's,
  because `ImageRef::framing` maps *source*-pixel space and a reduced buffer under the raw framing
  draws the picture at a fraction of its size. `color::framed_transform` is the one place the two are
  composed and both backends go through it.
- **The canvas shrinks the page's pictures to fit vello's atlas, and the export does not** (§15 D745).
  vello keeps every picture a scene draws in **one 8192-pixel square atlas** (`ATLAS_EDGE`, upstream's
  `MAX_ATLAS_SIZE` pinned to a version), and when the next one will not fit it sets that picture's
  position to `None` and carries on — *"there's nothing we can do"*, in `resolve_pending_images`' own
  words: no error, no `Result`, no log. Three ordinary 4500 × 3000 photographs need three shelves of
  3000 and the third has nowhere to go, so the canvas drew **1 250 opaque pixels of 1 875** while the
  layers row and the Fill swatch showed all three — those read the store, and only the canvas reads
  the atlas. So `ImageStore::prepare` computes **one integer factor for the whole page**
  (`images::atlas_downscale`), searching *upward from 1*: full resolution until it stops fitting, then
  shrink. From the store's own decoded population and **not from what a frame draws**, since a factor
  derived from visibility would resharpen a photograph when its neighbour scrolled off; one factor
  rather than one each, since per-picture factors make the page's photographs disagree about
  sharpness and make the answer depend on placement order. The fit test is a **shelf** packing where
  vello uses a guillotine allocator, which is safe in exactly one direction — *the shelf fitting
  implies the guillotine fitting* — and costs a photograph shrunk when it need not have been. ⚠️ **The
  budget makes the loss not happen; it does not make it visible.** `ScenePainter::has_image` is
  answered by the store, so D179's placeholder still cannot fire for an atlas failure, and past
  `MAX_ATLAS_DOWNSCALE` = 64 the silent drop returns.
- **`ImageStore::new()` never previews; `ImageStore::interactive()` does**, and `CanvasRenderer` is its
  only caller — `ondin-export`'s `png()` takes the plain one. The safe default is deliberately the
  inconvenient one: an export that quietly wrote a downsampled photograph is the defect here that no
  visual check would find. **`wants_frame()` says a promotion is pending and `canvas::draw_canvas` owes
  it a `request_repaint`**, since the promotion happens in a later frame's `prepare` and the frame that
  releases a slider is routinely the last one egui draws.
- **Derived buffers are evicted by two rules, because there are two kinds of waste.** A preview is one
  position of a slider nobody will return to and goes as soon as it is stale; a full buffer cost real
  work and goes only under its own budget (`ADJUSTED_BYTES`), **stale first and within each the least
  recently asked**. That budget bounds a genuinely different thing from `DECODED_BYTES`:
  every derived buffer is recomputable from a decode, so it is a working-set bound where the decode
  budget bounds waste. Anything derived from a picture the store no longer holds goes with it.
  ⚠️ **The budget is enforced where a buffer is *inserted*, not only from `prepare`** — `trim_derived`
  is the one place that reads it and `pixels` calls it as well as `evict_derived` does (§15 D596).
  Being only in `prepare` meant it bounded nothing at all on every path that prepares once and then
  reads, which is every non-interactive caller: `png::png` and `png::raster_of` build a store, prepare
  it once and hand it to the renderer, so an export and a library cover grew one full-size buffer per
  distinct `(ImageId, AdjustKey)` the walk visited. **And it takes a live buffer when there is no
  stale one**, because on such a path every entry is live — a floor of `PREVIEW_FLOOR`'s kind here
  (§15 D160) would refuse to evict at all. What that costs, where a working set genuinely exceeds the
  budget, is a recomputation rather than unbounded growth.
- **A thumbnail is a third answer, deliberately not `pixels`** — `ImageStore::thumbnail(&ImageRef,
  edge)` cuts a square of `edge` device pixels and touches neither the ask clock nor `wants_frame`,
  because a sixteen-point chip going through `pixels` would promote a full-resolution adjustment pass
  for a picture nothing is drawing at size and keep the app repainting on a row's behalf (§15 D189).
  It reduces first and adjusts second — the opposite order to the canvas, and they do not commute —
  over a `THUMB_BASE = 128` copy cut **once per `ImageId`** into a third map beside `entries` and
  `small`, since `reduced` is O(width × height) whatever its target. That copy is evicted with the
  *picture* rather than with the last adjustment of it, one step further out than `small`'s rule,
  because a thumbnail leaves no derived entry to keep it alive. Orientation and the crop are applied
  and the framing mode is not: a chip has no box for Fill and Fit to argue about, so what it shows is
  a centre-crop. The egui texture is the app's half of the seam (§9.2).

**Placing** (`Tool::Image`, `tools::create_image`, §9.4):

- **The tool is not a persistent mode, and it is the only one on the rail that is not.** Arming it *is*
  picking files: the rail button and `Ctrl+Shift+K` run one action, which opens the dialog and arms the
  tool only if something loaded. Each click then places one of the loaded images, in pick order, and
  when the last one is placed the tool hands back to Select. Arming a placement tool with nothing to
  place would be a cursor whose clicks do nothing.
- **The cursor carries the count.** `Bitmap::Loaded(Remaining)` is the drawing tools' own crosshair
  with a chip hung off its bottom-right saying how many pictures are still to place — exact to 99,
  `99+` beyond — and the plain crosshair when the queue is empty, which is the same "failed to disarm"
  moment the bullet above rules out. The badge is drawn for a *single* remaining image too, where the
  number alone tells the user nothing: without it `Tool::Image` and the six drawing tools show the
  identical bitmap while a click means something else entirely (§15 D236, D9).
- **The loaded images live on the app, not in the tool.** `Tool` is a `Copy` enum every match on it
  would have to carry, and picking files is one event while placing them is several.
  `choose_tool` clears them for anything but `Tool::Image`, which is the one line that makes Escape,
  `V` and any other rail button all put them down.
- **A click fits, a drag draws.** The click is the loaded-cursor gesture: the image is centred on the
  point, at `fitted_image_size` — shrink to fit, **never scale up**, against the frame under the point
  or, on bare canvas, the viewport. Both halves are traps rather than refinements: read as "always fill
  the frame" it lands a 32px icon enormous and blurry, and without it at all a 6000px photograph arrives
  six thousand units wide and ungrabbable. The viewport is the fallback because it is the only bounded
  thing there is, and *original size* is one right-click away whichever the fit was measured against
  (§9.4, §15 D305 — it is a context-menu row now and not a card one). A drag lays out its own box
  and the image fills it at whatever
  aspect was drawn, because a drawn box is an instruction. Both gestures are the same arms the Text
  tool uses, for the same reason: a shape abandons a click and these must not.
- **The file is read, hashed and decoded before the tool is armed**, so a file that cannot be drawn
  never becomes a placement, and the decode supplies the intrinsic size the fit rule measures. The id is
  `sha256:<hex>` of the **encoded** bytes, through `ring` — already in the app's tree via `ureq`/`rustls`
  — because the id goes in the file and `sha256sum` on an exported original should reproduce it.
- **Placing the same file twice adds a reference, not a second copy**: the caller asks
  `Document::has_image` and omits the `AddImage`. That is the whole payoff of a content-hashed key, and
  `build::missing_image_ops` is the same question asked of a whole paste — a picture the target already
  holds is recognised rather than stored twice, and an id from *another* document is the same key for
  the same bytes, so nothing is remapped on arrival (§15 D280).
- **The layer is named for the file, and a picture that arrives without one is numbered `"Image N"`.**
  A filename is real identity and is kept; a paste has none to keep, and calling every one of them
  "Pasted image" named a layer for how it got here rather than for what it is (§15 D187). The name is
  resolved at the call site by `canvas::image_layer_name`, not by `CreateNode { name: None }`, which
  would produce "Rectangle 4" — an image is a *fill* on a Rect and the kind is all core can see.

**Dropping and pasting** (§9.4, §15 D183) are the other two ways in, and they share the place path:

- **One loader, three ways in.** `load_image_bytes(bytes, ext, name)` is everything after "here are the
  bytes and what to call them" — hash, sniff, decode, name — and reading a file is the thin wrapper over
  it. A drop usually carries a path and sometimes only bytes; a paste carries neither, which is why the
  format sniffing takes an `Option<&str>` extension rather than a path — and why the name is an
  `Option<String>` the placement fills in rather than a string the loader invents (§15 D187).
- **Dropping or pasting onto a *selected* shape replaces that shape's picture and keeps its framing**;
  anywhere else makes a layer. The selection is the rule for all three ways in, and it keeps the
  destructive reading opt-in. Only a single file replaces.
  **A locked layer is not a target** (§15 D463): `canvas::image_drop_target` asks
  `query::is_effectively_locked`, so a drop or a paste onto a locked picture makes a new layer instead
  of repainting one. That guard is the drop's own rather than image editing's — neither gesture enters
  the mode, so neither asks `edited_image`'s question — and it is the door the mechanism went without
  from D183 until 2026-09-07, `toggle_locked` leaving the selection in place, which makes
  *select → lock → paste* three ordinary acts.
  A **drop must also land on the shape**: the selection-alone arm is the *chord's* paste, which has no
  pointer to address a shape with, and a drop falling
  through to it replaced whatever was selected wherever it was released (§15 D184). **On Windows no event
  carries the position at all**, so `canvas::drop_point` reads the desktop cursor through `GetCursorPos`
  and maps it into egui's screen space against the viewport's `inner_rect` (§15 D241); a drop there aims
  and replaces like any other. The viewport centre is what is left when that reading fails or the drop
  lands off the canvas.
  **The context menu's *Paste here* is the third gesture and it is aimed like the drop** (§15 D224): it
  has a pointer *and* a selection, so it requires both — a selected shape under the press — and lands a
  new layer at the press otherwise. Right-clicking bare canvas and choosing *paste **here*** cannot
  sensibly mean "replace the picture over there", which the chord in that same state does mean.
- **A drag of files over the window announces which of the two a release would do** — an outline round
  the frame the picture will land in, a pill naming the outcome, and the hover outline on the shape that
  would be replaced (`canvas::draw_drop_indicator`, §15 D184). The frame is `target_artboard`'s answer
  for the landing point, the one `create_image_at` would parent by; a landing on bare canvas, or a frame
  not wholly on screen, falls back to a border inside the canvas edge. The count in it is of files, not
  of pictures, because whether a file is an image is a question about its bytes and they are not read
  until the drop.
- **A pasted image is re-encoded to PNG before it is hashed.** The clipboard hands over decoded RGBA, and
  there is no encoded original to store or to hash; PNG because it is lossless and one of the four. So a
  paste's id is the hash of *our* encoding and does not dedupe against the same picture placed from a file.
- **SVG is refused rather than rasterized**, sniffed from the leading bytes and reported separately from a
  file that could not be read. That report is the whole reason for the sniff — *"could not read" would
  be a lie about a file that reads perfectly well and is simply not an image* — and until 2026-09-09 it
  was a lie for the commonest file there is (§15 D671). 🚨 **There is one predicate**,
  `svg_in::looks_like_svg`, which the paste path has always asked of a clipboard string; the drop path
  carried a second implementation that answered `false` for a `<!DOCTYPE svg …>`-first file, so the
  same drawing was *"Could not read"* when dropped and became layers when pasted. `app::looks_like_svg`
  is the **byte-to-`str` adapter** over it and nothing else: the 512-byte cap and the lossy decode are
  this side's own, because they are about bytes. The predicate skips an XML declaration and any run of
  comments before the root — a generator comment between the two is what Illustrator writes — and
  **refuses a byte-order mark deliberately**, that being a different question, since a BOM reaches
  `roxmltree` too and admitting one here would trade a wrong refusal for a parser error. *Open, and it
  wants a real file rather than an argument.* The parser's branch exists now (§7, §15 D394), so more
  files reach the *not an image* message than reach the failure one.
- **A refusal says which of the two things went wrong, and carries the numbers** (§15 D677). *"Could
  not read"* is the answer for a file that will not read off disk and for bytes that are not a picture;
  it is a **lie** about a picture the decoder handled perfectly and a renderer bound refused, and it
  was that lie for every one until 2026-09-09, because `ondin_render::images::DecodeError` had no
  reader anywhere in the workspace and both callers of `insert` dropped it with `.ok()?`. A 70000 × 100
  panorama is 34 KB of good PNG and is refused only because `vello_cpu`'s `Pixmap` is `u16`-dimensioned
  (`MAX_EDGE`), so what it needs to hear is *"panorama.png is 70000 × 100; the largest Ondin can draw
  is 65535 on a side"* — the numbers **and** the limit, because *"too large"* sends somebody back to a
  file to guess. `TooMuchPixelData` gets its own sentence for the same reason it is its own variant: a
  different bound with a different remedy. `app::ImageRefusal` is the two-way question the three
  message sites ask; `paste_image` deliberately says nothing, its bytes being the app's own encode, so
  a refusal there is a bug rather than something to explain. **A multi-file failure is one sentence per
  file** rather than one list of names, which is the whole point — two files can fail for two reasons
  in one drop.

**On disk** (§5.11): the table is written *last*, sorted by id, one entry per record, with embedded
bytes as **base64** rather than serde's array-of-numbers. Last because the image lines are the ones that
never change; base64 because `Vec<u8>` through `serde_json` is four to six text bytes per byte, one per
line pretty-printed. A document with no images writes no key at all, so adding the table changed no
existing file's bytes (invariant 9). **Still one file, and emphatically not a zip** — a zip looks like
the compromise between a file and a folder and is the worst of the three for version control, since
compressing and reordering makes every save a fresh opaque blob with no useful delta; a folder is fine
for git and loses the portability that is the cost which actually bites on Windows. Base64 lines at the
end of one JSON file keep both, which is the whole reason the table sits where it does.

### 5.6 Transform & resize semantics (Figma baseline)

- `transform` carries translation, rotation, skew and flip. **It does not carry scale in normal
  editing.** Scale is the one factor kept out, and for a reason the others do not share: a layer's
  size must be one number in one place (its geometry), or a stroke thickens when its group is
  resized. Skew is admitted because it has no geometry field it could live in instead — there is
  nowhere else to put a lean.
- Interactive resize edits *geometry* (`SetGeometry`: rect/ellipse size, path points scaled, text
  box size) — stroke widths and children are unaffected, matching Figma.
- A resize moves the text **box**, never the text size — and **a scale may not change which of
  `TextSizing`'s three states a layer is in**. Which one it is in is the user's answer to "who decides
  this box" (§5.4), so `tools::scale_geometry` — the step group resize, selection resize and skew all
  share — hands text to `tools::scaled_text_sizing` ahead of the generic path and returns. ⚠️ **A
  railed node answers one arm earlier still, and did not until 2026-09-07** (§15 D472): on a rail
  `TextSizing` is inert, so `Auto` produced no patch at all and a railed child came out of a group or
  selection drag with a bare `SetTransform` — standing still while its ribbon went on pinning the
  container's width, which came out 47% short of the drag. That arm edits the **rail**, which is what
  `resize_to_handle` had been doing since §15 D405 and this door was not; the two derive their boxes
  differently (`anchored_box` over `Resolved` there, `tools::railed_box` here, that function having no
  `Resolved`) and share `tools::railed_resize`.
  **Off a rail**, `tools::scaled_text_sizing` scales each axis exactly when the *user* authors it:
  `Auto` has nothing at all, `AutoHeight` has only its wrap width, `Fixed` has both. The layer still
  travels with the box on either arm, because the transform half of the edit is the caller's and
  happens regardless. ⚠️ **That sentence opened *"That function"* until 2026-09-15, and had been
  naming `railed_resize` ever since the railed ⚠️ above was inserted between the pronoun and its
  antecedent** (§15 D790). `railed_resize` holds no `TextSizing` at all — on a rail the mode is
  *inert*, which is what the inserted passage itself says, so the sentence contradicted the paragraph
  directly above it. **A pronoun is a citation with no name in it, and it rebinds silently when prose
  grows above it**: nothing resolves `That function`, and the edit that broke this one changed not
  one character of it. Answering before the generic path is load-bearing, not tidiness:
  `tools::resizable_size` reports `Size::ZERO` for auto text and `(w, 0)` for
  auto-height, and the `max(1.0)` floor below it — there so a resize cannot drive a shape to nothing —
  rounded those zeros up, so resizing a group containing one silently converted it to `Fixed(1×1)` or
  `Fixed(w × 1)` and collapsed it to a sliver showing about one character.
  `tools::tests::scaling_a_group_leaves_auto_sized_text_alone` and
  `scaling_a_group_scales_an_auto_height_child_without_fixing_it` hold both halves.
  The early return is about the *box* and nothing else: under the Scale tool auto-sized text still
  takes the new **font size**, because `tools::scale_scalars` runs ahead of the return, so a scaled
  group's label scales with it (§15 D70).
  ⚠️ **On a rail that ordering is a trap, and `railed_resize` has to be handed the type the
  transaction will *leave*** (§15 D604). It converges its scale against a box `railed_box` genuinely
  lays out, so a solve against the kind it found converges on `layout(new rail, old font)` while the
  document ends up with `layout(new rail, new font)`. `tools::kind_to_solve_against` applies the
  gesture's own photographic factor to the four text scopes first, at **both** rail doors. Solved
  against the current kind, a `BottomRight` drag under the Scale tool slid the held corner
  `(9.58, 15.00)` out from under the pointer where the Select tool's identical drag landed it to the
  bit — which is the control saying the solve was right and the composition wrong. Only the kind the
  solve *measures* moves; the box it measures from is still where the node is now.
  🚨 **And the anchor is the corner the *handle* holds, which for three corners out of four is not
  the box's origin** (§15 D789). `railed_resize` translates the solved rail so that corner lands
  where `want` puts it, reading it off `Handle::anchored` — of **both** boxes, since the held edge is
  `origin + width` on one side and `origin + 0` on the other, so the two offsets differ by exactly
  the extent residual the translation exists to absorb. Pinning the **origin** instead is right for
  `BottomRight` alone and hands the residual to the held corner everywhere else: a `BottomLeft` drag
  to a tenth of the width slid it **10.37 units**, the width residual to a hundredth. The solve is
  deliberately exact on placement and close on extent, so **whichever corner the translation names is
  the one the gesture keeps its promise about.**
- **Dragging a text layer's own handle is the gesture that authors its box, and *which* handle decides
  how much of it.** `tools::resize_to_handle` gives the box the width the drag asked for either way;
  whether the **height** also becomes the user's is the handle's business, because a side handle owns
  one axis and says nothing about `y` (`Handle::anchored`). So dragging the right edge of an auto-width
  layer gives it a wrap width and leaves the lines deciding the height — `AutoHeight`, which is what
  Figma does and which no gesture could previously reach — while a corner or a top/bottom handle
  authors the height and produces `Fixed`. Already-`Fixed` text stays fixed under a side drag: the rule
  is about height *authorship*, not about the handle alone (§15 D148).
- **The inspector's W and H are that same gesture with the pointer typed in**, so they share the rule
  rather than restating it: `tools::resized_text_sizing` takes the new size and one boolean —
  *does this number author the height* — and both `resize_to_handle` and the panel call it. W says no
  and H says yes, except that with the proportion lock on W drives H as well and is therefore a corner.
  The fields exist for all three sizing modes, reading `query::local_box` like the handles do rather
  than the `sizing` field, which is what gives an `AutoHeight` layer a door onto its authored width
  (§15 D297).
- Group resize recurses geometry edits into children (`tools::resize_group`, one transaction): each
  descendant's position within the group scales with the box and each leaf's geometry scales with
  it, so the group's own transform comes out untouched and a resized group is still a group of
  ordinary nodes. It is **exact at every angle**, including the case that used to be approximated: a
  child rotated off-axis inside a group scaled *non-uniformly*. Squashing a turned rectangle makes a
  parallelogram, and the transform can now say so. The mechanism is `tools::split_geometry_scale` —
  carry the node bodily through the intended scale, then split the result with `build::Basis::exact`
  (§5.7a), putting rotation, skew and flip in the transform and the residual diagonal into the
  geometry. The two together reproduce the intended matrix exactly, because the RQ decomposition is
  exact for any **invertible** matrix. ⚠️ **That word was missing here, and in `split_geometry_scale`'s
  own doc, until 2026-09-10** (§15 D714): `Orientation::to_affine`'s determinant is always ±1, so
  `orientation · diag(sx, sy)` can offer a second column of zero and nothing else once `sy` is zero,
  and a rank-1 basis has one that is not. `Basis::of` returned a plausible split for such a matrix and
  had no way to say it could not represent it, so one turn rewrote a 40×40 rect **1 unit tall at 63°**
  with every number finite. `Basis::exact` answers `None` there and on the sub-`DEGENERATE` arm, and
  every caller **refuses per node** — the member that cannot be split is left where it is and the rest
  of the gesture proceeds, which is `tools::scaled_about`'s answer to the overflow case (§9.4, §15
  D481). The same mechanism serves a multi-selection resize
  (`tools::resize_selection`, §9.4), which is where it matters most: a *selection* is exactly where
  unrelated, differently-turned layers end up together. §15 D50 has what this replaced.
- **A leaf whose geometry *is* its shape scales that geometry** (`tools::resize_geometry`): a `Line`
  or a `Path` has no authored `size` and no children, so it belongs to neither of the two paths above
  and used to fall through to `resize_group`, whose body iterates *children* and therefore produced
  an empty transaction — handles that drew, armed and did nothing (§15 D98). The scaling itself is
  `scale_geometry`'s, which can only work about the node's **origin**, and a path's box is usually
  nowhere near its origin; so the node's transform takes the correction `anchor·(1 − S)`, split by
  `split_geometry_scale` exactly as group resize splits its own, which is what keeps a mirror through
  a handle in the transform as a flip rather than in the geometry as a negative size. The routing is
  **structural** rather than a fourth list of kinds — no authored size *and* no children — so an
  empty group answers it too and gets the same nothing it always did. It is spelled once, in
  `tools::resize_layer`, which `canvas::resize_tx` and the inspector's W/H fields both call (§9.4), so
  a typed number and a dragged handle cannot come to mean two different things about the same shape.
  The kind that actually arrives here is a `Path`: a lone `Line` has endpoint handles rather than a box
  (§9.4, §15 D99) *and* no W/H fields — its own field is an `L` writing through `move_line_end` instead
  (§15 D229) — so neither route reaches it, and inside a multi-selection either
  kind goes through `resize_selection` instead.
- **A handle dragged past the corner it is anchored to flips the shape, and the flip *is* the sign of
  the scale factor.** `tools::resize_factors` hands `scale_along` a signed distance from the anchor and
  only the *magnitude* is clamped, so a negative factor reaches `split_geometry_scale`, which peels the
  reflection into the transform's `Orientation::mirror` and still hands the geometry a positive scale —
  the rule at the top of this section. Every caller of `resize_factors` used to throw that sign away, a
  `Group` included; §15 D102 has both of the places it was lost, and why fixing one of them was not
  enough.
  🚨 **The rule is unqualified and the paragraph above explains only *one* of the two resize paths,
  which is how the other went eleven months without obeying it** (§15 D753). A childless leaf with an
  authored size — a `Rect`, a `Text`, an image-filled layer — never reaches `resize_factors`: it goes
  through `tools::resized_box`, whose extent is `(at - held).abs()` and whose origin reflects the box
  across the anchor, so the box lands on the far side with **no sign left to become a mirror**. Same
  world box to the unit, `Mirror::X` against `Mirror::None`. `resized_box` now **reports** the
  crossing and `resize_to_handle` composes a reflection about the new box's own centre. ⚠️ **The
  crossing test is a sign comparison against `span - 2·held` and not `at < held`**, which is the
  neighbouring `edge` closure's question — which side of the anchor the box lies on — and agrees with
  *crossed* only for a handle on the high side; `Handle::Left` holds the **right** edge. ⚠️ Alt is the
  same rule with the centre as the anchor, and type on a rail is the one exclusion, its flip being
  §15 D406's `on_path_flip`.
- **The split must be done on the node's LOCAL transform**, after projecting back through the
  parent — never on the world matrix. Splitting in world space and projecting the result afterwards
  leaves the parent's basis wrapped round the outside of it, which puts scale back into the
  transform by another route.
- A node's own transform never holds scale, but a **world** basis can: a sheared parent with a
  turned child multiplies out to a basis with scale in it. Anything reading a world basis back
  therefore has to carry that residual rather than rebuild from the angle alone (§9.4's inspector
  does).
- A skew is also asked for directly: `Ctrl`-dragging a side of the selection box leans it, and the
  inspector has a Skew field (both §9.4). A plain resize never produces one — that is a different
  verb and has to be requested.
- **The scale tool (Figma's `K`) is built, and it does not multiply the transform either.** That was
  the design this document carried for it, and it would have broken the rule at the top of this
  section: a scale in the transform is a layer whose size is in two places. So `tools::Scaling` is
  `Geometry` — every gesture above — or `Photographic`, which is the same geometry recursion plus one
  extra step (`tools::scale_scalars`) that multiplies the *scalars* a resize deliberately leaves
  alone: stroke widths, dash patterns, per-side widths, corner radii and font size, all by the
  geometric mean of the two box factors. §9.4 has the tool and §15 D70 the reasoning, including why
  one number rather than two and why a radius is scaled from the stored radius.
- **A frame's scoped guides (§5.5) join that list, and are the one member scaled by the axis factor
  rather than by the mean.** `tools::scaled_guides`, called from `scale_scalars` so it sits behind the
  existing `Scaling` fork. The offset from a frame's origin is an absolute length, so a plain resize
  leaves it alone and a photographic scale multiplies it — a guide down the middle of a frame that
  stayed at 100 while the frame doubled to 400 would no longer be down the middle, and that is exactly
  what the Scale tool promises. But a stroke width has no direction where a guide's position is a
  coordinate on one *named* axis, so it scales the way a path's points do (a vertical guide by the x
  factor, a horizontal one by the y): the geometric mean would drift a guide off the feature it was
  placed against under any non-uniform scale.
  ⚠️ **So the call is gated on the `Scaling` fork itself and never on the mean** (§15 D694). It sat
  behind `Scaling::scalar`'s `Option` until 2026-09-09, and that answers `None` for two unrelated
  reasons — a Geometry drag, which is a resize and must leave a guide alone, and a Photographic one
  whose mean is within `SCALE_NOOP` of 1, which is a scale and must not. A photographic `(2.0, 0.5)`
  therefore scaled a 400 × 200 frame to 800 × 100 and left its centre guide at 200. Everything else in
  `scale_scalars` genuinely does not move at mean 1, so the early return is right for the rest of the
  list and was wrong for exactly this member of it.

### 5.7 Operations

```rust
pub enum Operation {
    // ids are minted by the caller (TransactionBuilder + IdSource) and carried in the op:
    CreateNode  { id: NodeId, parent: NodeId, index: usize, kind: NodeKind,
                  transform: Option<Affine>, name: Option<String> }, // None: numbered — §5.7b
    DeleteNode  { id: NodeId },                       // removes subtree
    // paste / duplicate / import — nodes arrive with freshly-minted ids, validated as a tree:
    InsertSubtree { nodes: Vec<Node>, parent: NodeId, index: usize },
    Reparent    { id: NodeId, new_parent: NodeId, index: usize },
    Reorder     { id: NodeId, index: usize },
    SetTransform{ id: NodeId, transform: Affine },
    SetGeometry { id: NodeId, geometry: GeometryPatch }, // size, corner radii, path, line end, text sizing
    SetText     { id: NodeId, content: String, spans: CharSpans, para_spans: ParaSpans },
    SetTextStyle{ id: NodeId, style: TextStyle, spans: Option<CharSpans> }, // character defaults
    SetTextSpans{ id: NodeId, spans: CharSpans },      // character overrides, content untouched
    SetParagraphStyle { id: NodeId, paragraph: ParagraphStyle, spans: Option<ParaSpans> }, // paragraph defaults
    SetParagraphSpans { id: NodeId, spans: ParaSpans },           // per-paragraph overrides
    SetBlockStyle{ id: NodeId, block: BlockStyle },    // vertical align, trim, overflow, max lines
    SetName     { id: NodeId, name: String },
    SetVisible  { id: NodeId, visible: bool },
    SetLocked   { id: NodeId, locked: bool },
    SetProportionsLocked { id: NodeId, locked: bool }, // resize holds the ratio; §5.3, not SetLocked
    SetPivot    { id: NodeId, pivot: Option<Pivot> },  // transform origin; None = the box centre, §5.3
    SetOpacity  { id: NodeId, opacity: f32 },
    SetClip     { id: NodeId, clip: bool },           // frames only; see §5.3
    SetMask     { id: NodeId, mask: bool },           // this layer masks the run above it; §5.3.
                                                      // ONE node, not a run: being masked is a fact
                                                      // about where a sibling sits, so the inverse is
                                                      // a plain SetMask back. Refused with
                                                      // WrongKindForOp on a kind that cannot be one —
                                                      // §15 D282 for why this one is refused where
                                                      // SetClip lets an inert flag sit.
    SetMaskMode { id: NodeId, mode: MaskMode },       // §5.3. NOT an argument of SetMask: the mode is
                                                      // remembered while the flag is off, so it is
                                                      // writable on a layer that is not a mask, and
                                                      // `changes_ink` is true there too — §15 D288.
    SetFillRule { id: NodeId, rule: FillRule },       // non-zero or even-odd — §15 D239. Its own op
                                                      // rather than part of a geometry patch, being a
                                                      // property of no particular kind: a Path, a
                                                      // Boolean and a frame all have an interior where
                                                      // GeometryPatch is matched against the kind.
                                                      // `changes_ink` is true — which parts of the
                                                      // shape are inside is a geometry question wearing
                                                      // a paint-shaped op — and `absorb` refuses it
                                                      // (§6.2).
    SetFills    { id: NodeId, fills: Vec<Fill> },
    SetStrokes  { id: NodeId, strokes: Vec<Stroke> },
    SetEffects  { id: NodeId, effects: Vec<Effect> },  // the whole stack — §5.3a, §15 D333. For
                                                       // SetStrokes' reason: a reorder, a removal, a
                                                       // visibility toggle and a tuned number are one
                                                       // op with one inverse. Gated on the ROOT only,
                                                       // not on takes_paint — a group has no fill and
                                                       // a blur over one is ordinary. `changes_ink`
                                                       // is true, and it is the one paint-adjacent op
                                                       // that changes ink OUTSIDE the layer it names.
    // SetArtboardBackground was here and is gone: SetFills targets a frame — §15 D400
    SetExports  { id: NodeId, exports: Vec<ExportSpec> }, // the files this layer produces — §7, §15 D274.
                                                          // The whole list, for SetStrokes' reason: a
                                                          // reorder, a removal and an edit are then one
                                                          // op with one inverse. No kind gate — "can this
                                                          // be exported" is a question about bounds, and
                                                          // `changes_ink` is false, since nothing drawn
                                                          // reads it.
    // the ops with no node to name — the ground and the guides belong to the document (§5.5):
    SetCanvasBackground { background: peniko::Color },
    AddGuide    { guide: Guide },
    RemoveGuide { id: GuideId },                      // inverts to AddGuide carrying the whole guide
    SetGuidePosition { id: GuideId, position: f64 },
    SetGuideColor    { id: GuideId, color: Option<peniko::Color> },
    SetGuideScope    { id: GuideId, owner: Option<NodeId>, position: f64 }, // both, or neither — §5.5
}

pub struct Transaction(pub Vec<Operation>);   // applied atomically = one undo entry

pub struct ApplyOutcome {
    pub inverse: Transaction,   // apply to undo
    pub dirty: DirtySet,        // the nodes the ops wrote — §5.9's `update` expands to descendants
}

pub enum OpError {
    NoSuchNode(NodeId), DuplicateId(NodeId), InvalidParent, WouldCycle, IndexOutOfRange,
    BadOpacity, BadExportSpec, WrongKindForOp, ArtboardPlacement, MalformedSubtree,
    EmptyGeometry, BooleanAbandoned,  // §15 D736 — empty is the user's to fix; abandoned is not
    NoSuchGuide(GuideId), DuplicateGuide(GuideId), BadGuideOwner(NodeId), /* ... */
}
```

- `apply` is **atomic**: validate every op against staged state; on any error mutate nothing. It buys
  that with `let mut working = self.clone();` — a whole-document clone per committed edit, and per undo
  and per redo, which go through the same function. That is O(nodes) with a small constant **and it must
  stay that way**: `ImageSource::Embedded` holds an `Arc<[u8]>` precisely so the image table is a
  refcount bump rather than a memcpy of every photograph. It was a `Vec<u8>` until 2026-08-22 and cost
  **10.2 ms per nudge at 60 MB of images**, in release (§15 D301). *Anything else large put in a
  `Document` field owes the same question before it lands there.*
- `apply` computes the inverse from pre-state (`SetTransform` inverse captures the old transform;
  `DeleteNode` inverse is an `InsertSubtree` carrying the captured nodes with their **original
  ids** at the original position — id preservation on undo falls out naturally).
- **The dirty set names the nodes the operations *wrote*, and the expansion to descendants belongs to
  `Resolved::update`** (§5.9, §15 D590). `op_set_transform` used to enumerate its own subtree into it,
  which is the same walk `update`'s `collect_subtree` performs — and the duplication cost more than a
  walk, because it left `update` unable to tell *why* a node was dirty: its text pass ran over the
  expansion, so nudging a group of twenty text blocks re-shaped all twenty for a change that cannot
  move a glyph. Four ops still dirty a subtree and each has a reason the node alone cannot carry:
  `SetClip`, `SetMask` and `SetMaskMode` change how everything under the node is *drawn*, and
  `SetGeometry` on a frame changes what its children are clipped to. The two structural ones
  (`InsertSubtree`, `DeleteNode`, and `Reparent` for both parents) enumerate what they touch because
  every one of those nodes is genuinely new, gone or moved. Everything else inserts the node it wrote,
  and its parent where the parent's union bounds move.
- Because ids ride inside ops, replaying a transaction anywhere yields the same result — the
  multiplayer-readiness property (§12). There is no id allocation inside `apply`, so no
  `RestoreSubtree` special case and no `created` back-channel: creators know the ids they minted.
  **`CreateNode { name: None }` is the one field that is resolved against the destination**: it means
  "number me among my new siblings" (§5.7b), so two replicas replaying it from diverged states agree
  on the structure and the ids and can disagree on the string. §15 D127 has why that was accepted.
- **`SetText` carries both span lists**, because a span is a byte range into the content: commit the
  string on its own and every override past the edit point describes the wrong characters. The paragraph
  list is there for the identical reason and not by analogy — a paragraph reads the value in force at its
  first byte. Styling *without* editing is `SetTextSpans` / `SetParagraphSpans` instead, so an undo of
  "make this bold" or "indent this paragraph" cannot restore different text.
- **The two *style* ops carry an optional span list, and only their inverses ever fill it in.** Setting
  the defaults re-states the overrides against them (`Spans::restated`), because a span equal to the old
  default was never stored — so an override that has just become an echo is dropped, correctly and
  invisibly. `None` asks for that re-statement and is what every forward caller passes; `Some` installs
  exactly the list given, which is how an undo puts back the span the drop removed. Without it the
  re-statement was one-way in both scopes (§15 D163).
- `SetCanvasBackground` is the exception to every "ops target a node" reading: it carries no
  `NodeId`, `op_set_canvas_background` is infallible because there is no id to miss and no kind to
  be wrong, and it dirties nothing — `Resolved` holds transforms and bounds, and neither depends on
  the colour behind the frames. Its inverse is the previous colour (§15 D28).
- The five **guide** ops are the other ops with no node to name, and they dirty nothing either: a
  guide is not rendered (§9.4), so there is no cached bound and no scene fragment to invalidate.
  They still validate like everything else — `AddGuide` refuses an id the document already has and
  the other four refuse an id it does not (`DuplicateGuide` / `NoSuchGuide`), so a whole
  transaction naming a stale guide fails atomically rather than half-applying. `RemoveGuide` inverts
  to an `AddGuide` carrying the **whole guide**, not just its position, so undoing a delete restores
  the colour the user had chosen as well as the place it sat.
- **`SetGuideScope` moves the owner and the position together because they cannot be separated.**
  `position` is *read in* the owner's space (§5.5), so a transaction that changed the owner and left
  the number would reinterpret the same coordinate in a different space — a guide 40 units down a
  frame would mean 40 units down the canvas for as long as the intermediate state lasted, and the
  inverse would be built from that state. It inverts to itself carrying the old pair, so dragging a
  guide across a frame's boundary is one undo step and the return trip is exact.
- **`AddGuide` and `SetGuideScope` both validate the owner** (`BadGuideOwner`, §5.5), and that check is
  what makes **op order inside a delete transaction load-bearing**: `apply` inverts a transaction by
  reversing it, so a transaction that deleted a frame *before* removing its guides would invert to
  `[AddGuide, InsertSubtree]` — the guide re-added while its owner is still missing, which the check
  refuses, failing the whole undo. Guides first, therefore, which is what `build::guides_of` documents
  and `app.rs::delete_selection` does; `undoing_a_frame_delete_restores_its_guides` asserts **both**
  orders, because the wrong one deletes perfectly well and only breaks Ctrl+Z.
  - ⚠️ **Naming an owner is not the only way to break the rule, and the other way is answered by a
    post-condition rather than by an operation** (§15 D491). `op_delete` never looked at `self.guides`,
    so a `DeleteNode` on a guide-owning frame was accepted and the file it saved never loaded again.
    `apply` now re-checks every guide's owner **after the last op and before `*self = working`** — over
    the whole guide list rather than the ops, because the rule is about the document. The position is
    the whole of the design: a per-op check would refuse a transaction that ends up **correct**, since
    the guides-first order never holds an orphan while frame-then-guides passes through one on its way
    to a valid document. That reverse order is legal, is what a caller might write, and is exactly the
    transaction `undoing_a_frame_delete_restores_its_guides` commits as its "wrong" order — wrong only
    for the undo.
    `deleting_a_frame_that_owns_a_guide_is_refused_or_still_loads` asserts the **round trip**
    rather than the error, so a future spelling that corrupts differently still fails it, and it
    carries the `guides_of` order as its control: a refusal that also refuses the correct spelling
    would be worthless.
- **`SetExports` bounds the values it stores** (`BadExportSpec`, §7, §15 D492) — a scale that cannot be
  a size and a `quality` outside `1..=100` are refused rather than written. A `Width(0)` that reaches
  the document becomes a row the panel offers, a filename asserting zero pixels, and a 1 × 1 file with
  nothing on it or in the exit code to say it was wrong. `document::export_spec_is_usable` is the
  predicate, and it is the same rule `ExportScale::from_label` and the CLI's parse were already
  applying to a *string*. The loader answers the same question by **dropping** the row (§5.11): the app
  should never author one, and a file that carries one should still open.
- **`Operation::changes_ink` classifies an op by whether applying it changes what is *drawn*** — the
  artwork, not the chrome round it — and `Transaction::changes_ink` is **any** of its ops, not all,
  since a transaction that moves a layer *and* renames it has a visible result. Exactly **eleven**
  answer `false`: `SetName`, `SetLocked`, `SetProportionsLocked`, `SetPivot`, `SetExports`,
  `SetLayoutGrids` and the five guide ops, and every one of them
  is **a no-op in `RenderOverrides::absorb`** (§6.2), deliberately — "the renderer
  has nothing to do with this" and "this changes nothing drawn" are one fact asked by two callers. Not
  one function, because `absorb` also has to separate the *patchable* ops from the structural ones and
  this question does not. ⚠️ **It is a subset and not an equality, and this bullet said *"the same
  eleven … if the two lists ever disagree, one of them is wrong"* until 2026-09-09** (§15 D659):
  `absorb` has a **second** no-op arm further down the same `match`, `AddImage | RemoveImage`, so its
  no-ops are **thirteen**. The two image ops answer `true` here and are absorbed there because
  `RenderOverrides` has no image table to patch — *"cannot preview this"* rather than *"nothing to
  preview"* — which is written out at both ends. That matters beyond tidiness:
  `EditorSession::has_gesture_preview` is `!overrides.is_empty() && …`, so **every** transaction
  `absorb` no-ops is invisible to `cancel_gesture`'s gate, and a repair list for that has to be derived
  from `absorb` rather than from this list. `[A7-L8-04]` certified the equality by hand-counting the
  first arm alone. The `match` is
  wildcard-free so a new op stops the build here, and
  `op::changes_ink_tests::only_the_chrome_operations_change_no_ink` pins the set as a list,
  because a stopped build does not stop its author picking the wrong arm. The caller is the selection
  chrome's edit-time hide (§9.4, §15 D128). ⚠️ **This count has now been wrong here twice, in two
  directions of the same mistake**: it said nine — here, in the test's own doc and in the test's
  fixture — until 2026-08-24, having missed `SetExports` when that op arrived, and then said ten until
  2026-09-07, having missed `SetLayoutGrids` the same way. The drift the list exists to catch, twice,
  inside the thing that catches it. **Recount every copy against the `match` when an operation is
  added**; no gate reads a number in prose, and the only copy any gate reads is the fixture's
  `assert_eq!(invisible.len(), 11)` (§15 D336). ⚠️ **The count is now written in five places and has
  gone stale in three of them**, which is D336's own closing advice arriving for the second time: if it
  moves again, prefer *deleting* the number to updating it and let the fixture be the record.
- **`Operation::changes_nothing(&self, doc)` asks whether applying it would leave the document exactly
  as it stands, and `Transaction::changes_nothing` is *all* of its ops, not any** (§15 D428). The
  transaction is the unit because a *Hide* over a mixed selection is a `SetVisible` per layer, the
  already-hidden ones individually no-ops and the whole hiding something — so a per-op filter would
  drop operations out of a step whose inverse then puts back a different set. It is sound to ask each
  op about the document as it stands rather than about what its predecessors would leave, because if
  every predecessor changes nothing then that *is* the document it would see. This `match` is
  wildcard-free too, and **`false` is the safe answer**: a wrong `true` silently drops an edit, where a
  wrong `false` only commits an undo step nobody wanted. A missing subject and the kind gates `apply`
  enforces both answer `false`, so a commit that would have *failed* still fails and still reports;
  equality is of the **value written**, so `-0.0` equals `0.0` and `NaN` equals nothing, which keeps a
  non-finite operation reaching `NonFinite` (§15 D421). An **empty** transaction answers `false` — that
  is the committer's separate question (§9.3). The caller is `EditorSession::commit_inner`.
- Grouping/ungrouping are composite transactions (§5.7a), not dedicated ops.
- Validation rejects: cycles, a frame parented by a group, out-of-range indices, unknown ids, duplicate ids,
  malformed subtrees, opacity out of range, ops applied to an unsupporting `NodeKind`.
- `InsertSubtree` validates the *whole* subtree, not just its root: every internal parent/child
  pair goes through the same kind rules as `CreateNode`, no node may be a second `Root`, no node
  may be listed as a child twice, and opacities must be in range. It is the op paste, undo-of-
  delete, import and (later) MCP write tools all funnel through, so anything it lets past becomes
  a corrupt document that the tree walks then have to survive.

### 5.7a Composite builders & the world-space facade (`build.rs`)

Users and agents think in world space and in whole intents ("group these", "put it here"); the
model stores local transforms and primitive operations. `build.rs` is the single translation
layer, and it lives in core — not the app — because the UI, MCP write tools, and the future
command line (§13) all need the identical projections, and a second copy would drift.

```rust
pub fn local_for_world(doc, res, id, world: Affine) -> Affine;      // the one world→local conversion
pub fn place_at_world(doc, res, id, world) -> Result<Transaction>;  // §8.4's adapter
pub fn move_by_world(doc, res, ids, delta) -> Result<Transaction>;
pub fn reparent_preserving_world(doc, res, id, new_parent, index) -> Result<Transaction>;
pub fn group(doc, ids: &mut IdSource, members) -> Result<(Transaction, NodeId)>;
pub fn mask(doc, ids, members, key: Option<NodeId>) -> Result<(Transaction, NodeId)>; // wraps 2+ in a
                                              // group, flags one as the mask; returns what to select
pub fn ungroup(doc, id) -> Result<Transaction>;
pub fn ungroup_all(doc, ids) -> Result<Transaction>;  // several, ONE tx — simulated, not concatenated
pub fn outermost(doc, ids) -> Vec<NodeId>;   // members with no ancestor in the set
pub fn guides_of(doc, ids) -> Vec<Operation>; // the RemoveGuides a delete owes — FIRST in the tx, §5.7
pub fn image_ids_in(nodes: &[Node]) -> Vec<ImageId>;  // sorted, unique, hidden fills included
pub fn missing_image_ops(doc, held: &[(ImageId, ImageEntry)]) -> Vec<Operation>; // AddImage for what
                                              // this document lacks — FIRST in the tx, §5.5a

// bulk property edits over a selection — the apply-once rule for *properties*
pub fn subtree_nodes(doc, ids) -> Vec<NodeId>;               // outermost, then each subtree in full
pub struct ColorUse { pub color: Color, pub uses: usize, pub nodes: Vec<NodeId> } // slots, then layers
pub fn colors_in(doc, ids) -> Vec<ColorUse>;                 // distinct solids, most-used first
pub struct PaintAt { pub node: NodeId, pub target: PaintTarget, pub index: usize } // two lists, an index
pub struct GradientUse { pub brush: Brush, pub uses: usize, pub nodes: Vec<NodeId>, pub at: PaintAt }
pub fn gradients_in(doc, ids) -> Vec<GradientUse>;           // the same census over the ramps
pub fn paint_at(doc, at: PaintAt) -> Option<Brush>;          // the brush in one place
pub fn recolor(doc, ids, from: Color, to: Color) -> Transaction;      // by exact RGBA bytes
pub fn repaint(doc, ids, from: &Brush, to: &Brush) -> Transaction;    // by whole brush — not the same
pub enum PaintTarget { Fill, Stroke }
pub fn paint_targets(doc, ids) -> Vec<NodeId>;               // through a group, stopping AT a frame
pub enum PaintShown<T> { List(Vec<T>), Mixed }               // ::list / ::is_mixed / ::unpainted
pub fn shared_fills(doc, ids) -> PaintShown<Fill>;           // the whole list, or a disagreement
pub fn shared_strokes(doc, ids) -> PaintShown<Stroke>;
pub fn shared_over_fills<T>(doc, ids, of: impl Fn(&Fill) -> T) -> Option<T>;   // over *every* paint
pub fn shared_over_strokes<T>(doc, ids, of: impl Fn(&Stroke) -> T) -> Option<T>;
pub fn edit_fills_all(doc, ids, edit: impl Fn(&mut Fill)) -> Transaction;      // in place, each list
pub fn edit_strokes_all(doc, ids, edit: impl Fn(&mut Stroke)) -> Transaction;  // keeping its own shape
pub fn set_fills_all(doc, ids, fills: &[Fill]) -> Transaction;        // exactly this list, to each
pub fn set_strokes_all(doc, ids, strokes: &[Stroke]) -> Transaction;
pub fn set_opacity_all(doc, ids, opacity) -> Transaction;    // outermost only — opacity composes
pub fn set_corner_radius_all(doc, ids, radius) -> Transaction;    // subtree — a radius does not
pub fn shared_corner_radius(doc, ids) -> Option<f64>;        // agrees to RADIUS_AGREEMENT, not ==
pub const OPACITY_AGREEMENT: f32;   // how near two values a readout calls them one — the panel's
pub const RADIUS_AGREEMENT: f64;    // own `_shown` twins read these two, D607
pub fn any_rect_in(doc, ids) -> bool;
pub fn any_paint_in(doc, ids) -> bool;                       // asked of the Stroke panel too — D400
pub struct Properties { pub fills: Vec<Fill>, pub strokes: Vec<Stroke>, pub opacity: f32 } // appearance
pub fn properties_of(node: &Node) -> Option<Properties>;     // None for a group — none to give
pub fn paste_properties(doc, ids, props) -> Transaction;     // the three set_*_all above, composed

pub fn align(doc, res, ids, target: Rect, axis, edge) -> Transaction;
pub fn distribute(doc, res, ids, axis) -> Transaction;  // equal gaps — but never a reorder, so an
                                                    // overlapping set gets even *leads* instead, D487
pub fn flip(doc, res, ids, axis) -> Transaction;    // mirror across the union's centreline — or a
                                                    // single layer's pivot, if one has been placed
pub fn z_order(doc, ids, mv: ZMove) -> Transaction;
pub fn skew_x(radians: f64) -> Affine;   // skewX: +x displaced in proportion to +y
pub fn skew_y(radians: f64) -> Affine;   // skewY: the gesture on a vertical edge, said directly
pub struct Orientation { pub angle: f64, pub skew: f64, pub mirror: Mirror } // ::of / ::to_affine
pub struct Basis { pub orientation: Orientation, pub scale: Vec2 }           // ::of(Affine)
```

Two properties every one of these upholds, both of which a naive implementation gets wrong:

- **A structural edit must not move anything on screen.** Plain `Reparent` keeps the *local*
  transform, so it teleports the node by the difference between the two parents. `group`,
  `ungroup` and `reparent_preserving_world` all re-project.
