- **An edit must apply to a node exactly once.** When a multi-selection contains both a group and
  something inside it, operating on each independently moves the inner node twice. `outermost`
  filters covered descendants and every multi-node *transform* builder routes through it.

**And a builder that dissolves *several* containers simulates rather than concatenating**
(§15 D521). `ungroup_all` is `ungroup` in a loop over a `Document` **clone advanced by each
transaction as it is built**, because `ungroup` reads the container's own position among its parent's
children: the second container's index is measured against a child list the first one's ops have
already spliced, and a container nested inside an earlier one has a different parent and a different
local transform by the time its turn comes. That is the rule `layers::plan_layer_move` and
`insert_subtrees` already follow, paying a whole `Document` clone rather than a map of child lists
because an ungroup rewrites transforms as well as parentage; the clone is skipped for the
single-container case, which is every ungroup but a multi-selection. ⚠️ **Concatenating against the
original does not merely interleave, and the obvious assertion cannot see it**: measured, the second
container's children land at stale indices *inside* the run the first splice made and the last child
is pushed off the end, while **every world position is still right**, because the wrong indices still
name the right parent.

**A property edit needs the same rule read differently, and that is what `subtree_nodes` is.**
`outermost` alone is the wrong filter for a colour: it hands back the group, which has no paint of
its own (§5.3), and the shapes the user can plainly see inside it go unchanged. So the members are
reduced to the outermost ones first — that is what stops a node selected alongside its own ancestor
being visited twice — and then each of those subtrees is walked in full. The walk is a deterministic
pre-order with children pushed in reverse so they pop in document order, because an operation list
has to replay identically on another replica (§12) and so cannot depend on the order a `HashSet`
felt like iterating in. ⚠️ **The *roots* are ordered too, and were not until 2026-09-09** (§15 D646):
pre-order within one subtree was never the whole claim, since `outermost` returns its members in
**input order**, so a multi-root scope came back in whatever order the caller held it — pick order,
for every panel that passes a selection. They go through `all_in_document_order` first, and **only
when there is more than one**, that being the only case it can matter and a whole-document walk being
what it costs. `set_opacity_all` is the deliberate exception that proves the pair are
different questions: opacity **composes** down the tree, so setting 50% on a group and on each of
its children lands at 25%, and it therefore takes `outermost`. A corner radius does not compose, so
`set_corner_radius_all` takes the subtree.

**How near two values have to be for a readout to call them one lives here too, and that is what
`OPACITY_AGREEMENT` and `RADIUS_AGREEMENT` are** (§15 D607). A second copy of that rule is exactly
what went wrong: core compared both with `==` while `inspector.rs` used `< 1e-6` and `< 1e-9`, and
**only the panel's copy ever ran**, so the tested rule was one no user could reach. The two numbers
differ on purpose — an opacity field formats as `{v:.0}%`, so a part in a million is the same number
on screen, where a radius is a length in document units and a billionth of one is below anything a
drag or a parser can author. There is no `shared_opacity` here any more; it had no caller anywhere in
the tree, tests included, and the readout is `inspector::shared_opacity_shown` alone.

`colors_in` is the census behind both the Group Colors panel and the picker's document-palette chips
— the same question asked of a selection and of the root, which is why it lives here rather than in
either panel (`picker::document_palette` is now a call to it with the root as its scope, where it
used to be a second implementation nothing in this document mentioned). **The scope is the caller's,
and the panel's is not simply the selection**: a single selected container is the box the question is
asked *about* rather than part of the answer, so the panel passes its children (§9.4, §15 D401), while
the chips pass the root and are unaffected. **Solids only**, because that is
what `recolor` can act on: a gradient is not one colour, so a row claiming it was `#EB6E5A` would
recolour something the user never pointed at. **`gradients_in` is its twin over exactly the paints it
leaves out**, keyed by the whole `Brush` — a gradient's identity is its stops *and* its geometry, so two
ramps of the same colours at different angles are two gradients and merging them would report a count no
selection could match. Both are thin wrappers over one private `census(doc, ids, key)`: one walk with a
key function rather than one function per key, because the two answers have to agree about which paints
and which layers they found and in what order, and the layer-dedupe rule is the fiddly part of that.

**A gradient row is keyed by a place, so the census reports one.** `PaintAt { node, target, index }` is
`Copy + Eq` and small enough for a UI slot to carry where a whole `Brush` is not (§9.4). **Two lists and
an index, on every kind**: a frame used to need the caveat that its one background answered to *fill 0*,
and that went with the field it was about (§15 D400). `census` keeps the **first** place each
entry was met and does not update it on later hits, because first is what is stable to name;
`GradientUse::at` carries it and `ColorUse` ignores it, a colour being a key already. `paint_at` reads the
brush at a location and answers `None` when the place has gone, which is what tells a slot pointing at it
to close. `repaint` then changes every use of a whole brush — **not** a generalisation of `recolor`, which
matches the exact RGBA *bytes* the colour census keys by: two match rules for two keys, and folding them
together would make one of the two kinds of row disagree with its own edit (§15 D135).
**Hidden paints are counted**, because a recolour that skipped them would let
the old colour reappear the moment the fill was switched back on. `recolor` matches on the exact RGBA
bytes `colors_in` counts by, so what the panel lists and what the edit changes cannot disagree.
`ColorUse` carries **both** numbers a caller can want: `uses` counts paint slots and `nodes` the
distinct layers, in document order. **The layer a row names is the node the paint sits on**, never its
container — so a frame's own ground names the frame and nothing inside it, which is what would be wrong
if the census ever walked a frame's contents into the frame's row
(`a_frames_background_names_the_frame_as_its_layer`, which asserted nothing at all from D400 until §15
D480). They are not the same number — a shape whose fill and stroke share
a colour is two uses and one layer — and `nodes` is carried out of the one census walk rather than
re-derived, since the panel would otherwise walk the tree again per row per frame to answer a question
this walk already had in hand (§9.2, §15 D71). It is what cost `ColorUse` its `Copy`.

**Paint has its own walk, `paint_targets`, and the rule it encodes is that a group is organisation
while a frame is a thing.** A group has no paint of its own and exists to hold layers together, so a
paint edit passes straight through it — and through the root — to the shapes inside; a frame is
*rendered*, its background and properties are its own and its contents are *its* contents, so the
walk stops **at** the frame and takes the frame as the target. Setting a fill over a selected frame
colours the frame, not everything in it. This is deliberately not `subtree_nodes`, which remains
right for the census: "what colours are in here" does mean everything inside a frame, while "paint
these" does not. ⚠️ **That is a statement about the walk and not about the Group Colors panel's
scope, and the two were confused in the code until 2026-09-01**: `subtree_nodes` from a frame does
reach everything inside it, and what changed is that the panel no longer starts the walk *at* the
selected frame (§9.4, §15 D401). The census function is unchanged. Frames cannot sit inside groups
(`can_parent`), so no frame is ever reached by
passing through one — and a frame *inside a frame* is not reached either, because the walk stops at
the outer one (§15 D62).

**One layer's appearance is liftable, and `Properties` is the three fields that means.** Fills,
strokes and opacity — the payload behind *Copy properties* / *Paste properties* (`shortcuts.md` §7,
`context-menus.md` §3). Position, size, rotation, the name, the pivot and the lock are excluded
because they say *which layer this is* rather than how it is drawn, and geometry is excluded for a
second reason: a corner radius lives in `NodeKind`, so it would be a per-kind bridge rather than a
field (§15 D257). `properties_of` **refuses a group** rather than answering with an empty list, which
is `paint_targets`' own distinction — an empty appearance is a well-formed payload that *clears*
whatever it lands on. It asks one predicate to decide that; it asked two while a frame was not
`takes_paint`, and lifting the appearance off a two-fill frame now carries both fills (§15 D400). `paste_properties` is not a fourth walk: it is `set_fills_all`,
`set_strokes_all` and `set_opacity_all` composed, so the fills and strokes reach through a group and
stop at a frame while the opacity goes to the outermost members alone, and the row's scope is the two
rules this section already states rather than a third. Each of the three skips the targets that
already agree, so pasting an appearance a layer already has is an empty transaction and no undo step.

**What is shared is the whole list, not the first brush.** `shared_fills` and `shared_strokes` answer
with the `Vec<Fill>` / `Vec<Stroke>` every target agrees on, so two layers that
both start red but differ in their second fill do **not** share a fill list — a panel claiming they
did would delete one of them on the next edit. `set_fills_all` and `set_strokes_all` give every
target *exactly* the list, which is what keeps the reading believable: what was shown is then true of
all of them.

**Any disagreement at all is `Mixed`, and the only empty panel is one where nothing in scope is
painted.** `paint_shown` returns `Mixed` the moment two targets differ and needs no second pass to
check whether they are all painted: empty lists are all equal to each other, so reaching a
disagreement at all proves something in scope has a paint for the stand-in row to stand for. It went
the other way first — an unpainted target among painted ones fell back to the empty state, on the
reading that a stand-in needs *every* target to have something behind it — and that was reported
straight back, because it is the commonest disagreement there is: one layer with a stroke and one
without came out as "No stroke", which is false of half the selection and false in the direction that
matters, since the stroke it denied is the one on screen (§15 D53). What a mixed row then
says is asked property by property — `shared_over_fills` / `shared_over_strokes` fold a getter over
**every paint of every target** rather than one row of each, which is what lets a selection that
disagrees about how many fills it has still report the colour they share, and in which **a target with
no paint disagrees with every value** rather than being skipped: a layer with no stroke has not got the
other one's 4pt weight, so that selection reads mixed in every property at once instead of reporting
the lone stroke's numbers as shared. Absence is a value here, and the only one that agrees with
nothing. What the row writes is
`edit_fills_all` / `edit_strokes_all`, an **in-place** edit that leaves each target its own list
length, order and untouched properties. That is the non-destructive half of the bulk paint API and the
whole reason a mixed row is a property editor rather than an overwrite (§9.4, §15 D53). A frame takes
that edit like anything else, and used to fork on the kind and pull only the *brush* back out of the
stand-in its background read as — that stand-in carried no `visible` flag, so "hide every fill in the
selection" silently skipped the frames in it (§15 D400).

**A frame's fills are its fill list, and no verb here needs a case of its own for them** (§15 D400).
`paint_targets` is the one scope, for fills and strokes alike: a `strokeable_targets` filter sat
between it and `shared_strokes` / `shared_over_strokes` / `edit_strokes_all` / `set_strokes_all` while
a frame could be stroked and not filled, and it went with the `takes_stroke` that was the whole of that
difference (§5.3), as did the `any_strokeable_in` the app hid the Stroke panel by. `shared_fills`,
`set_fills_all` and `edit_fills_all` read and write `Node::paint().fills` on a frame exactly as on a
rectangle — which is what lets one gesture fill the frames and the shapes in a mixed selection, and
what the inspector has drawn under a single *Fill* header since §15 D397 — while `shared_strokes` and
`set_strokes_all` have reached a frame's outline since it grew one (§15 D144).
⚠️ **The known limitation this passage carried is gone with the field it was about**: a frame held one
background rather than a list, so on a shared list of two the frame took the first while the shapes got
both. It takes the whole list. **Gone with it is `build::fills_seen_as`**, the `pub` mapping that
presented the one background as a one-entry list so the app's `DisplayNode` — a node plus a live
gesture's overrides, and not a `Node` — could be asked what the committed tree was asked; it is
`paint.fills.clone()` once a frame keeps a real list, so its six callers read the field.

The other `shared_*` reads answer with the value when every node in scope agrees and `None` when they
do not. Every one of these emits **one** transaction
(invariant 5) and every one skips no-op writes, so a field that loses focus without having been
edited produces nothing rather than an undo step made entirely of writes that change nothing.

`Basis` and `Orientation` belong here for the same reason: `transform` may carry a reflection and a
skew (§5.6), and reading rotation back as `atan2(b, a)` is wrong about both. A mirrored basis has a
negative determinant, so the bare angle is nonsense and rebuilding the transform from it silently
drops the mirror; a sheared basis' second column is not square to its first, so a rebuild from the
angle throws the lean away as well. `Basis::of` is the one place the decomposition is written —
`Orientation::of` is `Basis::of(t).orientation`, the inspector's rotation and skew fields go through
it, and so must anything else that round-trips an angle.

**The split is RQ, by Gram–Schmidt**: every invertible 2×2 factors *uniquely* as
`R(θ) · skewX(k) · mirror · diag(sx, sy)` — four parameters for a four-coefficient matrix, so it is
exact for any matrix a well-behaved editor produces and for any a foreign file brings in, provided it
has four *independent* coefficients. That exactness is the property everything else leans on: it is
what lets a world-space edit be pushed onto a node whatever its parents have done to it, instead of
being approximated (§15 D50).
🚨 **This sentence used to drop the qualifier in its second clause — *"so it is exact for any matrix
whatsoever"* — and the code was faithful to that** (§15 D714). It is the one place where the correct
premise and the wrong conclusion sit in one sentence, which is why it is worth spelling out: the four
parameters only span the space when the matrix is invertible. `Orientation::to_affine`'s determinant
is always ±1, so `orientation · diag(sx, sy)` can offer a second column of **zero** and nothing else
once `sy` is zero, and a rank-1 basis — `[1, 2, 2, 4]`, whose second column is `(2, 4)` — has no
exact split at all. **`Basis::of` is total and lossy; `Basis::exact` is partial and exact**, answering
`None` for a rank-1 basis and for one under `DEGENERATE`, and the choice between them is whether the
caller is *reporting* a basis or *rewriting* one. The inspector's angle and scale readouts want a
number for a collapsed node — 0° rather than a blank — and are `of`'s reason to stay total.
⚠️ **Two of them rewrite and are not yet converted**: `inspector::multi_angle_tx` and the skew half of
`inspector::inspector_transform` rebuild a whole transform from `of`'s split and commit it through
`build::place_at_world`, which never reaches `split_geometry_scale`'s guard. D714 has the fix and why
it is a UI ruling rather than a one-line change. `Basis`
keeps the residual `scale`, always non-negative, since the sign of a reflection stays in
`Orientation::mirror`; the transform then takes the `Orientation` and the node's geometry takes the
`scale`. `skew` is in radians in `(-π/2, π/2)` with SVG/CSS `skewX` semantics — the matrix
coefficient is `tan(skew)`, displacing +x in proportion to +y, which in the document's y-down space
leans the *bottom* of a shape to the right. That convention was picked so the SVG writer needs no
sign fixing, and it is verified end to end: a 25° skew emits `matrix(1 0 0.4663 1 …)`.

`R(θ)·FLIP_Y` and `R(θ+π)·FLIP_X` are the *same* reflection, so `of` reports whichever axis leaves
the smaller angle: flipping an upright layer vertically must not make the inspector claim it is
rotated −180°. The skew is the same in both readings, so admitting one does not disturb that rule.

### 5.7b Layer names (`naming.rs`)

Four things generate a name and nothing else does: **creation**, **duplication**, a boolean's
label following a change of operation (§9.4), and an image layer's `"Image N"` — which is the one of
the four core does not resolve, for the reason the `Some` bullet below gives. Everything else that
writes a name is the user typing one. The rule behind all of it: the app owns the names it generated, the user owns the names they
typed.

- **`CreateNode { name: None }` means "number me among my new siblings."** `Document::op_create`
  resolves it through `naming::created_name` against `Document::child_names(parent, except)`, so
  three rectangles drawn in one frame read "Rectangle 1", "Rectangle 2", "Rectangle 3". **Every
  generated name carries a number, the first one included** — a bare "Rectangle" beside a
  "Rectangle 2" reads as though the first were somehow special, and it costs the layers panel its
  symmetry for nothing. The number taken is the **first free** one rather than the next after the
  highest, so deleting "Rectangle 2" hands that name to the next rectangle. Neither needs stored
  state: both are read back out of the names present, where a per-kind counter would have to be saved
  and one that is not saved resets silently on reload.
  ⚠️ **That resolution is what makes a bulk create quadratic, and it is the binding cost of a large
  paste** (§15 D446). `child_names` walks every sibling into a fresh set once per child created, so
  applying *n* children to one parent is Θ(n²): a 32,000-shape SVG is **38 ms of import and 62.6 s of
  `Document::apply`**, on the egui UI thread. Recorded rather than fixed — the chokepoint *is* the
  per-parent rule below, so removing the scan is a decision about names and not a repair; it is open in
  `roadmap.md` under *Per-edit cost*.
  ⚠️ **The search wraps to 1 at `u32::MAX` rather than running off the end** (`naming::free_name`,
  §15 D433). That is belt-and-braces for a *create*, whose `from` is always 1, and load-bearing for a
  **copy**, whose `from` is parsed out of a string the user typed: a layer renamed
  `Rectangle 4294967295` and duplicated needed one iteration to overflow — a panic out of core on the
  UI thread in debug, and in release a `Rectangle 0`, which is a name `numbered` refuses to parse.
  Wrapping is `created_name`'s own rule and keeps the answer inside the series; the line past it
  answers a *duplicate* name, which is legal here, rather than one the parser rejects.
- **Numbering is per parent.** Document-wide numbering yields "Rectangle 137" in a large file for no
  benefit, and names repeating across parents is already an accepted state — the layers panel shows
  ancestor rows for a search hit precisely so one can be located (§9.2).
- **A builder that wants a specific name passes `Some`,** and inside core only two do: the body
  `build::flatten` and `build::outline` share carries the layer's own name across (a flattened
  "Subtract 1" is still the subtract the user built, and an outlined "Badge" is still the badge), and
  `flatten`'s union arm numbers the result against the siblings that *survive*
  its own deletes. Everything else passes `None` — **including every layer of the starter document**. Its
  frame was `Some("Frame")` and its text layer `Some("Heading")`, and each was then the one layer of its
  kind in the app whose name did not match what the tool makes; both are numbered now, "Frame 1" and
  "Text 1" (§15 D127). **The app adds one more**, and it is the only generated name resolved outside
  core: an image layer is named by `canvas::image_layer_name` before `tools::create_image` builds the
  transaction, because `None` here would be resolved against the *kind* and an image is a Rect (§15
  D187). `"Image"` is deliberately absent from `GENERATED_NAMES` for the same reason — that list is the
  inverse of `default_name` and a stem no kind produces would make it a lie.
- **A duplicate keeps a typed name and increments a numbered one** — "Badge" copies as "Badge",
  "Rectangle 2" as "Rectangle 3". Decided from the string by `naming::copy_name`, never from a
  stored "this one is automatic" bit. `build::CopyNames` holds the answers and emits a `SetName` for
  the **copied root only**, because a duplicated group's children are unique within the *new* group,
  which is what per-parent numbering means. It is an accumulator rather than a plain function
  because several copies in one transaction cannot see each other in the document — nothing has been
  applied yet — and both copy paths keep one: `insert_subtrees` (paste, `Ctrl`+`D`) and the
  Alt-drag's `canvas::clone_tx`, which builds its own `InsertSubtree`.
- **The strict test and the loose one are different questions and must not be unified.**
  `naming::generated_stem` / `is_boolean_label` ask "is this a string we would have written", which
  is what `build::set_boolean_op` needs before overwriting a name (§9.4): getting it wrong renames a
  layer the user named. `copy_name` asks only whether a name *looks* numbered, and its false
  positive is benign — "Badge 2" duplicated as "Badge 3" is what was wanted.
- **A name has to be one there is something to show, and that is `naming::usable`** (§15 D644). It
  trims, answers `None` when nothing is left, and turns every interior whitespace character into one
  ordinary space; runs are *not* collapsed, because "Hello   World" is what somebody typed. Both
  rename fields had always refused an empty name — the layers panel's (§15 D54) and the inspector's,
  which carries the reason: two surfaces for one edit have to agree on what a name is. **SVG import
  was a third door and agreed with neither**, installing `""` and `"   "` verbatim for a layers row
  with no label at all, so `svg_in::element_name` asks this now. ⚠️ **`None` rather than a repaired
  string is the point at that site**: `op_create` turns it into a generated name, which is what an
  element carrying no `id` already gets. ⚠️ **One home and two copies**: the two fields still
  hand-roll `trim`/`is_empty`, so this is where the rule is *written* and not yet where it is
  enforced.
- **Uniqueness is never load-bearing.** Nothing in the workspace resolves a node *by* name; every
  lookup is by `NodeId`, and §13 states outright that a name is a disambiguated fallback. So
  reparenting a layer into a parent that already holds its name collides and renames nothing, and
  the numbering is a courtesy rather than an invariant (§15 D127).
  ⚠️ **That is exactly why the SVG writer puts a name in `data-name` and never in `id`** (§7, §15
  D611). An `id` must be unique in its document and must be an XML `Name`; "Rectangle 1" is neither.
  The one place a name generated here leaves the document is therefore also the one place that would
  have had to sanitise and uniquify it, and nothing in this section is prepared to promise either.

### 5.8 History

```rust
pub struct History { undo: Vec<Transaction>, redo: Vec<Transaction>, run: Option<Shape> }
```

- `commit(doc, tx)`: `out = doc.apply(&tx)?; undo.push(out.inverse); redo.clear();`
- `undo`/`redo`: pop, apply, push the returned inverse to the other stack — symmetric, no special
  cases, because `apply` always returns the inverse.
- **`redo.clear()` is what stops a redo being applied to a document that has moved on since the undo.**
  Commit A, undo it, commit B, press redo: without it the stack still holds the transaction that redoes
  A, so a `SetTransform` re-writes a stale value *and* pushes its own inverse, leaving a step the user
  never made (§15 D480, `a_new_commit_drops_the_redo_stack`).
- **`run` is the merge window `commit_into_run` folds into**, and what it holds is the **shape** of the
  last commit: one `Operation::shape_key` per operation, which is the operation's variant, the *field*
  inside it where the payload names one, and the subject. A merge is refused unless the shapes are
  equal, because keeping the older inverse only restores both edits if the second overwrote exactly what
  the first did. ⚠️ **The field is part of the key and has to be** (§15 D482): a discriminant names the
  variant, which is the field set for 22 of the 23 overwriting operations and is not for `SetGeometry`,
  whose payload is itself a field selector — a size edit and a corner-radius edit on one node merged, and
  one undo restored the size and stranded the radius with an empty stack. **And `shape_key` is not
  `Operation::overwrites`**, which answers *"which node does this operation write"* for two app callers
  and `None` for every guide operation: `SetGuidePosition` keys a run here, so a held arrow key on a
  guide is one undo step, and a guide is still not a node anywhere else.
- ⚠️ **No structural command can use the run at all**, and that is a property of `shape` rather than a
  policy: a merge is refused unless the shape exists, and `shape` needs `overwrites()` on **every**
  operation, which is `None` for `Reparent`, `DeleteNode` and `CreateNode`. So an ungroup, a paste and
  an image drop have to fold their parts into **one** transaction *before* committing — the run cannot
  fold them afterwards, and *"use `commit_run`"* is never the answer for a verb that changes the shape
  of the tree (§9.3, §15 D521, D522).
- **The three things that end a run** are a
  plain `commit`, `end_run()` — the caller's half of the policy — and **an undo or a redo**. The last is
  load-bearing in both directions: an undo that left the shape standing lets the next edit fold into the
  step *before* the undone one and discard its own inverse, and `redo`'s copy sits **before** its `pop`,
  which is the whole of what that copy does — a redo press with *nothing to redo* still ends the run
  (§15 D480, which pins each and has why the third is otherwise unreachable).
- History lives in core and is shared by app and MCP: one timeline, AI edits and user edits
  interleave in it and both undo through it.
- Unlimited depth in v1; `DeleteNode` inverses hold full subtrees, so a size/entry cap is a known
  future knob (park).

### 5.9 Resolved (derived layer)

```rust
pub struct Resolved {
    world: FxHashMap<NodeId, Affine>,
    world_bounds: FxHashMap<NodeId, Rect>,   // stroke-expanded, world space
    ink_bounds: FxHashMap<NodeId, Rect>,     // world_bounds grown by the effect stack — see below
    inner_ink: FxHashMap<NodeId, Rect>,      // ink_bounds BEFORE this node's own effects escape (§15 D341)
    text: FxHashMap<NodeId, TextLayout>,     // parley layouts, invalidated via DirtySet
    boolean: FxHashMap<NodeId, BezPath>,     // combined outline per Boolean node, its own local space
    failed: FxHashSet<NodeId>,               // booleans whose arithmetic was abandoned (§15 D239)
    index: rstar::RTree<BoundsEntry>,        // leaves = paintable nodes
}
impl Resolved {
    pub fn rebuild(doc: &Document) -> Self;
    pub fn update(&mut self, doc: &Document, dirty: &DirtySet);
    pub fn ink_bounds(&self, id: NodeId) -> Option<Rect>;
    pub fn text_layout(&self, id: NodeId) -> Option<&TextLayout>;
    pub fn invalidate_text(&mut self, doc: &Document);
    pub fn mask_path(&self, doc: &Document, id: NodeId) -> Option<BezPath>; // in the PARENT's space
}
```

- ⚠️ **Six maps, a set and an index** — and the listing above showed **five fields**, omitting
  `inner_ink`, `boolean` and `failed`, none of which appeared anywhere else in this document either,
  so a reader checking a count against §5.9 came up short and found nothing to correct it with. Each
  is a *different question* rather than a convenience: `world_bounds` is
  the box you are **editing**, `ink_bounds` is what is **drawn** (§15 D334), and `inner_ink` is what an
  effect *layer* must be big enough to hold before its own padding — the only one of the three a
  caller holding a **different** effect stack can use, which is the preview path and is why sizing a
  buffer from `ink_bounds` clipped the very blur being scrubbed (§15 D341). `failed` is a set beside
  `boolean` rather than an absence in it, because "no entry" would otherwise mean both *"an
  intersection that is correctly empty"* and *"an upstream panic"* (§15 D239). **The count is
  load-bearing in prose**: §15 D764 turns on there being six, and D741 and `roadmap.md` each proposed
  "a fourth map" and "a fifth map" for what would be the seventh and eighth.
  ⚠️ **Both of those proposals were declined on 2026-09-15 and the count stays at six** (§15 D778) —
  D741's local-box map and D510's rounded-outline one. **A seventh map is a decision rather than an
  optimisation**, and the reason is this bullet: `update` has to keep every one of them equal to
  `rebuild` for the life of a document, while `ondin-core/tests/resolve.rs`'s
  `assert_resolved_matches_rebuild` compares only **four** of the six — `boolean` has a fixed-fixture
  differential and `inner_ink` is compared by nothing anywhere — so a new map joins a partial guard.
  D778 carries what would re-open the question.
- No `FontContext` is threaded through: `core::text` owns a thread-local parley engine and returns
  layouts carrying the exact `peniko::FontData` blob parley resolved, so the renderer draws glyphs
  straight from it.
- `update` consumes `DirtySet`, in this order: re-shape the **dirty** nodes' text, recompute world
  transforms parents-first, recompute bounds children-first, then propagate bound changes up to the
  root. ⚠️ **The text pass is the one step that does *not* run over the subtree expansion** (§15
  D590). A descendant's world transform depends on a dirty ancestor and a descendant's *layout* does
  not — `text::layout` reads `TextRef::of(node.kind())` and nothing else — so re-shaping the
  expansion meant a nudged group of twenty text blocks paid twenty parley shapes per keypress for a
  change that cannot move a glyph. `core::text::shapes()` is the counter that makes this assertable;
  nothing else can see it, since the layouts produced are identical either way and the differential
  against `rebuild` is green under both.
- ⚠️ **The affected set carries each node's depth, and the parents-first sort caches its key** (§15
  D594). `collect_subtree` records depth as it descends — a child's is its parent's plus one, free
  there — into an `FxHashMap<NodeId, usize>`, and the sort is `sort_by_cached_key` over a lookup.
  Both halves are load-bearing: `sort_by_key` calls its key function on **every comparison** and the
  old key walked the parent chain to the root, which made the incremental path **4.8×** the full
  `rebuild` at depth 20 and **47×** at depth 200 — per commit, so on every held arrow key, undo and
  redo. `sort_by_cached_key` alone takes 93% of that out and still leaves `update` three times the
  price of the `rebuild` it exists to avoid, because the walk runs once per node; recording the depth
  is what removes the walk. **`rebuild` needs no sort at all**, its recursion putting parents before
  children structurally, which is why it wins outright the moment depth costs anything. The quantity
  is **depth**, not node count: 402 nodes at depth 200 cost more here than 4,000 flat ones, so any
  cost model that denominates this path in nodes is describing something else.
- **The text cache is load-bearing.** Bounds, hit-testing and the scene walk all read it. Without
  it every text node re-shapes several times per frame, and text shaping dominates the pipeline.
- **Font arrival invalidates it — the arrival of a font the document *names*.** Shaping resolves
  against whatever families are registered, so a layout computed before a font downloaded used the
  fallback face, and without the call bounds, selection rectangles and hit-testing keep describing
  the wrong face forever. ⚠️ **The app called `invalidate_text` for any registration at all until
  2026-09-08** (§15 D591), which is §5.4a's rule read as far as the comma: the picker registers
  preview faces for families the user is merely scrolling past, so a scroll re-shaped the whole
  document repeatedly for faces that cannot change a glyph of it. `FontPoll::touches` against
  `OndinApp::document_families()` is the gate now. `invalidate_text` itself is still whole-document —
  the family half is enforced at the call, not inside — which is the coarser half of §5.4a's sentence
  and costs one walk of a document that had work to do anyway.
- Local bounds per kind in `geometry.rs`; expand by half stroke width + miter allowance.
  **A bounds function's `None` means *no measurable extent*, not only *no geometry*** (§15 D495):
  `world_bounds_of_parts` and `world_bounds_of_path` pass their answer through `geometry::measurable`,
  which asks that the rect be **ordered** and **finite**, and either test alone lets half the bad boxes
  through — a `NaN` in the transform comes back inverted rather than empty, and an overflowing but
  perfectly finite affine comes back ordered and infinite. A node so measured is out of the spatial
  index, out of the cull and out of *zoom to selection*, which is the honest description of a layer
  whose extent is not a number; a clamped box would instead put a click target on the artwork.
  `transform_rect` stays total and says so, several of its callers having a `Rect` to return and
  nowhere to put the absence.
  ⚠️ **One arm reached `transform_rect` raw until 2026-09-09** (§15 D667): the placeholder box a
  failed boolean still draws, where `query::local_box` composes child transforms itself and so
  produces an ordered *infinite* rect from operand transforms every guard on the operation accepts.
  It goes through `measurable` now. 🚨 **And the rule is stated a second time on purpose, at
  `resolve::build_index`** — the writer guards what it *stores*, the index guards what it *accepts*,
  however the map came to hold it. That is a deliberate exception to this document's usual preference
  for one statement per rule, and the argument is that `world_bounds` is derived from geometry as
  well as from transforms and the doors onto a non-finite one are not enumerable. It is not
  belt-and-braces: `rstar`'s `AABB::from_corners` takes its corners component-wise, so an *inverted*
  rect normalises to the **maximal** box and makes the node a candidate for every spatial query for
  the life of the session.
  ⚠️ **`ink_bounds` needed no guard for D676's door and does need one for D685's**, which is the same
  sentence arriving twice with opposite answers. D676: `effect::escaped` mapped the radius as an
  ellipse with `(x² + y²).sqrt()`, and the **square** overflows at about `1e154` where the product
  itself is finite to `1e308` — so a legal radius, a `scale(1e155)` `affine_is_finite` accepts and a
  world box `measurable` accepts produced an ink box of `(−inf, −inf, inf, inf)`. It is `f64::hypot`
  now, the same value by a route that cannot overflow, so the box stays finite **and stays right**;
  a `measurable` there would have refused a question with a perfectly good answer. D685 is the door
  where the *answer* really does overflow — a radius near `f64::MAX` — and both ink stores end
  `.and_then(geometry::measurable)` for it, so a bound that is not a number is stored as the
  **absence** D495 chose rather than as an infinite box or, worse, as the unchanged one.
- **`mask_path` is the outline a mask clips with, in its *parent's* space** — the space its siblings
  are drawn in, so it can be handed straight to `push_layer` under the parent's world transform or
  written into a `<clipPath>` beside the parent's `<g>`. It answers the **`Shape`** mode only: an alpha
  mask has no geometry to ask for, since what masks is the ink it lays down (§5.3, §6.2, §15 D288). The arms are `boolean::operand_of`'s plus one:
  a **`Text`** node contributes its glyph outlines, which is the arm a boolean deliberately does not
  have and the case masks are largely for. A `Group` or `Root` contributes the **union** of its
  children, never a concatenation. `None` means *masks nothing* — a hidden mask, an empty text node,
  an empty group, a cancelled boolean — never "clip everything away", which would make hiding a mask
  look like deleting the artwork. Filled non-zero, the rule the same outline is filled with when the
  layer paints. §15 D282 has the nested-mask conservatism this leaves.
- **A masked layer keeps its own world bounds; its *container* gets only what the mask lets through.**
  `world_bounds` is not reduced by any clip, a mask included — the answer a frame clip has always given
  its children, conservative because a clip only removes ink, and the box you drag the layer by. But
  `resolve_subtree` and `recompute_bounds` clip each masked child's *contribution* to the box the
  governing mask **clips with**, so zoom-to-fit on a mask group frames the picture rather than the
  photograph behind it. `query::local_box` mirrors that, or the handles and the snapping would
  disagree. §15 D283 has the split and what it costs. ⚠️ **That box is `resolve::mask_extent`, and it
  was the mask's *own* box until 2026-09-07** (§15 D460): a mask **group** narrows its own box with the
  mask inside it, where `mask_path` skips that inner mask and clips with the un-narrowed union — so a
  container was reported at a tenth of the region its children draw in, and since culling reads these
  boxes its whole subtree went unpainted while still being on screen and clickable. The helper is arm
  for arm with `mask_path`, `query::mask_extent_local` is its local twin, and keeping those lists of
  arms together is what stops the rule drifting from the clip again.
  ⚠️ **And the mask itself contributes *nothing* to that union — it lends the clip, not its own
  rectangle** (§15 D494). Until 2026-09-07 the mask child's own box went in un-narrowed alongside the
  boxes it clipped, which is invisible while the mask is the smaller of the two and reverses the rule
  the moment it is not: a 1000×1000 mask over a 100×100 picture reported the group at 1000×1000, where
  what the group *shows* is the 100-unit square. Five arms had it — `recompute_bounds`' box and ink,
  `resolve_subtree`'s box and ink, and `query::local_box` — because two passes cross two kinds of
  bounds. **A group whose only child is a mask therefore has no box at all**, which is the honest
  answer rather than an oversight: it draws nothing, so *zoom to selection* and the marquee have
  nothing to measure.
- **`ink_bounds` is the second bounds cache, and the split is the point** (§5.3a, §15 D334).
  `world_bounds` keeps meaning *the box of the thing you are editing* — the selection outline, the
  inspector's W and H, snapping, the rulers, the marquee and the R-tree all read it, and a shadow must
  not move any of them: softening a blur would grow the reported height, and a snap would catch on a
  shadow's edge. `ink_bounds` is that box grown by `effect::stack_escape` at **every level of the
  subtree** — measured from the children's *ink* rather than from the box just stored, or a shadow one
  level down would be forgotten by every ancestor — and it is what **export** frames from
  (`ondin_export::extent`, §7) and what the SVG writer's filter region is written from — ⚠️ **padded,
  since 2026-09-10, for a stack's inner shadows** (§15 D742): a filter's *working* region is not this
  box, because an inner shadow's primitives have to be evaluated outside the shape they never draw
  outside of, and §7 has the mechanism. The two are
  equal for the overwhelming majority of nodes, which is why it is a second map rather than a wider
  first one: nothing carries an effect until someone adds one. A masked child's *ink* contribution is
  clipped to the governing mask's **ink** extent — `mask_extent` over `ink_bounds` rather than over the
  world boxes — and not to its box, since a blurred mask passes ink beyond its own outline and too
  small is the one error these bounds may not make. ⚠️ **That last rule was broken by the escape
  itself until 2026-09-07** (§15 D473): `stack_escape` took a plain union of the per-effect escapes,
  where §6.4 composes a drop shadow's silhouette out of the already-blurred layer — so a 40×40 rect
  under a layer blur and a drop shadow claimed a `y1` escape of 46 where the ink reaches 64. And
  **the box is also the buffer** (`grow_to_escape` ends `device_ink.intersect(grown)`), so the shadow
  was not merely mis-culled but drawn with a ruled edge across it at 38/255. The escape is taken per
  §6.4 stage now (§5.3a).
  ⚠️ **A non-finite escape is *swallowed* here rather than propagated, and the guard for it is at the
  operation** (§15 D641). `effect::escaped` splits the insets back into an offset and a radius, so an
  infinite escape gives `inf − inf` — `NaN` — and `f64::min` answers the non-`NaN` operand, so every
  edge contributes zero and the box comes back **unchanged**: a layer whose blur reached everywhere
  reported the bare geometry. The repair is `build::effect_is_finite` at `SetEffects` and
  `InsertSubtree` (§4 invariant 8), **not** an infinite box here — that is the failure D495 removed,
  and the two rules this section holds are easy to read as one: *too small is the error these bounds
  may not make* is about erring **among numbers**, while a bound that is **not** a number is an
  *absence*, which `escaped`'s signature has no room for. `reach(f64::NAN)` is `0.0` by the same
  convention, so a `NaN` radius was always a benign no-op and only the infinite one lied.
  🚨 **An infinite escape can also be *derived* from finite fields, and that door was open for a day**
  (§15 D676, closed by D685). `stack_escape` summed `deviation(radius).powi(2)` over the visible layer
  blurs and rooted it, so a radius past about `2.7e154` — finite, and therefore accepted by
  `effect_is_finite` at both its doors — made the sum infinite and landed `escaped` on exactly the
  swallow above. The operation guard cannot see it, because the field it weighs *is* finite, and
  `f64::hypot` does not apply, the operands being a fold rather than a pair. **The fold is the
  classical overflow-safe one now** — divide through by the largest deviation, sum squares that are
  all `≤ 1`, multiply back — with **two things behind it**: `escaped` answers the *unbounded* rect for
  an escape whose insets are not all finite, and both ink stores pass their result through
  `geometry::measurable`, so that rect becomes an absence. 🚨 **Of the two overflows this bullet now
  records, the derived one was the dangerous one**: D676 answered an infinite box, which makes
  everything draw and every raster enormous, and D685 answered the **original** box, so the cull drops
  artwork that is on screen — the one error these bounds may not make.
  **Culling reads `ink_bounds`** (`scene::paint_node`) — see §6.3. This line said the opposite until
  2026-09-07, having been written while the cull did read `world_bounds` and never restruck when D334's
  sweep fixed it on 2026-08-24.
- Property-tested: `update` after any op sequence ≡ `rebuild` from scratch, for transforms, bounds
  **and text layouts**, over randomized op sequences including text creation and restyling — and
  including `SetMask`, which is the one op in that mix whose effect on a box travels **sideways**, so
  the two passes reach the same container union by different routes, and `SetEffects`, which is the
  one that travels **outwards** and has a second map to agree about. ⚠️ **What it cannot say is whether
  the rule those routes agree about is right**: both passes narrowed by the mask's own box instead of
  the box it clips with, identically, and this property held throughout (§15 D460). A differential
  between two implementations of one rule guards a change to either and is silent about the rule.
  `a_shadow_moves_the_ink_box_up_the_tree_and_leaves_the_editing_box_alone` states the split directly.
- Known cost: `update` rebuilds the whole R-tree (`bulk_load`) rather than patching entries. Fine
  at current scale, and the first thing to fix when node counts grow — parked in §14.

### 5.10 Queries

```rust
pub fn hit_test(res: &Resolved, doc: &Document, p: Point, slop: f64) -> Vec<NodeId>;
pub fn nodes_in_view(res: &Resolved, view: Rect) -> Vec<NodeId>;
pub fn bounds(res: &Resolved, id: NodeId) -> Option<Rect>;      // world AABB, from Resolved
pub fn local_box(doc: &Document, res: &Resolved, id: NodeId) -> Option<Rect>;
pub fn pivot_world(doc: &Document, res: &Resolved, id: NodeId) -> Option<Point>;
pub fn group_chain(doc: &Document, id: NodeId, inside: Option<NodeId>) -> Vec<NodeId>;
pub fn is_within(doc: &Document, id: NodeId, ancestor: NodeId) -> bool;
pub fn is_effectively_locked(doc: &Document, id: NodeId) -> bool;   // this node, or any ancestor
```

- `hit_test` = R-tree candidates → **exact geometric test** (point-in-path for fills, distance ≤
  half-width for strokes, glyph-box test for text), topmost-first, respecting visible/locked.
  The exact tests live in `geometry.rs`, not in callers. Both flags are read **through the ancestors**
  (`is_effectively_interactable`), so a layer inside a hidden or locked group is unpickable.
- **`is_effectively_locked` is the lock half of that, and it is `pub` because the whole app needs it**
  (§15 D321). **A locked group locks its contents** — that is what a lock on a container means, not a
  convenience laid over it — and until 2026-08-23 the only ancestor-aware reading of the lock in the
  tree was private to `hit_test`, so every refusal in the app asked `Node::locked` and stopped at the
  node's own flag. Everything that refuses an *edit* asks this — **and so does the one label that
  explains such a refusal**, `canvas::draw_size_badge`'s padlock, which is the only thing on the canvas
  that says why the handles will not move and so has to answer the same question they did (§15 D348).
  The two things that must not are the
  lock control itself and its label, which write the own flag and would otherwise offer *Unlock* on a
  layer that is not locked. A node the document does not hold answers **`true`** — a refusal rather
  than a licence. **Locked alone, deliberately not visibility**: hiding says "do not draw", locking
  says "do not change", and a hidden-but-unlocked layer is fully editable (`context-menus.md` §5.9).
- `slop` is a picking allowance in **world** units, and **every kind spends it**: each arm of
  `geometry::contains_local` adds it to the ink's own reach (`stroke_expansion + slop`) as a band
  reaching *outward*, on top of whatever interior the shape has. It used to be the `Line` arm alone, on
  the grounds that a filled shape has an interior to aim at; a stroked shape with **no fill** has none,
  and is grabbed by its outline or not at all (§15 D115). ⚠️ **This sentence was false for `Text` until
  2026-09-07** (§15 D483): D115's sweep missed that arm and its own enumeration of the rewritten arms
  never named it, so the kind users click most tested its bare layout box — and a text node with a 40pt
  **outside** stroke reported world bounds 40 units wider on every side than a click could reach, a band
  of its own stated extent selecting nothing. It is the *caller's* number because only the
  caller knows the zoom — `canvas::pick_slop` is `PICK_SLOP_PX / camera.zoom`, so the band under the
  pointer is the same size on screen at any magnification, which no constant in world units could be —
  and `0.0` means exactly.
  It widens the **candidate query** as well as the exact test, which it has to: a horizontal line's
  cached bounds are a zero-height rectangle, so a point beside it never became a candidate at all
  (§15 D222).
- **Masking answers the hit test at both ends** (`query::masked_away`, §15 D284). A **mask is never
  hit**: it paints nothing, so there is nothing on the canvas to aim at, and a click where it sits
  belongs to whatever it is letting through — it stays selectable from the layers panel and by
  marquee, both of which go through bounds rather than through here. And **masked content is hit only
  inside its mask**, or the clipped-away half of a photograph stays clickable over empty canvas. Every
  ancestor is asked, not just the node's own parent, because a mask two levels up clips this layer
  just as surely. ⚠️ **`outline_at` asks the same function, and did not until 2026-09-07** (§15 D456):
  it asked two of `hit_test`'s three questions and not this one, so the same two clicks answered
  differently through the two doors and the Text tool offered a mask as a rail (§5.4). It is asked
  *last* there, behind the cheap rejections, because it walks the ancestor chain and asks `mask_path`.
- **`outline_at`'s bound is in nodes and its work is in segments, so each segment is rejected by its own
  control hull first** (`query::seg_hull`, §15 D507). The candidate query is bounded — a `slop`-sized box
  through the index — but inside a candidate it solved the exact nearest point on **every** segment, and
  `PathSeg::nearest` is a quintic root-find per cubic: one imported path is enough, and `canvas::rail_at`
  asks it for the hover affordance and again for the click, so a frame can pay twice. A Bézier lies inside
  the hull of its control points, so a hull that is further from the pointer than the allowance cannot
  hold the nearest point and the solve is skipped; the threshold narrows to the nearest distance found so
  far. Measured in release, 2,000 segments went 0.160 ms/call to 0.041. ⚠️ **The hull rather than
  `PathSeg::bounding_box()`, which measured half as good** — the tight box is a root-find of its own — and
  a reject may only ever be *too generous*, since a hull that did not contain its curve would change the
  answer rather than the cost.
- `bounds` and `local_box` answer different questions and are not interchangeable. `bounds` is the
  axis-aligned world region a node covers — right for culling, snapping and marquee tests.
  `local_box` is the node's *own* rectangle in its own space, which is what a selection outline and
  its resize handles need: on a rotated node the first is a box the shape does not have. `local_box`
  also covers containers, by unioning children through their transforms — each masked child clipped to
  what its governing mask *clips with*, exactly as `Resolved`'s world box does it (§5.9, §15 D283,
  D460), through `query::mask_extent_local` rather than the shared helper because this function works
  in the node's own space throughout and composing the two would mean an inverse per child — which is
  the only way a group gets a box that rotates with it.
  ⚠️ **`bounds` is a map lookup and `local_box` is a subtree walk, and the chrome asked it fourteen
  times a frame** (§15 D741). Counted through one real frame with a 200-child group selected: **2,814
  calls for 201 nodes, exactly 14.00 top-level asks, and none at all with nothing selected.** In
  release that is 0.169 ms per frame at 1,000 children, 0.789 at 4,000 and **5.400 at 16,000**, about
  a third of a 16 ms budget.
  🚨 **Eight of the fourteen were one function asking twice for one box** (§15 D764):
  `canvas::selection_handles` asked `preview_local_box` for its own `box_` and then `preview_pivot`,
  which asks `preview_local_box` again — and `previewed_pivot` answers `Some` for any existing node,
  so the second walk was unconditional. `EditorSession::preview_pivot_in(id, box_)` takes the box the
  caller already has and `preview_pivot` is written in terms of it, so the two cannot disagree about
  what `pivot_point` is applied to. ⚠️ **D741's *"fourteen different functions … not one hoist away
  from being one"* was therefore false**, and the arithmetic in the review had said so: 0.6431 ms per
  selection-box build against 0.3490 ms per `local_box` call is a factor of 1.84, which is two walks.
  **Six asks remain**, and for those the fix would have been a new map on `Resolved` filled by the
  same children-first pass — it cannot be derived from `world_bounds` for the reason this bullet opens
  with. 🚨 **That map is declined** (§15 **D778**, 2026-09-15), on the six-ask arithmetic — about
  0.07 ms per frame at 1,000 children — and on the door below. ⚠️ **It would answer the resting frame
  only**: `session::preview_local_box` forwards here only while `overrides.is_empty()` and re-walks
  the children itself whenever an override is live, which is every frame of a gesture, so a cache is
  bypassed exactly when the handles are moving. **Six uncached walks a frame is the design**, and
  D778 carries the trigger that would re-open it.
- `pivot_world` is `local_box` composed with the node's own `Pivot` (§5.3) and its world transform —
  the point a rotation or a mirror should hold still, in the space the gesture is working in. It is
  here rather than in `build.rs` because it answers a question rather than building a transaction, and
  `build::flip` and the inspector's quarter-turn buttons both ask it, so neither can pick a different
  point from the one the canvas marker is drawn on.
- `hit_test` always returns a **leaf**: groups are not indexed (§5.9) and have no outline of their
  own. Turning that leaf into the node a click should *select* is a separate step, and `group_chain`
  is the tree walk it needs — the unbroken run of `Group` ancestors, outermost first. The policy on
  top of it is the app's (§9.4), but the walk is not, because MCP's future `select` needs the same
  answer. The app also *subtracts* from the list before it walks up: `canvas::pick_leaf` drops any
  frame that has children (§9.4, §15 D22). That is a picking policy, not a hit test — `hit_test`
  still reports the frame, because a query asking what covers a point must answer honestly.

### 5.11 IO

- Native format = JSON, currently **v4** (`io::CURRENT_SCHEMA_VERSION`). `schema.rs` defines a
  versioned DTO decoupled from in-memory types.
- **The library block is the first key after `schema_version`** (§5.11a). Its position is a decision
  about *reading* rather than about diffs: the dashboard lists a folder by reading each document's
  name, project and date, and `io::probe` reaches them from a 4 KB prefix without parsing the
  document. See §5.11a for why that matters on a synced folder.
- `save`: nodes emitted **sorted by NodeId**, stable field order → byte-identical re-saves
  (invariant 9). Guides are sorted by id for the same reason — the in-memory list is unordered
  (§5.5), so its order records what has been dragged out and undone rather than anything about the
  document. `load`: read `schema_version`, run `migrate.rs` chain, build `Document`, then verify
  tree integrity.
- ⚠️ **The version is compared in the header's own denomination and is never narrowed** (§15 D638).
  The header is whatever `serde_json` parsed, so it is a `u64`, while `CURRENT_SCHEMA_VERSION` is a
  `u32` — and casting before the comparison made `version > CURRENT` mean something other than what
  it reads as: `8589934592` (2³³) truncated to **0** and was migrated through the whole v0→v4 chain
  and opened, while `u64::MAX` was refused as *"unsupported schema version: 4294967295"*, a version
  the file does not claim. `IoError::UnsupportedVersion` therefore carries a `u64`, which is what
  makes the narrowing visible at all: with the payload wide, re-introducing the cast does not
  compile.
- **Integrity verification is total, not a spot check.** The in-memory tree walks
  (`subtree_ids`, `paint_path`, `resolve`) deliberately carry no visited set, because a document
  produced by `apply` cannot contain a cycle. That makes the loader the place where that guarantee
  is established, so it checks: root exists / is `Root` / has no parent; every non-root parent
  resolves; every listed child points back; **no node is listed as a child twice**; **every node is
  reachable from the root**; **no node is deeper than `io::MAX_TREE_DEPTH` (256)**; and every
  parent/child pair obeys the same kind rules operations do.
  Reachability and the duplicate check are what make cycles and orphan components impossible — without
  them a hand-edited file can satisfy parent/child consistency and hang the app.
- ⚠️ **The depth bound is the one check that is about the *stack* rather than about the tree, and it
  was missing until 2026-09-06** (§15 D416). Every other check bounds a shape; none of them bounded a
  depth, and the walks this list delegates safety to are recursive, so a ~2,000-deep document of
  nested groups passed all five and then killed the process with `STATUS_STACK_OVERFLOW` inside
  `Resolved::rebuild` — **an abort rather than a panic**, which nothing catches and which takes the
  session's unsaved work with it. It rides on the reachability walk, which was already visiting every
  node once. `svg_in` enforces a far tighter 64 at its own recursion, so an import can never build a
  document the loader would refuse. ⚠️ **A depth bound is not a size bound, and for a fortnight nothing
  was** (§15 D446): `<use>` instancing branches, so 843 bytes of markup expanded to 16,384 shapes and
  the cap on `<use>` nesting admits 65,536 — three instantiations per level rather than two is an
  allocation failure, which is an abort. `MAX_SVG_NODES` (50,000) is asked at the top of
  `node_ignoring`, the one choke point every emitted node passes, so a refusal never stops mid-element;
  past it the import stops and says so, which is that module's standing degradation.
  ⚠️ **And a size bound is not a *payload* bound** (§15 D459). Both of those count nodes, and what a
  node **carries** is a third quantity: every shape naming a gradient gets its own copy of the whole
  stop list, into the transaction, the `Document` and then the saved JSON, so 6,000 stops and 6,000
  rects is 452 KB of markup holding 864 MB — 2.4% of the XML budget and a rounding error against the
  emitted one. `svg_in::MAX_GRADIENT_STOPS` (256) is its only bound, and the list is **resampled** to
  it rather than truncated or refused, since truncating compresses the ramp into the front of its
  range; a file that reaches the cap is a generated one, and it is reported once as `approximated`.
- ⚠️ **The op door owes the same standard, and on one check it did not pay it** (§15 D423). The claim
  that "a document produced by `apply` cannot contain a cycle" rests on `op_insert_subtree` validating
  the set it is handed; it walked from each node to its listed children and never asked the converse —
  whether every non-root node **is** somebody's child — so a set composed from two `capture_subtree`
  snapshots taken at different moments inserted an orphan, which then panicked `DeleteNode`, `Reparent`
  and `Reorder` and saved a file the loader's own check (5) rejects. One comparison
  (`claimed.len() + 1 != nodes.len()`) closes it. *Two doors into the tree held to different standards
  is exactly what this section says must not happen.*
- ⚠️ **There is deliberately no finiteness check here, and that is a measurement rather than an
  omission** (§15 D421). One was written and removed as unreachable: `serde_json` writes a non-finite
  `f64` as `null`, refuses `null` where an `f64` is wanted, and refuses an overflowing literal like
  `1e999` — all at `from_value`, one function above the integrity walk. The whole of the protection is
  therefore at the operation (`OpError::NonFinite`, invariant 8), which is where it belongs anyway —
  ⚠️ ~~**and the operation does not yet cover paint**, so a `NaN` gradient stop is refused at the SVG
  importer rather than here or there (§15 D448). Invariant 8 carries the *Fix*.~~ **Paint landed the
  same day (§15 D451)**, so the claim that the whole of the protection is at the operation is true of
  every number the model carries rather than of coordinates alone.
- The save format and the MCP/AI snapshot (§7.3) are distinct schemas — never conflate them.
- **A purely additive field does not need a version bump.** `schema.rs` reuses the model's serde
  representation, so a new field there is on disk immediately; if it carries `#[serde(default)]` and
  the default is *what old files already meant*, every existing file still loads correctly and a
  migration step would be a no-op. `Stroke::align` is the first of these — v1 files have no `align`
  and default to `Center`, which is exactly how they were drawn. Pinned by
  `a_saved_file_without_stroke_align_loads_as_centred`. `Node::clip` is the same case, and so is
  `DocumentDto::canvas_background` (§15 D28) — the first additive field at the *top* level rather
  than per node: a file written while the ground was session state was drawn on the default, which
  is precisely what the default reproduces, so no migration step is owed. Pinned by
  `a_saved_file_without_a_canvas_ground_loads_with_the_default`. `DocumentDto::guides`
  (`#[serde(default)]`, §5.5) is the same case again and the plainest of the three: a file written
  before guides existed had none, which is exactly what the empty default reproduces.
  `Node::proportions_locked` (§15 D41) is the fourth: a bare `#[serde(default)]` like `align` and
  `guides` rather than a named fn like `clip`'s, because while the lock was session state no file
  recorded it, so every node in every existing file meant `false`. It is also the only one of the four
  with no normalization on load — `clip` is re-checked against the kind (`dto.clip &&
  dto.kind.clips_children()`), since its default says "yes" and would otherwise arrive with every group
  claiming to clip, whereas an unlocked flag is inert on every kind and needs no such guard. Pinned by
  `a_saved_file_without_the_proportion_lock_loads_with_nothing_locked`, which strips the key from every
  node of a saved fixture and asserts the reload is the same document *and* that every node — not just
  the resizable ones — came back unlocked.
  ⚠️ **`clip`'s normalization was owed on the way *out* as well, and was missing until 2026-09-09**
  (§15 D663): `op_set_clip` accepts an inert flag on purpose (§5.3, §15 D282), so the writer wrote a
  value the loader threw away and `save(load(save(d)))` differed from `save(d)` for every group
  carrying it, with no edit made. **A normalization at one end of the format only is a document whose
  bytes move the first time it is opened and saved**, which is invariant 9 read from the side it is
  easiest to miss. `DocumentDto::from_document` carries the projection now; the loader's copy stays,
  because it guards a hand-edited or foreign file rather than our own writer, and
  `an_inert_clip_flag_never_reaches_the_file` pins the pair.
  `Node::pivot` (§15 D55) is the fifth and the **strongest**
  of them: `#[serde(default, skip_serializing_if = "Option::is_none")]`, so an unmoved pivot is not
  merely defaulted on the way in, it never reaches the file at all — adding the field changed no
  existing document's bytes, which is invariant 9 read forwards.
  `a_document_with_no_moved_pivot_writes_no_pivot_field` asserts the string never appears in a save
  with nothing moved, and `a_moved_pivot_round_trips_in_both_variants` covers both `Pivot` variants,
  because which one a kind gets is a rule (§5.3) the loader must not quietly re-decide.
  `Stroke::sides` and `Stroke::dash_fit` (§15 D68, D69) are `pivot`'s strongest form again —
  `skip_serializing_if`, so a stroke on the whole outline and an unfitted
  pattern never reach the file, and adding both changed no existing document's bytes.
  **`Node::mask` (§5.3, §15 D282) is that strongest form yet again, and the plainest reading of it**:
  a file written before masks existed had none, so `#[serde(default)]` alone is what every one of its
  nodes meant — no named default function, unlike `clip`, whose default says "yes" — and
  `skip_serializing_if` keeps the key out of every document with no mask in it, so the field changed no
  existing file's bytes. `the_mask_flag_is_absent_from_a_document_that_has_none` asserts both halves.
  It is normalized on load the way `clip` is (`dto.mask && dto.kind.can_mask()`), which here guards a
  hand-edited or future file rather than our own default, since nothing writes a mask onto a frame —
  `a_mask_on_a_frame_does_not_survive_being_loaded` is that half. **`Node::mask_mode` (§15 D288) is the
  same form once more and adds one rule**: `skip_serializing_if = "is_shape_mask"`, so a document whose
  masks are all shape masks — which is every document written before the mode existed — carries no key
  and changes no bytes, and it is loaded **without** being gated on `mask`, deliberately, because the
  mode is remembered while the mask is off. `the_mask_mode_is_absent_until_something_is_not_a_shape_mask`
  asserts both directions.
  **`GuideDto::owner` (§5.5) is that form once more, and the reason there is no v4**: every guide in
  every file written before scoping existed ran the whole canvas, which is exactly what a missing key
  means, and `skip_serializing_if` keeps a document with no scoped guide byte-identical to what it was
  before the field existed. `a_document_with_no_scoped_guide_writes_no_owner_field` pins that half.
  **`ImageRef::fit`, `crop`, `tile_scale`, `orient` and `adjust` (§5.5a) are that form once more**, so an image
  placed before framing — or before orientation, which arrived the same way and needed no bump either
  (§15 D182), or before adjustments, which arrived the same way again (§15 D186) — keeps its exact
  line in the file.
  `a_chosen_fit_is_written_and_the_default_one_is_not` pins **both** halves,
  because they are different claims: the default staying out is what made framing additive, and the
  chosen one going *in* is the half a `skip_serializing_if` gets wrong by being aimed at the wrong
  predicate — silently, since the document would then load with the crop thrown away and look like the
  crop gesture had not committed. Three predicates rather than one, because the parameters live beside
  the mode rather than inside it (§15 D178): an image cropped and then set back to Fill writes its
  rectangle while one that has never been cropped writes nothing at all, which is what
  `only_the_parameters_that_were_changed_are_written` asserts from the absence end. `adjust` carries a
  predicate of its own *and* one per slider, so a picture with one moved value writes that value and
  no other six (`a_neutral_adjustment_is_no_pipeline_and_no_bytes`, both halves).
  **`Stroke::miter_limit` is the weaker kind and the first of those**: `#[serde(default =
  "default_miter_limit")]` with no skip, so every stroke in every file now carries a `miter_limit`.
  A ratio that is not 4 has no "absent" reading, so there is nothing for the field to vanish *into*;
  the cost is that an old document re-saves with a key it did not have, which is additive on load but
  is not the bytes-forwards guarantee the other three make. Invariant 9 is untouched either way —
  it is about a re-save of what was loaded. `a_stroke_on_every_side_writes_no_sides_field` pins the
  two that claim to vanish, `a_saved_file_without_the_new_stroke_fields_loads_as_it_was_drawn` strips
  all three from a saved fixture and requires the reload to be the same document, and
  `per_side_widths_and_a_mitre_limit_round_trip` covers the other direction — including `Custom`'s
  four widths, which live inside the enum variant rather than beside it.
  **`NodeDto::exports` (§7, §15 D274) is `pivot`'s strongest form once more, and at both levels**:
  `skip_serializing_if = "Vec::is_empty"` on the node's list, and again on every field of an
  `ExportSpec` but `format` — so a document nobody has set up to export carries no key at all, and a
  layer that exports a plain 1× PNG writes `{"format":"Png"}` and nothing else.
  `export_settings_round_trip_and_cost_nothing_when_empty` pins all three halves: the key never
  appears in a document with no exports, a list round-trips through a save, and an undo brings the
  file back to the **exact bytes** it had rather than to something equivalent.
  ⚠️ **A spec whose scale or quality cannot be one is *dropped* here, where the operation refuses it**
  (§5.7, §15 D492). The asymmetry is this file's own rule for a value that is decoration: refusing the
  whole document over an export preset would lose the artwork to save the recipe, which is the same
  bargain the out-of-range `opacity` clamp makes two fields up. It is not repaired either — `Width(0)`
  has no defensible non-zero reading — so the row goes and the panel shows one fewer. Invariant 9 is
  untouched, being about a re-save of what was loaded.
  **`NodeDto::effects` (§5.3a, §15 D333) is that same form once more** — `skip_serializing_if =
  "Vec::is_empty"`, so a document nobody has put an effect on carries no key and no version bump was
  owed. `an_effect_stack_round_trips_in_order_and_costs_nothing_when_empty` pins both halves, and its
  fixture is deliberately **two entries of the same kind on an artboard**: a loader that deduped by
  kind, or a field folded into `Paint`, or an op gated on `takes_paint`, each fails there and nowhere
  else in that file.
  A bump is still required for anything that changes the
  meaning of an existing field, or whose default would silently alter old documents.
- **Guides are verified too, but not against a tree** — there is none for one to corrupt. The loader
  rejects a malformed guide id, a duplicate one, and a non-finite position; a guide far off the side
  of the artwork is legal, because panning reaches it. Their ids come out of the same reservation
  the nodes' do (§5.2), so a guide loaded from a file can never be re-minted over. It also rejects an
  `owner` that is dangling or is not a frame, rather than **promoting** the guide to global: a scoped
  guide's `position` is read in its owner's space, so with no owner it has no place at all, and
  quietly making it a world coordinate would move the line to somewhere nobody chose. Refusing here
  is also what keeps every drawing and snapping site free of a fallback for a state
  `check_guide_owner` will not let `apply` produce.
- **v1 → v2** is the first migration that moves real data: a rect's scalar `corner_radius` became
  per-corner `corner_radii` (§5.3), and the step spreads the one number over all four corners —
  which is what it always described. Pinned by
  `migration_spreads_a_v1_corner_radius_over_four_corners`. Renaming a field is exactly the case the
  bullet above excludes from "purely additive": `serde` would have dropped the old key and defaulted
  the new one, quietly squaring off every rounded rectangle ever saved.
- **v2 → v3** is the text attribute model (§5.4). Most of the growth is additive and rides
  `#[serde(default)]` + `skip_serializing_if`, so a uniform text node writes no `spans`, no
  `para_spans`, no `paragraph` and no `block` at all — pinned by
  `a_uniform_text_node_writes_no_spans_paragraph_or_block`. (`para_spans` arrived after v3 had shipped
  and needed no bump of its own, being additive in exactly this sense; §15 D163. So did
  `ParagraphStyle::marker` and `ParagraphStyle::level`, both `skip_serializing_if`, so a document with no
  list is byte-identical to what it was before either field existed; §15 D169, D172.)
  Two fields changed *shape*, which is what the bump is for:
  - `line_height` was a bare multiplier and is now `Option<Length>`. The step reads a v2 number as
    `Em(m)`, which is exactly what it meant; left to serde the key would have been dropped and the
    field defaulted to `None`, silently retyping every document ever saved to the font's own leading.
    Pinned by `migration_reads_a_v2_line_height_as_a_multiple_of_the_font_size`.
  - `align` moved out of the character defaults and into the paragraph scope. **The physical value is
    preserved rather than mapped to the new `Start`/`End` pair**: an old file said *left*, and turning
    that into "the start edge, whichever that is" would flip the alignment of the first RTL document
    anyone opened. Pinned by `migration_moves_align_into_the_paragraph_scope_without_relabelling_it`.
  The loader also **clamps both span lists to the content** rather than rejecting a file whose ranges
  outrun it (`a_span_reaching_past_the_content_is_clamped_on_load`): a stale range is a hand-edit or an
  older writer's rounding, not a corrupt tree, and clamping loses nothing a designer would notice. The tree
  checks are the ones that must refuse. ⚠️ **Clamping to the content means clamping onto its *character
  boundaries* too, and that half was missing until 2026-09-06** (§15 D422): a span ending inside a
  multi-byte character loaded with no complaint and then panicked on every render, in `text::cased_text`
  and again in parley's style builder. `Spans::clamped` therefore takes the **content** rather than its
  length, and snaps outward so the styling the file asked for covers the whole character it half-named.
  It is not a loader-only repair: `op_set_text` and `op_set_text_style` call the same function, so a
  fix placed at the loader alone would have left the live-editing door open.
  **The same pass canonicalizes each span's *value*** (§5.4, §15 D443), which is what keeps a
  hand-edited `Em(0.020000000000000004)` from fragmenting the stored list against a typed `Em(0.02)`.
  ⚠️ That defect is smaller than the one it was filed as: the *read* path was always immune, because
  `values_in` resolves each cut through `set_on`, so the panel never reported *Mixed*. What was lost is
  the span list's own invariant (2), and therefore a save writing two spans where the document has one
  value.
- **v3 → v4** is a frame's ground leaving `NodeKind::Artboard` for `Node::paint` (§5.3, §15 D400):
  `{"Artboard": {"size": …, "background": <brush>}}` becomes `{"Artboard": {"size": …}}` with the brush
  moved into that node's `fills` as `{"brush": …, "visible": true}`, a `null` background contributing no
  fill — which is exactly what it meant. This is v1's case again rather than an additive one: serde would
  drop the old key and default the new list to empty, quietly stripping the ground off every frame ever
  saved. ⚠️ **The brush is *prepended*, and that matters on exactly one shape of file.** The list is the
  z-order, bottom first, and a background painted behind everything; a v3 frame could not hold a fill at
  all — `SetFills` refused an `Artboard` — so today the list is always empty and prepending and appending
  are the same operation. The rule is written the strict way so that a file a future reader hands this
  step does not get its ground painted on top of its own artwork. Pinned by
  `migration_moves_a_v3_frame_background_into_its_fill_list` and a null-background sibling; ⚠️ **the
  flip is the one worth knowing** — removing the fill-write while still removing the key leaves the
  *kind* assertion green and fails only the colour assertion, with `left: []`. That is the shape of a
  migration that silently never ran, and nothing else would say so, there being no
  `deny_unknown_fields` here.

### 5.11a The library block (§15 D362)

- **A document knows its own library identity, and it is the only document state that is not about
  drawing.** `core::meta::DocumentMeta` — `id`, `name`, `project`, `created` — is a top-level key in
  the `.ondin`, written second, after `schema_version`.
- **It is in the file because the base folder syncs.** The library's root is user-settable precisely
  so it can be a Drive, Dropbox or OneDrive directory (§9.6); a fact that lives anywhere else does not
  arrive on the user's second machine, and a library there with every document named by its slug and
  no project assignments is not the same library. The cache directory is for what is *derived*.
- ⚠️ **The other edge of that: a copy of the file is a copy of the identity.** Anything that duplicates
  a `.ondin` outside the app — a sync client resolving a conflict, an Explorer paste — produces a second
  document with the same name, the same project and the same id, which the dashboard draws as two
  identical cards. That is why a conflict copy has to be recognised from its *filename*
  (§9.5, §15 D375), the only thing about it that differs. *Duplicate* inside the app mints a new id and
  is not affected.
- ⚠️ **Nothing in it may be written by a clock.** Byte-identical re-saves (invariant 9) are what make
  the format diff well, and one modified-at stamp written by the save path would end that for every
  document at once. Every field changes only when the **user** renames the document, moves it between
  projects, or creates it. An edit time is read off the directory entry, where it already is.
- **Not an `Operation`, so outside undo.** A rename is a library action taken from the dashboard,
  often while the document is not open; routing it through `apply` would put an entry in the wrong
  document's history and make `Ctrl+Z` in the editor undo what the file browser did.
  `Document::set_meta` writes it directly and reports no `DirtySet` — nothing about the drawing
  changed.
- **Additive in `NodeDto::pivot`'s strongest form** (§5.11): every field is `Option` +
  `skip_serializing_if`, *and* the whole block is skipped when empty, so a document that has never
  been through the library is written byte-for-byte as it was before the field existed. No version
  bump was owed.
- ⚠️ **`io::load` never mints a missing `id`.** A loader that filled one in would make loading
  non-deterministic — the same bytes twice would give two documents that disagree about who they are.
  A pre-library file loads unfiled and the app gives it an identity the first time it files it.
- ⚠️ **An `id` is 32 lowercase hex characters and a file that says otherwise loses it** (§15 D419).
  `DocumentMeta::is_wellformed_id` is the shape `library::ids::mint` produces and the only shape
  anything has ever minted; `DocumentMeta::sanitized` drops an id that is not it, rather than refusing
  the document, because `None` is an ordinary state every pre-library file is already in. This is a
  **security** check and not a tidiness one: the id is joined as a *path component* by the crash
  snapshot, the version pin and the cover cache, so `"id": "../my-cool-design"` makes `atomic::write`
  rename attacker-chosen bytes over a real document, and on Windows an absolute id makes `Path::join`
  discard the base entirely. **Applied at both boundaries, and the second is the one that matters
