  most**: `io::schema::into_document` is the load path, and `io::probe::meta_in_prefix` is the
  *scan's* reader, which never loads the document and feeds `library::cover::key` for every card the
  dashboard draws — the door that opens itself. The three app writers ask `library::ids::is_minted`
  before joining, so a fourth reader that bypasses both boundaries still refuses.
- **`io::probe::meta_in_prefix` reads the block from the first 4 KB of a file** and answers `Found` /
  `Absent` / `Inconclusive`. Three outcomes because "there is none" and "I could not tell" lead to
  different work, and because a zero-byte read from an unhydrated cloud placeholder must never be
  cached as "this document has no name". Hand-rolled rather than `serde_json`, for the one reason that
  matters: serde must parse a *complete* value and a prefix is by construction incomplete.
- ⚠️ **The three answers are not three shades of the same thing, and the one caller treats two of them
  as opposites** (§15 D485). `library::scan::read_meta` maps `Found` to the block it read, `Absent` to
  a **healthy pre-library document** with default metadata and `Entry::unread = false` *without opening
  the file*, and only `Inconclusive` to a full `std::fs::read` + `io::load`, which is the one path that
  can report the file unreadable. So the rule is: **`Absent` is a positive claim that this is one of
  ours and carries no block**, and everything the prefix cannot definitely account for — not an object,
  a stray byte where a key belongs, a duplicate `meta`, a block that will not deserialize, a prefix that
  ran out — is `Inconclusive`. A wrong `Inconclusive` costs a slow scan; a wrong `Absent` is the
  dashboard asserting a renamed PNG is a healthy document.
- ⚠️ **A duplicate `meta` key is refused rather than resolved**, because `serde_json` keeps the last and
  the probe would return on the first, and the two key different things: the probe fills `Entry::meta`
  and so `library::cover::key`, while the recovery snapshot and the version history use the *loaded*
  document's. Matching serde's rule would still diverge for a second block past `root` or past the
  prefix. Seeing a second key at all is why the walk defers its return to `root` — one key further, the
  writer putting `root` immediately after `meta`.
- ⚠️ **`Absent` is the one place key order is trusted.** `schema.rs` emits `meta` before `root`, so
  reaching `root` first means there was none — a claim about files this crate wrote. A hand-reordered
  file costs the dashboard a filename instead of a typed name and heals on the next save. That is the
  **only** wrong answer this variant is allowed to give.

---

## 6. ondin-render

### 6.1 Layout

```
ondin-render/src/
├─ lib.rs
├─ renderer.rs     # Viewport, RenderOverrides
├─ gpu.rs          # VelloGpuRenderer (vello + wgpu) — interactive canvas
├─ cpu.rs          # VelloCpuRenderer (vello_cpu) — PNG export, CI, headless
├─ scene.rs        # trait ScenePainter + the one document->scene walk, culled
├─ effects.rs      # the effect passes — one specification, read by both backends (§6.4)
└─ color.rs        # the ONLY color conversion point; pin-time verification tests
```

### 6.2 The boundary

```rust
pub struct Viewport { pub view: kurbo::Rect, pub pixel_size: (u32, u32) } // zoom is derived

pub trait ScenePainter {
    fn has_image(&self, id: &ImageId) -> bool;
    fn fill_path(&mut self, transform: Affine, path: &BezPath, brush: &peniko::Brush,
                 framing: Option<Framing>);
    fn stroke_path(&mut self, transform: Affine, path: &BezPath, stroke: &StrokePaint<'_>);
    fn draw_text(&mut self, transform: Affine, run: &TextRun<'_>);
    fn push_layer(&mut self, transform: Affine, clip: Option<&BezPath>, rule: ClipRule,
                  opacity: f32);
    fn push_mask_layer(&mut self);   // DestIn: what is already in the enclosing layer survives in
                                     // proportion to the alpha drawn in this one — §6.2, §15 D288
    fn push_effect_layer(&mut self, transform: Affine, bounds: Rect, effects: &[Effect]);
                                     // filtered before compositing — §5.3a, §6.4. `bounds` is the
                                     // node's INK box in `transform`'s space. DEFAULTED to a plain
                                     // push_layer, so a backend without the passes draws the artwork
                                     // unfiltered rather than dropping it. Both backends override
                                     // it since §15 D339; the default is now the recording painters'
    fn pop_layer(&mut self);         // ⚠️ closes an effect layer OR an ordinary one, and a painter
                                     // that keeps effect frames must count which — §15 D338
}
```

- `Viewport` stores `view` + `pixel_size` only; zoom falls out of their ratio (no redundant field
  to keep in sync).
- **One world unit is one pixel at 100% zoom.** It has always been how the model behaves — zoom is
  `view` measured against `pixel_size`, so 100 units across 51.94 device px *is* 51.94% (§15 D33) —
  but it was never stated as a rule, and nothing depended on it until the editor grew a pixel grid.
  Two things now do, both in §9.4: `grid.rs` draws a one-unit lattice and `snap::to_pixel` rounds to
  one-unit multiples. Those are the same lattice seen twice — what the app *shows* and what it
  *honours* — so if either picks a different pitch the other is lying. A different unit is a change
  to this rule, not a local one.
- **Brushes, not colours.** Paths carry `peniko::Brush` through unchanged, so gradients work.
  Gradient coordinates are authored in the node's own local space — the same space as the path — so a
  gradient the app itself made needs no brush transform. ⚠️ **An *imported* one may carry one**: a
  `GradientBrush`'s affine is a squash for the elliptical radial gradient peniko's two circles cannot
  express, so both backends set a brush transform from `color::brush_to_backend`'s second answer
  whatever the variant, rather than only for a picture (§15 D412). ⚠️ **And its stop offsets are made
  monotonic on the way through** (`image::make_stops_monotonic`, §5.5a, §15 D455) — neither backend
  normalises, so this is the last place the rule can be stated once for both, and a descending ramp is
  not a wrong picture but a flat fill of the first stop's colour. **An image is the other exception**: its
  coordinates are its own pixel grid, which knows nothing of the shape it is filling, so every draw
  carries a `Framing` beside the brush — the map from source pixels into that same local space, the
  extend the fit implies, and the clip a letterboxing `Fit` needs (§5.5a, §15 D178). `StrokePaint`
  and `TextRun` each carry one for the same reason. It is `None` for a solid, for a gradient, and for
  an image the document has no table entry for — which costs nothing to get wrong, since the same
  missing entry means the store cannot produce pixels and the fill is diverted to the placeholder
  before the framing is used.
- 🚨 **Which *resolution* a picture is wanted at is the one thing the two backends are meant to
  disagree about, and it is the only such thing** (`color::Resolution { Source, Atlas }`, §15 D745).
  `color.rs` exists so they cannot differ — one conversion, one monotonic-stops repair, one framing
  composition — so the exception is a parameter on `brush_to_backend` rather than a second code path:
  the GPU painter asks for `Atlas` (`ImageStore::atlas_pixels`, shrunk so the page's pictures fit
  vello's 8192-pixel atlas, §5.5a) and the CPU painter for `Source`, because `ondin export --png` has
  no atlas and must write the picture the user placed. **A canvas that softens a photograph and an
  export that does not are both correct**, and a reader finding them different should reach for this
  rather than for a bug.
- **`has_image` is the one question the walk asks the painter rather than tells it.** The store of
  decoded pixels belongs to the backend and the geometry belongs to the walk, so a picture that cannot
  be drawn is answered here and *drawn* in `scene.rs` — one placeholder from one description, rather
  than one per backend to keep in step (§6.3, §15 D179).
- **Layers, not folded alpha.** `push_layer`/`pop_layer` handle frame clipping and node opacity.
  Folding opacity into each child's alpha is only equivalent when nothing overlaps; two overlapping
  half-transparent children must not show through each other. Layers cost real work, so one is
  pushed only when a node actually clips or is below full opacity.
  ⚠️ **`clip: None` means the render target's own pixel box, and a backend that needs a shape must
  use that one** (`gpu::layer_shape`, §15 D612). vello demands a shape for every layer where
  `vello_cpu` takes the `None` as it stands, so only the GPU backend substitutes — and it must not
  substitute a *big* rectangle in the node's space, since an ancestor scale shrinks that in world
  terms and turns "no clip" into a clip. The target's box is the one shape no transform can shrink,
  it is what "unbounded" means for a surface with edges, and `GpuScenePainter::limit` already
  follows the layer stack so a nested effect buffer gets its own. `push_mask_layer` takes the same
  shape from the same function: two spellings of "unbounded" one function apart is how the two came
  to mean different things.
- **A mask run is a layer of its own, nested *inside* whatever the parent already pushed**
  (`scene::MaskRun`, §15 D282). It cannot be folded into the parent's clip: a parent has one clip for
  all of its children and a mask has one for a *run* of them, so a frame with two masks in it needs
  three clips over three stretches of one child list. It closes and reopens with the parent's layer,
  for `escape_clip`'s reason and in step with it — mask first out, mask last in — since a child on its
  way out of a frame draws unclipped *and* unmasked, in its own place among its siblings.
  `scene::mask_geometry` is the override-aware **mirror** of `Resolved::mask_path`, the relationship
  `build_of` has with `svg_of`, so a mask being dragged clips where the pointer is; ghosts carry
  `GhostNode::mask` and `GhostNode::mask_mode` for the same reason, so an Alt-drag copy of a masked
  group previews masked in whichever mode it is in.
- **The two mask modes are two layer arrangements, and `MaskRun::kind` is which** (§15 D288).
  `RunKind::Clip(BezPath)` is a shape mask: one layer carrying the outline as its clip, and the mask
  itself never drawn. `RunKind::Alpha(NodeId)` carries **the node, not geometry** — an alpha mask is not
  geometry, what matters is the ink it lays down, so the only way to ask for it is to draw it — and it
  arrives at the **end** of the run, because the mask composites *over* what it masks and what it masks
  has to be there first. The alpha arm's run layer carries **no clip**: it is an isolation group, so the
  composite reaches the run's own drawing and not the page behind it. `push_mask_layer` is then one
  `BlendMode::new(Mix::Normal, Compose::DestIn)` that both backends take on their own `push_layer`, so
  this is one mechanism rather than two and the GPU path needs nothing vello does not already do. It is
  a method of its own rather than a fifth parameter because it takes none of `push_layer`'s other
  decisions — no clip, no fill rule, no opacity. Neither mode reads the mask node's **own opacity**: for
  a shape mask the outline says which pixels survive and nothing about how much, and for an alpha mask
  the opacity is already in the ink by the time it is drawn, so folding it in again would apply it
  twice. One asymmetry to keep: a shape mask with no geometry masks *nothing*, while an **alpha mask
  with no ink legitimately erases the run** — that is the mode being honest, not a case to guard.
  ⚠️ **That asymmetry is about ink and not about the eye icon, and only the shape arm used to know it**
  (§15 D566). A **hidden** mask masks nothing in *either* mode — it is the first case §15 D282's rule
  names — and the shape arm got it from `mask_geometry`'s opening visibility test while the alpha arm
  asked nothing, so `end_run` pushed a `DestIn` layer over a node that draws nothing and the empty
  composite multiplied the whole run's alpha away. Hiding a 100×100 mask over a 200×200 rect left
  40,000 pixels in `Shape` and **0** in `Alpha`, while `query::hit_test` and `Resolved::world_bounds`
  went on answering as if the mask were there. Both arms now ask `scene::visible`, one named rule
  rather than the same line written twice, which is how the two came to disagree.
- **An effect layer is the outermost of a node's layers, and both positions are load-bearing**
  (`push_effect_layer`, §5.3a, §6.4, §15 D333). *Outside the clip*, so a clipping frame's own drop
  shadow falls outside the frame instead of being cut off at the very edge it exists to escape — the
  SVG writer needs a wrapper element for exactly this reason, and the two are one decision spelled
  twice (§7). *Outside the opacity*, so the shadow is cast from the layer as it actually appears: a
  half-transparent layer casts a half-transparent shadow rather than a solid one from a ghost. The two
  orders happen to agree for a plain fade and part company the moment a `Filters` row is in the stack,
  which is why this one is written down. The layer is pushed only when
  `effects::any_ink` says a pixel could change — **not** `!effects.is_empty()`, or every layer that
  has ever had an effect added and switched off pays for an offscreen buffer forever — and only when
  the node has cached bounds, so a node in the frame it was created in draws **unfiltered** rather
  than not at all. **A ghost gets its own in `paint_ghost`**, measured by `scene::ghost_ink` rather
  than looked up in `Resolved`, which has never seen it: without that an Alt-drag copy of a shadowed
  layer draws flat for the whole drag and gains its shadow at the instant of release, which is the same
  class of twitch the snapping rule below is about. ⚠️ **`ghost_ink` is `effect_bounds`' three arms and
  has to be** (§15 D567): it read `geometry::local_path(&ghost.kind)?.bounding_box()`, which answers
  `None` for `Root | Group | Text | Boolean`, so the `?` swallowed the computation and a ghost of any
  of those pushed **no effect layer at all** — a shadowed *group* previewed flat for the whole drag,
  which is the very twitch the sentence above claims this prevents. And an outline's box is not the
  ink's box: `geometry::world_bounds_of_parts` is what `Resolved` measures a leaf with, stroke
  expansion included, so a 40pt-stroked ghost's buffer was 20 units short on every side. A container's
  box is its children's, each grown by that child's own stack; a boolean's is `GhostNode::path`; every
  other kind goes through `world_bounds_of_parts`; and the growth is `effect::escaped`, the same
  arithmetic `effect_bounds` applies, because invariant 5 requires the two to land on one number.
  ⚠️ **Pushed at the top and popped at the *end* of `paint_node`, so every early return owes it a
  pop** (§15 D436). There is one: the `Boolean` arm, which returns from the middle because a boolean's
  children are operands rather than artwork. It unwound the clip/opacity layer and the mask run
  through `close` and asserted about the outer opacity layer, and left the effect layer open — so a
  drop shadow on a boolean made **the boolean and every layer after it** vanish, on the canvas and in
  `ondin export --png` alike, everything following being drawn into a layer that was never
  composited. Not folded into `close`, which is also called inside the children loop where the layer
  must stay open: it belongs to the whole node, not to a mask run. `paint_ghost`'s twin arm is unwound
  the same way, and **that unwind is load-bearing now rather than a precaution**. It was written while
  `geometry::local_path` answering `None` for `Boolean` meant it could not fire — a fact about a
  function two modules away, not about the arm, which is exactly why it was written rather than argued
  away — and `ghost_ink` ended that: a boolean ghost's box comes from its own `GhostNode::path`, so the
  layer is pushed and the pop is what keeps D436's bug out of the preview (§15 D567). ⚠️ **The comment
  in `scene.rs` still says it cannot fire.** *Fix the code comment.*
- **`RenderOverrides` is how a gesture is drawn** (invariant 5): per-node patches (transform, kind,
  paint, **effects**, opacity, visibility, re-shaped text) plus *ghosts* — artwork that does not exist yet, which
  is what a shape being dragged out with a create tool is and what the copy an Alt-drag carries is —
  plus one value belonging to no node,
  `canvas_background: Option<Color>`, absorbed from `SetCanvasBackground` so a drag in the picker
  previews the ground live (§15 D28). It is not part of the scene walk: the backdrop is the clear
  colour, handed to the renderer separately, so the override rides here only to reach that caller.
  It counts towards `is_empty`.

  **A ghost is a subtree, not a leaf.** `Ghost { parent, index, node }` separates the attachment point
  from the artwork, and `GhostNode` carries everything the walk reads off a `Node` — transform, kind,
  paint, effects, text, opacity, visibility, clip, mask — plus its own `children`, so a ghosted frame previews with
  its contents *and* clips them (`scene::paint_ghost` handles a ghost's clip layer and opacity the
  way `paint_node` does, and **stops at a `Boolean`** the way `paint_node` does too). It also carries
  the one piece of geometry a kind cannot state: `path`, a boolean ghost's combined outline, evaluated
  once when the subtree is built beside the shaped text and for the same reason — the walk must be
  handed derived geometry rather than compute it per frame (§9.4, §15 D94). The single childless leaf
  this replaced was all a shape tool needed, and it is what forced Alt-drag to move the original
  rather than the copy (§15 D40). One consequence is
  load-bearing: every setter looks in the **ghost forest before** the node map, because a transaction
  that adds artwork and then places it (`build::insert_subtrees` follows its `InsertSubtree` with a
  `SetTransform` for the new root) names a node the document has never seen — left to the node map
  that transform becomes an override keyed to an absent id and is dropped in silence, previewing the
  copy sat exactly on top of the original it came from. **The readers owe the same order**, which is
  newer and was missed once: `transform_of` answered `Affine::IDENTITY` for a ghost id — a ghost has
  no override entry, precisely because `absorb` writes into the ghost — and nothing drew wrong from it
  until a boolean began evaluating over a ghost operand (§15 D94). **`InsertSubtree`'s `index` is
  honoured**, and `scene::paint_node` interleaves ghosts among their parent's real children by it
  rather than drawing them last. Drawing last was the same z-order only while every caller appended;
  a copy that lands immediately above its original previews between that original and whatever sits
  over it (§15 D42, which recorded the gap and kept it until something asked).

  Two properties make it trustworthy rather than merely fast:

  1. **Built from the pending transaction.** `RenderOverrides::from_transaction` projects the exact
     `Transaction` the gesture will commit, so preview and result cannot describe different edits.
     A differential test builds the scene both ways — overrides over the untouched document, and
     the transaction actually applied — and requires the draw-call streams to be identical.
     ⚠️ **A live text session takes the one other door, `from_transaction_shaped`, and the
     differential does not cover it** (§9.3, §15 D592): the same projection with the session's
     already-shaped `TextLayout` handed in instead of re-derived, which is why that argument is a
     whole layout keyed to a `NodeId` — the property above then rests on the caller building both
     from the same `parts()`, and it does.
  2. **It refuses what it cannot represent.** The line runs *through* the structural ops rather
     than around them: one that only **adds** artwork is a ghost (`CreateNode`, `InsertSubtree`),
     because nothing in the committed tree changes and there is no node whose absence the walk has
     to fake. One that **moves or removes** an existing node — delete, reparent, reorder — is not
     representable at all, because a patch cannot say "somewhere else" or "not there". Those, and
     values `apply` would reject, return `None`, and the caller shows no preview at
     all. A missing preview is recoverable; a lying one is not. **`SetClip`, `SetMask` and
     `SetMaskMode` refuse for a
     third reason**, structural in the sense that matters here: each changes which *other* nodes the
     walk clips, where an override is a patch on one node. Nothing sets any of them mid-gesture — all
     three are a click on a panel — so refusing costs a preview nobody asks for (§15 D282, D288).
     **`SetFillRule` is the seventh refusal and the only one refused for neither reason** (§15 D239):
     it patches one node and nothing else, so it is not structural, but there is no `NodeOverride`
     field for the rule and adding one would buy a live preview of a control that is a click. It is
     also emitted by `build::boolean` when that makes an `Exclude`, and a boolean is committed rather
     than dragged out. *If anything ever scrubs the rule, the fix is a field here rather than a change
     of category* — and the seventh is why this list must not be collapsed into "the structural ops":
     six of the seven refusals are about structure in one sense or the other and one is about a
     missing field, so `absorb`'s arms are the record of which is which.

  **`SetEffects` is patchable, and its arm also marks the node moved** (§15 D333). The patch is the
  whole stack, as the op is; the *moved* mark is the part that is not obvious, and it is there because
  an effect reaches outside the layer it hangs on, so the cached bounds no longer cover where the ink
  lands. Every number in an effect popover is a scrub, so without this arm each of them is the
  unscrubbable field of §15 D245 — and it was `absorb`'s `match` being wildcard-free that forced the
  decision rather than letting it be forgotten: the missing arm was the single compile error in the
  workspace.

  Refusing is not the same as ignoring, and the five guide ops (§5.7) are the case that draws the
  line. A guide is egui chrome rather than scene content (§9.4), so there is nothing here for one to
  patch — but returning `None` for them would blank the preview of everything *else* in the same
  transaction. They are absorbed as no-ops returning `Some`, and the app previews a guide being
  moved from its own gesture state instead (`OndinApp::shown_guide`). `SetPivot` sits in that same
  arm, beside `SetName`/`SetLocked`/`SetProportionsLocked`, and for a stronger reason: the pivot is
  *baked* by whichever gesture reads it rather than composed into the world transform, so the
  renderer has nothing to do with it at all and what a pivot edit previews is chrome (§15 D55). The
  canvas drag draws that chrome from the live pointer; the origin *fields* have no pointer of their
  own to draw from, so `EditorSession::pivot_preview` carries the pending value beside the overrides
  and `preview_pivot` reads it — without which a field re-reading its base from the committed node
  cannot be scrubbed at all (§15 D245, D247).

  ⚠️ **There is a *second* no-op arm and no document mentioned it until 2026-09-09** (§15 D659):
  `AddImage | RemoveImage`, which brings `absorb`'s no-ops to **thirteen** against `changes_ink`'s
  eleven (§5.7). It is **the only no-op here that is not also invisible** — an image op changes what is
  drawn — and it is a no-op because `RenderOverrides` has no image table to patch, the two honest
  answers being this or refusing the whole preview. Refusing is worse: a transaction that places an
  image is `AddImage` *and* a `CreateNode`, so declining would blank the preview of the shape as well
  as the picture in it. What it costs is that a previewed image is not visible until the commit lands,
  which nothing exercises yet — placing is a click, not a drag. *If something ever drags one, the fix
  is a preview table on the overrides, the shape `canvas_background` already has here.*
  `overrides.rs · every_no_op_of_absorb_is_a_no_op_and_two_of_them_still_change_ink` pins all
  thirteen and asserts its own list lengths; what it cannot do is prove there is no fourteenth, which
  needs a value of every `Operation` variant and is `op.rs`'s fixture's job.

  Empty overrides reduce the walk to the committed document exactly — the world transforms it
  composes down the tree are bit-identical to `Resolved`'s, so export is unaffected. **One transform
  is deliberately not**: an axis-aligned box whose device edges do not already land on whole pixels
  is rounded onto them (§6.3, §15 D197), which is a function of the viewport and so could never have
  come out of `Resolved` at all. A box already on the grid is returned untouched, which is what keeps
  the sentence above true wherever it can be — not an optimisation, since the round trip through the
  base transform's inverse perturbs an untouched matrix in the fourteenth decimal and
  `assert_preview_matches_commit` compares exactly.

### 6.3 Backends

- **GPU (`vello`)**: owns `vello::Renderer`; the app supplies the `wgpu` device/queue (shared with
  egui). Build path: z-order walk, culling any node whose **ink** bounds miss the viewport (§5.3a,
  §15 D334 — the paragraph below has why it is that box and not the editing one) — which
  also skips its whole subtree *when those bounds cover it*, i.e. a group (whose bounds are its
  children's union), a frame that clips (whose bounds are the limit of what its children can
  paint), or a **boolean** — whose bounds cover its subtree *exactly*, the walk stopping dead there
  because its children are its operands rather than artwork, which makes it the strongest member of
  the list and not a doubtful one. ⚠️ **It was missing from that list until 2026-09-08** (§15 D536):
  a boolean has children, does not clip and is neither `Group` nor `Root`, so the predicate came out
  `false` and every boolean in the document was walked, `paint_shape`d and encoded on every frame
  wherever the view was — 800 parked booleans issuing **801** fills against a group document's **1**,
  each fill also cloning a whole `BezPath`. The list has never been observable in a fill count for a
  *group*, whose descendants are culled leaf by leaf whatever it says, which is why nobody saw it be
  wrong. A frame with `clip` off is none of the three, so its contents are walked (§5.3), and a node
  holding a ghost is never culled at all, since cached bounds cannot know about a layer that does not
  exist yet (§15 D27) — pushing world
  affines and peniko/kurbo data into the scene (near-zero
  translation: the model already speaks kurbo/peniko), opacity and artboard clipping via layers,
  text via the glyph-run API from the cached parley layouts. v1 rebuilds the in-view scene per
  frame; the fragment-caching seam stays in `scene.rs` for later.
- **CPU (`vello_cpu`)**: same `scene.rs` walk, no GPU, deterministic output → used by PNG export and
  `ondin serve`. This removes GPU-in-CI entirely, and is what makes a raster golden possible at all
  (§11 — none is written yet). **Deterministic at a fixed SIMD level, and the export path fixes it**:
  `cpu.rs`'s `export_settings` pins `Level::baseline()` through `RenderContext::new_with`, because
  with the level merely detected a *stroked path* rasterizes differently under AVX2 from the way it
  does under SSE4.2 or the scalar fallback — measured at 17 differing bytes over 7 pixels of the
  exported buffer, worst channel delta 9, all of it on near-transparent edge pixels. Every other
  primitive measured — fills, gradients, blend layers, glyph runs — is level-invariant. The pin is
  **export-only**: `rasterize_glyph_run` keeps the detected level for the font picker's live preview
  strips. ⚠️ **It also *declines* rather than truncating** (§15 D586): `RenderContext` and `Pixmap`
  take `u16` dimensions and this reached them through a bare `as u16`, which wraps — 8 × 70,000
  returned 142,848 bytes for a caller holding a `ColorImage` that wanted 2,240,000, and epaint
  asserted on the UI thread. It answers `Option<Vec<u8>>` and refuses anything past
  `MAX_RASTER_SIDE`, which is this crate's constant (§7). `baseline()` is target-derived, so byte-comparability holds across machines of one
  architecture (§15 D304) — **and one pinned `vello_cpu`**, the `=0.0.9` → `=0.2.0` bump having moved
  that same stroked path and nothing else (§15 D414). `cpu.rs`'s `raster_settings` spells out all four
  rasterizer settings at **every** `vello_cpu` call site rather than only the export one — the flush is
  where a default would bite silently — so no upstream default can move a raster unannounced.
- **Effects: both backends implement them, from one specification** (§5.3a, §6.4, §15 D333, D339).
  `CpuPainter::push_effect_layer` renders the layer into an offscreen `RenderContext` sized
  from the walk's ink box — clamped to the enclosing target **grown by the escape**
  (`effect::buffer_box_within`), so an effect on a layer mostly off-screen costs the visible part *and*
  keeps the silhouette that casts into it; clamping to the bare target loses the shadow of a layer
  scrolled out of view (§15 D342) — but never past **the page's own pixel count**, because the escape
  is measured in device pixels and therefore grows with the zoom without any bound at all: a layer
  covering the viewport gives its escape up rather than the GPU, at a measured cost of one part in 255
  on a quarter of one per cent of pixels (§15 D402) — and, when the layer's own blur is wide enough to
  have destroyed the detail,
  at a **coarser resolution** than the device's (`effect::buffer_downscale`, §15 D395), because a
  gaussian of deviation σ carries nothing finer than σ and the convolution otherwise grows without
  bound as someone zooms in, to the point of tripping the GPU's watchdog — runs `effects::run` over
  its `Pixmap`, which is already premultiplied sRGB
  and therefore borrowed rather than converted, and composites the result back through
  `ImageSource::Pixmap`. It keeps a **stack** of `FxFrame`s, and `base` is the *current* target's
  rather than the page's, saved on push and restored on pop: a backend that left `base` alone would
  draw the layer's contents at the page's coordinates inside a buffer that starts somewhere else, i.e.
  mostly off the edge of it. The offscreen route is taken even for the two effects `vello_cpu`'s own
  `push_layer` filter could serve, so that all four go through one mechanism on both backends.
  ⚠️ **The buffer's *size* comes from one function too, and it is capped by resampling rather than by
  truncation** (`effects::effect_buffer`, `effects::MAX_EFFECT_BUFFER_SIDE` = 8192, §15 D744). Both
  backends said `.min(u16::MAX as f64)` — a number neither can build: eight times the GPU's
  `max_texture_dimension_2d`, so a large layer allocated scratch textures past the limit and **wgpu
  validation aborted the process** where the CPU backend and both exports drew the document correctly;
  and 127 pixels past `cpu::MAX_RASTER_SIDE` on the other side. Past the cap `k` grows until both
  sides fit, which is D395's mechanism rather than a new one — **truncating cuts the silhouette a
  shadow is cast from**, so the shadow comes off a stump and the defect reads as a rendering bug
  rather than as a bound. The number is fixed rather than the device's own maximum for D395's reason:
  two backends must choose the same buffer for one drawing, and a device limit is a property of
  whoever opened the file. It is also vello's `MAX_ATLAS_SIZE` (§5.5a), so one number bounds the
  effect scratch textures and the image atlas alike.
- **The GPU backend does the same thing one step later, because a `vello::Scene` is a recording**
  (§15 D339). `GpuScenePainter::push_effect_layer` redirects drawing into a **sub-scene** with the
  same clamped box, the same outward rounding and the same scale taken from the composed device
  transform; `pop_layer` closes it into an `EffectJob` and puts a `draw_image` of a fresh atlas slot
  in the enclosing scene. After the walk, `VelloGpuRenderer::resolve_effects` rasterizes the jobs,
  runs `fx_gpu`'s compute passes over each, and points its slot at the result with
  `Renderer::override_image` — **deepest nesting level first**, since a frame is recorded as it pops,
  so a nested layer's texture is registered before the scene that draws it is rendered. The slots are
  unregistered at the end of the frame: they are keyed by blob id and every frame mints new ones.
  ⚠️ **On the renderer that will *draw* the slot, which for a nested layer is not the page's** (§15
  D404). A layer's result is drawn by the scene it popped back into — the page for a top-level layer,
  the **parent layer's own sub-scene** for anything deeper — and that sub-scene belongs to a
  level-above pass with an atlas of its own. Registering only on the page's made vello panic with
  *"Tried to draw an invalid empty image"* the moment one effect layer contained another, from the day
  effects landed until 2026-09-01. That is why the passes are **planned before any of them runs**: a
  level's consumers are the passes of the level above, which have not happened yet, and `Holder`
  records where each slot went so the unregister reaches the same atlas.
  ⚠️ **One vello pass per *renderer*, and that is a correctness rule** (§15 D344). vello's image atlas
  evicts a resident image that has not been *drawn* for two resolve passes, and every
  `render_to_texture` is one — so a renderer doing N passes a frame loses any picture that
  appears in only one of them, which is how an image fill came to draw nothing whenever any layer on
  the page carried an effect. Sibling layers are packed into as few textures as possible
  (`Scene::append` at each slot's origin) and rasterized together, and **every pass takes the next
  renderer**, built on demand. That leaves every renderer — the page's included — at one pass a frame.
  The passes read their slot out of the packed texture through `fx_gpu::Slice`, so nothing is copied
  on the way in. Measured: 20 effect layers cost the same as eight — flat in the layer count **so
  long as the level packs into one texture**. 🚨 **That proviso was not in this sentence, and §15 D402
  is what put it there**: the page-area budget below splits a level whose layers outgrow the page, so
  above that line the layer count changes the pass count again (§15 D776).
  ⚠️ **How many renderers that costs was never observed until 2026-09-15, and for a *nested* document
  it is the nesting *depth*** (§15 D763). `VelloGpuRenderer::pass_high_water` records the busiest frame's
  demand; on an RTX 4070 Ti, one blur is **1** pass, a blur inside a shadow **2**, three deep **3** —
  so a realistically nested drawing pays about `3 × 7 ms` of pipeline build **once in the life of
  the process** and holds three renderers. ⚠️ **One `Renderer` is a 6–8 ms band measured on an
  otherwise-idle adapter, and 15 ms for the first in the process** (§15 D763, D777); **D344's
  *"84 ms to build"* does not reproduce**, against the same `AaSupport::all()` default and the same
  pinned vello 0.9.0, and that entry records no profile, machine or version to adjudicate it by.
  🚨 **The condition is load-bearing**: the same build is **48–65 ms** when the on-device test suite
  is contending for the adapter, about seven times over, which is contention rather than drift —
  `--test-threads=1` reproduces the idle figures exactly. 6–8 ms is the number this paragraph's
  arithmetic wants, the app not building renderers from thirteen threads, but **a band quoted
  without its condition is how the wrong one gets carried forward** (§15 D777). 🚨 **The sibling case is the one the budget below is about,
  and it is the unbounded half** (§15 D776): many layers at *one* level whose combined area exceeds
  the page, where depth is bounded by how deeply a designer nests and area is not. Measured the same
  day on the same card — 32 blurred squares at one level demand **11** passes on a 100×100 page,
  **3** on a 200×200 and **1** on a 400×400 — so the count is a **ratio**, total effect-buffer area ÷
  page area, and **the depth figure above answers only the nested case**. Nothing anywhere caps the
  pass count. ⚠️ At a full page the binding constraint is the shelf *row* rather than the ink, `pack`
  weighing the packed texture's bounding box: at 1920×1080 the break falls at about forty overlapping
  on-screen effect layers, which is reasoned from `pack` and not measured at that size.
  🚨 **Bounding the renderers and reusing them is declined** (§15 **D779**, 2026-09-15). Those two
  figures together make the bill a **one-off hitch** — about 77 ms on the frame that first demands
  the worst `K` ever measured here, and nothing after it — while a pool has to answer D344's
  correctness rule rather than a cost, and D344's symptom was a pasted image drawing nothing from
  the second frame onwards. **If the hitch is ever felt, build renderers off the critical frame
  rather than share one across passes**, which leaves the rule above intact.
  ⚠️ **What bounds a pass is the page, not the layer count** (§15 D402). `pack` starts a new chunk
  rather than let one exceed the page's own pixel area, because vello's intermediate buffers are fixed
  sizes and it cannot report an overflow: `render_to_texture` neither reads the bump allocators back
  nor returns an error, so past that capacity the fine shader **hangs**, Windows resets the GPU after
  two seconds, and the app dies in whatever the next frame touches first. The unit of a pass was the
  nesting *level* until that budget existed, which is why the renderers are handed out per pass now —
  splitting a level without splitting the renderers would put D344's bug straight back.
  ⚠️ **Straight alpha at the two ends and premultiplied in the middle**, which is the one place the
  backends genuinely differ at the seam. `vello_cpu`'s `Pixmap` is premultiplied, so the CPU backend
  hands its buffer to `effects::run` untouched; **vello's GPU output is straight** — measured, not
  assumed — and its image atlas takes straight alpha too, so `fx_gpu` brackets the stack with a
  `premul`/`unpremul` pair.
  **Culling reads `ink_bounds`, not `world_bounds`** (`scene::paint_node`), so a layer whose own box
  has left the viewport is still walked while its shadow reaches into it. This paragraph carried the
  ⚠️ opposite as an open defect until 2026-09-01; the fix D334 asked for is in, in all three of the
  readers that entry names — `paint_node`, `plan::raster_size` and `plan::raster_opts`. ⚠️ **The
  record was the last thing to follow, and it took three passes**: D334's index line was restruck on
  2026-09-06, and §5.9's and §7's copies of the same claim on 2026-09-07. **Four passages said the
  cull read `world_bounds` for a fortnight after it stopped** — which is what a `Fix` verdict costs
  when the fix lands and nothing restrikes the places that asked for it.
- GPU output is *not* expected to be byte-identical to CPU output in general — the two rasterizers
  antialias differently, so any fractional or rotated edge disagrees. GPU correctness is covered by
  an on-device suite the default run skips for want of an adapter
  (`cargo test -p ondin-render -- --ignored`).
  **The effect passes are the exception, and deliberately**: `fx_gpu`'s shaders quantise on the same
  8-bit ladder as `effects.rs` and convolve with the kernel the host builds from the same function,
  so where the rasterizers have nothing to disagree about the effects have nothing either.
  `tests/fx_gpu.rs` compares the passes over one buffer and allows **one** channel — the cost of the
  premultiplied round trip the GPU path needs and the CPU one does not — and
  `gpu_effects::both_backends_draw_the_same_shadow` renders a whole document through both and asserts
  **exact** equality on a fixture placed on integer pixel boundaries for exactly that reason.
- **Axis-aligned boxes are rounded onto whole device pixels.** vello computes coverage per path and
  alpha-blends each path independently, so where two shapes share an edge that falls at fraction `f`
  across a device pixel, `f(1−f)` of whatever is *behind* both leaks between them — a lighter line
  down the join, peaking at a quarter of the fill→backdrop contrast. `scene::snapped_box_world`
  adjusts the world transform of a `Rect` or an `Artboard` so its device edges are integers, against
  the grid `scene::device_base` derives from the viewport — **the same affine both painters apply on
  top of the walk's** (`cpu::CpuPainter::base`, `gpu::GpuScenePainter::base`, each computing it
  inline), so those three have to stay in step or the walk snaps to a grid nothing rasterizes on.
  Everything rounds to *one* global grid, so anything that abutted still abuts and the edge they now
  meet on carries no antialiasing to conflate. The snapped transform is the node's own ink only — its
  background, its clip and its stroke, so those cannot part company — and never its children's, which
  snap on their own terms against the same grid; a ghost snaps by the same rule as the node it will
  become. Only `Rect` and `Artboard`, and only where the device transform is a pure scale and
  translate, so rotated pairs, ellipses, polygons and paths still conflate.
  **Two boxes are exempt, and they are exempt together** (`RenderOverrides::unsnapped`, §15 D272):
  image editing's chrome ghost and the layer it is glued to. Rounding rebuilds a box's *scale* from
  its rounded span, so two rectangles of different sizes round differently — and the offcut is a
  continuation of the layer drawn several window-widths wider, where a half-pixel miss over the
  window becomes a whole pixel out at its far edge. Reported as the ghost sliding 1–2px as the crop
  was dragged. Neither opts out alone: making them *equal* is the requirement, and the layer's
  rounding is computed here from the device base, so the only place the two can agree is by both
  standing out. What it costs is this seam mitigation on one layer for as long as somebody is looking
  at its crop — which is the trade in the other direction, since snapping is what makes edges step
  rather than glide.
  `scene::SNAP_BOXES_TO_DEVICE_PIXELS` is the switch. §15 D197 has the measurements, what was ruled
  out, and the two guards that are load-bearing.
- **Every visible paint is drawn, and the order is fills then strokes.** `paint_shape` walks
  `fills` in `Vec` order and then `strokes` in `Vec` order, skipping the ones switched off, so the
  last element of each list is the last painted (§5.3). Text is one pass over the *same* shaped runs
  per visible fill — never re-shaped, §5.9 — and falls back to black when it has none, because ink
  that vanished with its last fill would read as the text itself having gone. A `Line` skips fills
  entirely, having no interior. ⚠️ **A frame is the one kind that may not fall through to that tail**,
  and the fill loop is therefore written twice on purpose (§15 D400): the tail fills *and then* strokes
  in one place, while a frame's fills go behind its children and its strokes over them and outside its
  own clip (§15 D144) — two different depths of the walk, so the loop is in `paint_shape`'s frame arm
  and the stroke call stays in `paint_node`. A rule added to one of the two loops is owed to the other.
  Pinned by `all_visible_paints_are_drawn_fills_first_then_strokes`,
  `a_hidden_paint_is_skipped_and_the_rest_keep_their_order` and
  `a_line_stacks_its_strokes_and_ignores_its_fills`; §15 D56 has the milestone in which this walk drew
  the first visible paint of each list and nothing else.
- **Stroke alignment is built, not delegated.** No 2D backend in the stack has it — not vello, not
  `vello_cpu`, not SVG — so `scene.rs` constructs it: stroke at **twice** the width, which reaches a
  full width either side of the outline, then clip away the half you do not want. What survives is
  exactly one width of paint on the chosen side. Inside clips to the shape (non-zero); outside clips
  to the shape *plus* an enclosing box taken **even-odd**, which is "everything but the shape".
  Even-odd rather than a reversed-winding trick for two reasons: the direction the user drew a path
  in is unknown, and a shape with a hole gets the right answer (the hole is outside). **That
  enclosing box has to clear the *ink*, not the shape**: `scene::outer_bounds` takes a `reach`, and
  `scene::miter_reach(width, limit) = width · limit.max(1.0)` is what states it, because the doubled
  stroke's half-width *is* the nominal width and a mitre runs that far times the limit out from the
  vertex. Padding by the shape's own extent alone left the ring's outer edge *inside* a wide stroke
  and cut rectangular bites out of it (§15 D97). This is why
  `ScenePainter::push_layer` carries a `ClipRule` and `StrokePaint` carries no alignment — by the
  time a stroke reaches a backend it is always centred. Alignment needs a closed outline to have an
  inside, so `geometry::stroke_align_applies` gates it and open shapes draw centred; the renderer,
  the SVG writer and the inspector all ask that one function, so they cannot disagree about which
  shapes qualify. Verified at the pixel level, not by call sequence:
  `stroke_alignment_puts_the_paint_on_the_right_side_of_the_outline`. A `Boolean` is answered **by
  kind** there rather than measured, because measuring goes through `local_path`, which cannot build
  its outline (§9.4, §15 D93); that case is pinned through the *markup* instead —
  `an_aligned_stroke_on_a_boolean_exports_with_its_clip` asserts the `clipPath`, since the clip is the
  whole construction — and is one of the booleans still owed a pixel comparison.
- **A per-side stroke is one call per edge, along an open path.** `geometry::side_path(kind, side)`
  returns the **open** `BezPath` a side occupies, with each corner arc split at its 45° midpoint so a
  rounded rect's top edge owns half of each top corner — what CSS does with `border-top` against
  `border-radius`, and the only cut that lets two sides of different widths meet cleanly. Cutting at
  the straight edge instead leaves a rounded rect's corners bare, which reads as four gaps rather
  than a border. The radii come back off `RoundedRect::from_rect(…).radii()` rather than being
  clamped again locally, so a side's arc is the same curve the fill uses; a zero-radius corner
  contributes its sharp vertex. The walk therefore separates **what gets stroked from what the
  alignment clip is built from** — the same path for a whole outline, and different per side, because
  "inside" is a question about the *rect* and not about the edge. For the
  same reason `closed` is asked of the **kind** rather than measured off `path`: a side path is open,
  but the shape it belongs to is not. `StrokePaint` carries no `sides` field, exactly as it carries no
  alignment — by the time a backend sees a stroke it is one path and one width (§15 D68).
- **One alignment clip per *run* of same-aligned strokes.** `scene::paint_strokes` walks the stroke list
  and pushes one clip layer for each maximal run of consecutive strokes that agree about alignment, so
  two outside strokes share one mask and one complement path where they used to build one each per
  frame. Runs and not a sort, because the list order **is** the z-order: grouping across a differently
  aligned stroke would move paint. All four sides of one per-side stroke ride that stroke's clip, as the
  SVG writer already had them. §15 D146 has the measurements, including the finding that the clip was
  never the dominant cost — building four side paths a shape a frame is.
- **Type strokes, on the outline of its own glyphs.** `ondin_core::text::outline` builds that outline
  from the cached layout (no re-shaping) and the text branch of the walk hands it to the same
  `paint_strokes` a shape uses, so `StrokeAlign::Outside` on a text node is outlined type and not a
  special case. Built at the render boundary and **only when a visible stroke exists** — it costs about a
  microsecond a glyph, which is why the gate is load-bearing. Neither backend's glyph-stroking call is
  used: it would only buy the centred case, and alignment needs a clip built from the outlines anyway
  (§15 D145).
- **The dash pattern reaching a backend is resolved, not the model's own.**
  `geometry::resolved_dashes(stroke, width, path)` is where the two things §5.3 refuses to store are
  turned into numbers, and it takes the width *actually being laid down*, so a `Custom` side's own
  width decides its dots and its fitting. A zero-length dash — which is how a dot is stored — draws
  nothing under `Cap::Butt` or `Cap::Square`, so those two get a square dot one width long with the
  gap shortened to match: the **period is preserved**, which is what keeps the spacing field meaning
  one thing under all three caps. And `dash_fit` scales the pattern through
  `geometry::fitted_dashes` so a whole number of periods spans the outline — the *nearest* count,
  not the floor, since flooring can stretch every dash by a full period where nearest moves each by
  at most half of one. The cost is the path's `perimeter` at render and export time. Fitting is
  measured **per subpath**, not against the whole path: a fit scale is a property of one closed run and
  one `dashes` array cannot say two things, so `geometry::dash_fit_pieces` splits a multi-subpath path
  into one piece per subpath with that subpath's own pattern — and answers `None`, cloning nothing, for
  every stroke that has no fit to disagree about (§15 D69, D147).
- **Ink at least as wide as the shape is thin is filled, not stroked.** Every alignment arm of
  `paint_stroke` goes through `scene::lay_stroke` rather than calling `ScenePainter::stroke_path`
  itself, and past its gate — `width >= min(bbox)`, closed paths, solid patterns — it expands the
  outline with `kurbo::stroke`, drops the expansion's inner contours (`outermost_subpaths`), appends
  the outline's own path, winds every subpath alike (`wound_alike`) so a non-zero fill is a plain
  union, and fills that. Below the gate nothing changes and the backend's own expander does the work.
  This is the fix for a very wide stroke leaving a hole in the middle of its own ink, and §15 D131 has
  the measurements, the two simpler constructions that do not work, and why the gate cannot fire late.
  **The SVG writer does not have it**: it hands `stroke-width` to the consumer, so at these widths an
  export and the canvas can disagree (§7).
- **The mitre limit passes straight through** as the ratio it is stored as (`StrokePaint::miter_limit`
  → `kurbo::Stroke::with_miter_limit`), in both backends. Nothing in the render path knows about
  degrees; that conversion belongs to the panel (§5.3).
- **An image fill is framed by the walk, and each backend is told in its own idiom.**
  `scene::framing_of` resolves one `Framing` per draw, reading the intrinsic size from the
  **document's image table and not from the decode cache** — the table stores it precisely so that
  layout never waits on a decode (§5.5a), and the walk *is* layout: a picture mid-decode must frame
  at the size it will be, or every image jumps on the frame it first appears. vello takes the
  transform per call as a `brush_transform` and composes `transform * brush_transform`, which is why
  the framing is computed in the node's local space; `vello_cpu`'s paint transform is **context
  state** instead, so `apply_paint` sets it on **every** call — the framing for an image, and
  `color::brush_to_backend`'s second answer otherwise, which is the identity for a solid and the
  brush's own transform for a gradient (§15 D412). Left standing, an image's framing would go on
  transforming the next shape's gradient; it was cleared with `reset_paint_transform()` until an
  imported ellipse needed a transform of its own, and setting it unconditionally is what keeps the
  rule in one arm rather than two. The extend belongs to the fit and is put in force at the boundary by
  `color::apply_framing`/`color::framed_sampler`, **never written back into the model**, so the two
  cannot drift; quality and alpha stay the model's. The pixels come from `ImageStore::pixels` and not
  from `get` — the fill's own adjustment resolved, which may be a reduced preview while a slider moves
  — **except on the GPU, which asks `atlas_pixels` for the same buffer shrunk to the page's share of
  vello's atlas** (`color::Resolution`, §6.2, §5.5a, §15 D745), the one resolution the two backends are
  meant to disagree about; so `color::brush_to_backend` hands back a `(Brush, Affine)` pair and `color::framed_transform`
  composes the framing over the buffer's own grid; neither backend may set a brush transform without
  it (§5.5a, §15 D186). `scene::clipped` wraps the single draw a
  letterboxing `Fit` asks for (§15 D178). And `paint_strokes` takes its frame as an explicit `Rect`
  rather than deriving `shape.bounding_box()`, because outlined **type** is stroked along its glyph
  outlines and framed in its text box (`layout.bounds()`) — deriving it would put a picture at one
  scale through the letters and another behind them.
- **A picture that cannot be drawn is a drawing, not a skipped call.** `scene::fill_or_placeholder` is
  the one place a *fill* becomes ink — a shape's own fills and an artboard's background both go through
  it — and where `ScenePainter::has_image` says the store has no pixels it hands off to
  `scene::paint_missing`: `ondin_core::missing_placeholder`'s grey ground on the shape, then a layer
  clipped to the **shape's own path** with the cross and the rim stroked inside it, so an image fill in
  a circle stays a circle. It goes through `fill_path`/`stroke_path` like artwork, so `ondin export
  --png` carries it and both backends draw it from one description. A **stroke** or a text run painted
  with a missing picture still draws nothing, deliberately: the placeholder is a statement about an
  area and a stroke has none. §15 D179 has the merged three states and the repair. ⚠️ **"Draws
  nothing" is a `return`, not an omission, and the CPU backend did not make it until 2026-09-06** (§15
  D437): `apply_paint` answers `false` for a brush that resolved to nothing, `fill_path` and
  `stroke_path` return on that answer and `draw_text` discarded it — and since `vello_cpu`'s paint is
  *context state*, the run came out in the previous node's colour rather than in nothing. Every golden
  agreed, the CPU backend being the reference.
- **Color (`color.rs`)**: document colors (sRGB straight alpha) are converted to whatever each
  backend's contract requires — determined by *reading the pinned versions' docs and verifying with
  a pixel test*, not assumed. If a backend accepts sRGB `peniko::Color` directly, the conversion is
  identity — the point is the single choke point plus the test.

### 6.4 The effect passes (`effects.rs`)

**One implementation of the pixel arithmetic, read by both backends** — and that is a dependency
fact rather than a preference. `vello` 0.9 has no filter of any kind beyond
`draw_blurred_rounded_rect`, so the GPU canvas has to grow its own passes whatever happens, and
`vello_cpu` 0.2.0 implements only `GaussianBlur` and `DropShadow`, single-primitive graphs only — no
`ColorMatrix`, no `Composite`, so neither colour filters nor an inner shadow can be expressed there
at all. ⚠️ **That was re-checked at the `=0.0.9` → `=0.2.0` bump rather than renumbered** (§15 D414):
the filter module grew `flood`, `offset` and `shift`, and neither of the two missing kinds is among
them, so the argument holds for the same reason it did. Leaning on the library for the two it has would mean **two implementations of blur** on the
two backends §3 exists to keep identical. So these functions are the specification, the CPU backend
is the reference, and the GPU shaders are written against it — `fx.wgsl` has one entry point per step
of `effects::run`, in the same order, over the same premultiplied 8-bit values, with the gaussian
kernel built by `effects::kernel` on the host and handed to the shader as a buffer rather than the
formula being evaluated a second time (§15 D333, D339). `tests/fx_gpu.rs` runs the two over one
buffer and compares the bytes.

⚠️ **`ondin-export` reads two of these functions across the crate boundary and that stays**
(§15 D702, **D783**). `svg.rs` calls `effects::filter_matrix` once from the `<filter>` emitter and
`effects::any_ink` twice, which is why §3's graph says SVG needs `ondin-render` and not core alone.
**Moving the two into `ondin-core` was proposed and declined**: §3 permits it — both are pure over
`ondin_core::effect` types — and this paragraph is what refuses, because the move splits the
specification, leaving `filter_matrix`'s twenty coefficients, in the order `fx.wgsl` packs them five
to a row, in a crate that has no backend to hold them to. **The dependency comment was corrected
instead**, that being the cheaper of the two and what its reader actually needs.

`Surface { px: &mut [u8], w, h }` is the seam: RGBA8, deliberately neither `vello_cpu::Pixmap` nor a
`wgpu::Texture`, since both backends can hand over a slice and neither should own the type. Its
constructor **asserts** the length rather than debug-asserting it, because the bug class here is an
off-by-one on a stride, which in release silently shears the picture instead of failing.

Two conventions are pinned in that module because they are invisible when wrong:

- **Pixels are premultiplied.** Blurring straight alpha mixes the colour of fully transparent pixels
  into their neighbours and draws a halo round every soft edge — which reads as "the blur looks
  dirty" rather than as a bug in a convolution. Invariant 7 governs what the *document* stores; this
  is downstream of `color.rs`, where the conversion has already happened.
- **Filters run in sRGB, not linear.** SVG's `color-interpolation-filters` defaults to `linearRGB`,
  so every filter we emit says `sRGB` explicitly (§7) — matching what `svg::adjust_def` already did
  for image adjustments. Blurring in linear light is arguably more correct and is emphatically not
  what any design tool does: matching Figma matters more than matching physics here, and the three
  writers agreeing matters more than either.

**`run` is two stages, not one fold**, and the SVG writer is arranged the same way for the same
reason. `Filters` and `LayerBlur` transform the layer's own appearance in list order; every shadow is
then cast from *that* result and merged behind it or over it. The one-fold version — each effect
reading whatever the previous one produced — is the obvious spelling and it is wrong in a way the
markup shows plainly: an inner shadow following a drop shadow takes its silhouette from the layer
**plus the shadow**, drawing a second inner edge along the shadow's outside. Casting every shadow
from the layer is also what Figma does, and what anyone stacking two shadows at different distances
expects.

⚠️ **The bound has to be computed the same way, and it was not until 2026-09-07** (§15 D473).
`effect::stack_escape` took a plain union of the per-effect escapes, which is right for two shadows —
side by side out of one silhouette — and wrong for everything this staging *composes*: two `LayerBlur`s
run one after the other convolve at `σ = √(σ₁² + σ₂²)`, and a shadow cast from `graphic` starts from a
silhouette already stage-1 wider on every side. Measured, a 40×40 rect under
`[LayerBlur { radius: 12 }, DropShadow { offset: (0, 40), blur: 4 }]` claimed a `y1` escape of 46
where the ink reaches 64 — and since that box is also the **buffer** the pass works in, the shadow came
out with a hard edge at 38/255 rather than merely mis-culled. The escape is taken per stage now and
§5.3a states the arithmetic. **This paragraph and `stack_escape` are one decision written in two
places**: reordering the stages here is a change to that function too, and nothing fails if only one
of them moves.

`filter_matrix` composes a `Filters` row into the 4×5 `feColorMatrix` array — the layout SVG takes
and the one `AdjustPipeline` already uses, so the writer emits it with no rearranging — in the order
**brightness → contrast → saturation → hue**, which is the order the panel lists them in. Matrix
composition does not commute, so that order is part of the specification: the canvas, the raster
export and the file have to pick the same one. The luminance weights are the spec's sRGB
0.213/0.715/0.072 and **not** the 0.299/0.587/0.114 of the older NTSC formula, which is the likelier
thing to type from memory and is a visibly different grey. `device_sigma` returns **two** deviations,
because a non-uniform scale blurs unevenly: a node's transform carries no scale (§5.6) but the
viewport does, an export at 2× does, and a skew in an ancestor does — one averaged sigma makes a blur
on a skewed layer round rather than leaning. `spread_alpha` is a **box** dilation, which is what
SVG's `feMorphology` does, so the export and the canvas are boxy in the *same* way rather than one of
them being right alone — **and it takes two half-widths for the reason `device_sigma` takes two
deviations** (§15 D601). It took one, `spread * scale.0.max(scale.1)`, so a 10-unit spread at
`scale = (4, 1)` drew 40 device pixels on *both* axes where the vertical wanted 10. The factor is the
ratio of the two column norms `push_effect_layer` computes, so it is unbounded rather than a
rounding, and `tools::side_shear` is a shipped gesture that produces one.
⚠️ **The bounds were the half that was already right, which is what turns this into a ruled line
rather than a shadow that is merely too thick.** `effect::escape` has always added the spread in
*document* units per side, so `escaped` maps it through the linear part of the world transform as an
**ellipse** and allocates `spread × scale` per axis — 40/10 for that case, correct, and disagreeing
with the ink. `grow_to_escape` ends `device_ink.intersect(grown)`, so the surplus 30 device pixels on
the short axis were cut off with a straight edge. §5.9's *"too small is the one error these bounds
may not make"* was kept by the bounds and broken by the **drawing**: the same symptom as D473's, from
the opposite direction, and with no bounds arithmetic to look at.
⚠️ **And the spread's half-width is bounded by the buffer it runs in, which nothing bounded until
2026-09-09** (`effects::spread_steps`, §15 D615). `n` is in **device pixels** — the authored number
times the zoom — and the only cap anywhere was `inspector::MAX_OFFSET`, a range the panel shares
with the **Offset** fields, which cost O(1) per pixel where a spread costs Θ(n): one shadow with
`blur: 0` at `spread: 10_000` and zoom 256 measured **1 092.7 ms** on a real adapter. The cap is
`extent − 1` per axis and it is **exactly lossless**, because both backends read outside the buffer
as empty: once the window covers the line a dilation can find nothing further and an erosion has
already met a zero, so no picture changes and only work that could not have changed one is stopped.
Both backends take it from the one function, as they take `k` and the buffer box from one. What it
does *not* do is make the cost sublinear — Θ(w·h·n) for `n` up to the buffer's own size stands, and
running the dilation on `shadow_downscale`'s coarse grid the way the blur does is a real
approximation and a decision still open.

🚨 **An inner shadow is complemented at the *tint*, never at the silhouette, and that is a decision
rather than an arrangement** (§15 D742). The silhouette both kinds of shadow are cast from is the
graphic's own alpha; `255 - v` happens once, in the last pass before the confine. Inverting first —
which is the obvious spelling and is what shipped until 2026-09-10 — puts two edge rules in
contradiction: the offset lookup calls outside the buffer *fully casting* while `convolve`,
`spread_alpha` and `coarsen` all call it *transparent*, which for an inverted silhouette means the
opposite thing. On a shape whose ink **is** its own bounding box the inverted silhouette is zero in
every pixel the buffer holds, so at offset `(0, 0)` the lookup's branch never fires and the render is
pixel-identical to no effect at all; both backends agreed, so `tests/fx_gpu.rs` stayed green over two
implementations of one wrong picture. ⚠️ **What makes the late complement need no edge flag anywhere
is that every pass between the two commutes with it** — `blur(255 − v)` padded with 255 is
`255 − blur(v)` padded with 0 for a normalized kernel, `coarsen` is a box average of the same shape
including its partial blocks, `upsample` is bilinear with weights summing to one, and a dilation of
the complement is the erosion of the original. **A pass inserted between them that is neither linear
nor a max/min with a matching identity breaks that argument**, and nothing would say so. It also puts
`spread_alpha`'s `grow` back on the operand it was written for — `(spread > 0) != inner` is a rule
about the *shape's* alpha, so against an already-complemented buffer a positive spread on an inner
shadow thinned it instead of thickening it. The GPU spells the same decision by sending `inner` to
`Pass::Tint` rather than to `Pass::Silhouette`.

**A shadow's own blur is bounded where the layer's buffer may not be** (`effect::shadow_downscale`,
`effects::blur_coarse`, §15 D403). σ in device pixels is the authored deviation times the zoom, and
D395's buffer downscale is forbidden to a shadow — the artwork composited over it stays sharp. The
silhouette is not that artwork: it is an alpha field on its way to becoming a gaussian of deviation σ,
so past twice the budget it is box-averaged into `ceil(σ/24)`-pixel blocks, blurred at σ/k, and read
back bilinearly. **The half-block is the whole of the read-back** — a coarse sample stands at the
centre of the block it averaged — and getting it wrong shifts every shadow by half a block, which
looks like a shadow creeping as the zoom changes rather than like a bug. Both backends take `k` from
the one function, as they take the buffer box from one — **and its size, since 2026-09-10**
(`effects::effect_buffer`, §15 D744), the two hand-kept copies of that arithmetic having each capped
at `u16::MAX`, which is eight times what the GPU can build; the GPU spells the three steps as `coarsen`,
a blur dispatched over the coarse grid, and `upsample`, with the coarse grid living in the top-left
corner of a full-size scratch texture so every slot stays one size.

🚨 **The resample's own cost claim has a precondition, and the shader shipped for nine days without
it** (§15 D743). Dispatching `coarsen` over the coarse grid, one thread per block, makes the total
work one read per source pixel — *while `k ≤ min(w, h)`*. Past that the grid is **1 × 1**, a single
thread walks `k²` taps over a buffer of `w·h`, and the pass becomes the full-size spelling D403 was
written to avoid: **116.3 ms** for one shadow at `k = 1 334` against **0.45 ms** once both loops stop
at the **source** rather than at the block, at settings the panel and the view both permit. Both
backends bound them there now. **Bounding the loop skips exactly the taps the range check skipped, so
no value moves**, and the divisor stays `k²` — the transparent-off-edge rule, not an oversight.

**Both of those numbers are capped, because a document is allowed to hold a deviation no stage
downstream of it can survive** (`effect::MAX_SHADOW_BLOCK` = 4096, `effect::MAX_KERNEL_RADIUS` = 512,
§15 D454). `<feDropShadow stdDeviation="1e30">` imports with nothing reported, saves, and reloads —
and the dashboard rasterizes every document in the base folder, so one such file is a hang at launch
rather than a bad drawing somebody asked for. The two caps bound different things and neither covers
the other: `coarsen` was Θ(k) whatever the surface it walked, and behind it the kernel is `2⌈3σ⌉+1`
taps with nothing else to stop it. ⚠️ **D743 bounded that walk, so `MAX_SHADOW_BLOCK` is now a
correctness cap rather than a cost one** — `coarsen` costs `w·h` however large `k` is, and what the
cap still buys is that `k as i32` above `i32::MAX` wraps *negative*, runs neither loop and draws no
shadow at all, which is the arm that is silent rather than slow. The kernel's cap is asked in
`effects::kernel_radius` — **the one function both backends' blurs go through**, which is why one
guard closes the GPU as well: both backends reach the allocation almost at once now, where before it
was the CPU hanging in `coarsen` first and the GPU building the kernel on the host immediately. Reaching either cap means something upstream failed, and
what it buys is that the failure is the cheapest wrong picture rather than a frame that never returns.

Pixel-tested end to end through the CPU path (`ondin-render/tests/effects.rs`): the shadow's colour
and position, alpha falling off across the blur rather than stopping at an edge, a blur spreading
past the layer's own edge, a `Filters` row changing colour and not extent, spread growing the
shadow, an inner shadow staying inside the layer's *ink* and not merely its box, an inner shadow
reaching **all four edges** of a rect at offset `(0, 0)` — the shape whose ink is its own box, which
the ink test above cannot see and which drew nothing at all until D742 — a positive spread thickening
an inner shadow *inwards*, and a stack with no
ink compositing identically to no stack at all. The SVG suite reads the filter graph instead —
what the file *says* against what the renderer *draws* — and neither suite would notice if only the
other were right, which is why both exist.

---

## 7. ondin-export

- **SVG** — pure `svg_of_reported(doc, res, origins: &[NodeId]) -> Export`, of which
  `svg_of(…) -> String` is the shim that keeps only the markup and
  `svg(doc, res, artboard: Option<NodeId>)` is one call: a whole document is the root on its own and a
  single artboard is that artboard on its own. **`Export` is the writer's side of `svg_in::Import`'s
  `skipped`/`approximated`** (§15 D780): `svg`, plus `approximated` — the picture differs — and
  `round_trip` — the picture is right and re-reading the file gives a different document. The shim is
  that way round because the report is the new thing and every existing caller wants the markup; the
  two callers that face a user, the export card and *Copy as SVG*, ask for the report and word it
  through one helper in the same two-clause shape as the paste message on the reader's side. What a **set** adds is a *selection* — a viewBox over
  the union of their world bounds, and each subtree emitted under its own **parent's** world
  transform, so several layers from different frames land where they sit relative to one another.
  Order is the caller's and is kept, because the output has to be byte-stable (invariant 9) and
  because SVG has no z-index: a selection handed over out of document order comes back restacked.
  Nothing is deduplicated here either — the caller's filter is **`build::in_document_order`**, which is
  `outermost` plus exactly that ordering, since this function cannot know whether a repetition was
  meant and cannot check the order at all (§15 D259, D267). **Both halves are the caller's and both
  were once missed**: no caller met the ordering half until 2026-08-20, `Selection::ids` being pick
  order, so a selection made front-to-back exported upside down. **The parent's transform is what the walk's
  `outer` means**: `emit_node` composes `outer * node.transform()`, so passing the origin's *own*
  world applies its local twice, which a scoped export did until 2026-08-20 (§15 D258).
  Structurally faithful: groups
  and artboards become nested `<g>` elements carrying their *local* transform and opacity, shapes
  inside them use local coordinates, a clipping artboard gets a `clipPath`, and gradients become real
  `<linearGradient>`/`<radialGradient>` defs — carrying `gradientTransform` where the brush has one and
  omitting it at the identity, which is the attribute's own default, so no existing file's markup moves
  (§15 D412), and writing the stop list **clamped monotonic on a copy** (§5.5a, §15 D455), which is the
  writer's own question — *what does this file mean* — answered SVG's way, with the model untouched. **A *sweep* has no SVG 1.1 equivalent and is approximated as a
  `<radialGradient>` whose radius comes from the shape** (§15 D647): its payload is a centre and two
  angles and no radius at all, so the only honest source is the node's own box, measured to its
  **farthest corner** — half the diagonal covers the shape from the frame's centre and from nowhere
  else — and pulled back through the brush transform first, `cx`/`cy`/`r` being read before
  `gradientTransform`. It is the one arm here that asks `paint_frame` for a box, which is why the
  caller gates the call on the kind. Nesting is not cosmetic — group opacity is only
  correct on a `<g>`, since per-child opacity fades each child separately.
  **A mask becomes a `<clipPath id="mask-{id}">` plus a `<g clip-path="url(#mask-…)">` wrapping the
  run of siblings above it, and emits no element of its own** — the markup shape of `scene::MaskRun`,
  and the mirror this writer is written to be (§5.3, §15 D282). No transform is written on either:
  `clipPath` is `userSpaceOnUse` by default and the space in force where the `<g>` is referenced is the
  parent's, which is the space `Resolved::mask_path` answers in. No `clip-rule` either, because SVG's
  default is non-zero and that is what the canvas fills the same outline with. A mask whose path is
  `None` wraps nothing and the run carries on unwrapped, which is the canvas's reading of `None` as
  well. That is the `Shape` mode; **an `Alpha` mask is a
  `<mask id maskUnits="userSpaceOnUse" style="mask-type:alpha">` holding the layer's own markup**, with
  `<g mask="url(#…)">` over the run (§15 D288) — because what masks is the ink, and drawing it is the
  only way to say that in SVG. ⚠️ **`mask-type: alpha` is load-bearing**: SVG's `<mask>` defaults to
  *luminance*, so without it every alpha mask exported would silently become the one mode this app does
  not have, and would look right whenever the mask happened to be white. It is written as the CSS
  property rather than the presentation attribute of the same name, which has the poorer support. No
  emptiness test on this arm, matching the canvas — but ⚠️ **a `visible()` test, which this arm did
  not have until 2026-09-09** (§15 D648, D566, D282). Emptiness and hiding are different questions:
  an alpha mask that lays down no ink erases the run and that is the mode being honest, while a mask
  the user has switched off has not been asked to erase anything. Without the guard the arm opened a
  `<mask>` and filled it by calling `emit_node` on a node `emit_node` returns early for, so hiding a
  mask exported the whole drawing erased — the reading D282 forbids, fixed on the canvas in D566 and
  left standing here for a day, so one document drew one picture and exported another. The `Shape`
  arm gets it from `mask_path` and always had. **Its region is written explicitly too, and for the
  same reason a filter's is** (§15 D458): `<mask>` defaults to the same `-10%,-10%,120%,120%`, and
  under `userSpaceOnUse` a percentage is a fraction of the *viewport* read as a length in the current
  user space — which inside a transformed `<g>` is that group's local space, not the page, and
  everything outside the region is mask value 0. Measured in Chrome, a group under `scale(0.1)` kept
  its masked artwork only to x = 43 of 400, and one translated a thousand units with its children a
  thousand back lost all of it. The region is the **mask's own** `ink_bounds` mapped into the
  referencing node's local space and inflated a tenth — the mask's box rather than the run's, because
  outside it the mask draws nothing and its value is 0 there whatever the region says. A mask with no
  ink keeps the absent region, since it erases the run wherever it is evaluated. `<clipPath>` takes no
  region, so the `Shape` arm has none.
  **An effect stack becomes one `<filter id="fx-{id}">` and a `<g filter="url(#fx-…)">` wrapping
  everything the node emits** — one filter per node rather than one per effect, since the whole stack
  composes into a single graph (§5.3a, §6.4, §15 D333). Three properties of it are load-bearing, and
  the markup is well-formed in every wrong version. **The region is written explicitly**,
  `filterUnits="userSpaceOnUse"` from `Resolved::ink_bounds` mapped into the wrapper's space **and
  then padded for the stack's inner shadows** (`svg::inner_working_pad`): SVG's default region is
  `-10%,-10%,120%,120%` of the object's box, which crops any real shadow — a 24px blur on a 40px icon
  loses most of itself. 🚨 **The pad is not slack, and the ink bounds alone were wrong here** (§15
  D742): outside the region SVG defines every primitive's result as transparent black, so a region
  equal to the layer's ink left the `feComponentTransfer tableValues="1 0"` that inverts the alpha
  nothing outside the shape to invert from — and on a shape whose ink *is* its own box, which is a
  rect, a frame, an image or a text node, that is the whole region and the file drew nothing. **A
  filter's working region and the layer's ink bounds are two quantities** — where the primitives are
  evaluated against where the result lands (§5.3a) — and an inner shadow is the one effect for which
  they differ. The pad is `reach(blur) + |spread| + |offset|` over the visible inner shadows, uniform
  and generous rather than per-side, because the closing `feComposite operator="in"` confines the
  result and no extra region area can draw. **The wrapper is outside the clip**, because SVG applies
  `filter` before `clip-path` on one element, so an attribute on the node's own `<g>` would draw a
  clipping frame's shadow and then cut it off at the frame's edge; it is also the only position that
  works for a shape whose markup is several elements (`emit_stacked`). It carries **no transform**, so
  the region is described in the node's *parent's* space, which is the space `effect_region` composes
  for. And **a `<filter>` with no primitives renders its element as nothing at all** — not as a no-op —
  so a stack whose entries are all switched off or all neutral must emit no filter rather than an
  empty one; where the stage-one graph has changed nothing and no shadow survives, an attribute-less
  `<feOffset/>` is the shortest way to say "unchanged". The graph is built in the same **two stages**
  the CPU pass uses and for the same reason (§6.4), and every filter carries
  `color-interpolation-filters="sRGB"`, the spec's default being `linearRGB`.
  ⚠️ **That identity primitive is load-bearing on the *reading* side too, and the graph now comes back
  in.** `ondin_core::svg_in::effects_of` reads a `<filter>` as a whole effect stack — the shadow
  chain drop or inner, a lone `<feDropShadow>`, a lone `<feGaussianBlur>`, `<feMerge>` as assembly,
  and a bare `<feOffset/>` as an **empty** stack rather than as a skip (§15 D411) — so respelling
  "unchanged" as anything else would make a stack that resolved to nothing arrive as a reported loss.
