  Document order is the stack order both sides agree on: the `feMerge` lists the results *differently*
  (behind, layer, in front), so it is deliberately not what the reader takes the order from. **One
  effect is written and cannot be read back, and that is a decision rather than a gap**: a `Filters`
  row's `feColorMatrix` is not invertible — brightness and contrast are both a scale on the same
  channels, so one matrix answers to any number of pairs — and such a stack is skipped whole and
  reported rather than guessed at.
  Doubles as a model-completeness gate: **everything the model expresses must round-trip to valid
  SVG**, and anything it can only approximate must say so out loud rather than silently substitute
  (gradients were flattened to mid-grey for two milestones and the gate reported success).
  ⚠️ **"Out loud" meant *in a doc comment* until 2026-09-15, which is not out loud at all** (§15
  D780, `[S8.1-L7-05]`). The reader had `Import::skipped`/`approximated` from the day it was written;
  the writer returned a bare `String`, so the five features it knows it cannot say exactly — a sweep
  gradient as a radial one, a shadow's spread as a square kernel, type on a rail whose glyph placement
  is the viewer's, a flipped rail as a reversed path, an image fill as a `<pattern>` — reached nobody
  but a developer reading this module. They reach the export card and *Copy as SVG* now, **and in two
  lists rather than one**: the last two are *round-trip* losses and not approximations, because a
  reversed rail is the identical drawing (§15 D406) and the `<pattern>` lands exactly where the
  document puts it, measured in a browser — so what is lost is the *document* coming back, not the
  picture. Calling either "approximated" sends a user after a bug that is not there.
  🚨 **The report is read off the node in `emit_node`, under the visibility guard, and deliberately
  not in `collect_defs`** — which already walks every origin, already carries a `&mut` and already
  sees all five, and which has **no visibility guard** on purpose, an unreferenced def being harmless.
  A report built there announces a sweep gradient on a layer the file does not contain. The shadow arm
  carries three conditions for the same reason — a zero spread emits no `feMorphology`, an invisible
  effect is skipped by `effect_def`'s loop, and the whole `<filter>` is absent unless `effect_region`
  could answer — since **each is a way to warn about markup that is not in the file**, which is what a
  report that restates a rule instead of observing one does.
  `ondin-export/tests/fidelity.rs` pairs every reported claim with the markup that caused it, so the
  report cannot drift from the writer.
  ⚠️ **That gate is exactly as wide as the tests in `svg_roundtrip.rs` that call `svg_of`, and one of
  them did not** (§15 D650): `an_imported_clip_path_is_empty_outside_the_clip` reads hand-authored
  markup, which makes it a renderer test and not a binding, and it was standing in for the writer's
  own `<clipPath>` spelling — emitted at **top level** rather than inside `<defs>`, which nothing had
  ever read back. **Both sides of a hand-written fixture agree about what SVG looks like**, so a test
  in that file which does not call the writer binds nothing, however much its name reads like it.
  ⚠️ **A layer's *name* is part of what round-trips, and it reached the file for the first time on
  2026-09-09** (§15 D611). `svg_of` never called `Node::name()` — the only ids in the output are the
  `grad-`/`img-`/`clip-`/`mask-`/`fx-` ones this writer synthesises from `NodeId::to_wire` — while
  `svg_in` reads an element's `id` **as** the layer name at six sites, so a document with named layers
  exported and re-imported came back with every layer unnamed and nothing anywhere said so. It goes in
  **`data-name`**, written by `name_attr` at the three places this writer opens an element that *is* a
  node: the leaf in `emit_shape`, the container `<g>` in `emit_node` — the **outer** one in the
  split-clip case, the inner existing only to hold the clip apart from the transform — and
  `emit_stacked`'s `<g>`, whose children are that node's own paints and must not carry it. An unnamed
  node writes nothing, as every other attribute here does at its default. **Not `id`**: that would put
  free user text into the same namespace as the synthesised ids above, where a layer someone named
  `clip-601d_2` shadows a real `<clipPath>` and silently redirects its own frame's `url(#…)`, and it
  would mean mangling ordinary names on the way out and reading them back mangled. `data-*` is valid
  markup every viewer ignores and the **writer** round-trips the name byte for byte. **The reader
  prefers it and still falls back to `id`**, which is not a compatibility shim — `id` is where
  Illustrator and Inkscape put a layer's identity, and reading it was right before and is still
  right. ⚠️ **The reader has one exception to byte-for-byte and it is deliberate** (§15 D644): it
  goes through `naming::usable` (§5.7b), so a name that is blank or only spaces falls through to the
  numbering and any other whitespace in one comes back as a space.
  ⚠️ **"Valid" starts at the number, and nothing was enforcing that until 2026-09-07** (§15 D508).
  `svg::fmt` is the single formatter every number here goes through, and both its arms printed a
  non-finite one verbatim — `NaN` and `inf` are not SVG `<number>`s, so **one anywhere makes the whole
  file unparseable**. It floors to `0` now, a wrong-but-drawable file beating an unopenable one, the
  same trade the `-0` case makes. **The floor is not the whole answer and must not be taken for it**:
  `effect_region` composes `transform * world.inverse()`, so a node scaled flat wrote a `<filter>`
  region of `NaN`s, and a *floored* region is a region of no area — which the spec renders identically
  to an unparseable one, i.e. the referencing element not at all. A singular world transform therefore
  writes no filter, and the artwork exports unfiltered, which is what `ScenePainter::push_effect_layer`
  does for the same case. ⚠️ **The predicate is `build::affine_is_invertible` since 2026-09-15** (§15
  D762) and was `determinant().abs() < f64::EPSILON`, which is not "singular" at all: a relative
  epsilon against a quantity in squared world units, so at large coordinates it could never fire and
  the guard this paragraph describes was silently absent.
  ⚠️ **The reader's `fill`/`stroke` cascade follows CSS's rule for an invalid declaration, and did not
  until 2026-09-07** (§15 D493). `svg_in::resolve` inherits a style and overrides it property by
  property; every arm but two read `prop(…).and_then(parse_len)`, so a value they cannot read leaves
  the inherited one standing, while the two paint arms assigned the *result* of the parse — and `None`
  is that struct's spelling for **unpainted**, so `<g fill='#00ff00'><rect style='fill:var(--brand)'/>`
  came back with no fill rather than green. The parse guards the assignment now. ⚠️ **Three meanings
  share that one `None` and only the value's own text separates them**: `none` and `transparent` mean
  unpainted, and an unresolvable `url(#…)` is a valid declaration with a dead reference, which SVG
  itself leaves unpainted (§15 D477) — so keeping the inherited paint there would put **opaque black**
  under a missing image, the very failure D477 is named for. `!important` is stripped one level down in
  `declaration`, because it is a *specificity* input and this reader is a lookup rather than a cascade
  engine, so the marker could only ever make a good value unreadable.
  ⚠️ **A `<style>` element is every one of its text children joined, and reading `roxmltree`'s
  `text()` truncated it** (§15 D544). That accessor answers the first child *and only when it is a
  text node*, so an XML comment inside the sheet ended it there — and a **leading** one,
  `<style><!-- … --></style>`, the legacy idiom, lost the sheet whole and sent every classed shape in
  the drawing to SVG's initial `fill`, which is **black** rather than nothing, with `skipped` and
  `approximated` both empty. The join is owned (`svg_in::style_sheets`) and built by `import` **above**
  the `Builder` it is handed to, because `Css`'s rules borrow it and Rust drops in reverse declaration
  order; a sheet split across two text nodes has no single `&str` in the document to point at. **This
  is not what the lookup-rather-than-a-cascade-engine rule is about** — that decides which *selectors*
  are read, not which bytes of the sheet reach the parser. **A paint that is genuinely
  unreadable is reported**, through a fourth flag beside `Css::complex`, `Gradients::patterns` (§15
  D477) and `Gradients::resampled` (§15 D459) — one `skip` for the file rather than one per element,
  and `skip` rather than `approximate` because the paint is not there in some other form. It is a
  `Cell`, being the only one of the four that is a fact about the *elements* rather than about the
  defs, and so the only one set while the gradient table is already borrowed.
  ⚠️ **A stated `stdDeviation` of zero is a value, and it used to refuse the whole `<filter>`** (§15
  D572). `deviation_of`'s guard was `> 0.0` where only the `is_finite()` half was doing the junk-file
  job it was written for, and all three callers propagate a `None` with `?` — so a hard-edged offset
  shadow, `<feDropShadow dx="1" dy="1" stdDeviation="0"/>`, which `effect::Shadow` holds exactly at
  `blur: 0.0`, arrived as `skipped: ["filter"]` with the layer unshadowed. A lone zero blur now joins
  the bare `<feOffset/>` as an identity primitive rather than a reported loss, and a **negative**
  deviation is still refused, which is what SVG says. 🚨 **Widening it opened a hole in `shadow_chain`'s
  refusal, which read presence and not effect**: *"neither moved nor softened"* was
  `!seen_offset && !seen_blur`, sound only while a zero refused the file one function away, so a zeroed
  `feOffset` plus a zeroed `feGaussianBlur` became a chain with two primitives, both flags set and no
  effect at all — a solid slab imported exactly on top of the artwork, which nothing downstream would
  object to because it is a valid shadow that happens to be invisible. The test is on the **values**
  now, with `spread` deliberately left out of it so the rule stays exactly the one it was.
  `flood-color="currentColor"` is read too: it is a *reference* rather than a colour, so it resolves
  against the **referencing** element's `color`, threaded down from `chrome` because a `<filter>` lives
  in `<defs>` and inherits nothing of its own.
  ⚠️ **A `<text>`'s own `opacity`, `display`/`visibility` and `filter` reach every run it splits into**
  (§15 D573). A positioned `<tspan>` becomes a node of its own and carries none of the three, so
  `<text opacity="0.3" display="none">A<tspan x=… >B</tspan></text>` imported with only the **first**
  run faded and hidden and `skipped` empty — a diagram pasted from a file that hides a layer arriving
  with half of it on screen and nothing saying why. `chrome` takes the outer element beside the run's,
  which is the treatment `text_node`'s `outer` transform already had and which the three chrome
  properties were never moved with. It **composes** rather than replacing: opacity multiplies as SVG
  nests it for groups, `display` and `visibility` hide if either says so, and `filter` is the one that
  cannot — two filters are a graph where the model holds one effect stack per node — so the run's own
  wins where it states one and the `<text>`'s is used otherwise.
  ⚠️ **A `<tspan>` is read at whatever depth the file states it** (§15 D575). The walk read exactly
  one level, so a tspan inside a tspan had its whole style dropped — no colour, no size, no weight,
  with nothing in `skipped` or `approximated` — while its **text** arrived, the collection underneath
  being already `descendants()`, which is exactly what made the loss silent. The content is
  flattened into pieces first, and the piece is one per **text node** rather than one per element:
  it carries the innermost element the characters came from and that element's resolved style, so
  `<tspan>x<tspan>y</tspan>z</tspan>` is three pieces and `z` reads the *outer* tspan's style. That
  is the shape the one-per-element reading cannot express at all, and it is what makes the depth stop
  mattering.
  ⚠️ **Whitespace in a `<text>` is collapsed to XML's four characters and no more, and it was
  Unicode's twenty-three until 2026-09-09** (§15 D660). `push_collapsed` asked `char::is_whitespace`
  — the `White_Space` property — while its own doc said *"XML whitespace collapsing"*; XML's `S`
  production is `#x20 | #x9 | #xD | #xA` and CSS's `white-space: normal` collapses the same four, so
  the reader was wider than both specifications. Four of the twenty-three are exactly the characters
  an author reaches for *because* they are not ordinary spaces: `10\u{00a0}km` imported as a
  **breakable** `"10 km"`, a figure space and a narrow no-break space became ordinary ones, and a
  leading ideographic space vanished outright — a pasted price or measurement the source deliberately
  kept unbreakable came back breakable, with nothing in `skipped` or `approximated`. `XML_SPACE` is
  the one constant, and **`text_node`'s two trims share it**: on the wider set a `trim` *removed* a
  leading separator rather than collapsing it, which is why the ideographic row lost a character
  where the others lost only a distinction. The two must not drift, because `lead` re-bases every
  span's byte range onto the trimmed string (§15 D396).
  ⚠️ **A duplicate id is first-wins, which is what a browser does — and one of the reader's three id
  maps did it** (§15 D642). `Gradients::collect` builds `ids` (every element carrying one, read by the
  `<use href>` resolver, by `filter="url(#…)"` and by `gradient_chain`'s `href` walk), `clips`
  (`<clipPath>` **and `<mask>`**) and `by_id` (the resolved gradients the fill and stroke paths ask
  for). Only the first was written `entry().or_insert()`, under a comment stating the rule; the other
  two were plain `insert`s, i.e. last-wins — so one document had **two** answers for `#g`, and the
  common path had the wrong one. Measured against Chrome on two `<linearGradient id="g">`, red then
  blue: Chrome paints red and Ondin painted blue. The rule is *the only answer that does not depend on
  document order twice*, and it is stated here because a comment beside one of three implementations
  held neither of the others.
  **A shape with at most one fill and one centred whole-outline stroke is one plain element** with
  `fill` and `stroke` attributes — the markup this writer has always produced, and the overwhelming majority of
  shapes. Anything else goes to `emit_stacked`: a `<g>` carrying the node's transform and opacity, then
  one element per visible paint in the §6.3 order, strokes with `fill="none"` so a later one cannot
  paint over the fills beneath it. The transform and the opacity move up to the group because the
  several elements are all the one shape — they must share one user space, which is also the space a
  `clipPath` reads its coordinates in, and fading them separately would let the lower paints show
  through the upper. `write_element` is the single per-kind element writer both paths share, so there
  is no second place for a polygon to round differently from the canvas. **`fill-rule` rides with the
  fill through `with_fill_rule`, on *both* arms, for the same reason.** It was on the plain arm alone
  until 2026-09-06, so whether an even-odd shape exported as even-odd depended on how many paints it
  happened to have: an `Exclude`, whose rule is derived rather than stored (§15 D239), given an
  ordinary aligned stroke left the plain arm and exported **non-zero — which for a symmetric
  difference is a union**, every hole filled in, while the canvas drew it correctly (§15 D438).
  Two shapes pay for the model-completeness gate. SVG has no stroke alignment either, so a
  non-centred stroke is built the same way the canvas builds it (§6.3) — a `<clipPath>` plus a
  double-width stroke inside it — and that construction is `align_clip`, applied **per stroke**
  (`sa-<node>-<i>`), so the id carries the paint's own index and hiding one does not renumber the
  others. (The canvas shares one clip across a *run* of same-aligned strokes for the cost of it, §15
  D146; here the cost is a few lines of markup rather than a per-frame path build, so the simpler
  per-stroke form stays.) An outside clip's
  outer ring carries the same mitre allowance the canvas gives it, off
  `effective_sides(…).max_width(s.width) · miter_limit`: the two must agree or a wide stroke exports
  differently from the way it was drawn (§15 D97). **There is one width at which they now do disagree,
  and it is stated rather than fixed**: past `scene::lay_stroke`'s gate the canvas fills an expanded
  outline instead of stroking it (§6.3), where this writer still hands `stroke-width` to the consumer
  and leaves the expansion to whoever renders the file — so an SVG of a 309pt stroke on a 200×120 shape
  is only as correct as that renderer (§15 D131). A **per-side**
  stroke is the third such shape and mirrors the walk exactly: one `<path>` per edge from
  `geometry::side_path`, which is why the `plain` fast path now also requires
  `effective_sides(…).is_all()` — a stroke that is not the shape's outline can never ride the shape's
  own element. All the sides of one stroke share that stroke's single alignment `clipPath`, since they
  are one paint and a clip each would be three more identical defs. A **fitted dash on a multi-subpath
  path** is the fourth: one `<path>` per subpath with its own `stroke-dasharray`, because an element
  carries one pattern and a fit scale belongs to one closed run, so `plain` also requires
  `dash_fit_pieces(…).is_none()` (§15 D147). A **frame's border** is the fifth and the only one that
  changes the group structure: it must be painted over the contents and *outside* the frame's own clip,
  so a frame with both becomes two `<g>`s — outer with the transform and opacity, inner with only the
  `clip-path` — and the border's `<rect>` goes between them, gated on both being present so nothing that
  never stroked a frame moves by a byte (§15 D144). A **text stroke** rides the `<text>` element itself,
  keeping the output re-shapeable, and an aligned one is clipped against the glyph outlines
  `ondin_core::text::outline` builds — the same path the canvas strokes (§15 D145).
  `stroke-dasharray` likewise
  carries the **resolved** pattern (§6.3): SVG can express neither a zero-length dot nor "fit to
  corners", so both arrive here already turned into numbers, per edge where the edges have their own
  widths. `stroke-miterlimit` is emitted **only when the join is Miter and the limit is not 4**,
  which is SVG's own default and kurbo's: writing it unconditionally would restate what every
  existing export already meant. This list used to give a second reason — "and the golden SVGs are
  byte-compared" — which was false for as long as it stood, there being no goldens then, and was
  corrected to say so along with the prediction that the omission would survive goldens arriving.
  **They arrived on 2026-08-22** (§11) and it did: the second reason is true now, and the branch still
  rests on the first alone. And a gradient's
  slot name carries the paint's index (`grad-<node>-fill-0`, `-stroke-1`), including when there is
  only one: the slot has to name *which* paint now that there can be several, and spelling the first
  one `fill` would leave two ways to write the same thing. §15 D56 has the rest.
  **`Defs` is insertion-ordered and deduped through a set** (§15 D593): the order
  is what invariant 9's byte-stability and every §11 golden rest on, so the `Vec` cannot become a map
  — and the *membership* question cannot be a scan of it, because `collect_defs` asks once per
  gradient fill, per gradient stroke, per image (three ids), per effect stack and per text rail, which
  made D defs cost Θ(D²) comparisons over ids sharing a long common prefix. At 16,000 defs that was
  **87% of export time** while the bytes emitted grew exactly linearly, and the output is
  byte-identical either way, so no golden can see it.
  An **image** fill is a `<pattern>`, which is a paint server exactly as a gradient is — so it goes
  through the same `Defs` machinery (`image_id`, spelled like `gradient_id`), `paint_attr` names it in
  the `fill` or `stroke` attribute, and `write_element` learnt nothing. The tile is the source's
  **intrinsic pixel box** and the whole framing is the one `patternTransform` — omitted when it would
  print as the identity, through the `matrix_attr` an element's own `transform` goes through — so the
  markup never learns which of the four modes it is. **Inside the pattern is a `<use>`, not the
  picture** (§15 D595): the payload is one `<image id="pix-<hash>">` per distinct `ImageId`, written
  once in `<defs>` however many nodes show it, carrying `ImageEntry::href` — the encoded original as a
  `data:` URI, or a link's path as written (§5.5a). Keying the def per node *per slot* meant thirty
  shapes on one photograph wrote thirty base64 copies of it, a **26.6×** export against a document
  whose own size is flat because `ImageId` is a content hash. ⚠️ **The per-node `<pattern>` is not the
  duplication and stays** — its `patternTransform` is that node's framing — and the `opacity` and
  `filter` sit on the `<use>`, which is where they have to be once the `<image>` is shared. No
  `width`/`height` on the `<use>`: those apply only to an `<svg>` or a `<symbol>` reference, and the
  `<image>` already carries the tile. An **adjusted** picture
  gets a `<filter>` def as well, hung on that `<use>` and never on the pattern (which would colour
  whatever the pattern fills), carrying an `feColorMatrix` and an `feComponentTransfer` straight off
  `ImageAdjust::pipeline` — each stage only where it is not the identity, no `feFuncA`,
  `color-interpolation-filters="sRGB"` because a filter's default working space is linear, and a
  filter region pinned to the element's own box because the default is 10% larger each side and would
  bleed between tiles. An unadjusted one emits no filter and no reference to one (§15 D186). A pattern always tiles where three
  of the four modes want `Extend::Pad`, which costs nothing the app can author, and a **letterboxing**
  picture is as much a reason to stack as an aligned stroke is: the clip belongs to one paint, so
  `plain` also fails when any visible fill or stroke's framing asks for one. The frame a picture is
  framed against mirrors the walk's three cases — an artboard's own box, a text node's **layout
  bounds**, and otherwise the outline's bounding box. An image *fill* the document's table cannot
  answer for exports as the **missing-image placeholder** — `emit_missing`, the same ground, ink, width
  and cross the canvas paints, off the same `ondin_core::missing_placeholder`, with a `clipPath`
  (`mi-<node>-<slot>`) of the shape round the cross and the rim — never as a `url(#…)` naming a def
  that is not in the file, and it is another reason to stack, three elements and a clip being more than
  a `fill` attribute can carry. The writer's unresolvable set is **smaller by construction**: only a
  dangling id reaches it, since a link goes out as its `href` and undecodable bytes are the viewer's
  problem with the encoded original. A **stroke** with an unanswerable image still writes `none` at
  `paint_attr`'s image arm, as the canvas draws nothing for one. An artboard *background* used to do
  the same and was the one place the two writers disagreed; it does not since a frame's ground became
  an ordinary fill, which goes through the same `emit_missing` a shape's does (§15 D179, D400).
  ⚠️ That arm was written as `fill="none"` first and caught by reading the emitter against the walk —
  `scene::fill_or_placeholder` takes a frame's fills and a shape's alike, so a frame whose picture had
  gone showed the grey cross on the canvas, wore the amber glyph in the layers panel, and exported a
  hole. §15 D185 has the rest. **That is one of the two recorded divergences between this writer and
  the scene walk, and since 2026-09-15 there is a gate for their shape** (§15 D781, `[A1-L7-07]`):
  `ondin-export/tests/two_walks.rs` compares the **ink set** — which nodes each walk decided to put
  paint down for — through a unique solid colour per node, so neither walk reports on itself. Both
  recorded divergences were of exactly that kind, which is why the differential is scoped to it and
  not to all eleven decisions this emitter re-makes; §4's invariant 11 has the boundary argument.
  🚨 **No gate in this workspace looks at image markup, so a change to it is checked in a browser.**
  The §11 golden holds one node of every kind and **no image**; `svg_in` has no `<pattern>` handling
  at all (`[A5-L6-01]`), so the round-trip suite cannot read one back; and nothing here renders SVG.
  What stands in is the technique `CLAUDE.md` records for checking an *import*, pointed at the writer:
  export the document, rewrite a copy by hand into the shape being replaced, serve both over HTTP,
  draw them into canvases and difference the pixels. That is what said the `<use>` hoist above is
  identical and not merely valid — 10,800 opaque pixels, 0 channels differing (§15 D595).
- **PNG** — `png(doc, res, vp) -> Vec<u8>` via `VelloCpuRenderer` + PNG encoder. No GPU anywhere in
  this path. It shares the walk, so it needs no rule of its own about a picture that cannot be drawn:
  the placeholder is ink and lands on the pixels, which is where a hole would do the most damage and
  therefore where it is pinned (§6.3, §15 D179). Shapes, artboard backgrounds, images **and text** are
  all rasterized — the walk hands a `TextRun` to `ScenePainter::draw_text` and `cpu.rs` fills its
  glyphs; the module doc said text was deferred until 2026-08-20, long after its own
  `text_rasterizes_ink_pixels` had been written to assert otherwise (§15 D264).
- **PNG of a selection** — `png_of(doc, res, origins) -> Option<Vec<u8>>`, the raster mirror of
  `svg_of`. A viewport cannot express "only these layers", so this is not a framing trick: it walks
  from each origin through `scene::build_of`, whose `build` is one call with the root on its own. Two
  properties follow and both are wanted — **ancestor clipping does not travel** (the walk starts at the
  layer, exactly as `svg_of`'s emitter does, so the two writers agree), and **nothing behind is
  painted**, artboard background included, which is what puts a selection export on transparency
  without a flag. **1:1 and no scale argument**: world units are px by implication, so one device pixel
  per world unit is the framing that needs nothing decided. ~~A multiplier is a *control* that wants
  somewhere to live before it wants a parameter.~~ **It has one since 2026-08-21** — the Export panel
  (§15 D274) — so the parameter is real and sits on `RasterOpts` below; this stays the 1:1 shortcut.
  ⚠️ **And it is now a shortcut with no production caller**: *Export as…* was the last one and went on
  2026-08-22 (§15 D264), leaving only `ondin-export/tests/png.rs`. `ondin-export` is a library and this
  is `pub`, so nothing will ever warn. `crate::extent` is the shared union both writers frame
  from, so a viewBox and a pixel grid cannot come to describe different boxes (§15 D264). **It unions
  `ink_bounds`, not `world_bounds`** (§5.3a, §15 D334): an export is a picture of what the layer
  *draws*, and framing from the editing box crops a drop shadow off at the layer's own edge. The two
  are equal for any layer with no effect beneath it, so no existing file changed.
- **Snapshot (AI handoff / MCP projection)** — `snapshot(doc, res) -> Snapshot`, serde-serializable.
  Stable documented schema: id, kind, name, local+world transform, world bounds, paint summary
  (gradients described with kind and stops; an image by the id that keys the table — its content hash,
  so it also says when two fills are the same file — plus its framing mode, its alpha, and the
  adjustments that are not at rest, absent entirely when none is), full text style
  (family, size, weight, italic, line height, alignment, sizing), children ids, artboard membership,
  and a `warnings` list carrying font families the machine does not have. Versioned independently
  (`snapshot_version`, currently **9**: 3 was the text attribute model, 4 the image detail and 5 its
  adjustments, both bumped on
  the precedent of 2 because a variant growing detail is what that bump was for, §15 D185, D186,
  **6 is masks**, §15 D282, **7 the mask *mode***, §15 D288, **8 the effect stack**, §15 D335, and
  **9 a frame's ground leaving `Geometry::Artboard`**, §15 D400);
  decoupled from the save schema. `NodeSnapshot::pivot` is skipped when unset and reports the
  **resolved local point** rather than the model's fraction-or-point enum (§5.3): a reader is asking
  where the thing turns, and which of the two ways the model stores that is a detail of how it
  survives a resize. Additive and write-only, so it needed no bump of its own. ⚠️ **It is the one
  field in this projection that *derives* rather than reads** (§15 D651): a fraction is resolved
  against `local_box`, and a node with no measurable box — an empty container — falls to `Rect::ZERO`,
  so its fraction reports `[0, 0]` whatever it says. Not reachable from the UI, recorded rather than
  endorsed, and pinned by the test that makes the derivation observable at all. **`NodeSnapshot::mask`
  sits beside `clip` and is the reason for 6**, on 5's own argument and more strongly: a reader that
  has never heard of masks gets *two* statements wrong about one page — the mask described as a shape
  sitting there in its own fill when nothing of it is drawn, and every layer above it described as
  whole when each is cut to that shape — where 5 was bumped for one such misreading of one layer. It is
  also **the first bump where an untouched document's snapshot changes bytes**, `mask` being reported
  for every node the way `clip` always has been rather than skipped when false; that is a reason for
  the number to move, since a consumer diffing snapshots reads the version first (§15 D282).
  **`NodeSnapshot::mask_mode` is 7**, and the same argument one step on: a reader on 6 knows the layer
  is a mask and describes a soft-edged alpha mask as a hard clip, which is wrong about every pixel
  along its edge. It is a **string** (`"Shape"`/`"Alpha"`) on `line_height`'s precedent — a name
  survives a mode being added where an integer discriminant silently shifts meaning — and owned rather
  than borrowed because this type is `Deserialize` too (§15 D288).
  **`NodeSnapshot::effects` reports the visible entries in compositing order** (§5.3a), skipped when
  empty, with a string `kind` on `mask_mode`'s rule and the **authored** numbers — a blur's radius,
  not the gaussian deviation — since those are what a caller would set. It is reported at all because
  the alternative is a projection describing a layer with a drop shadow as a layer with no shadow.
  It landed without a version bump, against this list's own precedent — 5 was bumped
  for `adjust`, which is likewise absent when neutral, on the grounds that a reader who has never
  heard of adjustments describes an adjusted photograph as the file it came from, and a reader on 7
  describes a shadowed layer as a flat one — and was **bumped to 8 the same day**, with the JSON
  golden regenerated (§11, §15 D335).
  **`Geometry::Artboard` lost its `background` on 2026-09-01**: a frame's ground is an ordinary entry
  in `NodeSnapshot::fills` now, arriving with every other layer's, and repeating it under the geometry
  would report one paint twice and leave a writer with two places to send it (§15 D400).
  **That is 9**, and it earns the bump on both of the grounds above at once: a reader on 8 looks for a
  frame's ground where the schema says it is and finds nothing there, describing a filled frame as an
  empty one, which is 5's argument; and an untouched document's snapshot changes bytes, which is
  exactly what 6 moved for, since a consumer diffing snapshots reads the version first.
  `every-kind.json` was regenerated for it (§11). ⚠️ **It went in without the bump on the first pass**
  and was caught by `arch-scribe` reading the change against `snapshot.rs` — the same read that found
  this passage claiming the current version was **7** with a live "fix by bumping to 8" instruction,
  four bumps after the code had done it. Two stale version numbers in one paragraph, neither of which
  any gate can see.
  `name` is *usually*
  distinguishing now that generated names are numbered (§5.7b) and is still **not unique** — the
  reason `id`, `parent` and `children` sit beside it, so a consumer can disambiguate by path or
  ignore names entirely (§15 D127).
- **The canvas ground and the guides are deliberately absent from all three.** SVG and PNG paint
  frame backgrounds only, because the ground is the surface behind and *around* the frames rather
  than part of the artwork, and a guide is scaffolding the designer worked against rather than
  something they drew; the snapshot schema is per-node and versioned separately, so carrying either
  there would be its own decision. Both are document state (§5.5) but not exported state — §15 D28.
  For the guides this falls out rather than being enforced: they are never in the scene walk at all
  (§9.4), so no export path could emit one by accident.
- **JPEG** — `jpeg::encode_rgba8(rgba, w, h, quality)`, and **no renderer of its own**: everything up
  to the pixels is `png::raster_of`, so a JPEG and a PNG of the same layer at the same scale differ
  in exactly one step. There is no second framing rule to drift and no second place for a trim or a
  pad to round differently. The encoder is `image`'s, already compiled here through `ondin-render`'s
  decode cache (§5.5a), so it declares an edge rather than adding a tree. **Alpha is dropped, not
  flattened here**: JPEG has no alpha channel and the matte a transparent pixel should land on is a
  *decision* — the export's background — made in `plan` and composited before the encoder sees
  anything (§15 D274).
- **Finishing a raster** — `png::raster_of(doc, res, origins, RasterOpts)` is what `png_of` is now a
  1:1 shortcut for. `RasterOpts` carries a **scale**, an optional **background** composited under the
  artwork, **trim** and **pad-to-square**; it is *resolved* rather than being the spec itself,
  because `Background::Frame` needs the tree to answer and `Width(512)` needs the subject's box, and
  both are decided in `plan`. The three finishing steps run **trim → pad → composite** and the order
  is the whole of their meaning: trim reads alpha, so a background that filled it in first would make
  the trim a silent no-op; a pad applied before the trim would have its own padding trimmed off; and
  compositing last covers the artwork and the padding in one pass rather than two that have to agree.
  The pixel count is capped per side at `png::MAX_RASTER_SIDE`, and **the cap is on the scale,
  not on each axis** — clamping the axes independently squashes a 100×50 asked for at 2000× into a
  square, which is the same picture at the wrong aspect ratio (§15 D274). ⚠️ **That constant is
  `511 × 128 = 65408`, and it is emphatically not `u16::MAX`** (§15 D434): `u16::MAX` is the value
  `vello_common` documents as the one it panics on, so the clamp written to prevent a panic caused
  one — through `--width 65535`, and through a plain 1× export of a document carrying a `1e30`-wide
  rect, which needs no flag at all. Both factors are vello's and neither is public.
  ⚠️ **The number itself lives in `ondin-render` since 2026-09-08 and `png::MAX_RASTER_SIDE` is an
  alias** (§15 D586): the limit is the CPU backend's, and while the argument for it sat here alone
  `ondin-render` made the same `as u16` mistake at a second site — `rasterize_glyph_run`, the font
  picker's preview strips. One number, one argument for it, two callers. **Two** tests re-measure it
  against the dependency now rather than one: `a_raster_at_the_cap_renders_on_either_axis` here and
  `cpu::preview_tests::a_strip_too_big_for_the_backend_is_refused_rather_than_truncated` there.
  **The finishing steps widen before they multiply** for the same class of reason: a
  side's squared byte count is `png::square_bytes`, in `usize`, because in `u32` it wrapped to zero at
  32768 and the copy then ran off the end of a zero-length buffer.
- **Plan** — `plan(doc, res, subjects, PlanOptions) -> Vec<PlannedFile>` is the **one place a saved
  `ExportSpec` is interpreted** (§5.3): a scale becomes a multiplier against a particular layer's
  box, `Background::Frame` becomes a colour by walking up to the enclosing artboard, and a layer's
  name becomes a filename sanitized for the strictest filesystem in play. **The spec's `prefix` and
  the layer's name are composed *before* that sanitizing**, not after, so a `/` means one thing
  across the whole path rather than making a folder in one half and a hyphen in the other.
  `PlannedFile` carries the
  pixel size the panel shows on the row and a `clamped` flag for a request the rasterizer could not
  meet. **`raster_size` and `raster_opts` measure `ink_bounds`, the box `extent` frames the render
  from** (§5.3a, §15 D334) — so the row predicts the file's size on a layer with an effect too, and a
  `Width(512)` scale resolves its factor against the box the file is actually framed on. ⚠️ This
  paragraph asserted the opposite as an open defect until 2026-09-07, both readers having been swept
  on 2026-08-24 with the cull beside them; see §6.3 for what that cost.
  `render(doc, res, file)` turns one into bytes; `zip(files)` packs a set. **Nothing here
  touches the filesystem** — the app and the CLI own that, which is what keeps the crate testable
  without one. **No two files in one plan share a name**: `ExportSpec::effective_suffix` separates two
  specs on one layer — the typed suffix when there is one, else the marker the scale derives, so the
  separation holds without anyone typing `@2x` — and
  a case-insensitive ` (2)` de-collision catches what it cannot: two layers can share a name, and a
  duplicated layer carries its original's specs by design. ⚠️ **That is a rule about names inside one
  plan and not about the folder's existing contents** (§15 D636). ⚠️ **`de_collide` claimed the wider
  thing until 2026-09-09** — *"nothing is silently overwritten"*, which no function in this crate can
  promise, its `taken` list being a local `Vec<String>` that dies with the `plan()` call (§15 D652).
  The plan has no filesystem to
  consult, so a file already in the destination is replaced by whichever writer runs next.
  **Two doors write with no dialog behind them and both owe a count**: the panel's *folder* arm, which
  reports `Exported 4 files (2 replaced) — … → C:\…\assets` (§15 D636), and the CLI's `--all`, which
  prints `wrote 4 files to … (2 replaced)` (§15 D652). A *File* or an *Archive* was named in a save
  dialog a moment earlier and the OS has already warned, so those two are the deliberate exclusions.
  `folders_from_names` reads `/` in a
  layer's name as a folder separator and is **off by default**, because it changes what a name means.
- **CLI** — `ondin export <file> [--svg|--png|--json] [--scale <n>|--width <px>|--height <px>] [-o
  out]` runs all three with no
  window and no GPU. `ondin export <file> --all [--scale-override <2x|512w|512h>] [--folders] [-o
  dir]` runs the **document's own**
  export
  settings instead — every layer that carries any, at the formats and sizes the file says. It is a
  different command rather than a fourth format, and refusing `--all --png` is what says so.
  ⚠️ **One document, and `-o` takes a filename rather than whatever token comes next** (§15 D670).
  A second positional is **refused**, naming both files, rather than overwriting the first — a build
  step whose glob matched twice would otherwise export the wrong document into the right name — and
  `-o` refuses an argument beginning with `-` for the reason the size flags already do one argument
  earlier. Taking it unconditionally did not merely mis-set the output: the token never reached the
  top of the loop, so the unknown-option arm could not object either, and `ondin export doc.ondin -o
  --png` **lost the format flag** and wrote SVG bytes into a file called `--png`.
  ⚠️ **With no `-o` it writes into the folder holding the `.ondin`**, falling back to `.` only when
  that path has no parent — which in the library is a project folder the user keeps other things in,
  and is why `--all` is the door that most needs its replacement count (§15 D652). Neither document
  stated the default until then. **Exit
  code 1 when the run produces no files**: a build step that silently succeeds without producing its
  output is the failure noticed three commits later. ⚠️ **That rule was written as *"nothing in the
  document is set up to export"* and the code matched it, which is narrower than the failure it names**
  (§15 D531): the gate asked whether any layer carried *settings*, not whether any file was *written*,
  so a document whose only exporting layer had no ink — an empty group, a fully hidden layer, a
  zero-size shape — carrying a **raster** spec exited 0 having written nothing and not even created the
  output directory, with the skip reported on stderr. The gate is on the rendered set now. Only raster
  specs can be skipped this way; `plan::render`'s SVG branch always produces a file, so an SVG spec over
  an empty group writes one and exits 0, correctly.
- **The three size flags are the panel's three questions**, `ExportScale`'s variants reaching the one
  export route that could ask none of them — the panel has had the whole ladder per row since it was
  built and `--all` has always honoured it, but the one-off `--png` was pinned at 1× by a
  `viewport_over` call (§15 D360, D361). They are **refused rather than ignored** where they cannot
  apply — on `--svg`/`--json`, and on `--all` — and **only one at a time**, three answers to one
  question being no place for a precedence rule nobody would remember; the same flag twice is the same
  refusal, where `--png --svg` takes the last one, because two formats have an obvious ordering and two
  sizes do not. The derived output name is **not** decorated with `@2x`: that marker is `plan`'s way of
  separating files written in one go, and letting a flag rename this command's single output would make
  `-o` the only way to know where the bytes went. `Width`/`Height` are resolved against the same box
  the render frames, so the multiplier is taken where the drawing is measured rather than twice.
- **`--scale-override` is what `--all` gets instead**, and it means something different: the size flags
  *are* the size, this **overrules** one the document carries, so the file goes on deciding which
  layers export and at what formats. It takes the export row's own vocabulary read backwards
  (`ExportScale::from_label` — `2x`, `512w`, `512h`, and a bare number meaning `x`), so one argument
  covers all three questions and what a designer reads off a row is what a build script types. It
  lives in `PlanOptions` rather than in the caller because **a scale is half the filename** through
  `ExportScale::marker`, and forcing the multiplier after planning would render at 1× under names still
  saying `@2x`. **Specs that become identical collapse to one file** — a layer at 1×/2×/3× forced to 1×
  is one asset three times, and de-collision would otherwise write two files of junk — and that dedupe
  runs *only* under an override, so an unforced plan is byte-for-byte what it was.
- When `viewport_at`'s cap takes a size down, the command **says so on stderr** and names what it
  actually wrote, which `plan` already did — in the **spec's own vocabulary**, so a clamped `--width
  200000` is reported as `200000w` rather than as the `655.350×` it resolved to and nobody typed.
- **In the app, one door and not two.** There was a one-off beside the repeatable — *Export as…* on
  every layer's context menu and `Ctrl+Shift+E`, the save dialog picking the format — and it was
  **removed on 2026-08-22** (§15 D264). It asked where, what format and at what size on every use and
  remembered none of it, which is exactly what the panel below answers from the layer, so it had
  become the slower of two routes to the same file rather than a second kind of export. The whole
  verb went, not just the row: a chord with no menu row is a verb nothing announces.
  ⚠️ **`Ctrl+Shift+E` is unbound but not free** — plain `Ctrl+E` is *Flatten*, so the `!m.shift` on
  that arm is the only thing between a hand reaching for the old chord and a dissolved selection, and
  it now reads like a guard against nothing. `a_stray_shift_on_ctrl_e_does_nothing_rather_than_flattening`
  is what holds it. **`scene::build_of` is not affected**: the removed row paid for that walk and
  *Copy as PNG*, the panel, the CLI and the goldens all stand on it.
- **In the app, the repeatable** — the inspector's **Export** panel (§9.4), which edits the layer's
  own `exports` list and produces it, and since the removal above **the only door onto a one-off
  export file** as well as onto a repeated one. **The destination follows the file count** — one file gets a save dialog with a name already
  in it, several get a folder and are written into it individually — and *Export as ZIP* is a second
  button appearing exactly when there is more than one file, because a zip of one file is a thing you
  have to unpack to get back what you already had. ⚠️ **A planned path is a folder *and* a name, and
  both destination arms had it wrong** (§15 D656): with `folders_from_names` on the path carries a
  `/`, so `save_dialog_target` sends the folder half to `set_directory` and only the name to
  `set_file_name` — and only when that folder already exists, platform dialogs differing on a start
  directory that does not resolve. The write side creates it for **both** destinations, which it did
  for only the folder one, so a layer named `icons/close` exported fine as one of several and failed
  on its own. *Export all* (`Ctrl+Alt+E`, and a row on the page
  menu) re-runs every layer in the document into the folder the last export went to, with no dialog
  after the first time (§15 D274). **Every layer means every layer, nesting included** — a layer with
  export settings inside another layer with export settings is its own file, because a spec on a nested
  layer is a deliberate instruction and the two produce different pictures. So the panel and the CLI
  both collect through `build::all_in_document_order`, which is the document ordering **without**
  `outermost`; the *selection* door (`export_subjects`) keeps that filter, where a group and a child
  both picked would plan the child twice (§15 D267, D516). ⚠️ **That sort is where the ordering comes
  from, and the walk that finds the layers has none** (§15 D649): `all_in_document_order` collects its
  input into a set before re-walking the document, so `exportable_layers` may gather them in any
  order, and a `.rev()` there claiming otherwise is a rule stated where it is inert.

## 8. ondin-mcp

### 8.1 Topology — the app is the server

The document lives in a running Ondin process (GUI or headless). Therefore **the Ondin process
hosts the MCP endpoint**; agents connect to it. Concretely:

- The running process listens on a local socket: **Unix domain socket** (Linux) / **named pipe**
  (Windows), at a well-known per-user path, with a discovery file
  (`$XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/ondin/<pid>.json` / `%LOCALAPPDATA%\ondin\run\<pid>.json`) recording endpoint +
  open document path.
- A thin **stdio proxy** (`ondin mcp-proxy`) bridges agents that expect to spawn an MCP server over
  stdio: it connects to the running instance's socket and forwards. If no instance is running it
  exits with a clear error naming `ondin serve`.
- Multiple documents/instances: proxy picks by document path argument, else the single running
  instance, else errors listing candidates.

### 8.2 Headless mode

`ondin serve <file.ondin>` opens a document with **no window**: core + history + CPU renderer +
MCP endpoint. Same op queue, same tools — an agent can build/edit/export a document on a CI box or
a machine with no display. This falls out of the headless-core invariant and is a first-class v1
deliverable.

### 8.3 Concurrency model

- The owning process holds `Document` + `History` + `Resolved` on its main thread.
- All mutations funnel through a single-writer **op queue**:
  `mpsc<OpRequest { tx: Transaction, reply: oneshot<Result<ApplyOutcome, OpError>> }>`.
- MCP handlers (async, own thread/runtime) build transactions with their session `IdSource`, submit
  to the queue, await the reply. The GUI pumps the queue every frame; `serve` pumps it in its main
  loop. One source of truth, one history, AI edits appear live on the canvas through the same path
  as UI edits.
- No MCP handler ever touches `Document` directly (invariant 10).

### 8.4 Tools

Phase 1 — read/export (ship first):
`get_document() -> Snapshot`, `get_node(id)`, `list_children(id)`, `hit_test(x,y)`,
`get_bounds(id)`, `get_selection() -> Vec<NodeId>`, `export_svg(artboard?)`, `export_png(viewport)`.

Phase 2 — write (1:1 with operations/composites):
`create_node`, `insert_subtree`, `delete_node`, `reparent`, `reorder`, `set_transform`,
`set_geometry`, `set_text`, `set_text_style`, `set_fills`, `set_strokes`, `set_opacity`,
`set_visible`, `set_name`, `group(ids)`, `ungroup(id)`, `duplicate(id)`, `undo()`, `redo()`,
`set_selection(ids)`.

Selection is app state, not document state (§9.3) — but it is deliberately part of the MCP surface,
because "the selected layer" is how humans will phrase almost every AI request. The MCP layer reads
it from (and writes it to) the owning process's session state, never the `Document`.

Notes: `create_node`/`insert_subtree`/`duplicate` return the new ids (the handler minted them, so
it knows them). Snapshot exposes world transforms so agents can compute local placements; a
convenience `place_at_world(id, world_transform)` adapter is allowed in core if agents struggle.

🚨 **The two phase paragraphs above are parsed by a test, and editing them can break the build**
(§15 D726). `ondin-mcp/src/tools.rs` holds the same twenty-eight names as `PHASE_1` and `PHASE_2`, and
a `#[cfg(test)]` module there `include_str!`s this file and diffs both phases **in order** — the
second copy having sat here unreadable to any gate, in a crate deferred to M6, for as long as the
lists could quietly drift. The parser anchors on each phase's opening sentence, takes the paragraph up
to the first blank line, and reads **every backticked token in it as a tool name**, dropping any
signature at the `(`. So: do not reword either opening sentence, do not reflow a phase paragraph into
the one below it, and do not put a backticked aside inside one — the *Selection* and *Notes*
paragraphs are outside the parse and are where such a thing belongs. A rename here fails at the
comparison, and a moved heading fails loudly at the parse rather than silently comparing two empty
lists.

## 9. ondin-app

### 9.1 UI chrome — decision record

**Decision: `egui` for v1.** gpui (Zed's framework) was evaluated and parked, not rejected:

- gpui now supports standalone Windows/Linux apps and its widget quality is the benchmark. But it
  renders through its **own** backends (Metal / blade / DirectX), not wgpu. Our canvas is
  Vello-on-wgpu; embedding it in gpui means cross-API texture sharing (DX shared handles / Vulkan
  external memory) — deep per-platform plumbing — or a per-frame CPU readback, which is
  disqualifying for a 60 fps canvas. It is also pre-crates.io-stable (git dependency recommended,
  breaking changes routine).
- egui composits with a wgpu canvas trivially (Vello renders to a texture; egui draws it via a
  paint callback — a proven pattern) and is good enough for v1 chrome: layers tree, inspector,
  color editor.
- Honest expectation: egui is a **medium-term commitment, not a placeholder** — UI toolkits are
  rarely swapped in practice. The strict boundary (no egui types in core/render/export/mcp) is what
  keeps a future migration (gpui once wgpu-composable or via its wgpu fork, or Xilem once mature)
  survivable. Revisit post-v1.

**Harness decision (M5a, 2026-07-22): use `eframe`, not raw `winit`+`egui-winit`+`egui-wgpu`.**
A deliberate refinement of §2's raw listing. Rationale: the thing we commit to is *egui*, not
eframe; eframe only owns the window + wgpu device + event loop. The Vello canvas renders to its own
wgpu texture (needed regardless, to composite under egui chrome), so eframe imposes no canvas-perf
penalty and the 120fps target is gated by Vello, not eframe. egui itself (via eframe) provides
keyboard/IME/viewports for Command Mode and text. Crucially the swap back to raw winit stays cheap
because the boundary rule confines egui to `ondin-app`: only "who creates the window/device/loop"
(main.rs) would change. Raw winit would only win for frame-perfect present control or a
host-owned event loop — neither applies to a standalone app. eframe 0.35 note: the `App` trait
method is `ui(&mut self, &mut egui::Ui, &mut Frame)` (not `update`), and panels are the unified
`egui::Panel::left(..)` shown into a `Ui` (no `SidePanel`).

**Every control the chrome grounds wears one hairline, and it is resolved against its own ground
(2026-08-29, §15 D386).** The design writes it as `1px solid color-mix(in srgb, var(--color-text) 8%,
transparent)` on a box that is already `text 5%`, and CSS paints a background *under* the border area
— so a translucent border composites over the element's own fill, not over what the element sits on.
`theme::color::FIELD_BORDER` is that 8% over `FIELD` (62), which is what `ui::field_frame`,
`ui::button_face`, egui's `widgets.inactive.bg_stroke` and the popup surfaces all stroke with;
`CARD_BORDER` is the same 8% over `CARD` (53), for the three strokes that enclose a card ground rather
than a field one. **The two differ because the rule makes a border brighter the brighter its ground**,
which is not a disagreement to fold away — 62 round a resting card would read as the lit edge hover
already means. Where a control's ground is *translucent* the composition happens by painting order and
the stroke stays translucent: the dashboard's search field and a `ui::segmented` track are both
`text_a(20)` over their own ground, and land on the same 62. **Sliders, switches and the Align row's
buttons carry no hairline at all**, which is what the mock draws and what the eye wants of a control
that is a track rather than a box.

**And the hover ground is one name, `theme::color::HOVER` (52, 52, 54), read by four places that have
to agree** (§15 D484). Two of them are `theme::install`'s `w.hovered` fills, which is what egui itself
paints for every stock widget; the other two are hand-rolled — `ui::icon_button_padded` for the tool
rail and top bar, `ui::button_face` for the field-row family — plus `inspector::template_cell`. ⚠️ **It
was a literal at all four and named at none until 2026-09-07**, so a change to any one of them would
have split the hover into a stock grey and a hand-rolled one with every gate green, and `CARD_BORDER`'s
(53, 53, 54) sat one level away in `theme::color` where a reader would have looked for it.

**And a hairline lands on the *device* grid rather than in point space, which is one predicate and two
bases** (§15 D46, D479). `ui::hairline_on_pixel_centre` answers whether a line this wide at this scale
wants its centre on a pixel *centre* or on a pixel *edge* — the parity of `floor(width × ppp)`, the
device width — and `ui::hairline_in_column` takes the nearest grid position of that parity. That is
what the three chrome rules ask for (`ui::rule`, `inspector::popup_rule`, `settings::section`): each
draws a 1pt line into a 1pt allocation between two galleys, so the constraint is two-sided — land on
the grid, and do not drift so far doing it that the ink leaves the column. `rulers::snap_across_axis`
shares the predicate and **rounds** instead, a guide having no column to stay inside and taking the
nearest grid line to where the user put it. ⚠️ **The predicate is the shared thing and the base is
not**: swapping one for the other moves the ink by up to a whole device pixel — 1pt at 100% — which is
D46's own failure by a second road, and is why these are not one helper with four callers.
`snap_across_axis` has **two** subjects since 2026-09-07 (§15 D484): the guides and the pixel grid,
which had hand-inlined it as `round() / ppp + half` with the half unconditional — right only because the
grid's line is one device pixel wide and so never reaches the even branch, which nothing in `grid.rs`
said. So the base parked for its own decision (`roadmap.md`) now moves grid ink as well as guide ink.

**And one height: `ui::CONTROL_H`, 28, everywhere.** ⚠️ **The popovers were 26 and three constants in
three files argued for it** — *shorter than the card's 28px fields, which is what keeps a popup of nine
sections from towering over the panel it belongs to*, which is also what the mock draws. Overruled: a
popover hangs *beside* the card it opened from, at the same width, so every control in it being two
points shorter than the control that opened it is not a distinction a reader can attribute to anything
(§15 D386). A tall popover is a tall popover, and it already scrolls. The colour picker went with them.
A `ui::segmented` track is handed `ui::SEGMENT_CELL_H` instead, which is this less the two points of
padding it adds at each end. The remaining short controls are deliberate and are not fields: a swatch
chip, a badge, the layers tree's 26pt rows.

**One rhythm, and the Transform card sets it.** X beside Y is `ui::CARD_COL_GAP` (7); X/Y above W/H is
`ui::CARD_ROW_GAP` (9). Every panel, card and popover follows both — it is the row on screen for every
selection, so it is the one the eye measures the others against. ⚠️ **The column gap is spelled twice
per row** and both spellings have to move together: once as `item_spacing.x`, once inside the row's own
`(available_width() - GAP) / 2.0`, and changing only the first pushes the last control a point past the
card, at which point `Ui::horizontal` wraps it onto a line of its own. Inside a popover the *third*
number is `ui::SECTION_LABEL_GAP` (5), which holds a small-caps eyebrow to the control it names and
nothing else; `ui::labelled` is what keeps that apart from the row pitch, and `POPOVER_SECTION_GAP` is
`CARD_ROW_GAP` — the eyebrow is what separates one section from the next, not a number. **The Export
panel's list is the one deliberate exception** and argues for itself below: a row plus its size caption
is one unit at 3, and one unit sits 6 from the next, because what has to read there is *this caption
goes with the row above* rather than *these are two controls* (§15 D274).

**The app icon is two artefacts, not one (2026-08-20).** Source art lives in `icons/` at the
repository root, and both halves are needed because neither reaches the other's surfaces:

- **The window.** `main::window_icon` decodes `icons/convertico-Ondin_256x256.png` to RGBA and
  hands it to `ViewportBuilder::with_icon`. This paints the title bar, the taskbar button and
  Alt-Tab. It is not optional in the presence of the resource icon below: winit registers its
  window class with `hIcon: 0` and does **not** fall back to the executable's icon, so without
  this call a running Ondin shows the generic Windows application glyph. One size has to be
  chosen, because `WM_SETICON` receives the same pixels for `ICON_BIG` and `ICON_SMALL`; 256 is
  the largest the set offers, and the OS downscales.
- **The executable.** `crates/ondin-app/build.rs` runs `winresource` (a build dependency; it
  shells out to the Windows SDK's `rc.exe`) to compile `icons/convertico-Ondin.ico` into
  `ondin.exe`'s resource table, where Explorer, a pinned taskbar button and a file association
  read it — none of which have a window. It must be the `.ico` and not a PNG: a resource icon is
  a container Windows picks a size *out of*, and winit has no way to consume one. The same script
  sets `ProductName`/`FileDescription` to "Ondin", overriding `winresource`'s default of
  `CARGO_PKG_NAME`; Windows shows `FileDescription` as the application name in Task Manager, so
  the default would read "ondin-app" there.

The build script failure is fatal rather than a warning, on the grounds that the MSVC toolchain
already requires the same SDK for `link.exe` — an icon missing on some machines and not others is
the failure mode worth refusing.

### 9.2 Layout

```
ondin-app/src/
├─ main.rs         # CLI: gui (default) | export | serve | mcp-proxy; eframe bootstrap
├─ app.rs          # OndinApp: window layout, top bar, tool rail, Action dispatch, file IO
├─ session.rs      # EditorSession: Document, History, Resolved, IdSource, Selection, Camera,
│                  #   save state, status. NO GPU — see below
├─ atomic.rs       # write(): temp file, sync_all, rename — every record the app keeps (§9.5, §15 D378)
├─ canvas.rs       # CanvasRenderer (the wgpu texture) + all canvas interaction and overlays
├─ cursor.rs       # the canvas cursors the OS has no usable one for (§15 D9)
├─ grid.rs         # the pixel grid: a one-world-unit lattice, the faintest chrome layer (§9.4)
├─ input.rs        # Mode + Action: mode-aware keyboard routing (§9.3)
├─ measure.rs      # Axis + Measure: the Alt-hover measure (all four pairings, §15 D201, D203) and the
                  #   gaps a spacing snap draws; pure Rect geometry, snap.rs's sibling and never its
                  #   dependent (§9.4, §15 D198, D200)
├─ menu.rs         # the context-menu registry — Item, Spec, Group, build — plus the app half that
                  #   opens, draws and dispatches one (`context-menus.md`, §9.4, §15 D214, D215)
├─ preview.rs      # in-flight gesture state (Drag, Handle, PenState/PenAnchor/PenSubpath/PenEdit,
                  #   TextSession) + PointSet, which is selection rather than gesture state
├─ prefs.rs        # Prefs: the settings that outlive a session, in config_dir()/ondin/prefs.json
├─ rulers.rs       # the two ruler bars + the ruler guides pulled out of them (chrome, §9.4)
├─ settings.rs     # the Settings modal — the home for preferences no panel is a door onto
                  #   (nudge step, fold-on-open, the web-font switch and the cache row; §15 D330)
                  #   — and the app's one form-in-a-modal card, which the dashboard's five modals
                  #   are drawn on too: card_modal, modal_title, modal_footer, section, caption
                  #   and the measurements (§9.5, §15 D368)
├─ snap.rs         # snapping: node bounds, ruler guides, text baselines, equal-gap spacing, and the
                  #   pixel grid under them all; draws its own transient lines and gap labels (Marks),
                  #   and those lines are NOT rulers.rs's guides — see §9.4
├─ view.rs         # Camera: pure screen<->world math
├─ fonts/          # mod.rs     FontService: system enumeration + Google Fonts catalog/download/
│                  #            cache/eviction (§5.4a)
│                  # queue.rs   the download pool's three-lane work queue (urgent FIFO, preview
│                  #            LIFO and bounded, prefetch FIFO and last; §15 D352)
│                  # preview.rs the picker's rows, rasterized in the family they name (§9.2)
├─ tools/          # pure transaction builders: create rect/ellipse/polygon/star/line/path/artboard,
                  #   resize (shape + group), rotate, pen_outline and its inverse pen_anchors
                  #   (+ pen_path, map_subpaths, rewrite_path)
├─ panels/         # layers.rs   docked layers tree (multi-drag reorder/reparent, rename, filter)
│                  # inspector.rs floating, individually collapsible property panels
│                  # picker.rs    the detached colour picker (solid / linear / radial)
│                  # paint.rs     pure Brush algebra shared by the two + the list-generic reorder
│                  #              (PaintList, PaintDrag, Slots, display_order, landing, reordered)
├─ ui.rs           # shared chrome widgets (cards, fields, segmented controls, colour ramps, Hsv,
                  #   and the dropdown frame and rows every menu shares — menu_check, MenuRow/
                  #   menu_row, menu_sep, menu_place, §9.4)
└─ theme.rs        # the Nocturne design tokens as egui Style/Visuals/fonts
```

**Chrome layout.** The top bar, layers pane and tool rail are `egui::Panel`s, so they reserve space.
The inspector is not: it is an `egui::Area` of independent cards drawn *after* the canvas, because
the design has the artwork running to the window edge with nothing but panels floating on it. Two
consequences worth knowing before moving it back: the canvas viewport is the full remaining window
(content can sit under the panels, and zoom-to-fit frames it there), and the Area shrinks to its
content, so the canvas below the last panel is live while the gaps *between* cards are not — which
is deliberate, so aiming at a panel can never deselect. One trap, since it cost a round: an `Area`
gives its contents a `Ui` whose `max_rect` is *the area's own size last frame*, so nesting a
`ScrollArea` (which fills what it is offered) inside one naively makes the pair converge on a tiny
scrolling box. `inspector_panel` re-establishes the column rect explicitly instead of inheriting it.

**Neither the layers tree nor the inspector column draws a scrollbar.** Both are
`ScrollBarVisibility::AlwaysHidden`: the wheel, the trackpad, drag-to-scroll, the tree's own
drag-to-edge scroll (§9.4) and any programmatic `scroll_to` all still work, and only the *drawing*
goes. The cards float on the artwork with no backdrop pane, so a bar down their side reads as the
edge of a container that is not there. The popovers inside the cards keep theirs — a list you page
through needs one to say how far down it you are (§15 D278, and D104 for the popover's own gutter).

**What toggles a panel is the whole header row, and a collapsed panel is its whole card.** A caret
and nine and a half points of small caps are a third of a 284px card, and the two thirds beside them
read as header while doing nothing; a collapsed panel *is* its header, so asking the user to find
the row inside it is a distinction without a difference. Both targets skip the header's action-icon
corner (`ui::CARD_MARGIN_X`, `ui::HEAD_ACTION_W`, `ui::HEAD_ACTION_PAD`), so a collapsed Fill still
takes a `+`. The two are **mutually exclusive** — `ui::section_head` takes a `sense` flag and
`inspector::panel` passes `open` — because overlapping click targets do not make a control generous:
both take the press and the panel toggles twice, back to where it started.

**The `+` is a 20pt glyph with a 40×32 hit target, and the header gives up exactly that band**
(`ui::HEAD_ACTION_PAD`, §15 D63). A one-shot button inside a target for the opposite action wants more
room than its ink, and here missing it collapses the panel you were about to add a fill to. The
padding is a *sense* rect only — the glyph and its box stay where the design puts them — and
`ui::icon_button_padded` senses the padded rect while allocating the unsensed box, because a clickable
20pt square inside a clickable 40pt one wins the hit test wherever it lies and would leave the padding
live everywhere except on the glyph (the trap `ui::menu_head` describes).

**A Fill or Stroke panel is open when it has paint in it and closed when it has none.** Empty, the panel
is a header and a `+`; expanded, it adds a line of grey text saying what the header already said — and
the `+` is reachable from the collapsed state, which is what makes that state a resting place rather
than a dead end.

**Asserted outright on a new subject, and on the transition otherwise.** Re-asserting it every frame
would make expanding an empty panel by hand impossible, since the toggle would be undone before it was
drawn, and the click would read as broken rather than as overridden. So within one selection the rule
fires once and the user's own toggle then wins; *changing* the selection is what re-reads the room,
because whether this layer has a fill is a fact about this layer and not a state to inherit from the
last one (§15 D64). `OndinApp::paint_synced_selection` is what notices the subject moved — nothing else
tells the panels, the same gap `layers_synced_selection` fills for the tree — and it is read **once**
per frame by `inspector_paint_panels`, which hands the answer to both panels, since a Fill that consumed
the change on its way past would leave Stroke thinking nothing had happened.
`OndinApp::paint_auto_collapsed` is the set recording which panels have already been collapsed for being
empty, so within one selection filling a list disarms the rule and emptying it re-arms it. The rule
itself lives in the free functions `sync_paint_collapse` / `open_paint_panel`, extracted from the methods
of the same name precisely so `inspector::collapse_tests` can exercise the real thing rather than a
restatement of it — the rule is addressable on its own terms, and a test of it should not have to stand a
panel up first (§15 D303, which retired the older reason that an `OndinApp` could not be built at all).

**Every card is salted with which card it is**, never with where it sits: `inspector::panel` pushes
the panel's title and `inspector::identity_card` pushes one shared salt for all four first-position
cards, so the ids inside a card survive the panel list changing with the subject — §15 D39 has what
went wrong without it. The identity card's kind glyph goes through `identity_glyph`, which nudges
`CIRCLE` down a point: Phosphor fits a circle inside the em box's cap height while `SQUARE` and
`FRAME_CORNERS` fill more of it, so centring every glyph by its layout box left the round one high,
and because the inspector swaps this glyph as the selection changes the card appeared to step up and
down. A per-glyph nudge rather than a shifted baseline — the other glyphs are already right.

**The layers tree is drawn front-to-back: the topmost layer is the top row.** `children` is z-order
with the last entry nearest the viewer (§5.3), so `layers_row` walks each child list reversed. Only
the *walk* is flipped — every index in that file is still a model index — which is why the
drag-and-drop arithmetic has to mirror it (`layers::resolve_drop`): a slot *below* a row on screen is
*before* it in the model, so the top of a container's list is `child_count` rather than 0.
`collect_visible_rows` walks the same tree without painting it, because a `Shift`-range is measured
along the rows as displayed; the two walks have to agree exactly, and §15 D54 has why that is a
standing drift risk rather than a solved one.

**A row's three controls — caret, eye, lock — are painted, not widgets, so one function answers both
"which is under the pointer" and "which did the press hit"** (`layers::RowTargets::at`, §15 D246). The
row is a single `Sense::click_and_drag()` region, so `Response::hovered` is about the *row* — it is what
makes the eye and lock appear at all — and nothing in it says where inside the row the pointer is. Each
control's x goes into a `RowTargets` as an `Option`, `None` where the row is not drawing it, and
`CONTROL_HIT` is the one band either side. Both questions going through that is the property worth
naming: **what lights up is what a click acts on**, where two hand-written comparisons are how a control
comes to glow somewhere it cannot be pressed. A control under the pointer paints `text::STRONG` — one
destination rather than a step from each of the four greys the three of them rest at — and no ground,
the row having a hover ground of its own.

**A row whose picture cannot be drawn wears its own kind glyph in `theme::color::WARN`** — the panel's
only warning colour, and the app's first (§15 D179). `layers::picture_missing` is the test, asked of
the **decode cache** rather than of the document so the row and the canvas placeholder answer one
question about one layer, and it counts visible fills and visible strokes — a frame's ground among the
fills since §15 D400, where it used to be chained on out of its own field, and with it every *other*
fill a frame can hold, which that chain could not have seen: the
canvas draws a placeholder only for a fill, but the row is a statement about the whole layer. Tinting
the existing glyph rather than adding a mark is what keeps it free — the icon is the one part of a row
that cannot be renamed away, and the row has no width to give.

**A row showing a picture draws it where its kind glyph would go** — a 16pt square in the 26pt row,
centred on `icon_x` so the icons down the tree stay one column and every name keeps its x (§15 D189).
`layers::picture_of` is the question, and it is deliberately narrower than `picture_missing` beside
it: the first visible **fill** only, no strokes, because that function asks
whether the layer is broken and this one asks what it looks like. ⚠️ **A frame's ground is in scope
now and was never an exclusion anyone decided** (§15 D400): this reads `fills`, a frame's ground lived
in a field of its own, and the comment justified the omission after the fact. A frame filled with a
photograph shows that photograph in its row, exactly as a rectangle filled with it does. **Rounded by the tessellator rather
than by a corner mask**, to `THUMB_RADIUS = 3` where the inspector's chip is masked to 4: a textured
`epaint::RectShape` carries its own `corner_radius` through tessellation and so needs to know nothing
about what is behind it, where `ui::mask_corners` paints the leftover corner in the *ground* colour
and a row's ground is three colours. The two radii are deliberately not shared, the chip's belonging
to `ui::swatch` and every colour in the app wearing it. The chip also wears a 1px translucent-white
hairline over that masked arc and the thumbnail wears none, for the same reason the radii differ: a
`Mesh` mask has no feathering, so the chip's corner would otherwise be a hard aliased step where the
tessellator feathers the thumbnail's. That hairline is **unconditional** — it is what keeps a chip
whose colour is near its own row from reading as a hole in the row, and a threshold would flick it on
and off mid-scrub (§15 D231). A dimmed row's thumbnail takes the same 40%
its glyph and name take, as a multiplier over the texture rather than as ink. ⚠️ **And the picture's
own `ImageSampler::alpha` is a second multiplier over the same texture, composed with that one rather
than competing with it** (`layers::thumb_tint`, §15 D784): the dimming says *this layer is out of
play* and the alpha says *this paint is faint*, which are facts about different things, so a hidden
layer holding a 30% picture is fainter than either alone. A rule that picked a winner would make one
of the two invisible exactly where the other was also true. It is a named function so the decision can
be asserted at all — the drawn thumbnail needs a decoded picture *and* a texture this pass's budget
did not defer, which is two pieces of machinery between a test and the rule.
No thumbnail — no picture, one the store cannot draw,
or one this pass's budget deferred — falls back to the glyph, which for the second is the amber one
above, so a missing picture and a thumbnail are mutually exclusive by construction.

**The texture is the chrome's and the pixels are the store's** (`thumbs::ImageThumbs`, a field on
`OndinApp` beside `previews`). It is `fonts::FontPreviews` again — a 2 ms per-pass budget, one upload
a pass whatever the budget says, and `request_repaint` on a deferral (§15 D160) — with one difference
that matters: it **sweeps**, because a `ThumbKey` carries seven scrubbable floats where a preview is
keyed by family, so one exposure drag walks hundreds of keys. `KEEP_PASSES = 3`, swept at the top of a
pass. Both the tree and the inspector's paint chip ask it, points in and device pixels out, so display
scale lands in the key rather than needing a field to invalidate against (§15 D189).

**A drag draws exactly one *mark* at a time: a line where the layer will land, or an outline round the
container it will land in** (§15 D67) — the destination container's own ink going blue below is not a
third one, which is the whole reason it is ink and not a box. **Both are `color::SELECT`**, the hue D13
reserves for "the app is talking about the selection": a selected row's kind glyph and its lit guide
leg already wear it (§15 D331), and a drop hint is the panel talking about a layer in exactly that
sense. A row getting *both* a line above and a line below is what must
never happen, because two lines round a row read as a box and a box is how the tree says "inside this
one". **And exactly one line may be drawn at each boundary**: two 1pt strokes at one y composite their
antialiased fringes into a visibly heavier band. Both are now true by construction rather than by a
rule each row applies to itself — the hint is painted **once, after the walk**
(`OndinApp::drop_hint`), and a boundary is named by its position *on screen*: `layers::boundary_y`,
where boundary *b* is the gap above `rows[b]`, so `n` rows have `n + 1` of them and none can be
reached from two different child lists (§15 D345). **That pair is the settled answer rather than a stage on the way to the paint panels' live
reorder** (§15 D306): the tree keeps its line, and porting the live-reorder idiom here is a decided
non-goal. What is *not* decided is the drawing — a more tree-like layers panel was still to come, and
D306 is scoped so it cannot be quoted against that. The first instalment of it is the width: **the
panel is 300pt, up from 250 on 2026-08-24** (§15 D330), because a row spends `layers::INDENT` — 31pt —
per level before it starts on a name, and at 250 a layer four deep had ~90pt to be legible in.
**Since 2026-08-25 that 300 is a *default* the user drags off** (§15 D349):
`Panel::default_size(prefs.layers_width).size_range(layers::MIN_W ..= MAX_W).resizable(true)`, 210 to
600, with the width written to `prefs.json` on the frame the drag *ends*. `MIN_W` is derived from the
row walk's own constants rather than chosen — what a *hovered* row at four levels has left for its
name. ⚠️ **That derivation had the wrong first term until 2026-09-07** (§15 D444): it subtracted the
header's `2 * PAD_X` where a row is narrowed by the tree's own `ScrollArea` gutter, half of it, so
every width figure in the constants' prose was 12pt pessimistic. Nothing on screen changed, the error
being wholly in the safe direction — but corrected, the four-deep row crosses zero at **194.5** rather
than 206.5, so the second of the two readings 210 was said to sit at no longer picks it. **210 stands**
and whether to re-tighten it is an open question for the maintainer, not something the arithmetic
decides — parked in `roadmap.md` under *Later · Parked decisions*, as a decision rather than a defect. ⚠️ Two things there are load-bearing and neither is visible in the source: the panel closure
calls `ui.set_min_width(ui.available_width())`, because a resizable `Panel` is sized from what its
content occupied and one that does not fill collapses to `size_range`'s **minimum**; and
