`default_size` must be called *before* `size_range`, or a hand-edited width is never clamped.
**The edge's highlight waits 200ms before it lights and the resize cursor does not** (`app::EDGE_DWELL`,
§15 D350): the splitter sits on the way from the tree to the canvas, so a highlight on hover fired on
travel, while the cursor is the affordance that says the edge is grabbable at all and is cheap to look at.
**The inspector column does not resize, and that is decided rather than pending** (§15 D351): its
width is a function of the *design* where the tree's is a function of the *document*, so widening it
would make fields wider rather than more informative. It is also an `Area` with no edge for a handle,
and `inspector_panel` re-establishes its column rect explicitly, so a user-set width would have to
become an *input* to that rather than something the layout discovers.
The second instalment
is the guides below, which arrived with a **design that asks for a 22pt indent** rather than 31 — the
pane went from 15 per level to a consistent 22 in the pass that drew the guides, which is coherent as
a *pair* since a guide says which container a row is in and the indent then need not. The app does not
follow it, the change having been asked for as *bigger* indents when 31 already is bigger — reported
rather than implemented, and then **decided on the machine: 31 stays** (§15 D331). Nothing in the guides
turns on the number either way; they are drawn from `layers::caret_column` at whatever the constant says.

**The drop follows the indent, both ways** (`layers::depth_range`, §15 D345). A gap between two drawn
rows is not one insertion point but a **run** of them — a level for each the two rows have in common —
and the pointer's *horizontal* travel picks which. The shallowest is the depth of the row **below** the
boundary, a hard floor because anything shallower would have to close containers the rows below are
still inside; the deepest is the depth of the row **above**, or the floor where that is deeper, which
is the "drop in as the first child of an open container" case. So a layer is carried out of a group by
taking it to the bottom of the group and moving left, and into one by moving right. ⚠️ **No row records
whether it is open, and `depth_range` must not start asking**: a container's children are drawn
immediately below it, so "the row below is deeper than the row above" and "the row above is expanded"
are the same statement about a tree, while a *collapsed* container has nothing of its own below it and
so takes a drop only through that row's own outline. `TreeRow::closed` is **not** that flag back again
and the difference is the whole reason one could go and the other had to come: an *open* container is
already written down in the row list, where a *closed* one is invisible in it — it has no rows below
it and neither does a leaf — and spring-loading below is the one thing that has to tell those apart.

**The x is a displacement from the grab, never an absolute reading** (`layers::depth_asked_for`): one
level per `INDENT` moved sideways from `press_origin()`, floored at 1 and then clamped into the
boundary's range. A row is picked up by its *name*, which at depth 1 already starts ~45pt in, so an
absolute x would ask for depth 2 before the pointer had moved. `LayerDrag::grab` is that origin — the
pointer's x and the *grabbed* row's depth, a drag carrying rows from several levels having no one
depth. **The line is then drawn at the chosen level's own column**, `rect.left() + indent_of(depth)` to
the panel's right edge, which is the only thing on screen saying which of the levels the drop means.

⚠️ **The level is held with hysteresis, not simply rounded** (`layers::STICK`, 0.65 of an indent). Plain
rounding has no threshold at all — 0.5 is where two levels are *equally close* — so a hand aiming at
neither, holding still or moving down the tree with a few points of sideways drift, sits on that edge
and the line flips frame to frame; reported as the line being "a bit twitchy". `depth_asked_for` takes
the level the drag settled on last frame and only leaves it once the pointer is more than `STICK` of an
indent away, then re-rounds to the nearest. The band is centred on the level being **held**, so it
travels with the answer: leaving level 2 rightwards takes 2.65 and coming back from 3 takes 2.35, which
is what makes this hysteresis rather than a wider dead zone. ⚠️ **The value fed back is the *unclamped*
one** — `drop_spot` answers with a `DropRead { spot, level }` where `spot`'s depth has been clamped into
what the boundary offers and `level` has not, and it is `level` that `LayerDrag::level` stores. Feeding
the clamped one back would let a boundary offering a single level quietly re-origin the gesture, so
dragging *over* a one-level gap would change what the hand's position meant on the far side of it.

**The container the line would land inside says so in its own ink** (`LayerDrag::lit`, read in
`layers_row` as `drop_host`): that row's name and kind glyph paint `color::SELECT` for as long as the
drop points into it. The line says *where* and on its own cannot say *which group*, two levels being
one 31pt step apart with nothing but indent columns to count. ⚠️ **It marks the destination parent**,
which during an outdent is several levels above the row under the pointer — not the row above the
line. Nothing lights at the top level, where the parent is the root and has no row. ⚠️ **And it is a
frame behind, necessarily**: a row's ink is painted while the walk is passing it, and an indent-aware
drop is not worked out until the walk is over, so the walk reads the answer the *last* one reached.
`layers_tree` copies `target` into `lit` at the top of the frame, in the one place `target` is thrown
away, which is what stops the two drifting — there is no second assignment that could forget. `lit` is
for painting only and must never decide where a layer lands; `target` is still cleared every frame so
that releasing off the tree drops nothing (§15 D19). ⚠️ **And nothing is read at all unless the primary
button is down *or being released this frame*** (§15 D471, D582): `drop_hint` returns before it touches `pointer_interact_pos`, because a
`LayerDrag` can outlive the release that should have finished it. Pressing the panel's own chord
mid-drag — `Ctrl+Alt+\`, or `Ctrl+\` for present mode — hides the panel on the very frame the chord
lands, and `finish_layer_drag` runs inside `layers_tree`, which is not drawn; `input::resolve` is
deliberately a pure function of one frame's events and `dispatch` hands `ToggleView` straight to
`set_view_switch` with no in-flight guard, where `Nudge`, `SizeStep`, `Delete` and `Enter` are all
intercepted in that same `match`. Without the button test the panel came back lighting a drop host and
painting a line for a pointer merely *resting* on a row, and the next ordinary click's release
committed the move. The guard is here rather than at the view switch because it closes the class: a
drag stranded by any future route is inert too, and in present mode `escape`'s first rung is
`self.present = false`, so the panel returns with the drag still live and only a **second** Escape
reaches `cancel_gesture`.

🚨 **The button test refused the release frame for a day, and that meant no drop landed at all**
(§15 D582). egui clears `pointer.down[Primary]` on the frame it *processes* the release, so a bare
`return` on `!primary_down()` skipped the one function that re-derives `target` on the one frame that
ends a drag: `finish_layer_drag` took the drag, found `target: None`, and returned silently. The guard
reads `primary_down() || primary_released()` and, when neither holds, **clears** the drag rather than
ignoring it — which is strictly stronger, since a stranded drag then dies on the first ordinary frame
instead of surviving until something else notices it. **A predicate over pointer state has to be asked
what it says on the release frame specifically**, because that is the frame the feature exists for,
and no gate in this workspace reads frame ordering.

**The drag ends on the primary button** (§15 D581): `layers_tree` asked `any_released()` — the
workspace's only one, against three `primary_released()` on the canvas — so clicking the scroll wheel
part-way through a row drag landed the drop wherever the pointer happened to be and left the still-held
primary controlling nothing. The **secondary** button is answered a layer up, `update` running
`cancel_gesture` before the panels and that clearing `layer_drag` by name; the middle button was the
one door with no answer at either end.

**The drop host outranks both selection and
dimming**, the way a hover beats a selection in the guides (§15 D331): a drag is a question being asked
now where the other two are states that persist, and a locked or hidden group still takes children, so
a host left at 40% would be the panel declining to answer.

⚠️ **A dim dashed outline round that row was built first and taken straight out again on the machine**
— *"let's remove the dotted outline, that doesn't sit right"*, replaced by *"only highlight the text
and icon of the group to blue"*. Two boxes in a panel that already uses one to mean "inside" is a
second vocabulary, which is what §15 D67 said when it refused this affordance in the first place;
colouring the ink says the same thing without adding one.

**The tree scrolls to a selection it did not make, and every door that makes one has to say so**
(`sync_tree_to_selection`, `layers_synced_selection`, §15 D581). A selection arriving from the canvas
is news: the chain is un-collapsed and `scroll_layers_to_selection` recentres the row, which is the
whole point of the field. A selection the *panel* just made is not, or the row under the pointer moves
out from under the hand that clicked it. **Three doors change the selection from inside the row
walk** — the click arm, the right-click arm and the `drag_started()` arm's `set_one` for a row that
was not already selected — and each owes the same line. ⚠️ **The drag arm did not carry it until
2026-09-08**, and the miss is invisible in the middle of a list because the recentre is gated on
`!clip_rect().contains_rect(rect)`: it needs a row only *partly* in the viewport, and then picking that
row up scrolls the whole tree, and every drop boundary in it, under a held pointer — 20.7 pt against
0.0 for a click ending in the identical selection.

**Resting a drag on a collapsed group for a second opens it** (`OndinApp::spring_load`,
`layers::SPRING_SECS`), so a branch that is not on screen can still be ordered within rather than only
dropped onto. It writes the same `collapsed` set a caret click does, and the branch stays open
afterwards. ⚠️ **Only the "inside this one" zone springs, not the whole row**: the row's edges mean
"between", and opening a branch there would shift every row below the pointer out from under a drop the
hand had already aimed at, where aiming at the middle is the one case in which opening is what was being
asked for — and the group's own row does not move when it does. Passing `None` **restarts** the wait
rather than pausing it, so a drag that crosses a group and comes back waits the full second again; two
visits of 0.6s do not add up to one of 1.2. ⚠️ **The `request_repaint_after` is the whole of the
timing** — egui only lays out a frame when something asks it to and a hand holding still asks for
nothing, so without it the clock would be read once, on the frame the pointer arrived. The drag already
requests a repaint every frame in `layers_tree`, which makes it redundant today and correct on the day
that changes.

**A level becomes a parent and an index in `layers::resolve_drop`.** One level in from the row above
means inside it, at the end of its child list (the top of it on screen); otherwise the row above is
walked up to the ancestor sitting at that depth (`ancestor_at_depth`) and *that* node's own slot is the
answer, which degenerates to the row itself when the drop is at the row's own level. ⚠️ **The no-cycle
check is asked of the destination parent, not of the row under the pointer** — during an outdent the
pointer sits on a dragged row's own child the whole way, so only the levels at or inside it are
illegal. `build::can_parent` still has to accept every carried row (§15 D54).

⚠️ **The pointer is bounded on the right only**, and the gap between two rows is a boundary rather than
a dead band. `layers::drop_spot` refuses an x past the row's right edge — past the panel is the canvas
— but deliberately not one to the *left* of it. The whole row is the drag handle
(`Sense::click_and_drag()` over `available_width()`), so a row can be picked up in the empty gutter
left of its glyphs, a few points from the panel's edge; one indent of leftward travel from there is off
the panel altogether, and containment would leave the outdent reachable from some grab points and not
from others. And it picks the first row the pointer has not passed the bottom of, not the row
containing it, because the rows do not touch and containment blanked the indicator for the frame the
pointer spent crossing each boundary.

**The tree draws its structure: a dashed guide down each open branch, and the path to the hovered or
selected row lit** (`layers::tree_guide_segments`, §15 D331). Three runs make up one row's guides — the
**trunks**, one per ancestor whose branch is still open, each crossing the row down the caret column of
the level it belongs to; the **connector**, the part of the *parent's* trunk above this row's elbow,
which is what makes the row hang off its parent rather than merely sit under it; and the **elbow**, a
horizontal run out of that column to the row's own leading glyph. All of it is 1.5pt of ink to 2.5pt of
gap at 8.5% of the text colour — under `theme::text`'s dimmest tier on purpose, because a hairline the
width of a caret's stroke in the gutter of every row must not compete with the names.

⚠️ **Every run starts with a dash, and the junctions depend on it.** `Shape::dashed_line` opens with
ink at the path's start, so a run beginning at a **junction** — an elbow, or the top of a row — puts
ink through it whatever the arithmetic either side works out to; the rhythm is per-run, as the design's
per-row backgrounds are, and what that costs is one dash of double length at each junction, which reads
as the junction being marked. It shipped the other way, with the below-elbow run phased to continue the
lattice the row's top had started, and the reported symptom was *"a slight gap on the vertical lines
where they meet the horizontal ones"*: a 2.5pt gap opening exactly where the eye follows the line round
a corner, to keep a rhythm nobody can count. The other half of that report is `layers::ELBOW_CLEAR` —
the elbow starts one dash-gap clear of the trunk's own ink rather than half a point off it — and the
third cause was the snap: the elbow's y goes through `layers::elbow_y` because the vertical is *split*
at it and the horizontal is *drawn* on it, so snapping one and not the other put the junction half a
device pixel out of true.

**A guide runs down `layers::caret_column`**, which is the whole reason that is a function. The guide
for level *n* is the trunk of an ancestor at depth *n* and it is drawn in that ancestor's
*descendants'* rows, so the line and the caret it hangs off have to agree about where the column is
from rows that never compute each other's geometry.

**They are worked out after the walk rather than during it**, because every one of them is a statement
about rows *other than* the one being painted: the trunk crossing this row belongs to an ancestor
several rows up, whether it carries on depends on a row below, and whether it is lit depends on which
row the pointer is over — which a top-down walk only learns when it reaches it. The walk collects a
`layers::TreeRow` per row it draws and one pass over that list answers all three; **the drop hint is a
second reader of the same list, for the same reason** (§15 D345). It also means a **filtered**
tree gets the guides of what is *shown* for free: the structure is read off the displayed order, and
`matching_rows` already keeps the ancestors that locate a hit.

⚠️ **A trunk whose branch has already closed is not drawn at all**, and this is the one place the
drawing departs from the design's markup. There a row carries a stub-height background for *every*
level, which is right for the fixture it was drawn against — no ancestor in it dies above a deeper row.
Read as a rule it leaves a fragment in mid-air: with `A → B → C` each an only child, A's trunk ends at
B's elbow, so a stub in A's column in C's row is a dash under a line that stopped a row earlier.

**Hovering lights the path from the parent, not the whole ancestry** — the parent's trunk from the row
under the parent down to the hovered row's elbow, and below that elbow the same trunk goes back to
rest. That answers "which one is this inside" once, where a lit ladder down every ancestor answers "how
deep is this", which the indent already says.

**A selected row lights the same path in `color::SELECT`** — the blue its own kind glyph wears, so the
leg and the glyph are one statement about one layer, and a layer picked on the *canvas* lights its leg
because `session.selection` is one selection for the whole app. Full strength rather than a tier of it:
a dashed hairline inks 37% of its length, so the blue reads as a tint without being mixed as one.
Sharing the hover's path *shape* is what makes the precedence expressible, and there is exactly one
rule with one exception (`layers::GuideInk`, whose three variants are that ranking):

- **Hover beats selection, one run at a time.** The pointer is a question being asked now where a
  selection is a state that persists, and a hover that could not be seen over a selected leg would
  leave the panel unable to answer it. So hovering a row *between* a selected row and their shared
  parent greys the trunk down to the hovered row's own elbow and leaves the rest of the leg blue — the
  colour changes at the elbow, which is the point at which the two paths part.
- **A selected row under the pointer keeps its blue.** It is already the row the panel is talking
  about, so there is nothing for a hover to add.

**On by default and switchable** (`Prefs::tree_guides`, the Settings modal's *Show tree guides*). The
indent says how deep a row is and nothing about *which* of the rows above it the row is inside, which
is the question a nested document actually raises — so the guides are what the panel is for. Off is for
the reading the ink costs: a hairline per level in the gutter of every row is ink the panel did not
have before, and a shallow document pays for a structure it does not have.

**The line sits in the middle of the gap between the rows, not on either edge** (`drop_line_y`). The
rows do not touch — `item_spacing.y` is 1 in the tree — so "the boundary between these two" has two y
coordinates, and half a gap in from whichever edge is named lands both on the same one. Sibling
boundaries had a single owner and never noticed; the boundary a frame shares with its topmost child was
reachable from **two lists** (the top of the frame's own, and beside the frame in its parent's), so it
had an owner in each and showed the discrepancy. ⚠️ **That report is unreachable rather than fixed** —
`boundary_y` names a boundary by its position on screen and asks for only one of the two edges — but
the arithmetic is not therefore optional: reaching for `rect.top()` again moves the line a pixel at
*every* boundary rather than at one. It is also simply where a line between two things
belongs. Snapped to whole device pixels afterwards (`snap_across`), the care `ui::rule` takes over its
hairline and for the same reason. **2pt wide** (`layers::DROP_LINE_PT`, §15 D345): it shipped at 2,
went to 1 to match the outline that means "inside" — at 2 that pair "read as belonging to different
controls rather than as two answers to one question" — and is back, because at one point it is a
hairline the eye has to hunt for, which is the wrong trade for the single most important thing a drag
has to say. ⚠️ **The outline has not moved and is still 1pt**: that pairing argument was about two
strokes of equal length, and it is weaker than it looks here, a 1pt outline running the whole way round
a 26pt row where a 2pt line is one short horizontal run. The outline is the thing to re-read if it is
ever reported as looking thin beside the line.

**Folding the whole tree is one button that reads the room**, not two: with a tree of any size whether
it is open is obvious at a glance, so a control that looks and does the other thing costs one button
instead of two (`tree_is_all_collapsed` / `toggle_collapse_all`). Its glyphs are
`arrows-in-line-vertical` and `arrows-out-line-vertical` — gather these together, push them apart. The
carets it replaced said "this row is open", which is a claim about one row that a tree-wide control has
no business making. ⚠️ **Both halves ask `tree_containers` and that is the enforcement of the sentence
above, not a tidiness** (§15 D674): the glyph is the exact negation of the press's `anything_open`, so
*"what counts as a container"* is one definition rather than two that agree today. `tree_is_all_collapsed`
re-inlined that filter until 2026-09-09, which made the coupling this paragraph asserts a hope — widen
one and the arrow points one way while the press does the other, with nothing in between to disagree.
It also drops a second full `subtree_nodes` walk per frame, the glyph being read on every frame the
panel draws where the toggle's walk is per click.

**A top-level row leaves room for the caret whether it has one or not** —
`caret_room = has_children || depth == 1`. Below the top level a childless row reclaims those 16px,
which reads fine where the indent has already said how deep you are. At depth 1 it does not: a frame
with a caret sat further right than a loose shape above it and read as that shape's *child*, and now
that a shape can live at the root beside a frame (§5.3) that is a pairing the top level shows
routinely.

**A `ui::value_field` is one box: the number's, with the prefix painted into a strip reserved beside
it.** The prefix used to be a widget laid out ahead of the number, which left the leftmost 15–20pt of
every field inert, and that is where the hand goes, because the label is what says which number this is
(§15 D63). `Prefix` is therefore a *measurement and a galley* rather than a widget. The strip is made by
advancing the cursor — `ui.add_space(inset)`, then a `DragValue` sized `full - inset` with
`spacing.button_padding.x` at **zero** — and the galley is painted back into it after the value.
Painting it ourselves is what keeps the glyph on *both* faces of a `DragValue`, and reserving the room
as `button_padding` instead is what used to make a three-digit stroke weight widen the whole inspector
(§15 D73). **`Prefix::Text` is 13pt, not the design's 10.5** (§15 D63).

**The number sits beside its prefix rather than at the far end of the field** — `Align::Min` on the
inner layout, `left_to_right` otherwise centring it in the box the reserved strip widened. The reason
is the same one that makes the strip scrub: the prefix is what says *which* number this is, so the two
have to read as one control and not as a label and a value at opposite ends of a box. This lived in
`value_field_f64`'s comment rather than in this document until a field needed an exception to it, and
one does: a **metered** field branches to `Align::Max` (§9.4, §15 D190), because a number in the
middle of a field the bar is also crossing reads as a label *on* the bar, and a prefix that is a word
rather than a glyph would land it somewhere different in every row of the card.

**The whole field scrubs, the prefix included** — and buying that back is why `value_field` owns its
number, `value: &mut N` plus a `ui::Scrub`, rather than taking a finished `DragValue` (§15 D75). The
reserved strip sits *outside* the `DragValue`'s box, which is the whole reason the field no longer grows
with its contents, so the only way that strip can scrub is a **second claimant**: `ui.interact` over it,
the pointer's own delta at the field's speed applied to the value, and `wrap_scrub` as for the digits. A
strip shows the same `ResizeHorizontal` cursor, so the two
halves are one control in both gestures; the strip's response is `union`ed into the number's, so a
caller's `dragged()` / `drag_stopped()` / `changed()` — and so the edit valve (§9.3) — cannot tell them
apart. `N` is egui's `Numeric`, so the `f32` opacity fields and the `f64` rest read alike at the call
site, and internally it is all `f64`, written back **only on a real change** so an `f32` field is not
rewritten every frame with the round trip's error. The strip's id is `ui.auto_id_with("prefix-scrub")`
and never `ui.id().with(…)`, which is the *containing* Ui's and so shared by every field in the row
(§15 D76).

⚠️ **The strip and the unit are sensed `Sense::CLICK | Sense::DRAG` and `Sense::CLICK`, spelled as
bitflags on purpose: the constructors `Sense::click_and_drag()` and `Sense::click()` are those flags
`| FOCUSABLE`, and neither of these rects may be a tab stop** (§15 D290). Only the `DragValue` in the
middle has a keyboard face, so focus on either of the others lands on something that paints no focus at
all — a suffixed field was three stops, and tabbing X → Y in the Transform panel took two presses with
the first going nowhere visible. `ui::transform_row_tests::tabbing_a_row_of_fields_steps_from_digits_to_digits`
drives real Tab events across a plain field and a suffixed one and asserts that **no id but the two
sets of digits is ever focused**, which is the form that also catches a fourth rect acquiring
`FOCUSABLE` later. *Read `Sense`'s flags rather than its constructors' names before adding an
interactive rect to a field.*

**A `DragValue` that sits on chrome somebody else drew has both its own faces stripped, in one place**
(`ui::strip_drag_value_chrome`, §15 D723). It has two: the resting face is a `Button`, grounding
itself from `bg_fill`/`weak_bg_fill` and outlining from `bg_stroke` across all four widget states, and
the keyboard-editing face is a `TextEdit`, grounding from `extreme_bg_color` and outlining in
`selection.stroke` once focused. `value_field_f64`, `badge_field` and `bare_drag_value` each held a
verbatim copy of the sequence with its own paragraph, so one rule read as three contracts. 🚨 **The
width goes and the *colour* stays, and that distinction is a reported bug**: `selection.stroke` is
also the colour `paint_text_selection` writes into the galley's vertices, so `Stroke::NONE` — being
transparent — turned every selected digit invisible and left an opaque selection block with nothing
in it, where a zero-*width* stroke is skipped by the tessellator and the outline goes either way. What
it deliberately does **not** touch is the selection *fill*, which is what shows a field is being typed
into, nor text colour, padding or spacing — `badge_field` inverts its ink because a light pill needs
dark digits, and that is its business. `ui::selected_digits_are_never_painted_transparent` drives real
pointer and key events through all three helpers and reads the glyph alphas out of the mesh.

**One number sets how sensitive every scrub is** — `ui::SCRUB_SCALE`, applied through `ui::scrub(base)`,
which every `Scrub` puts its base rate through and the picker's plain `DragValue`s still call directly.
The rates the fields ask for are *relative* to each other and were each chosen against the quantity they
edit (a line height wants 0.02 where a coordinate wants 0.5), so retuning the overall feel has to scale
them together rather than re-decide twenty-two judgements.

**Whole units under the hand, any number from the keyboard.** `ui::Scrub` carries the rounding rule
beside the speed: `Scrub::whole(base)` settles a drag to 0 decimals, `Scrub::fine(base, decimals)` to a
stated few, and `.range(r)` clamps *after* the rounding, since a rounded value can step outside a
fractional bound. **An inverted range is put the right way round and a `NaN` bound drops the range
altogether** (§15 D462), both at `.range(r)` rather than at the clamp: `f64::clamp` asserts
unconditionally on either, and a panic inside `eframe`'s update closure costs everything since the last
`.recovery/` snapshot. Swapping is what `DragValue::clamp_value_to_range` already does, so the two
spellings of the rule agree; dropping is the honest reading of a bound nobody can compare, `f64::min`
answering the non-NaN operand and so turning one `NaN` bound into a range pinned to a single number.
⚠️ **A range bounds what a gesture or a keystroke can reach; it does not rewrite what
the document already holds** (§15 D425). egui's default is the other way round —
`clamp_existing_to_range` is `true`, applied on every frame — so a stored value outside the range was
silently pulled to the nearest end and the widget's own rewrite was then reported as a **user edit**
and routed through the valve: an imported blur radius of 1200 became 1000 on the frame the panel first
drew it, with nobody touching anything. `value_field_f64` sets it `false` for all 82 numeric fields at
once, which is §5.3's *"clamped where the outline is built … not on the way in"* applied to the widget.
**`ui::badge_field` makes the same opt-out and it is inert** (§15 D475): it is the file's other numeric
control, both its production callers pass an unranged `Scrub`, and it opts out anyway so that the day
one of them takes a range is not the day the field silently acquires the behaviour. ⚠️ **`ui::bare_drag_value`
makes it too, and there it is inert for a reason nothing enforces** (§15 D552): that helper is handed a
*finished* `DragValue`, so a ranged one arrived carrying egui's default, and all four of its production
callers pass `.range(0.0..=100.0)` — every one an alpha percentage that stays inside it only because an
alpha is 0..1 by construction. **The two plain `DragValue`s left take both decisions from
`ui::plain_drag_value`**, a constructor carrying this opt-out and `expr::eval` for the fields that
cannot go through `value_field`. One of the two was not inert at all: the picker's radial CX/CY, where a
centre the document may legitimately hold outside the shape (`paint::radial_centre` clamps nothing, so
an imported `cx="1.5"` reads back as `1.5`) was painted as `100` and then committed as `1.0` by a bare
click, which `picker::radial_centre_tests` now pins. **A constructor rather
than one more line, because the field beside it was safe by accident**: the angle field's producer ends
`rem_euclid(360.0)`, so the difference between the two fields in one popover was that one producer
normalises and the other does not. **The Type panel is
where the rule is tested twice**, because it reaches the widget by three routes and has no second
guard the rewrite would trip. ⚠️ **`char_valve` carries `edit_valve`'s engagement latch since §15
D523 and this sentence is amended rather than deleted**: the latch commits on the falling edge of a
*gesture*, but the valve's third arm commits a `changed()` frame on a control that was never engaged
— which is exactly the shape of an egui-initiated rewrite, **measured rather than reasoned since §15
D803**, the opt-out removed and all three arms instrumented with the third the one that fires — so
the opt-out is still the whole of what stops the library writing to the document there
(`typography::…::a_stored_tracking_outside_the_fields_range_is_not_rewritten_on_an_idle_frame`).
⚠️ **The Layout grid panel is the third place it is tested, and the two image-card fields are a
fourth door nothing drives** (§15 D539). Three of the four grid fields carry a range the model does
not — `count` is `1..=1000` where the field's own doc says *"Zero draws nothing rather than being
refused"* — so merely selecting the frame rewrote `count: 0 → 1`, `margin: −8 → 0` and
`size: 0.5 → 1.0` and pushed an undo step apiece, with autosave and the crash snapshot writing the
repaired document back. The image card's *Scale* is the same shape: its floor is `cover_scale` and
its value `crop_scale`, two numbers that are equal at cover and part afterwards, since
`crop_reframed` holds the picture's scale fixed while the frame moves. **Both were closed by the one
line above before either was tested**, which is the argument for testing them: the door is in a
shared widget three panels away from every range that needs it.
Everything integral by nature takes `whole` — X/Y/W/H, rotation and skew for one layer
and for a multi-selection alike, the five corner radii, a polygon's side count, opacity %, font size, a
guide's position, the stroke weight and per-side widths, the dash numbers and the mitre angle. The
rounding is keyed on the **drag** and never on focus, and typing is not rounded at all, which is what
keeps a hairline or 33.3% askable. `Scrub::fine` has two callers: line height at `(0.02, 2)`, where
whole units would give 1, 2, 3 and nothing usable between, and the star's inner-ratio percentage at
`(0.25, 1)` — a ratio being the one quantity here that is not integral by nature (§15 D75).

**And what is typed can be arithmetic: a width of `135 * 2` reads 270.** `expr::eval` is every
numeric field's parser — `+ - * /`, brackets and a sign, **evaluated once and forgotten**, which is
§13 decision 1's rule arriving in the inspector rather than in the command bar; the field keeps a
number and nothing about the sum. It is deliberately a calculator and not a language: there are no
identifiers of any kind, because a grammar that grows them is how `parent.width` ends up
half-implemented here instead of in the Luau `vm.md` designs. It is a **superset of egui's own
parser** — whitespace inside a number is still a thousands separator (`1 000`), U+2212 is still a
minus — which is what let it become the default for every field; it therefore goes on *before* a
caller's `build` closure, so a field that has to parse something other than a number can still take
its parser back. A trailing unit (`%`, `°`, `px`, `pt`, `em`) is **dropped rather than converted**,
which the fields that format their own unit into the digits need — those three each carried a
hand-rolled `trim_end_matches(['%', ' '])` parser and no longer do.

🚨 **The descent is bounded at 64 levels, and the bound is about the *stack* rather than about
expressions** (§15 D669). It recursed once per `(` and once per leading `-` with nothing counting, and
a stack overflow is not a panic: nothing unwinds, so a pasted run of punctuation took the process down
with `on_exit`'s `disk_settle` and the library writer's `Drop` unrun — **the unsaved document and the
crash snapshot both**, which is the one failure the recovery machinery of §9.5 cannot cover. The count
lives in `unary`, the one rule on both recursion cycles, so a rule added later that recurses through
the grammar at all is bounded without anyone remembering to bound it; past the limit the field does
what it already does with an expression it cannot read and leaves the value alone. ⚠️ **64 is chosen
against what a field can plausibly hold and not against the measured stack figure** (~500 bytes per
bracket in a debug build), so the guard does not depend on which thread the parse happens on. Depth is
a property of an expression's *shape*: `1+1+1+…` a thousand times over stays at one level.

**Dropping it is right wherever the field has only one unit, and there is now exactly one place that
does not.** Geometry is px and only px — decided rather than deferred (§15 D358), which is what closed
`roadmap.md`'s *Units* section — so the sole pair that can be confused is typography's `Length`, `Px |
Em`, whose em face writes its digits as a percentage. There `12px` typed into a field showing `%` read
as twelve *percent*, and `150%` into a `px` field as a hundred and fifty px. `expr::eval_in(text,
Unit)` is the parser those four fields take back: it carries which unit each token was **written** as
and rejects the whole expression when one disagrees, so the field keeps the value it had (§15 D359).
It refuses `em` in a percent field too, though a percent field is an em field — the digits differ by a
factor of a hundred, and that conversion is what the unit chip beside the field is for.
Half-typed input is rejected rather than read leniently: fields update while editing, so `135 *` is
parsed on the way to `135 * 2` and must not be read as 135. A non-finite answer is rejected for the
same reason a range is clamped after rounding — `1/0` would otherwise show as the field's maximum.
`ui::bare_drag_value` puts the same parser on the fields that do not go through `value_field`, and
the two plain `DragValue`s left — the picker's gradient angle and its radial CX/CY pair — take it from
`ui::plain_drag_value` rather than naming it themselves (§15 D552).

**Functions — `min`, `max`, `avg`, `round` — were considered and declined**, recorded here so the
question is settled rather than reopened. A function earns its keep when an operand is *unknown at
typing time*: `min(parent.width, 500)` is worth having, `min(100, 200)` is a question already
answered by typing the operands. Every operand a field can see is a literal, so a function over them
computes something the person already knows — where `135 * 2` is work they cannot do at a glance,
which is the whole reason the arithmetic is here. The near miss is `round(135/7)`, covered by the
drag's own whole-unit settling and one retype. And the convincing example is always shaped like
"make them all as wide as the widest" — which needs a selection and a property read, not a function:
a command-bar sentence, answered in `vm.md` down to what a property read across a disagreeing
selection returns. **So the want to watch for is a *reference*, not a function** — "this field should
know a number it cannot see" — and it has a home designed for it already. Admitting `min(` would put
identifiers in this grammar and leave the app with two expression languages, the second one
undocumented and discoverable only by guessing which names exist.

**An operator's glyph changes as the sum is typed, and that is Inter, not us.** Typing `10 *` and
then `10 * 3` swaps the asterisk for a wider, figure-aligned one and lifts `+` and `−` a pixel onto
the digits' centre line — reported as a character that "looks like a different character was set in
place", which it is. egui 0.35 shapes through harfrust with the font's **default feature set**, and
Inter's `calt` substitutes those glyphs once figures surround them; there is no egui API to ask for
a different feature set, and the alternate is the better-looking of the two anyway. Nothing to fix,
recorded because the swap fires on exactly the keystroke that completes an expression and so reads
as the field doing it. `ui::operator_glyph_tests` pins it, and says so if a future Inter stops.

**No value field's precision comes from its drag speed.** egui derives one from the other by default —
`auto_decimals = (aim_radius / speed).log10().ceil().clamp(0, 15)` — which is a fair guess for a field
nobody has thought about and wrong here: it gave the geometry fields three decimals, and on the pass a
cursor wrap spends at zero speed it is `log10(∞)`, so the panel rendered fifteen (§15 D66). Every
scrubbable field therefore pins its own: `ui::number(n)` as a `custom_formatter` where trailing zeros
should be trimmed (`160`, `411.67`, `30.5`), or `max_decimals` where a fixed count is wanted. A field
with either is immune, because the range the guess feeds is then already fixed. *A new numeric field
needs one of the two — without it, the wrap will make it flash.* ⚠️ **And the rule is the twin field's
*spelling*, not merely "a formatter"** (§15 D725). The multi-selection Transform card pinned raw
`format!("{v:.2}")`s, which do not trim, so every number on it gained two trailing zeros the moment a
second layer was selected — `20.00` beside a single-layer `20` — and `inspector_multi_appearance`'s
corner radius pinned `{v:.0}` where its single-layer twin prints two decimals, so a shared **4.5 read
`4`**: the panel reporting a radius the document does not hold, over a control that steps by half
units and a photographic scale that carries corner radii. `a_number_reads_the_same_with_one_layer_selected_and_with_two`
asserts on the galleys of both cards over one document, because a test of `ui::number` passes while a
card calls something else. `Scrub`'s own `decimals` is a third
number answering a different question — where a *drag settles*, not how the value is displayed — and it
is stated rather than inferred for the reason §15 D75 gives; do not fold the two together.

**A scrub that runs into the window's edge teleports to the other side, so a drag never runs out of
room** (§15 D66). `ui::wrap_scrub` sends `ViewportCommand::CursorPosition`; the whole difficulty is that
egui derives `drag_delta` from the difference between successive pointer positions, so a teleport arrives
as a delta most of the window wide and cannot be told apart from a very fast flick. There is no hook for
correcting egui's idea of the pointer after the fact, so the artefact is not removed — it is spent on a
zero speed (`ui::scrub_speed_for`), which costs one pass of scrubbing per wrap and nothing else. Zero
rather than skipping the widget, because a `DragValue` at zero speed still *is* dragged and the gesture
survives the pass.

**Recognised by its size, not its timing.** The request reaches the backend only after `update` returns,
and the OS posts the resulting move whenever it gets round to it while the hand carries on generating
real events — so *which* pass the artefact lands on is not knowable, and assuming it was the next one is
the bug D66 records. `Wrap` therefore holds the distance the pointer was asked to jump, and a delta of
more than half of it is the teleport; nothing a hand does in one pass comes close. `wrap_pending` is a
pure read so that every field can consult it, and only `wrap_scrub` — which runs for the dragged field
alone — clears it. **The x axis only**: a field within a band of the window's top, which the inspector's
first panel very nearly is, would otherwise teleport vertically the instant a horizontal drag began.

**A value field is deliberately *not* where "an edit is happening" gets answered.** It was, for the
chrome hide (§9.4), and that seam could not see most of the edits it existed for: rotate and flip are
`field_button_sized` calls, the picker's saturation plane and hue bar are raw `ui.interact` regions, its
opacity field is `ui::bare_drag_value` and a stroke's position is an `egui::ComboBox`, so "is this
widget a value field" was answering a question nobody had asked. The question is asked of the
**transaction** now, at the committer (§9.3) — `Transaction::changes_ink` (§5.7) — and no field helper
takes part. §15 D128.

**Clicking a field selects all of it, hex fields included.** `DragValue` does this for free; a plain
`TextEdit` does not, so `ui::select_all_on_focus` applies egui's own recipe where egui does not — the
paint rows' hex and the picker's. Stored *after* the field has run and therefore taking effect from the
next frame, because the click that focused it also placed a caret and that write is the one to
overwrite. `DragValue` does the same.

**Every dropdown closes with the app's own chevron, never egui's arrow** (`ui::combo_chevron`, passed
to `ComboBox::icon`). egui paints a filled triangle in `fg_stroke.color` — the *interaction* colour, so
it brightened on hover and went full white with the popup open, which made the arrows the loudest thing
in a panel of dropdowns. The replacement is the Phosphor caret at 13pt in `text::DIM` — the same ink the
menu heads' caret uses, so one dim covers every "there is more here" in the app — fixed through every
state. `Style` has no field for a combo's icon, so this cannot be a theme default: **a new `ComboBox`
owes the `.icon(ui::combo_chevron)` call**, and nothing but review catches one that forgets.
⚠️ **The check is two greps and a comparison, not a number in a comment** (§15 D665): count
`ComboBox::from_id_salt` against `.icon(ui::combo_chevron)` over `crates/ondin-app/src` and read the
difference. `combo_chevron`'s doc used to close *"next to seven that do not"*, which was **seventeen**
by the time anyone counted — a coverage claim in a figure that rots on the day a dropdown is added,
which is the day it is being read. Run 2026-09-09: **23 constructions, 17 chevron calls, and four
`"probe"` combos inside `#[cfg(test)]` modules with none**, so the rule holds at every production
dropdown. ⚠️ Two traps in re-running it: the doc comment now *contains* both greps, so each returns
one hit more than the true count; and `combo_chevron_tests` calls the function **unqualified**, being
in the module that owns it, so a grep for `ui::combo_chevron` undercounts by exactly that module.

**And every dropdown's closed state is a `ui::glyph_and_text` job, never a bare string.** A bare
`WidgetText` is coloured by egui from the widget visuals, so it took `text::STRONG` at rest, full white
on hover and `ACCENT_100` when open — the family picker was the last one doing this, and it read a
shade dimmer than the variant field beside it and turned pale blue when opened. An explicit
`LayoutJob` bakes the two colours in, which is the same reason the chevron does not read state either.
The leading glyph names the control: `text-aa` for the family, `text-b` for the variant, `translate`
for the language, and the stroke row's three.

**Inside the *menu*, `ui::menu_rows` sets the row floor to `ui::MENU_ROW_H` (22 since 2026-08-20, down
from 24 — §15 D262) and zeroes the rows' `bg_stroke`.** Neither is a taste number: egui resolves a
`Button`'s frame per widget state and computes
its inner margin as `button_padding − bg_stroke.width`, so a hovered *or selected* row is laid out with
the border where a resting one is laid out without it — measured, 21pt of height against 23 and two points
of width — which is a dropdown whose rows move under the pointer and a popup that grows to its widest row.
The floor clears both natural heights; **dropping the border is what makes the two states geometrically
equal**, which is the stronger guarantee because it does not depend on where the natural size falls, and
the fill is the hover cue a menu row conventionally uses anyway. §15 D96 has the reports and the
measurements. **A floor only ever *raises*, so `MENU_ROW_H` is the row's height only while it stays above
the natural one** — `15 + 2 × button_padding.y`, which is 23 at the theme's padding of 4. It is the height
because every dropdown's own scope brings that padding to 0 or 2 first; a caller that leaves the theme's
value alone gets a 23pt row and no error, and lowering the constant alone would move nothing at all
(§15 D262). **Eleven popups call it — five in `inspector.rs`, six in `typography.rs`** (it read "all
eight, four and four" until 2026-08-20, and had been wrong for long enough that nobody could say when;
a count in prose is a premise the compiler never checks). The font family list is among them but takes
only the `interact_size` from it: it paints its *rows* by hand, which is why it was the one dropdown
that never had the fault (§15 D84). Six of the eleven set `button_padding.y` themselves on the line
after the call, which is why the helper must not — it runs first and would be overridden.
*Restoring a border to a menu row puts the shift back.*

**A control that does not apply is shown and disabled, never removed.** The inspector's rows divide their
width between fields and buttons, so a control that vanishes does not leave a hole — it widens the fields
beside it and moves the edge between them, and walking from one selected layer to several then slides
every number in the row sideways. **A whole card that returns early is the vertical form of it** and moves
everything below it instead, which is what the Align card did for the one selection with no target
(§15 D310). `ui::FieldButton::Disabled`, `ui::HeadAction::inert` and a dimmed
`HeadAction::toggle` are the three shapes of it, each carrying its reason in a tooltip because a dimmed
control cannot say why by itself. ⚠️ **Dimming is paint and nothing else, so the call site owes a
re-test after `.clicked()`** — `ui::button_face` allocates `Sense::click()` whatever the state, and
`FieldButton::Disabled`'s own doc says *"Callers must still ignore the click; this only draws the
state."* The adjustment sliders' resets, the undo/redo buttons and the two colour cards all do that
re-test, and it is the **only** guard refusing the write. §15 D740 measured it, and found that on the
canvas ground neither guard is observable from the document: the dead click commits
`SetCanvasBackground { DEFAULT }` over a ground already at the default and D428's `changes_nothing`
absorbs it, so what pins the dimming there is the glyph's colour and nothing else. **That tooltip has exactly two working spellings**, `on_hover_text`
never firing on a disabled response and a `ui.scope`'s response never being hovered at all:
`on_disabled_hover_text` where there is a `Response` to hang it on, which hit-tests the rect instead of
asking `hovered()`, and an explicit `Sense::empty()` claimant over the same rect where there is not
(§15 D182, D234). ⚠️ **That claimant senses nothing and is hovered anyway, and the reason is not the
one anybody writes down** (§15 D688): egui filters hit-test candidates on `senses_click()` /
`senses_drag()`, so a zero-sense widget never wins the hit test — it is granted hover by
`interaction.rs` while it sits **above** the top interactive widget under the pointer. **A claimant
works by being last, not by being interactive**, which is why it must be allocated *after* the
disabled scope. `Sense::hover()` is the same value spelled differently (`const HOVER = 0`) and is no
longer used anywhere in the app. A gate inside a gate goes through `ui::disable_unless`, because `Ui::disable`
*multiplies* the painter's opacity rather than setting it and a doubly-gated control would fade to 0.25
beside its neighbours' 0.5. **A control dims on two channels, and they must not compound either**: the
ink is `ui::resting_ink`, which paints `text::DISABLED` for an unusable control but defers to `MUTED`
where the surrounding `Ui` is already disabled, since a disabled scope fading `MUTED` *is*
`text::DISABLED` — 79 either way, against the 40 of both at once (§15 D235). §15 D134 is the rule,
its four applications, and the one thing it does not license — dimming a control that has a real
answer over a selection instead of deciding what the answer is. The colour picker's kind tabs are the case where the rule **reversed** a standing exception: a
slot that cannot hold a gradient used to get no tabs at all, which left a header holding nothing but a
close button and made the guide's picker read as a different, smaller panel rather than the same one with
two choices unavailable. `ui::segmented_enabled` and `ui::segment_label_disabled` are the widgets — a
per-cell `enabled` predicate, and a **third** label tier in `text::DISABLED` (the tier `icon_button`
already uses for a disabled glyph), because the resting label is what an *available* choice looks like.
`ui::segmented` delegates to the first of the two, so its eighteen existing call sites are untouched.
⚠️ **A disabled cell senses `Sense::hover()` and is therefore not a tab stop** (§15 D722). It was
`Sense::click()` either way until 2026-09-10, on the stated ground that the cell could carry a tooltip
explaining why it is unavailable — which the signature makes impossible, `segmented_enabled` returning
`Option<usize>` and the per-cell `Response` never leaving the function. What that bought instead was a
keyboard stop swallowing Return and Space and offering neither the click nor the explanation, since
`Sense::click()` is `CLICK | FOCUSABLE` (§15 D290 is the same fact read for the value field's strip).
The rect stays claimed, so the cell still reports hover for its ground; `Sense::hover()` *is*
`Sense::empty()` (§15 D688). **If the tooltip is ever wanted, `paint` gains the response** — widening
the signature is the honest way to offer it, and a sense nobody can read is not.

**Chrome never sets `CursorIcon::PointingHand`.** A web page uses the hand to mean "this is a link"; a
design tool's panels are all controls, so a cursor that changed on every header, icon button, swatch and
menu row said nothing and flickered constantly. The arrow stays put, and **the rule for the places a
cursor *does* change is that it has to mean something** — `Grab` on a paint row's reorder grip,
`ResizeHorizontal` on the layers panel's drag edge (§15 D349), on a numeric field's scrub strip and on
a gradient stop's handle in the picker, and the drawn bitmaps on the canvas (`cursor.rs`).
⚠️ **That list is an example and not a census, and this passage deliberately states no number.** It said "the
two places" until 2026-08-25 and there were already four claim sites, for a mechanical reason rather
than a careless one: a cursor is claimed through **two** APIs, `Context::set_cursor_icon` and
`Response::on_hover_cursor`, and a grep for the first finds neither scrub strip. Re-run
`grep -rn "set_cursor_icon\|on_hover_cursor" crates/ondin-app/src` rather than trusting a count here.

⚠️ **Nothing ever *withdraws* a cursor, and adding a withdrawal is how this breaks.**
`Context::end_pass` takes the viewport's whole `PlatformOutput` with a plain `std::mem::take`, so both
the icon and the bitmap start every frame at their `Default` and no claimant owes a reset; within a
frame the **last** writer wins. `canvas.rs`'s off-canvas arm used to answer "not me" by writing
`Default`, which erased the layers panel's `ResizeHorizontal` a few lines after it was claimed — the
canvas draws after the panel — and it was excused by a comment asserting the opposite of the first
sentence here (§15 D349). The sticky path the comment described is `PlatformOutput::take`, which
nothing on `end_pass`'s route calls.

**It reaches the canvas too**, which is where it is easiest to break: image editing's *Done* pill is a
plain button sitting on a surface where cursors legitimately change, and it shipped with the hand
before being caught on screen (§15 D270). A control that wants to answer the pointer does it with its
own ground. ⚠️ **The exception this paragraph used to name is gone, and so are three others** (§15
D371): `panels/typography.rs`'s *Show all features* reveal, the editor's brand mark, the breadcrumb's
project name and the dashboard's project card all set the hand until 2026-08-26 and none of them does
now. Re-running the census command above finds no `PointingHand` in production — the only one left in
the crate is inside the reveal's own test, which keeps the declined alternative measured so the arrow
reads as a decision rather than as an accident of egui.

**Chrome does not show the I-beam either, and that is a style flag rather than a habit.** egui's
labels are selectable by default, and `LabelSelectionState::on_label` claims `CursorIcon::Text` for
as long as a selectable label is hovered — so every panel eyebrow, caption and value label said
"text" about a piece of chrome, the headers most visibly, because that row is also the click target
that opens the card. `theme::install_style_into` sets `style.interaction.selectable_labels = false`.
**Off at the style, not per label**, because the alternative is a rule two hundred–odd `ui.label`
calls have to remember and the one that forgets is the one the eye lands on; `selectable` and `sense`
are separate fields, so labels that sense clicks are untouched. **A `TextEdit` is the one thing the
flag cannot reach, and the one thing that should keep its cursor**: it sets `CursorIcon::Text` itself
whenever it is hovered and interactive, and nothing writes over it. Chrome takes the arrow; a *field*
keeps whatever cursor says what it is. The inspector's frameless layer name is the case that fixes
the rule — with no frame, the I-beam is the only thing saying the card's heading can be typed in. It
was overridden to the arrow for one session and taken back on sight (§15 D277).

**Colour lives in `Hsv` (`ui.rs`), never in egui's colour types.** `Color32` is premultiplied 8-bit
and `ecolor::Hsva` routes through linearised light; both lose the RGB triple at low alpha, which made
every opacity nudge drift the hue. `color_to_egui` is one-way, for painting only.

**`paint.rs` holds the rules about how an edit rewrites a brush** — kind switching preserves stops,
opacity scales a ramp instead of flattening it, a linear gradient's angle is stored as the two
endpoints the model actually holds.
🚨 **It read *"owns **every** rule"* until 2026-09-15 and that was false, in the sentence a reader
relies on to conclude the two panels cannot drift** (§15 **D787**, `[S23.2-L3-04]`). The hex edit is
the counter-example: of the four ways `inspector::paint_hex_field` and `picker::hex_row` differ,
**three are rules about how an edit rewrites a brush** — what alpha goes out with a typed colour over
a set that disagrees, whether an unchanged colour is written at all, and whether an unrepresentable
colour is quantised before it is stored — and `paint.rs` holds **none** of them. What it offers that
path is `with_stops`, which takes the alpha decision as an *argument*. **The lift is `[S23.1-L1-05]`'s
and is not done**; until it is, this section describes a module that holds most of the rules rather
than one that holds all of them. ⚠️ **And `paint.rs`'s four geometry accessors speak the *shape's* space
where the brush may not**: a reader maps forward through `GradientBrush::transform` and a writer maps
back through its inverse, so an imported ellipse *moves* rather than turning round, and changing the
**kind** is the one gesture that discards the squash (§15 D412).
⚠️ **Both writers ask `build::affine_is_invertible` before mapping back, and the argument they used
to carry instead is the thing worth remembering** (§15 D713). It read that the inverse was safe
because `svg_in` bounds the transform's smaller singular value away from zero — true of `svg_in` and
not of the **field**, which has a second producer: `GradientBrush::transform` is `#[serde(default)]`
and nothing on load validates it, a singular matrix is *finite* and so passes `brush_is_finite` at
the op boundary, and `Affine::inverse` then put `NaN` in every endpoint. One click in the `CX` field
wrote a document that never opened again (invariant 8). A gradient whose space has collapsed to a
line has no centre and no angle to address, so both writers return the brush untouched and
`Transaction::changes_nothing` keeps it off the undo stack. **An argument that enumerates its
producers is false the day a second one appears, and nothing anywhere says so.**
⚠️ **And that predicate is the workspace's only spelling of the question since 2026-09-15** (§15 D762)
— the four `svg_in` and SVG-writer determinant tests D713 counted all call it now — so a fifth reader
of this field has one guard to ask rather than a number to pick.
It is unit-tested, and it is what keeps the inspector's
paint rows and the picker agreeing about the edits it does hold. ⚠️ **It is neither *pure* nor a
guarantee that they cannot disagree** (§15 D787): `paint::CharWrite` is `Valve(&egui::Response)`, and
`PaintDrag` and `Slots` carry `f32` screen spans off last frame's layout — and the two panels **have**
disagreed, `[S23.1-L1-02]` being the measurement of it over the hex field. **A promise that is
load-bearing while untrue is worse than no promise**, because the reader it is written for stops
looking. `PaintSlot` names *what* is
being painted, including the seven slots with no node behind them — `Canvas`, the document's ground
(§5.5, §15 D28); `Guide`, the selected ruler guides' colour — one `SetGuideColor` per guide in the
same transaction, and `Swatch::Mixed` where they disagree (§9.4); `Selection(PaintTarget, usize)`,
one row of the fill or stroke list the whole selection shares; `SelectionAll(PaintTarget)`, every
paint of every target at once, the row a disagreeing selection shows; `TextDecoration(DecorationSide)`,
a character attribute rather than an entry in any paint list (§9.4); `GroupColor([u8; 4])`, every
use of one exact colour (both §9.4, §15 D53); and `GroupGradient(build::PaintAt)`, every use of one
gradient, keyed by the **place** the census found it rather than by a value that would not fit in a
`Copy + Eq` slot (§15 D135) — that key names a node, but the row's anchor is still the root placeholder,
which is what puts it here. Each slot declares whether it takes gradients and
whether it takes an alpha, and the two are answered differently on screen: the alpha slider is simply
absent where it cannot be honoured, while the kind tabs are **present and disabled**, which is D134's rule
rather than an exception to it (§15 D18 has the reversal). `Canvas` and
`Guide` answer `false` to both: the ground is a single clear colour with nothing behind it, and a
guide is one hairline of chrome that has to stay visible over the artwork, so a slider fading it to
nothing would be deletion by the hard way. `GroupColor` takes no gradient for a third reason — it is
a row *in a list of solid colours*, so a gradient dropped into it is a value neither the list nor the
census that built it can express.

**Arrangement lives in `build.rs`, not the app.** Align, distribute and z-order are exactly what
that module is for — a user intent turned into one transaction — and MCP writes and the command line
will want the same three. What stays in the app is the one genuinely UI-shaped decision: *which box*
align works against — the **key layer**'s box where one is designated, the selection's own union with
several layers picked and none designated, the container's box with one (§15 D113). The key needs no
geometry of its own: aligning a layer to its own edge already lands it where it is, so `build::align`
never learns the feature exists. **The container is reachable with one layer only, and that is a decided
non-goal rather than a gap** (§15 D309): several layers have no single container, and aligning them one
at a time is what the third target would have meant anyway.

**Arranging a set never also reorders it: whatever is leftmost stays leftmost.** `build::sorted_along`
states the rule and `distribute` and `distribute_spacing` both lay out in the order it returns, which is
why it is spelled once. ⚠️ **With overlap that promise collides with the other two** — both extremes
held still, and equal gaps — and **the order is the one `distribute` keeps** (§15 D487): once the layers
overlap more than their own span the gap would go negative, and the **leading edges** are spaced evenly
instead, which holds the extremes as well. A slightly uneven overlap is a compromise; two icons trading
places is a result nobody asked for. The span is `max(trailing) − min(leading)`, **not** the last box's
trailing edge — sorted by *lead*, the last box is not necessarily the one that reaches furthest, which
is a background rect with two icons on it, and it read 140 for a set occupying 800.

**`build::distribute_spacing` is the one arrangement the key is an *argument* to** (§15 D243).
Equalising gaps is bounded by the two extremes and there is nothing in it for a designation to change;
naming the gap frees the whole run to slide, so one member has to hold still, and that member is the
key — everything before it on the axis packs backwards, everything after it forwards. With no key the
first member on the axis holds. **Two layers is enough**, where the even distribution needs three: two
have one gap and no interior. `build::gaps_along` is the readout beside it, returning every gap rather
than "the spacing, or `None`" — how close two numbers have to be before a panel calls them one is a
question about the panel, and the fold that answers it (`inspector::shown_gap`) lives there. **It takes
the boxes rather than the ids**, which is the same division as *which box does align work against*: the
panel feeds it `session::preview_world_bounds`, because a readout that comes from the committed tree
cannot move while its own scrub is previewing, and a signature over `(doc, res, ids)` could only ever
read the committed tree (§15 D245). The write beside it, `OndinApp::spacing_tx`, does read the committed
tree — deliberately, since an absolute target re-derived from its own preview would compound.
Z-order restacks each parent independently and computes its `Reorder` ops against the order the
previous ops leave behind, because each op's index is the slot *after* the node is lifted out — a
naive per-node loop silently scrambles a multi-selection. **A one-step move trades places with the
nearest *unselected* neighbour on that side, and a run of adjacent members moves as a unit** — so a
non-contiguous selection ends up further apart than it started rather than being gathered, and a
selection already against the end of the stack is not an edit at all. `build::restacked` walks from
the far end for that reason, and the neighbour clause is what stops a run at the very top swapping
within itself. ⚠️ **That rule lived only in a comment until 2026-09-09** (§15 D645), and the comment
had been checked on one of its two arms: `Backward` reached `z_order` from two test sites, one at
index 1 and one at index 0, and reversing its loop — which turns *Send backward* into *Send to back*
— left both green.

**`EditorSession` holds no GPU state, on purpose.** Three things depend on that: it is unit-testable
without a device (the id-collision, dirty-tracking and preview bugs were all invisible while it was
fused to `wgpu`); `ondin serve` (§8.2) needs exactly this state without a window, and a second
implementation would drift from the GUI's; and it is where §8.3's op queue plugs in. `canvas.rs`
borrows `session.render_inputs()` and owns everything device-shaped.

### 9.3 Data flow — the one-way valve

```
input event (winit/egui)
  -> tool updates PREVIEW state (no Document change)          # during gesture
  -> renderer draws Document + RenderOverrides(preview)
  -> on gesture end: tool builds ONE Transaction (ids minted via session IdSource)
  -> op queue -> Document::apply -> ApplyOutcome{inverse, dirty}
  -> History.push(inverse); Resolved.update(dirty)
  -> next frame renders committed state, preview cleared
```

- One gesture = one transaction = one undo step (invariant 5). A drag never floods history.
- ⚠️ **That was not universal until 2026-09-07, and both exceptions were commit *loops*** (§15 D521,
  D522). `app::ungroup_selection` committed inside `for group in groups`, so one `Ctrl+Shift+G` over
  two groups was two undo steps and one `Ctrl+Z` brought one of them back and left the other
  dissolved; `app::drop_images_at` called `create_image_at` per file, which commits its own, so three
  pictures dropped together were three steps, the first `Ctrl+Z` left two behind, and only the last
  was selected. Both build one transaction now, against a document **advanced as each part is built**
  rather than against the original, because both read structure back out of the tree — an ungroup
  reads the container's index among its parent's children, an image placement reads the child count,
  the sibling names and whether the blob is already embedded. ⚠️ **`commit_run` could not have
  repaired either, and cannot repair anything like them**: a run refuses to merge unless every
  operation `overwrites()`, which is `None` for `Reparent`, `DeleteNode` and `CreateNode`, so the
  mechanism is structurally unavailable to every command that changes the *shape* of the tree (§5.8).
  The folding has to happen in the builder.
- ⚠️ **And an interaction that changed nothing is *no* undo step** (§15 D428). `commit_inner` has
  always dropped an *empty* transaction — a click that turned out not to be a drag — and a no-op
  transaction is not an empty one: clicking into a value field and straight back out, and pressing a
  resize handle without moving it, both build a full
  transaction whose every operation writes back the value already there. Committing it dirtied the
  document, fired autosave and the crash snapshot, and left a step that undoes to the picture it undid
  from, so `Ctrl+Z` had to be pressed twice. The test is `Transaction::changes_nothing` (§5.7), asked
  **here** rather than at the hundred-odd doors that build transactions. ⚠️ **A no-op commit still
  clears the gesture preview**: it is the end of a gesture even though it is not an edit, and several
  callers rely on the commit alone to take the ghost off the canvas (§15 D109, D316, D317).
  ⚠️ **A third example stood in that list until 2026-09-08 and was never true** (§15 D532): a
  multi-row layers drop that lands the rows where they already are emits one `Reorder` per row that
  is *individually* a real move, so this guard answers `false` for it, correctly, and never covered
  it. It is guarded in the planner now, and it is the third of the class the bullet below names.
- ⚠️ **A press and a release with no travel is not an edit either, and that is a *third* mechanism
  rather than a restatement of the two above** (§15 D528). The empty transaction and `changes_nothing`
  both ask what the document would look like afterwards; this one asks whether the user asked for
  anything, and it is the only one that can answer a gesture whose zero-delta transaction writes a real
  value. The crop drags are the case that draws the line: `crop_tx` sets `fit = ImageFit::Crop`
  unconditionally, so a click in image-editing mode built a transaction that genuinely changed the
  picture's mode — `changes_nothing` says `false` for it and is right to — while moving no pixels,
  because a `Fill` picture's seed crop already *is* `cover_crop`. `canvas::gesture_travelled` is the
  test, measured in **world** space from a `grab_world` the press stores, since the threshold is a
  screen distance and a layer scaled 10× would otherwise need a tenth of the hand movement to count as
  a drag. It gates the **commit** and never the preview, which is free. Three `Drag` variants store the
  press for this and nothing else — `PointBox`'s `grab`, and `CropPan`'s and `CropResize`'s
  `grab_world` — and the rule was stated at each of them and nowhere as one rule until it was written
  here.
- ⚠️ **Three things a *per-operation* guard cannot see, and they are one class** (§15 D520, D528,
  D532). `changes_nothing` answers *"is each write a write of what is already there"*, which is a
  narrower question than *"did this gesture change anything"* in three separate directions, each
  needing a door of its own. **The transaction that is never built**: a zero nudge on the multi
  Transform card would be caught at the commit, but the cost is in the *building* —
  `tools::resize_selection` recurses into every descendant's geometry — and `build::local_for_world`
  is an inverse times a world matrix, so a move of nothing is not guaranteed to come back
  bit-identical to an exact comparison (§9.4, §15 D520). **The write nobody asked for**: a crop
  click's transaction genuinely changes the picture's mode, so the guard is right to pass it, and
  only travel can say the gesture never happened (the bullet above, §15 D528). **The composition
  that returns to where it started**: a multi-row layers drop at the boundary immediately after
  itself gives every row a `Reorder` to an index it is not at *yet* — all of them real writes, and
  net zero — so `layers::plan_layer_move` compares its own simulated child lists against the
  document after the loop and clears the ops, **only** when nothing was reparented, a reparent's
  `SetTransform` ops not being modelled by that simulation (§15 D532). **Each is guarded where it
  happens**, because none of the three is expressible at `commit_inner`. That is an argument *for*
  D428's one seam rather than against it: the seam catches what an operation can be asked about, and
  what it cannot be asked about is a fact about the gesture.
- ⚠️ **So a zero-travel release is answered by four routes and not by D428 alone — three of the six
  arms never reach that guard — and the census is a test rather than a paragraph** (§15 D696). Of
  `finish_drag`'s six committing arms,
  `Move` carries its own epsilon, `Skew` is caught by the **emptiness** test because `tools::side_shear`
  answers `None` for a zero drag, `Rotate` is guarded at its *producer* — `tools::rotate_node` compares
  coefficients and emits nothing for a zero turn — and only `Resize`, `LineEnd` and `RailOffset` reach
  `changes_nothing`. Two of the three are accidents of a producer's internals and neither is written
  down as a contract, so
  `canvas::zero_travel_release_tests::no_committing_drag_arm_spends_an_undo_step_on_a_zero_travel_release`
  asserts the **outcome** over all six and not the route, and a seventh arm added later has to join the
  table or fail it.
- The preview step costs O(nodes the gesture touches), not O(document): `set_preview` projects the
  pending transaction into `RenderOverrides` rather than cloning and re-resolving. **It composes over
  a live text session's transaction rather than replacing it** (§15 D609) — the session's operations
  first, the gesture's after, `RenderOverrides::absorb` being last-one-wins per field, so a field
  editing the session's own node wins the transform and leaves the uncommitted text alone.
- Text editing (Figma-verified behavior): placing a text node commits `CreateNode` immediately as
  its own undo step; each subsequent editing session (click in → typing → Escape / click out) is
  preview state driven by `core::text::TextEdit` and commits exactly **one** `SetText` transaction.
  So undo after typing restores the pre-session content (a fresh node left empty is removed
  instead), matching Figma's one-undo-step-per-editing-session model.
- ⚠️ **"Changed nothing" is measured against the document as it *last stood*, not as it stood when the
  session opened** (`TextSession::original`, §15 D584). A session is not the only writer to the node
  it is editing: the Type panel commits character and paragraph attributes straight to the document
  while a session is live, and each of the three helpers that re-open the editor afterwards
  (`canvas::text_session_restyled`, `…_after`, `restyle_session_with`, all through `restyle_session`)
  exists precisely because that has just happened. They re-based the **editor** and left `original` on
  the pre-session snapshot, so from the first outside commit `changed()` could only answer yes: one
  styling click, nothing typed, Escape — and a *"Text updated"* toast for an edit that updated
  nothing. `restyle_session` re-bases `original` onto the document now. ⚠️ **Onto the document and not
  onto the editor**: a live session is a commit *ahead* of the document, so re-basing onto the editor
  would make `changed()` answer no for text that has been typed and never committed, and Escape would
  throw it away. The undo half of that symptom had already been absorbed by `changes_nothing` at
  `commit_inner` (§15 D428); what the guard cannot reach is the status line, since an absorbed commit
  returns `Ok`.
- ⚠️ **Every exit from the editor commits the session first, and `go_to_dashboard` was not one of
  them** (§15 D415). A live editor holds its content and nothing else does — `preview_session` only
  calls `set_session_preview`, and `finish_text_edit` is the sole committer — so the save that walk
  takes on the way out wrote the document **without** what the user had just typed, and the line after
  it dropped the crash snapshot that was the last copy of it. `choose_tool` has carried the same guard
  since §15 D294 for the same reason: *a button that leaves the editor is an exit.*
- **A session's preview is kept as its own transaction** (`EditorSession::session_preview`, installed
  by `set_session_preview`) and is the one preview that
  outlives other people's gestures: it stands for content and styling not yet committed, so both places
  that would drop it — a commit and a right-click cancel — go through
  `EditorSession::clear_gesture_preview`, which is the single spelling of that exemption (§15 D109,
  D155, D168). Code that wants to ignore a preview reads *past* it (`committed_node`) and never clears
  it.
  ⚠️ **It was a `bool` beside one override set until §15 D609, and one flag cannot describe two
  previews at once.** A gesture laid *over* a live session is both, so `set_preview` replaced the
  session's content and `clear_gesture_preview` — "leave it where it is" — then left the released
  field's patch standing for the rest of the session. Keeping the transaction is what lets the first
  compose and the second rebuild. The gesture's half is a second field, `preview_holds_gesture`, and
  `has_gesture_preview` reads that rather than the negation of the session's: all four combinations
  are reachable.
- **It is built the same way a gesture's is, with one thing added: the layout the session has already
  shaped** (§15 D592). `RenderOverrides::from_transaction_shaped` takes an optional
  `(NodeId, TextLayout)`; `from_transaction` is the same call with `None` and is still what every
  gesture preview goes through. The argument exists because `set_kind`'s *"re-shape only when the text
  actually changed"* guard **cannot fire for a live session** — it compares against `doc.get(id)`,
  which is the last commit, and a session commits once — so every keystroke ran parley over the whole
  node a second time, 5.44 ms on top of 4.76 at 16,000 characters. `canvas::preview_session` passes
  `TextEdit::text_layout()`, the `extract` half of work already done. ⚠️ **A whole layout keyed to a
  `NodeId`, not a flag**: a layout that disagreed with the kind beside it would have the canvas
  drawing one thing while every measurement read another, so the argument is shaped to make that
  impossible to pass by accident and is derived from the same `parts()` the transaction is.
- Selection, hover, marquee are app state derived via queries — never document state. What a
  selection may *hold* has widened since guides arrived: `Selection` carries `ids: Vec<NodeId>`
  **and** `guides: Vec<GuideId>` — plus `key: Option<NodeId>`, which is a designation *within* the
  layer half rather than a third kind of subject (§15 D113) — and the first two are mutually
  exclusive by construction: every node
  mutator clears the guides, `set_guide` and `toggle_guide` clear the nodes. Nothing acts on both (no
  transform, no paint, no z-order in common), so a mixed selection would be a state with no
  operations, and the inspector, Delete and the canvas would each have to guess at it. Pinned by
  `selecting_a_guide_and_selecting_layers_are_exclusive`. The classification is unchanged: this is
  still app state, and a guide's *position* is the document's (§5.5).
- **The guide half is a list, and widening it changed nothing about the exclusivity or the emptiness
  rules.** `guides()`, `has_guide(id)` and `toggle_guide(id)` are the reads and the Shift+click
  mutator, `clear_guides()` drops the guide half and leaves the layers and the key alone (§9.4's guide
  lock is its one caller), and `set_guide` replaces the whole set. **`Selection::guide() -> Option<GuideId>` was deleted
  rather than kept**: it was the guide half's `single`, nothing wanted it once several guides could be
  picked, and a method whose whole meaning is "and is it the only one" is one a caller who means
  `has_guide` will reach for. `guides_multi_select_without_ever_reading_as_layers` is the pin for the
  line that had to survive the widening.
