- **There are now two emptiness questions, and chrome must ask the right one.** `is_empty`, `len`
  and `single` answer about **layers** — a guide selection reads as empty through all three *however
  many guides it holds*, which is what every caller gating node work (move, align, nudge, delete a
  layer) wants, since a guide is a subject for none of it. `Selection::nothing()` answers "no layers
  **and** no guides", which is the
  question a panel asks when it wants to know whether the inspector has a subject at all. The
  distinction is not academic: `picker.rs` used `is_empty` for the canvas ground's orphan rule, so
  opening the ground's picker with nothing selected and then clicking a guide left the picker
  floating beside the Guide panel, editing a colour whose field was no longer on screen.
- Inspector edits go through a preview→commit valve: dragging a slider previews, releasing commits,
  so a drag is one undo step. Keyboard nudges are instant single-op transactions. The colour picker's
  pointer targets add two cases the valve does not cover on its own, both in `picker::pointer_slot` — a
  *click* on the saturation plane sets neither `dragged` nor `changed`, so it goes straight to `commit`,
  and a *press* sets neither either, so the frames before the gesture travels far enough to be a drag
  preview through `preview_slot` (§15 D129). ⚠️ **The press arm claims the frame only where there was
  something to preview** (§15 D637): `preview_slot` returns whether its transaction was empty, which
  is what its doc had always promised and only the character-scoped route had computed, so a press
  whose write the slot refuses falls through to the valve instead of arming §15 D128's chrome retreat.
  Both bow out entirely once a gesture has been cancelled by right-click (§9.4), because the release
  still to come would otherwise arrive as an ordinary `drag_stopped` and commit the edit after all
  (§15 D31). **A cancelled frame spends the transition**: the valve reads and writes its engagement
  latch *before* that bail, or the frame that cancelled leaves the latch armed and the next frame —
  with the `Escape` key long gone from `input` — commits the edit the cancel had just thrown away
  (§15 D317). **"Ends" is a transition, not an event.** The valve asks whether the control is *engaged*
  — `dragged() || has_focus()` — previews for as long as it is, and commits on the frame that stops
  being true (§15 D316). Both halves of that test are load-bearing: a bare `Sense::click_and_drag`
  region is not a `Widget` and never reports focus, while a field being typed into is never dragged. It
  committed on `drag_stopped() || lost_focus() || changed()` until 2026-08-23, and a `DragValue` reports
  `changed()` on every keystroke and `lost_focus()` on **two consecutive frames**, so one typed width
  left five entries in the undo history — each writing the same final number, which is why the screen
  looked right and only the history was wrong. Previewing while engaged is what keeps a typed value live
  on the canvas, and it also gives a right-click something to cancel mid-type, since `cancel_gesture`
  tests `has_gesture_preview` (§9.4). **`Escape` never commits** — egui hands a `DragValue`'s typed
  number back rather than reverting it, so the valve refuses the commit on the frame that key is down,
  or the key that means *cancel* everywhere else would apply the edit (§15 D315). **And Escape in a
  focused field *does* reach the ladder in `OndinApp::escape`** — egui surrenders focus while
  processing input, so `egui_wants_keyboard_input` is already false by the time `input::resolve` runs
  — which means the key arrives at `cancel_gesture` and at the valve on the same frame. The cancel is
  what drops the in-flight preview; the guard covers the paths where the ladder stops at an earlier
  rung and never reaches the cancel at all (§15 D317).
- ⚠️ **There are three valves and the fix above reached one of them** (§15 D519, D523).
  `inspector::multi_valve`, which the
  multi-selection Transform card routes through and which exists separately for a reason §9.4 gives,
  went on committing on `drag_stopped() || lost_focus() || changed()` — the same expression, two
  hundred entries after it was removed here — so one number typed over a *selection* left five
  entries in the history where the same number typed over one layer left one. `typography::char_valve`,
  which every character-attribute field routes through and which exists separately because a live
  editing session is its own preview, was the third and was **worse**: it committed the intermediate
  values *to the document*, so a size typed as `100` put a one-point line through the artwork and
  then a ten-point one, two committed states and two undo entries for one number. Both carry the
  latch now, keyed the same way and read before the same bail, and `char_valve` gained the `Escape`
  refusal it had never had at all. ⚠️ **The falling edge of engagement arrives one frame before the
  number does**: a `DragValue` reports `lost_focus()` with its old value still in place and writes
  the parsed edit string back on the frame after, when the field is already disengaged, so a valve
  committing from the falling edge has to be handed the typed value by the field rather than read it
  off the response. ⚠️ **And `char_valve` has a third arm neither of the others needs**: a
  `changed()` frame on a control that was **never engaged** commits at once, the case a
  falling-edge-only valve has no transition to spend. That arm is guarded with `!lost_focus()` —
  otherwise a field *with* a latch falls through it and commits on the second of the two
  `lost_focus` frames the number an `Escape` had just abandoned (§15 D523). 🚨 **This sentence used
  to name the arm's users — *"the picker's hue slider and alpha strip reach it as raw sensed
  regions"* — and that half is false** (§15 D802). `picker::pointer_slot` answers a click through
  `write_slot` before it would reach `valve_slot`, so those controls never enter the valve on a
  click; a drag enters it as the engaged arm and its release as the falling edge, and on those
  frames `changed()` is never true. **Whether anything reaches the arm is open**, and deleting it
  breaks no test.
- ⚠️ **The durable defence against a fifth is a test, and it is written now** (§15 D524). One
  superseded expression survived in three hand-rolled valves *and* in a fourth line predicting what one
  of them would do, and was found four times by four unrelated accidents — a photographed undo history
  (§15 D316), a review sweep (D519), a doc comment written *about* the second (D523), and a grep run
  while writing *that* (D524) — with **no gate involved in any of them**, because nothing in the
  workspace compiles, lints or documents a commit *condition*.
  `app.rs · valve_condition_gate::nothing_commits_on_the_expression_d316_removed` is that gate: it
  reads every `.rs` file under `crates/`, blanks `//` comments so the prose that *explains* the
  expression does not trip it, and fails on any `lost_focus()` with a `changed()` within 160
  characters. **So a fifth site is named with its file and its line rather than found by accident.**
  ⚠️ **Windowed rather than line-matched, because `cargo fmt` wraps**: a condition long enough to be a
  problem is long enough to be split across lines, and a line-by-line pattern would have found **none
  of the four** — which is also why a search by hand has to be for the short token `lost_focus` and
  never for the expression, that being wrapped at a *different* point in each doc comment quoting it.
  The exemption is a `valve-gate-not-a-commit` marker in a comment beside the line and **not** a path
  in a list, for `deps_forbidden`'s lesson — a list of locations rots the moment a function moves,
  where a marker travels with the line and has to be re-justified by whoever writes the next one.
  ⚠️ **Five lines carry it and not one of them was a bug**: `inspector::interacting`, its inline copy
  in `canvas.rs`, the Type panel's opacity gate, `CharWrite::Valve`'s gate, and a `TextEdit` whose two
  terms sit in two *different* conditions — a text field genuinely does end when it loses focus, D316's
  rule being about numeric ones. That is the gate's whole cost and it is paid once.
- ⚠️ **"Every character-attribute field routes through `char_valve`" was false for one of them until
  2026-09-08** (§15 D569). The Type panel's variable-**axis** number field discarded the `Response`
  `value_field` hands back, so there was nothing for a valve to key on at all, and wrote through the
  *click* path — five frames of a prefix-strip drag, five commits, `undo_depth 0 → 5` — while
  `axis_slider` two functions below it was valved and carried a comment saying why. `write_axis`'s own
  `value == current` guard could never have absorbed it: `apply_char_attrs` sets no preview, so
  `current` is the last committed value on every frame and the two are unequal every time. The field is
  valved now, and the valve carries the `clear_at_default` the immediate write already had — without
  it, sliding onto the font's own value stores a coordinate where typing the same number drops one,
  and the same axis at the same value saves two different files depending on which control set it.
  ⚠️ **The rule is one function both arms read** (§15 D804): it was the same eight lines in
  `write_axis` and in `axis_valve`, only the valve's copy reached by a test, and it is now
  `axis_coords_after` — which is also the only form of it a test can reach without drawing the panel.
- **`edit_valve` reports whether it committed, and no caller may predict that for itself** (§15 D524).
  A caller that has to act *after* the commit — `inspector::valve_slot`, whose two retargets move a
  Group Colors row's key onto the colour it just became and follow the picker off a mixed row that has
  stopped existing — computed a `committing` of its own immediately
  before the call, under a comment saying *"the valve is what makes it true"*, and what it computed was
  the superseded expression: `true` on **every keystroke** of a typed colour, where the valve only
  previews, and `true` **twice** on an edit `Escape` had abandoned. So the row retargeted onto a colour
  the document did not have — which is the failure the paragraph beneath that line exists to prevent,
  caused by the line above it. **A predicate that predicts what another function will do is a copy of
  that function**, and copies drift; the fix is to ask rather than to correct the mirror. That is the
  same class as the three valves one level up, one abstraction down — a valve that re-implements a
  valve — and it is the shape to suspect wherever a condition is spelled in two places.
  ⚠️ **What the `bool` means is `EditorSession::commit`'s own answer, *"the commit took"***, which is
  `true` even when D428's `changes_nothing` drops the transaction underneath it. That is the right
  question for a caller asking *"has the edit ended?"* before comparing the colour itself, and the
  wrong one for a caller wanting to know whether the document moved.
- The colour picker keeps no colour of its own. It reads its target brush back through
  `display_node` every frame and writes each edit to the slot, so it tracks a live drag and cannot
  hold a stale value. What it *does* keep is intent the document cannot express: the selected
  gradient stop, the hue behind a grey (RGB has none), and a half-typed hex. Where the window sits
  is deliberately *not* in that set: it opens beside the field it edits, every time (§15 D24).
  `Picker::spawn` is that place and `placed` records whether the window has been put there yet, so
  the position is forced with `current_pos` on the first frame and left to egui from the second on —
  the card has no title bar, so egui owns the drag. Two details are what make that override actually
  land. The window declares a `default_size` height of *zero*, because egui's first-frame size
  estimate is otherwise clamped against the screen edge and the clamped position is what gets stored
  (D24). And a picker asked for by the `+` on a Fill or Stroke header has no row to sit beside yet,
  so the request is parked in `OndinApp::pending_picker` and claimed by the row it creates on the
  next frame (§15 D30). Retargeting an already-open picker keeps its
  position, which is what makes clicking through several fills on one layer read as one panel
  following the selection.
- **The preview-agrees-with-commit guarantee covers the render layer, not egui chrome.**
  `RenderOverrides::from_transaction` makes it structurally impossible for a *rendered* preview to
  describe a different edit from the transaction it came from, and a differential test enforces it
  (§6.2). An overlay painted with egui reads whatever gesture state it likes, so anything drawn as
  chrome that claims to show where an edit will land has to derive its geometry from the same function
  the transaction does. Nothing checks that for you; §15 D51 has the create outline that did not.
- Panels read through `EditorSession::display_node`, not the `Document`, so their controls show the
  in-progress value. Reading the document directly makes an accumulating control (a `DragValue`)
  snap back to the committed value every frame.
- **A multi-selection Transform field carries its own drag total, and that is a real difference from
  the single-layer path.** The single-layer fields need no such state: they read their number back
  through the render override, so the preview *is* the running total and each frame's edit is an
  absolute `SetTransform` computed from it. **The Rotation field is the one exception and it is a
  gesture latch rather than a total** (`inspector::AngleScrub`, §15 D206): reading the number back
  through the preview is exactly what breaks on a mirrored layer, because §5.7a relabels the reading
  by 180° mid-drag. Neither half holds over a selection, so
  `OndinApp::multi_transform_drag: Option<(MultiField, f64)>` holds how far the field in flight has
  been dragged, and every frame of the drag — the release included — builds the same transaction
  from the same **committed** base. `multi_valve` exists to clear the total when the gesture
  ends, and that is still the only thing it does that `edit_valve` does not: since §15 D519 it
  carries the shared valve's engagement latch, its `Escape` refusal and its ordering against the
  cancel bail, so the two differ in the total and in nothing else. §15 D53 has the failure that made
  this necessary: a release frame whose transaction came out empty and threw the whole drag away.
- **`OndinApp::shown_guide` is that same valve for guides**, and it has to exist separately because a
  guide has no scene fragment to hang a `RenderOverrides` patch on (§6.2). It reads the committed
  guide with either live edit applied over it — the canvas drag (`Drag::Guide`) or the inspector
  scrub (`OndinApp::guide_previews`) — and
  everything that draws or hit-tests a guide goes through it, so a gesture cannot move the line
  without also moving what a click on it will find. An `Alt`-copy is the one drag whose override is
  deliberately *not* applied, because the guide named then is the original and it stays where it is (§9.4).
  **The scrub half is a `Vec`, one entry per guide the
  edit names**, because an edit made with two guides selected is one transaction touching both: while it
  was a single `Option` only the last op previewed, the pair disagreed, and the position field reported
  `Mixed` about a guide it was in the middle of moving (§15 D142). **Every path that previews owes a fork
  into `preview_guide` beside its `set_preview`** — `edit_valve` for a drag and `preview_slot` for the
  picker's press, which is the fork that was missing (§15 D141): a `SetGuideColor` handed to
  `RenderOverrides` alone is absorbed as a no-op (§6.2) and nothing previews at all.
- X/Y, rotation and skew in the inspector are **world**-space for every **node** (Figma semantics),
  projected back to local transforms by `build::place_at_world`. **X and Y are the box's *corner*, not
  the transform's translation**: the two are the same point only for a kind with an authored size, and
  a `Boolean`, a pen `Path` or a `Group` has a box its own origin says nothing about (§15 D101). The
  edit is a world-space nudge — `translate(typed − shown) · world` — for the same reason. *"Every node"
  is the qualifier and it is load-bearing: there is exactly one non-node subject that departs from
  this, and it is the next bullet rather than a footnote somewhere else.*
- **A frame-scoped guide's position field shows its offset from the frame, not a world coordinate** —
  the one documented exception, and forced rather than chosen. Two reasons, either of which would be
  enough. A guide in a **rotated** frame has no world x or y at all (`rulers::guide_world_coord`
  answers `None`), so a world field would have nothing to put in it for precisely the guides frame
  scoping exists to support. And for a node the world position *is* the thing, whereas for a scoped
  guide the offset is what the user authored and the world coordinate is a consequence of where the
  frame happens to sit — so a field showing the consequence would take a typed number and then drift
  the moment the frame moved, which is the readout-that-lies `chip_label` already refuses for this same
  value. The ruler **chip** quotes the same number, so the panel and the ruler do not disagree *about
  the guide*; what the ruler *lattice* counts in is untouched, and so is `ruler_origin` (§15 D36, D137).
  The residue to know about: a scoped guide in an upright frame does sit over a lattice tick that reads
  a different number from the field beside it. That is the price, and it is the same shape of honest
  rough edge D36 records for its own band on a rotated frame.
  `inspector::guide_position_fields` carries the argument in full.
- **That field carries its own drag total, and the value it sets is *absolute*.**
  `app::InFlight::guide_position_drag: Option<(GuideAxis, f64)>` (§15 D785) is `multi_transform_drag`'s counterpart and
  exists for D51's reason exactly: the layout runs against the committed document every frame, so a
  field knowing only this frame's step commits the last step and loses the rest of the drag — and on the
  release frame the pointer has not moved, so that step is zero and the gesture commits nothing at all.
  Keyed by **axis**, because a mixed-axis selection lays two fields side by side. The absolute reading is
  the decided part: a drag sets every guide on that axis to the number shown, exactly as typing does, so
  a drag over a disagreeing pair *ends* the disagreement. That is the opposite of `multi_number`, which
  nudges a layer's X relatively over a mixed set and goes on saying `Mixed`; §15 D142 has why the two
  differ on purpose, and why the relative reading for guides lives on the arrow keys.
- **Input routing is mode-aware** (`input.rs`): every keystroke resolves against an explicit `Mode`
  (normal / text-insert; command — §13 — is a third arm of the same match) *and* against whether a
  chrome widget owns the keyboard. Both halves matter. Modality is the seam §13 needs and is
  expensive to retrofit; the focus check is what stops a layer-rename Backspace from deleting the
  layer being renamed. No key handling happens anywhere else, so the whole keymap is one function.
  **A modal owns the keyboard whole, and that is a third guard rather than the focus check**: while
  the Settings card, the *Unsaved changes* confirmation or the crash-recovery card is up,
  `input::resolve` is not called at all, because `egui_wants_keyboard_input` is `focused().is_some()`
  and a card of three buttons focuses nothing — so an arrow would nudge the selection and `Delete`
  would remove a layer behind the backdrop, where the user cannot see it happen. Two of those three
  arms were missing until 2026-09-07 (§15 D464), and the rule is the arm, not `resolve`.
  **A modal owns the *pointer* on the same terms, and that is not the backdrop's doing** (§15 D759):
  `raw.dropped_files` is filled from winit before any widget runs, so the `egui::Modal` backdrop that
  refuses every click does not touch a drop, and `take_dropped_images` — which is not an `Action` and
  so was never behind the keyboard guard — committed ops to the document behind the card. The
  condition is `OndinApp::modal_is_up` now, asked by both, because it was written out twice already
  and D759 wanted it a third time.
  **One thing outside it reads keys and is not the keymap**: `canvas::text_mode_input` takes raw events
  for the session's own editing keys — characters, Escape, Enter, Backspace, the arrows, `Tab`, which
  nests a list item, and the **clipboard trio**, which reaches the buffer here and nowhere else and is
  gated on Alt **and Shift** being up exactly as the keymap's own copy is (§15 D217, D204, D545) —
  Alt for `AltGr`, and Shift because `Ctrl+Shift+C` is this keymap's centre-align and `is_copy_command`
  no more examines Shift than it examines Alt. **`TextInsert` is *near* exclusive rather than exclusive**: no **bare** key resolves
  to an `Action` there, because a bare key in a session is a character, but a *modified* chord does —
  `Action::TextStyle`, the styling set `shortcuts.md` §10 asks for (§15 D211). `Tab` is the one of them
  the keymap *also* names (`Action::StepPoint`) and it stays in the editor's loop; the modes are
  the whole of what keeps the two apart (§15 D173). It owes the focus half of the guard even so, and
  shipped without it, typing a panel's digits into the document as well as into the field (§15 D167).
  **The chrome is not modal at all, and finishes the session rather than going dead with the chord**:
  `top_bar` consults `Mode` nowhere, so its *Undo*, *Redo* and *Save* buttons were live where their own
  chords are not — clicking Undo mid-session rewound the document under the editor, and on a node not
  yet committed it deleted the node being typed into, while *Save* wrote and **pinned a version** of a
  document without the typed text. Each of the three calls `OndinApp::finish_text_first` before acting
  now, as `choose_tool` and `go_to_dashboard` already did (§15 D466). ⚠️ **The button and its chord
  still disagree**, which is a gap rather than a decision: whether `Ctrl+Z` should be dead mid-session
  at all is unanswered here, and dimming the button would agree with the chord at the cost of a control
  that visibly does nothing.
  **Two `Action`s are resolved from the two signals one paste produces**: `Event::Paste` gives
  `Action::Paste`, and the `Ctrl`-without-Alt `V` **release** gives `Action::PasteRelease`, because
  `egui-winit` swallows the press and emits the event only for non-empty text, so a clipboard holding a
  picture and nothing else is otherwise unreachable (§15 D183). A text paste produces **both**, one frame
  apart, and the release is the *weaker* witness: `dispatch` acts on it only when the clipboard holds no
  text, which is the exact complement of the condition that decides whether the event exists. A
  same-frame flag stood here until 2026-08-18 and could not see the case that actually happens, so one
  text paste ran twice (§15 D219). **The `Ctrl+Alt+X` boolean is read
  from a release for the same reason and the whole clipboard trio is gated on Alt being up** — otherwise
  that chord cut the selection instead of excluding it (§15 D204). **`Ctrl+Shift+C` is the third binding
  read off a release**, `is_copy_command` swallowing that press the way `is_cut_command` swallows the
  other (§15 D212). ⚠️ **Reading the release is only half of such a binding**: the stolen press still
  arrives as an `Event::Copy`, so the loop above must decline it as well, or one keystroke centres the
  paragraph *and* overwrites the system clipboard — which it did until 2026-09-08 (§15 D545).
- **egui's own keyboard zoom is switched off** so that stays true: `theme::install` sets
  `zoom_with_keyboard = false`, because egui reads `Ctrl`+`+`/`−` itself and scales
  `pixels_per_point` — reported as "using ctrl and plus, or ctrl and minus, zooms the whole UI, panels,
  layers, toolbar, everything", while `Action::ZoomIn`/`ZoomOut` had been bound to those chords all
  along and were zooming the artwork at the same time. Turned off rather than worked around: the app
  owns the keymap, and a chord two layers both act on is the collision
  `input::boolean_key_tests::save_and_cut_are_not_booleans` exists to prevent. Display scaling stays
  the platform's business. *Anything else the app binds that egui also reads needs the same treatment —
  check `egui::Options` before adding a chord.*

### 9.4 v1 tools

Select (click, shift-click, marquee, select-all), hand/pan, move/rotate (`SetTransform`; Shift locks
a move to one axis and a rotation to 15° steps), resize by
any of four corner handles or four sides (`SetGeometry`, Figma-style — §5.6; Shift locks the
ratio, or releases it on a layer whose proportions are locked, Alt scales about the layer's transform
origin), **the transform origin itself** (a draggable pivot marker behind the Transform panel's
crosshair toggle, with two numeric fields appearing **under the layer's own bounding box**, in the size
badge's slot, while that toggle is armed — below),
**skew** (`Ctrl`-drag a side, Shift holds it to 15° steps — below),
**group resize** (recursive, §5.6),
**multi-selection resize, rotate and skew** (one box over several layers, below),
**scale** (`K` — the same gestures with stroke widths, radii and type scaling too, below),
frame/rect/ellipse/polygon/star/line, pen (`Path`,
straight *and* curved, with **corner↔smooth conversion** over a point selection — `tools::set_smoothness`,
where a smooth pair is *exactly* mirrored because that is what `is_smooth` means, §15 D250),
text (create + in-canvas edit with a real caret), group/ungroup, **frame
selection** (`build::frame` — a new frame sized to the selection's union, which is `group`'s sibling
and a second builder rather than a flag on it, §15 D249), alignment (to
each other with several layers selected, to the container with one, or to a designated **key layer** —
`Alt`+`Shift`+click, below), distribute (equal gaps, three
layers up) **and a named gap** (two layers up, packed outwards from the key), flip
horizontal/vertical (across the selection's own centreline, or a single layer's
pivot where one has been placed), quarter turns either way, z-order (one step or
all the way, `Ctrl`+`[`/`]`), alignment snapping with its transient snap lines, equal-gap spacing
snapping with the gaps it made quoted on the canvas, snapping to text baselines with a selected
node's baselines drawn, the pixel grid and
pixel snapping, rulers and ruler guides (`Shift`+`R` to show or hide the bars), the top bar's View
and Snap menus and present mode,
paint editing — stacked fills and strokes, each one drawn (§6.3), reorderable by its grip and
individually hideable by its eye, each solid or a linear/radial gradient with any number of
stops, edited in a detached picker — stroke width/join/dash/cap/alignment, corner radius (all four
together or one at a time), polygon sides, star points and inner ratio, opacity, artboard background,
**bulk property editing over a multi-selection** — transform, opacity, corner radius, the whole fill
and stroke list for all of them, and the Group Colors panel that recolours by colour (below),
cut/copy/paste and duplicate (`InsertSubtree`), Alt-drag to drag a copy out (§15 D40),
layers panel (drag reorder/reparent carrying the whole selection, double-click rename in place,
`Shift`-range and `Ctrl`-toggle row selection, visibility, lock, name filter, collapse/expand all —
below), keyboard nudge and the `Ctrl`+arrow size step, pan/zoom incl. zoom-to-fit, save / save-as / open
with unsaved-change protection and a save-state readout in the top bar.

**The wheel is split three ways** (`canvas::wheel_input`): plain scroll pans vertically,
`Shift`+scroll pans horizontally, `Ctrl`/`Cmd`+scroll zooms at the cursor — and `Alt`+scroll zooms too,
Adobe's spelling of the same gesture and a free alias, since no other wheel binding here reads Alt and a
bare Alt has no system menu bar to poke (`shortcuts.md` §9). It reads the raw
`MouseWheel` events rather than egui's smoothed deltas, and runs only while the canvas is hovered —
§15 D26 has both reasons.

**The right button abandons whatever gesture is in flight** — a layer being moved, resized or
rotated, a shape being drawn, a marquee, a row being dragged in the layers tree, a value field being
scrubbed in the inspector. The preview is dropped, so the layer returns to what the document already
says, and nothing is committed, so history never learns the gesture happened. That is the CAD/3D
convention rather than the drawing-tool one, and the reason to take it is that the alternative is
finishing an edit you already know is wrong and then undoing it, which leaves a step in the history
for something that should never have been an edit. It is the same rung of Escape's unwinding —
`OndinApp::cancel_gesture` is shared between the two so they cannot drift — and a strict no-op when
nothing is in flight, which is what leaves right-click-to-remove-a-gradient-stop alone. §15 D31 has
the part that is not obvious: cancelling cannot end the press. D168 has the other part: the test for
"is anything in flight" cannot be egui's own `dragged_id`, which a fast right-click has already
cleared by the time this is asked.
⚠️ **"Nothing is committed" is a promise about the whole gesture, and a *pending* one can outlive
the cancel and pay itself out later** (§15 D535). The two-digit opacity window (D210) is a gesture
with nothing held down: the first digit previews through `EditorSession::set_preview`, so
`has_gesture_preview()` is true and this is the rung `Escape` stops on — but `opacity_entry` was
absent from `cancel_gesture`'s clearing list, so the preview reverted on screen and
`fold_opacity_entry` committed 40% and an undo step when the 600 ms ran out. **A cancel has to shut
every window the gesture opened, not only drop its preview**, and the two are separate fields here
because one of them is a clock.

**The cancel is on the press and the menu is on the release** (`context-menus.md` §0 R1). Those are
the two halves of one right-click and exactly one of them ever pays out: a press that cancelled sets
`gesture_cancelled`, and `open_context_menu` refuses while that flag is up, so a right-click either
abandons a gesture or opens a menu and never both — no second flag was needed. **Spending the click
means the *selection* too**, which is why `canvas::canvas_context_menu` asks the flag at the top, where
the click is claimed, rather than leaving it to the one thing the function goes on to do: the layer and
guide branches set the selection *before* they reach `open_context_menu`, so a right-click that
cancelled a scrub over some other layer used to roll the edit back and select that layer (§15 D315).
**And it means the edit's own engagement latch**: `edit_valve` spends its transition on the frame it
bails, or the cancelled edit commits itself one frame later (§15 D317). R1 is a rule about the whole
frame, not about the menu.
Neither half could
move. The cancel has to stay on the press or the gesture runs on underneath a menu, and a menu drawn
on the press has that same release land *inside itself* and pick whatever row is under the pointer.
`OndinApp::secondary_press` is the position the press leaves behind, because egui delivers
`secondary_clicked` on the release and has forgotten where the press was by then; opening at the
press is what stops a click that jitters a few pixels shifting the menu out from under the hand.

**Context menus are one registry projected through six targets, not a menu written per door**
(`menu.rs`). `context-menus.md` is the spec — every row, its cost and its provenance — and it stays
the source of truth for the row set the way `shortcuts.md` does for the keymap; what belongs here is
the machinery. `menu::Item` is one enum of verbs, `Item::spec()` gives each its label, glyph,
accelerator and `Group`, and `menu::build` buckets whatever rows a menu asks for into the canonical
group order. A menu function therefore chooses *which* rows and never *which group they go in*, which
is what makes *Flatten* the same distance down the canvas menu and the panel menu rather than a
coincidence somebody has to maintain — **within** a group the emitted order is kept, so a row's
`Group` buys it a separator rather than a position (§15 D255). `Row::promote()` is the single
exception, for the rule that a verb a kind
lifts into its head is **moved** and not duplicated — *Ungroup* on a group, *Flatten* on a boolean —
and the return is `Vec<Vec<Row>>` rather than a flat list with separator markers in it, so an empty
group takes its separator with it by construction instead of by a rule at the draw site. Most rows
hand straight to an existing `input::Action`, which is what stops a row and its chord coming to mean
different things; the ones that do not are the ones a keyboard cannot express — *Paste here* at the
pointer, *Add point here* at the position the menu was opened at, the key-layer and base-operand
designations, the guide verbs — and the few `shortcuts.md` simply does not bind, which reach their
canvas verb directly rather than invent a chord for a `dispatch` to resolve (§15 D250, D256).
⚠️ **A field the registry cannot answer for is an absence, and it took a wildcard to make that untrue**
(§15 D675). `Item::spec`'s accelerator arm closed on `_ => "Ctrl+'"` and `menu::ViewState::get` on
`_ => self.grid` — a four-field struct against an eleven-variant `input::ViewSwitch` — so seven
switches would have drawn wearing the grid's chord and the grid's tick, four of them switches with
chords of their own. Both matches are exhaustive now, a chord comes from `ViewSwitch::accel()` beside
the label it already came from, and `Row::checked` takes an `Option` so a caller with no answer can
say so. **Nothing makes `accel` and `input::resolve` agree** — these are the menu's spellings and
`resolve` holds the bindings, `shortcuts.md` fixing how a chord is written — so the three are kept in
step by hand and by reading, which is worth knowing before trusting a printed chord.
⚠️ **And nothing asserted that the two menus between them *cover* the enum** (§15 D683):
`VIEW_MENU` and `SNAP_MENU` are hand-written arrays — 7 and 4 over eleven variants when D683 was
written — so a further one would compile, take a chord, and appear on neither menu. 🚨 **The check is
membership rather than cardinality** — a length sum passes for two arrays that both hold `Grid` and
neither holds `Present`
— so `every_view_switch_is_on_exactly_one_menu` asks each switch how many menus it is on and demands
one, which catches an omission and a duplication with the same assertion. ⚠️ **That twelfth variant
arrived with §15 D755** and is on the View menu, the arrays being 8 and 4 now; the numbers in this
sentence are D683's and the *test* is the thing that does not go stale. ⚠️ **It reached the canvas
menu a session later** (§15 D757), so `ViewState` holds **five** fields and `get` answers `Some` for
five switches and `None` for seven — the four-field figure above is D675's, as of its own repair, and
`ViewState`'s own doc keeps those numbers in the past tense for that reason. **Nothing pinned the
canvas menu's row set until D757**, which is how a switch came to be on one menu and not the other for
a session with every gate green; the test that closes it derives the expected set from `VIEW_MENU`
less `context-menus.md` §6.1's three deliberate excludes rather than listing it.

**No region opens a menu it did not claim** (R2). There is no global "any right-click opens
something": three responses read `secondary_clicked()` — the canvas, a layers row and the layers
panel's background — and `picker::stop_bar`'s right-click-to-remove-a-gradient-stop keeps the button
it already had. The canvas's single response resolves five of the six targets itself
(`canvas::canvas_context_menu`), in this order: a live text session, then a point selection, then a
guide (`guide_at`, which answers `None` while guides are locked, which is why the canvas menu carries
*Lock guides* itself — otherwise the setting could not be reversed from where it was set), then
`pick_at_pointer` → `pick_for_click`, then the page. **That last step is the same query a left-click runs
at the same pixel**, `Ctrl` deep-select included, so a menu cannot act on something other than what
it appears to be aimed at. ⚠️ **It asked `pick_leaf` alone until 2026-09-07** and so missed a frame's
name tag, which is the only handle an occupied frame has — its edge and its interior go through
`pick_leaf` too, so such a frame had no canvas menu at all and a right-click on the tag opened the
*empty-canvas* menu at the pixel a left-click selects the frame. `pick_at_pointer` is that chain
written once, for the click and the menu both (§15 D469). A hit inside the selection leaves it whole and a hit outside replaces it —
without the first half, right-clicking one of five picked layers to reach *Union* would silently
reduce the selection to one and produce nothing. Empty canvas does *not* deselect the way a
left-click there does, because opening a menu is not an edit and *Paste here* is the whole reason
that menu exists.

**One slot, so opening the next menu is what closes the last** (R4) — `OndinApp::context_menu`, the
shape `TopMenu` already has, and one slot across every floating thing rather than only across the
context menus: opening one clears `open_menu`, `picker`, `stroke_menu`, `type_menu`, `effect_menu`,
`export_menu` and `export_row_open`, all seven of which draw over the canvas it was aimed at.
⚠️ **It cleared the first four until 2026-09-08** (§15 D533), so a right-click left the effects
popover and the Export panel's own menu standing over the very canvas the menu was aimed at — and
neither dismisses itself on the way, both reading `PointerButton::Primary` only, so the secondary
click is invisible to them. **Image editing's card is deliberately not in
that set** (§15 D268), which is R4 applied rather than broken: R4 clears floating things somebody
*opened*, and that card is what a mode looks like — clearing it would leave the mode half-entered,
gestures still armed and outline still drawn with the controls gone. **That one exclusion is why the
clear and `OndinApp::a_popover_is_open` are two lists rather than one**: the lane test holds the six
popovers *including* the image card, the clear holds five of them plus the dropdown slot and the
picker, and a shared list would have to carry the exception — which is how a member comes to be
quietly excluded from one of the two (§15 D533). **There are three lists since 2026-09-19** (§15
D801): `OndinApp::a_popover_owns_escape` is the lane's six minus the same card, for the same reason
pointing the same way — `Escape` is how image editing is *left*, so a popover gate holding that key
would swallow the way out of the mode. Two consequences are not obvious. The release
that *opens* a menu would otherwise read as the click that dismisses it — D82's one-frame bug again,
and neither of `dropdown`'s exemptions catches it, since `any_click()` counts the secondary button
and a context menu has no head — so `ContextMenu::just_opened` makes the opening frame skip the
dismissal test. And **a click that dismisses a menu is spent doing so**: the canvas skips its mode
input and a layers row skips its click while a menu is open, or getting rid of a menu would double as
a selection change. ⚠️ **There is a third site as of 2026-09-08 and it is not a context menu** (§15
D558): the library screen's ⋮ popup and project-filter dropdown obeyed none of this, so a click aimed
at getting rid of one opened the document it landed on — the same rule, on a screen this section's
machinery does not reach, where the cost is a navigation rather than a selection (§9.5).

**An open menu is the first thing Escape unwinds, and it consumes the press** (R3).
`<OndinApp as eframe::App>::ui` handles that key itself and does not fall through to `escape`, so the
ladder cannot pay out two rungs on one keystroke — dismissing a menu opened by accident must not also
leave the group or drop back to Select, which is the very state the menu was aimed at. For the same
reason `input::resolve` does not
run at all while a menu is open, exactly as it already stands down for `egui_wants_keyboard_input`.
`self.present` stays first inside `escape` regardless — ~~`open_context_menu` refuses in present mode,
so the two can never contend~~. 🚨 **They contend now, and the menu wins** (§15 D756). That refusal is
gone, a context menu being the canvas answering a click and present mode leaving the canvas working
(§15 D750), so with a menu up in present mode the **first** Escape closes the menu and the second
leaves the mode. This arm is why: `ui` answers the key off `context_menu.is_some()` and returns, so
`escape` is never entered and its first arm is not reached. It is the order to want — had present
won, one press would have restored the whole chrome *underneath a menu that stayed open* — and it
falls out of the `return` rather than costing a line.

**A press that dismisses a floating thing is spent on it, and that is the rule rather than three
coincidences** (§15 D527). It holds at every door that reads the key, and the mechanism differs at each
because the floating things do: the context menu's arm at the top of the frame **returns**, the top-bar
dropdowns are a `dispatch` arm on `Action::Escape if open_menu != TopMenu::None`, the three modals are
gated out of `input::resolve` entirely (§15 D464) and answer `should_close()` at the bottom of the frame
instead, and the colour picker is `escape`'s own second rung inside an `else if` chain that can only pay
out one. ⚠️ **`TopMenu` was the one with no arm at all**, so one `Escape` over an open Zoom, View or Snap
menu closed the menu **and** dropped the tool to Select — R3's failure exactly, in a region R3 was never
extended to. ⚠️ **`egui_wants_keyboard_input` is not a substitute for any of these**: a dropdown opened
by clicking its head leaves `focused() == None`, so egui does not think anything wants the keyboard.
⚠️ **Those four were the doors that *read* the key, and it is nine since 2026-09-19** (§15 D801). The
five popovers R4 already knew about — `type_menu`, `stroke_menu`, `effect_menu`, `export_menu` and
`export_row_open` — were outside the enumeration because nobody had measured them, and **all five were
breaking the rule, in the two different ways the question predicted**. The three inspector popovers
cleared themselves on `key_pressed(Escape)` in their own popup and **did not stop the ladder**, so one
press closed a popover and dropped the tool — which is also how §15 D533's second consequence worked,
one press taking the context menu and the effects popover together. **The Export card's two read no
key at all**, so `Escape` left them up *and* paid out a rung: the one thing it should not, and none of
the thing it should. The mechanism now is a fifth one, `OndinApp::a_popover_owns_escape` gating an arm
in `update` whose **body is empty** — the popovers still close themselves later in the frame, and all
the arm removes is the second thing the press was doing. ⚠️ **It gates `Escape` alone and not the
keyboard**: a modal owns every key because the document behind it cannot be seen, and a popover sits
over a canvas the user is still looking at.

**The chrome is one row type for both surfaces.** `ui::MenuRow` adds an accelerator column, a checked
state, a destructive tint and a dimmed-but-hoverable state to what `menu_item` drew, and `menu_item`
is now that function with everything optional left off — the top bar's dropdowns and the context menus
are the same row drawn with different options on, which is the point: a row that is one height in one
door and another in the other is what makes two menus read as two apps. **Both allocate
`ui::MENU_ITEM_H`** — 24 since 2026-08-20, and one constant where the same 26 had been written out
three times, in `menu.rs` and twice in `app.rs`, so that the top bar moved when the context menus were
compacted rather than being the copy that got left behind (§15 D262).
A dimmed row senses `hover()` rather than `click()` so the sentence
saying *why* has somewhere to hang, which is `inspector::menu_action`'s trap met a second time.
`ui::menu_sep` is the hairline between groups — 1pt of `text_a(20)` with `SEP_AIR` either side, at
whole device pixels, **3 since 2026-08-20 and 4 before it**, so a separator costs the 7 of
`ui::MENU_SEP_H` (§15 D263). The rule stayed 1pt and only the air moved. ⚠️ **It said 1pt here and
painted one *device* pixel until 2026-09-10** (§15 D721): `1.0 / ppp` points, measured at **1.0 pt at
ppp 1.0, 0.667 at 1.5 and 0.5 at 2.0**, so at 200% a group rule was half the weight of the 1pt
`MENU_BORDER` round the same card — and of `field_frame`'s, `button_face`'s, `SEGMENT_BORDER` and
`inspector::popup_rule`, which are all 1pt. It is a **nominal point snapped to whole device pixels**
now — `round(ppp).max(1.0)`, `layers::snap_across`'s expression exactly — which is what the two
sentences above mean together; the snapping was never the defect and only the width was. ⚠️ **So it is
1.333pt at ppp 1.5 rather than 1.0**, deliberately: painting exactly a point there covers 1.5 device
rows, and a third of a point heavy and crisp beats exact and smeared. A bare `1.0` is the alternative
and is one constant away. **That total is a constant
because two places need it and only one of them draws it**: `menu_sep` allocates it and `menu::height`
adds it up, and they were two hand-copied `9.0`s a file apart with nothing keeping them equal.
`ui::menu_place` decides where the card goes: **flip, then round, then
clamp**, and the order is the whole of the function. Flipping is what a menu near an edge wants,
clamping is the only answer for a menu taller than the viewport where flipping merely changes which
end is lost, and **the clamp has the last word** because rounding a *clamped* value can push it back
out by a fraction of a point — half a pixel past the right edge is a menu with its last column cut,
where half a pixel off the pixel grid is only a hairline that looks soft. ⚠️ **This passage said
"clamp, then round" until 2026-09-09, with the argument for the opposite underneath it** (§15 D666),
as did `menu_place`'s own doc comment; the code has always been `snap(pos).clamp(…)`, so a reader
correcting the code to the design would have introduced the bug.
`ui::context_menu_chrome_tests::a_menu_is_clamped_after_it_is_rounded_and_not_before` pins it at the
one input where the two orders differ — every ordinary placement agrees under both.
It measures against `content_rect()` — egui 0.35's name for `screen_rect`, and
the better one, a row under a notch being as hidden as a row off the bottom edge. The height it
places is **computed** from the row and separator constants rather than measured, since the placement
is needed before the `Area` is shown and reading last frame's rect back would leave a menu opened
near an edge wrong for a frame. **A menu's computed size includes `ui::MENU_BORDER` on every side**,
because a `Frame`'s stroke grows its outer rect: the card paints `2 × 1pt` wider and taller than its
content plus its margins, and `menu::height` counting only the latter had `menu_place` clamping every
menu against a box two points short on both axes (§15 D263). The border is added inside `height` — its
contract is the height a menu *paints* at, and a menu is always in `menu_frame`. **On the width axis
the number went the other way: a card's named width is the width it paints**, so
`ui::menu_inner_w(card, pad)` takes the padding *and* the border off before `set_width`, and
`menu_place` is handed a plain `MENU_W` (§15 D307). One rule for every popover in the app — the context
menu's 210, the top bar's 150 and 160, `app::POPOVER_W`'s 272 — each of which was the content box until
2026-08-23 and so painted two points wider than `design/Editor.dc.html` draws it, with every placer that
reads a card's width (`menu_place`, `OndinApp::popover_left`'s 10pt lane clearance, the right-aligning
anchors) two points short of the ink.
`ui::context_menu_chrome_tests::a_menu_card_paints_the_width_it_is_named` drives all four `(width, pad)`
pairs through a real `menu_frame` and is the only thing in the suite that has ever pinned a painted
card width — **it pins the helper's arithmetic rather than the call sites**, so a new popover doing its
own subtraction would pass beside it, which is exactly how the eighth site survived the sweep that
converted the other seven. `menu::tests::a_menus_computed_height_is_the_height_it_paints` is what holds the
two together, by building the real frame and measuring it; the term-by-term test beside it was written
from the same arithmetic and agreed with `height` about a term neither of them had.
`theme::color::DANGER` (`#e0736b`) is the design export's one red and
sits on *Delete* alone, deliberately distinct from `WARN`: amber says a layer cannot be drawn as
described, red says this click removes it.

**Paste finally has a position.** `OndinApp::paste_at` centres the pasted layers on a world point,
which is what *Paste here* means and what `shortcuts.md` §7 has owed since `Ctrl+V` was written with
a fixed 20×20 offset. It measures from the **source** layers' bounds, so cut-then-paste-here falls
back to that fixed offset rather than inventing a rectangle for something the document no longer
holds. It asks the same three questions `paste` does and in the same order — a picture, then the app's
own subtrees, then text — because a row and the chord beside it must not come to mean different
things; the picture arm was missing until 2026-08-19 and the row was dimmed over one as well (§15
D224).

**Selection chrome shows the node's own box**, not the axis-aligned region it covers: the outline is
a quad and the four hollow handles sit on the shape's own corners, so resizing a rotated layer
changes its width and height rather than leaning it toward a rectangle. The model *can* hold a lean
(§5.6) — but a plain resize must not produce one, because it is a different verb and has to be asked
for; `Ctrl` on a side is the asking (below). The
sides resize one axis without drawing anything (§15 D14), and rotation is armed in the band just
*outside* a corner. The `W × H` badge quotes that box for a single selection — the same numbers the
inspector shows — and for a multi-selection the same oriented box the handles sit on, measured in its own
axes (below), so the badge had the right convention before the box existed to be quoted; it hangs off
whichever edge of that outline has its **outward normal pointing most steeply down the screen**, pushed
clear of it, with the label laid **along** that edge (D16, D49, and §15 D327 for the edge and D329 for the
angle). Choosing an *edge* rather than measuring a box inside a rotated frame is what makes the placement
survive a lean, no rotation holding a parallelogram square-on; and on a turned rectangle the chosen edge is
never more than 45° off horizontal, so the label stays inside the readable range D49 asked for and still
hops to the next edge at each diagonal. Only a sheared shape can make it steep, which is the trade
accepted against a pill lying across its own frame. Hovering outlines the
**exact** shape a click would select (`Ctrl` and `Ctrl`+`Alt` included, so the modifiers are
visible before you commit to them); a container lends the outline to every leaf it holds. It is
drawn at 3px against the selection box's 1.2px hairline — a transient answer to "what would this
click take" has to read at a glance over artwork of any colour, where the box marks something the
user already knows is there.
🚨 **That lending is what makes the ring's two filters load-bearing, and it had neither until
2026-09-09** (§15 D602). `canvas::stroke_outlines` recursed into every child of a container with no
bounds test and no visibility test at any level, so a pointer resting on a group resolved, built,
transformed and flattened a path for every leaf in it — 26 ms a frame at 16,000 leaves, and the *same*
26 ms with that group a million units off screen, up to twice a frame from here and from the key
layer's trace. It takes a `view` now, the camera viewport inflated by the ring's own stroke width
(`canvas::outline_view`), and rejects a subtree whose bounds miss it.
⚠️ **The reject copies `scene.rs`'s `bounds_cover_subtree` rather than approximating it**, which is
the detail a later reader would simplify into a plain bounds test: a group's bounds are the union of
its children and a *clipping* frame's are the limit of what its children may paint, so either may be
rejected whole — but **a frame with clipping off is neither**, and culling on its own box would lose
the ring on a child that is perfectly visible. The second filter is visibility, read through
`display_node` so a layers-panel eye **preview** counts, which the committed document this walk reads
does not see; it covers the entry node and everything under it and not the chain above it, which is
why `draw_key_outline` asks `shown_visible` before naming a node. ⚠️ **`draw_drop_indicator` is a
fourth door and still does not**, so a selected picture inside a hidden group is ringed while a file
is dragged over it.

**And all of it gets out of the way while a value in the inspector is being edited.** Scrub a width or
type a corner radius and the box, its handles, the size badge, the pivot marker, the hover outline and
the key layer's trace come off the artwork the edit is being judged against. `canvas::chrome_hidden` is
the one place that list lives and `app::ChromeHold` is a third *term* in it, beside a pen gesture and a
path under point edit, so it owns only the question of *when*. A scrub's 1.5s count starts when the
button comes **up**, so the chrome stays away for the whole drag however long it runs; a keystroke has no
duration, so each one restarts the count. It comes back on whichever comes first, that timeout or the
pointer moving **over the canvas** — over the canvas specifically, since travelling from one field to the
next must not bring it back — and `cancel_gesture` (the right button, or Escape on the same rung) brings
it back at once, a cancelled scrub having no result to look at. **Which edits count is asked of the
transaction and not of the widget**: every inspector control commits through `OndinApp::commit_edit` or
`edit_valve` (§9.3) — bar the identity row's *Group* and *Ungroup* buttons, which since 2026-09-08 call
the keyboard's own verbs and so reach `session.commit` and arm nothing (§15 D562) — and an edit arms the
hide if its transaction `changes_ink` (§5.7). So rotating 90°,
flipping and choosing a stroke's position take the box off as readily as a scrub does — a discrete edit
simply starts its count at once, having no duration — while the proportion lock, which draws nothing,
and opening the per-corner radius dialog, which commits nothing, leave it alone. Box trim is the one
edit that moves the box **without** moving the ink (D78), so it commits through `commit_chrome_edit` and
keeps its chrome: hiding the box there would take away the only thing there was to see. **And a control
has to have *done* something**, which is the other half of the same question and the half that shipped
missing: a valve is asked every frame with a transaction built every frame, so `app::edit_note` reads the
response beside the transaction — without it the resting X field renewed the hold for ever and the box
vanished whenever the hand stopped. §15 D128.
⚠️ **The rule is enforced by a test rather than by a habit since 2026-09-09** (§15 D679):
`only_the_layers_panel_commits_without_the_committer` reads the seven sources under `panels/` through
`include_str!` and demands that the set spelling `self.session.commit` is exactly `["layers.rs"]`. It
had been **false** — the guide card's Trash button (`inspector::remove_selected_guides`) committed
directly, which nothing anywhere could have said. ⚠️ **What the test cannot see is the two exceptions
named above**: both reach `session.commit` through an `OndinApp` method declared in `app.rs`, so the
grep passes over them honestly and this paragraph is the only thing that records them.

**A `Line` selected on its own gets its two ends instead of a box.** A box round a diagonal line has
four corners, none of them on the line, and rotating or skewing it says nothing a second endpoint
could not say better. **The rule is `canvas::lone_line`** — `None` unless the selection is **exactly
one** `Line`, since a line in a multi-selection keeps the union box and scales with it like anything
else — and `canvas::line_ends` places the two ends it names in screen space. The outline becomes a
segment along the line with a square handle at each
end, and dragging one moves that point (`Drag::LineEnd { id, which }`, `tools::move_line_end`). Shift
constrains to eighths of a turn about the *other* end, through the same `axial_corner` the line tool
uses while drawing, so a line is straightened the way it is drawn straight; snapping is the unshifted
case only, on both axes, because an endpoint travels freely where a resize handle is pinned to its
edge. **`canvas::selection_handles` returning `None` is the whole of how the box is suppressed** — the
corner handles, the four side bands, the `Ctrl`-skew, the rotate ring and every one of their cursors
hang off that one answer, and it refuses on `lone_line` rather than on `line_ends`, so a line whose
world transform will not resolve cannot fall through to the box arm (§15 D238) — and
`draw_size_badge` returns early for the same selection, because the
number it would quote is the bounding box's: "142 × 0" for a horizontal line, and for a diagonal the
extents of a rectangle nobody drew. The panel makes up part of the difference: X and Y report the
**start point** and the rotation field the **start-to-end angle** (below), so a line's position and
direction are both numbers even though the badge and the box say nothing. And it now carries the
**length** as well, in W's slot, which is the one measurement a line actually wants and which this said
neither surface had until D229 built it on 2026-08-19. §15 D99 has the asymmetry between the
two ends, which the model forces; D238 has the rule lifted out to where a test can reach it, and the
drawing that follows from it, which no test covers.

**A selected text node gets *two* boxes, and only one of them is a target.** New text is authored with
`BoxTrim::CapToBaseline` (§5.4), so its box hugs the letters rather than the leading around them —
which is what every gesture and every number then reads, the handles, align, distribute, snapping, the
size badge, the W/H fields and the Alt-hover measure alike. That leaves "where did the rest of the line
go?" unanswered, so `canvas::draw_text_line_boxes` outlines the **untrimmed** box as well:
`SELECT_DIM`, 1px, dashed at the guide extension's own 3/3, drawn *under* the trimmed box so the box
carrying the handles is the one that reads. The dash is that one deliberately — the relationship is
the same a frame-scoped guide's continuation has to its solid part, "this same thing, carried on past
where it stops mattering". Nothing is drawn when `untrimmed_bounds() == bounds()`, which covers an
untrimmed node and every `Fixed` one. Graphite draws both boxes for this reason; Figma makes trim a
per-node option and then has to explain the padding some other way. §15 D199 has the compatibility
decision that keeps old files untouched, and why cap-to-baseline leaves descenders outside the box.

**And its baselines are drawn, one hairline per line** (`canvas::draw_text_baselines`, §15 D355) —
`SELECT_DIM` again, 1px, spanning the *trimmed* box's width, drawn after the line box and before the
outline so they sit on top of the dashed box they are inside and under the tight box and its handles.
**Solid where the line box is dashed**, and the dash is what makes the pair read: dashed means
*notional*, a box that was taken away, where a baseline is the opposite — the line the type actually
sits on and the reference every other number here is derived from. Making the invisible reference
visible is half of "align to baselines"; the other half is that they are snap targets (below). One
switch governs both, *Snap to baselines*, which matters more for the drawing than for the snapping: a
forty-line paragraph draws forty hairlines, so whoever finds that noisy must be able to turn it off,
and the switch they will reach for is the one named after it. ⚠️ **A rotated text node shows its
baselines and cannot be snapped to them**, deliberately — see below.

**Two or more layers get one box, and a drag on it transforms all of them.** `canvas::selection_handles`
used to begin with `selection.single()?`, so handles appeared for exactly one layer and a
multi-selection could only be moved. The box over several has the **single-layer shape — a transform and
an extent** (`canvas::selection_frame_box`): the extent is the union of the members' *geometry quads*
measured in that transform's own axes, and the transform is whatever a turn or a lean has left the set at,
`IDENTITY` at rest, so at rest it is still the upright union. **A set's box is the union of the members
that *have* one, and is absent only when none does** (`canvas::selection_frame_extent`, §15 D505): an
empty `Group` — what a delete of its last child leaves, core pruning no containers — has no local box at
all, and one such member used to take the whole selection's chrome with it, so **Ctrl+A** over two rects
and one empty group drew no box, no handles and no size badge. A single layer keeps its own rotated box
(D15) because its handles should move the width and height the designer can see; a selection still has no
shared frame **in the document** — it is not a group, and its members may each be turned differently — so
there is nothing to read one off, and the upright union is the one box a resting set agrees on. What it
does have is a **session** orientation, carried on `Selection`, composed on each commit and given up the
moment the selection changes: a set whose frame snapped upright the instant the mouse came up would be
showing a box its own shapes had left behind. §15 D324–D326 have the arc, and the reason the extent is
measured from *quads* rather than from world bounds — an axis-aligned box does not survive being turned,
so an ink-based one would creep as the set moved, which is the original defect relocated rather than
fixed. The visible price is that the resting frame hugs geometry where it hugged ink, half a stroke width
tighter on each side of a stroked member, which is the single-layer frame's own rule. **A
multi-selection's *resize* runs on that same oriented box** (§15 D478): `canvas::selection_resize_box` is
`selection_frame_box`'s twin measured off the **committed** tree, `tools::resize_selection` takes a
`tools::SelectionBox { frame, extent }` and computes its factors and its anchor in the frame's own space
— `frame · S · frame⁻¹ · world`, both maps the identity on an upright set, so it is the old world-space
arithmetic unchanged there — and `canvas::resize_axes` maps the handle's outward direction through that
same frame rather than short-circuiting to the identity for a set, which is the shape the single-layer
arm has always used. It did none of that between D326 and D478, and the price was measured: a corner of
a 60°-turned pair landed **62.2243** units from the pointer and the corner opposite it, the one a resize
exists to hold still, moved 24.3782. The geometry-not-ink price above now belongs to the arithmetic as
well as to the chrome, and the three doors that resize a set from a *typed* number keep the upright union
deliberately — `OndinApp::size_step`, `inspector::scale_tx` and the multi W/H fields, because the box a
panel *reports* for a set is the upright one. What the gesture is transforming is *carried*
rather than looked up when it is applied: `preview::Target { Layer(NodeId), Selection }` replaces the
`id: NodeId` that `Drag::Resize` and `Drag::Rotate` used to hold, `Handles.id` became
`Handles.target`, and `resize_tx`, `rotate_tx`, `skew_tx`, `keep_ratio`, `snapped_resize` and
`resize_axes` all dispatch on that one value — so a drag cannot change what it is transforming
halfway through. `Drag::Skew` carries the same `Target` for the same reason.

**§5.6's rule that a transform never carries scale is what shaped the implementation.** The resize
could not be a scale multiplied into each node's transform, so `tools::resize_selection` is
`resize_group`'s mechanism with world in place of a shared parent: each root is carried bodily
through the scale (`scaled_about`, origin and basis both), projected back into its own parent, and
only *then* split by `split_geometry_scale` into the transform it may keep and the scale its
geometry takes. Four pieces are shared by both paths: `resize_factors` (the scale factors and the
anchor, including all of `symmetric` and `keep_ratio`'s anchor rules), `scaled_about`,
`split_geometry_scale` and `scale_geometry` (a leaf's size, a line's end, a path's points, or
recursion into a container). `resize_group` and `scale_subtree` are written in terms of them, and
their two tests pass unchanged, which is the evidence that refactor was behaviour-preserving; the
childless-leaf path `resize_geometry` (§5.6) is the fourth caller and needed nothing new. A root
turned off-axis under a non-uniform drag needs a skew to land exactly, and now gets one — which
matters more here than inside a group, since a selection is exactly where differently-turned layers
meet (§15 D50). **What a handle drag was asked for rides in one struct**: `tools::Resize { keep_ratio,
symmetric, scaling }` replaced the trailing `(bool, bool)` on `resize_to_handle`, `resize_group` and
`resize_selection`, which retires the `#[allow(clippy::too_many_arguments)]` both of the latter two
carried — the parts struct §15 D41 asked for before another argument was added, arriving as the Scale
tool's `scaling` became the ninth.

**`scaled_about` answers `Option<Affine>`, and a member whose product overflows is skipped rather than
costing the gesture** (§15 D481). `MAX_SCALE` bounds the *factor* a drag asks for and says nothing about
what the node already stores: a `Rect` holding `Affine::scale(1e308)` over a size of `1e-306` has every
stored coefficient finite and entirely ordinary world bounds, and one handle drag multiplies its basis to
`inf`, from which `Basis::of` hands back a `NaN` basis that invariant 8 then refuses for the **whole**
transaction. So all three call sites — `resize_selection`, `scale_subtree` and `resize_geometry` — refuse
**per node**: the member that cannot take the scale is left exactly where it was and the rest of the
selection moves.

**`split_geometry_scale` answers `Option<(Affine, f64, f64)>` for the same reason and one step later**
(§15 D714), and the two guards sit one function apart because they catch different failures of the
same gesture. `scaled_about` catches a basis whose product overflows to `inf`; this catches one that
is entirely **finite** and cannot be represented as `orientation × scale` at all — a rank-1 matrix,
whose second column no `R · skewX · mirror · diag(sx, sy)` can produce. `Basis::of` used to hand back
a plausible split for one, so `rotate_node` wrote `R(63.43°)` with `csy = 0` and `scale_geometry`
turned that into `(40 · 0).max(1.0)`: a 40×40 rect **1 unit tall at 63°**, from one turn, with no
`NaN` anywhere for invariant 8 to refuse. `build::Basis::exact` is the predicate (§5.7a) and all six
call sites refuse per node — `return Transaction(…)` for a single-node verb, `continue` inside a loop
over a selection — because §6.2's rule holds here too: a missing edit is recoverable and a lying one
is not. `tools::overflow_tests` and `tools::unrepresentable_basis_tests` are siblings on purpose.

**The Scale tool is Select with a different verb on the handles.** `Tool::Scale` sits in rail slot
three — with Select and Hand rather than with the shape tools, because it manipulates what is already
there — keyed `K`, glyph `resize`. Everything else about it is Select's: the click, the marquee, the
move, the rotate ring, the pivot marker. Only `Tool::scaling()` differs, and it is what
`canvas::resize_opts` puts in `tools::Resize`. That sharing is spelled once as `Tool::selects()`, which
five gates ask instead of `== Tool::Select` (the click, the drag start, the hover outline, the pivot
marker and `rulers.rs`'s guide lines), with the cursor sharing the two through one match arm — a tool
that answered yes in four of them would be subtly half-built. It is **proportional by default**: `canvas::keep_ratio`
treats the tool as "locked", so Shift releases it exactly as it does on a proportion-locked layer, and
released, the scalars take the geometric mean of the two factors. Its cursor is a drawn `Bitmap::Scale`
rasterized from the same Phosphor glyph as the rail button (D9), and it is the **rest** cursor only —
over a handle the directional resize arrows still win, because they say which way the box grows, and
what the tool does is invisible until something has been scaled. **Its verb has a numeric door too**,
the Transform card's Scale percentage below (§15 D311) — a field of its own rather than W and H
following the armed tool, because a W that meant two things would carry nothing to say which one, and
the cursor that says it is not visible while the pointer is in the inspector. **That door is open only
while the tool is held** (§15 D312): the row is drawn when `self.tool == Tool::Scale` and not
otherwise, so the panel says which verb is armed by what it *offers* rather than by what a permanent
field quietly means. §15 D70 has the rest.

**Adding a `Tool` variant is a change the compiler finds; adding a `NodeKind` is not — and the two
look like the same job.** Every predicate over `Tool` is one of three safe shapes: an exhaustive
`match` (the cursor dispatch, `create_tx`), a `matches!` over an explicit allow-list
(`drags_a_box`, `selects`), or a `match` whose wildcard is the answer a tool that has not opted in
wants (`scaling` → `Scaling::Geometry`). So a new variant either stops the file compiling or falls
through to the right default; adding `Tool::Image` changed no behaviour silently anywhere, which was
*checked* rather than assumed. `NodeKind` is the opposite and D87–D88 is where that is recorded: its
`matches!` lists answer a kind that is missing from them with a confident, wrong "no", and the
symptom is a feature quietly not applying rather than a build failure — which is why
`every_default_name_is_listed_as_generated` had to be given a wildcard-free `match` helper to make
`GENERATED_NAMES` fail loudly. The contrast is worth stating once, because the reflex each teaches is
wrong for the other: grepping every `matches!` after the build goes quiet is wasted work on the tool
side, and trusting the build is how a `NodeKind` sweep ends up half done.

**Arming a tool whose verb is *create* clears the selection** (`OndinApp::choose_tool`, §15 D294). You
are about to draw something, so there is nothing to be selected, and the chrome of whatever was picked
before — its outline, its handles, its size pill — is otherwise sitting under the box being dragged
out. The set is `drags_a_box`, reused rather than restated: Frame, Rect, Ellipse, Polygon, Star, Line,
Text and Image are exactly the tools the reason covers, and neither Text nor Image reads the selection
for anything (Text works off a hit test, Image off `pending_images`). The non-members are the point.
Select and Scale operate on the selection; Hand pans, and losing a selection to a pan is D293's mistake
one gesture over; **Node and ImageEdit are entered *from* a selected layer** — a double-click switches
to them with it picked and `edited_path` reads that selection to know its subject, so clearing would
empty the tool as it opened. The Pen is excluded deliberately rather than incidentally: it places
anchors one click at a time and never drags a box over anything. The clear fires on the tool *switch*,
so `place_image_action` — `Ctrl+Shift+K` and the rail's image button — clears too.

⚠️ **That gives `drags_a_box` a second consumer, and it changes what its test is for.** Answering only
"does a drag draw a box", a wrong *exclusion* was harmless; answering "does arming this tool delete the
selection", a wrong exclusion is destructive. `Tool::ImageEdit` turned out never to have been asserted
against the predicate at all and is in the exclusion loop now. *When a predicate gains a second
consumer, re-read its negative members rather than its definition.*

**And a tool switch abandons the drag in flight** (§15 D724). `choose_tool` cleared the text session,
the pen, `pen_bias`, `points` and `pending_images` — each by name, each with a sentence — and not
`self.drag`, so any tool key or rail button pressed mid-crop-drag left a live `Drag::CropResize` and
last frame's crop preview installed while `edited_image()` went `None` and brought the layer's
selection box and handles back. Three lines at the top of the function answer it: `self.drag`,
`self.alt_clone` — which the release will not clear, `finish_drag` reaching neither of its two
clearing sites once the drag is already `None` — and `clear_gesture_preview`, **not** `clear_preview`,
which would take a live text session's uncommitted content with it (§15 D109). ⚠️ **`Escape` was
already clean by ordering rather than by design**, its ladder reaching `cancel_gesture` before its own
`choose_tool(Tool::Select)` rung and that gate being the kind-agnostic `self.drag.is_none()` — so the
one route anybody would test was the one route that worked. 🚨 **It is deliberately not routed through
`cancel_gesture`**: that takes an `&egui::Context` `choose_tool` has not got across seventeen call
sites, and its gate answers for field scrubs and a Settings nudge, states a tool switch cannot be in
the middle of. What the two share is the **list**, not the funnel — which is `[A2-L7-02]`'s standing
cost, one privacy scope over 101 fields making *"is a gesture in flight?"* a hand-written list at
every site that needs one. ⚠️ **One of those sites has stopped being a list and this one has not**
(§15 **D785**): `cancel_gesture` asks `InFlight::any`, which is exhaustive by construction, while
`choose_tool`'s three lines are still three names chosen by hand. That is the narrow half of the
finding; the wide half — per-panel state, the field count, the single privacy scope — is untouched and
`[A2-L7-02]` stays open for it.

**A rotation sweeps the whole arrangement round one pivot** — the union box's centre, shared by every
member (`tools::rotate_selection`, per-member `rotate_node` about that one point) — rather than each
layer spinning where it stands. That pivot, how the proportion lock reads over a set, and where
`build::outermost` does and does not apply are the three things nothing in this document specified;
§15 D50 records each with its reasoning and its verdict.

**`Ctrl`-dragging a side skews.** The dragged side follows the pointer along its own length and the
side facing it stays put, so the box leans into a parallelogram (`canvas::skew_tx` →
`tools::skew_to_handle` / `tools::skew_selection`). **Sides only**: a corner has no side facing it
to hold still, so there is nothing a lean could mean there, and corners keep resize with the rotate
ring beyond them untouched. `Handles::armed` takes the modifier as a parameter and re-reads the side
bands with it, which keeps the one statement of the priority (D14) doing the deciding for the
cursor, the gesture and the hover outline alike. Ctrl was free here because it is otherwise the
deep-select modifier and handle bands are dispatched before deep-select; it is read at the **press**,
like the grab position and for the same reason (D29). **The lean is measured from where the press
landed** — `Drag::Skew` carries that point — and not from the box's centre, which is what it did until
2026-08-23: grabbing a side anywhere but its exact midpoint leant the shape by whatever angle the grab
already implied, before the pointer had moved at all (§15 D322). So the grabbed point follows the
pointer, which is the resize analogy honoured rather than merely invoked, and a second skew on an
already-leaning shape starts from zero. **Nothing snaps to the pointer**: the
pointer stands for an *angle* here, and a lean that catches on a guide is a lean whose number came
from somewhere the designer cannot see. Shift snaps to 15° steps instead, the same step a rotation
takes (D47). The lean is clamped to ±89°, a degree short of the quarter turn at which the shape
collapses onto a line and its matrix stops being invertible, and it is clamped rather than refused so
a wild drag pins at the extreme instead of snapping back. For a single node — shape *or* group — the
lean is in the node's own frame on its own local box, needing no recursion because everything inside
a container comes along with the basis; for a multi-selection it is a world-axis lean about the
shared upright union, so the set leans as one parallelogram — and since §15 D324 the **frame** leans with
it, drawn from the very shear `tools::side_shear` handed the shapes rather than re-unioned from the
preview. That sentence sat next to a frame that could not show what it described for as long as it existed. The cursor points **along** the side
(`Handles::screen_tangent`, the outward normal turned a quarter turn in the box's own frame, which on
a sheared box is not the same as turning the screen direction), which is what distinguishes it from
the resize cursor on the same band. §15 D52 has the design.

**The box is drawn dimmer than the layers it is drawn around**: 1px `SELECT_DIM` against the 1.2px
`SELECT` each member already gets for its own outline. It is derived chrome saying "these move
together" and must not compete with the artwork it encloses, each piece of which still shows its own
edge. A single layer's box is not drawn twice — its selection outline already *is* the box. `Handles`
deliberately does **not** keep the box's extent: everything that needs it recomputes from the
**committed** tree, because mid-drag the preview the corners come from already reflects the gesture,
and scaling relative to a box that is itself being scaled compounds every frame. And `snapped_resize`
excludes the *whole* selection from the snap targets rather than one node, so a multi-selection resize
cannot catch on the bounds of a layer it is itself scaling.
**A resize snaps only the axes its handle travels along**, which is `canvas::resize_axes`: the
handle's box-local outward direction mapped through the box's world transform, so a corner claims
both, an upright side claims one, and a rotated node's side claims both again because it really does
move in both. Snapping an axis the handle cannot move would shift the edge the handle is anchoring —
and where the geometry refuses anyway, it still draws a guide line for a match the gesture did not
make, which is what the **point box** did until 2026-09-09 by passing both axes unconditionally
(§15 D687). One answer for both boxes; a gesture that resizes owes this function the question.

**A move outlines the frame it would drop into.** `canvas::draw_frame_drop_outline` boxes any frame
that would adopt the selection if the drag were released now, at the hover outline's 3px
