`color::SELECT` and directly above it in the overlay stack, under the selection chrome: it answers
the same question about the thing under the pointer, and it must not read as the frame having become
selected. Frame membership follows the artwork silently (§15 D20), and until this the gesture said
nothing at all about a reparent that changes what clips the layer and where it sits in the tree. What
keeps it honest is that the adoption decision was **extracted** rather than reproduced —
`OndinApp::move_destination`, split out of `move_tx`, asked by the outline and by the commit with the
same snapped delta — so the outline cannot promise a frame the release does not deliver. Only frames
are outlined: leaving one for the root is equally a reparent, but the canvas is not a box that can be
outlined, and a layer coming *out* of a frame already reads as leaving the box it is visibly
departing.

**The artboard list the drop rule reads is memoized, and the key is `EditorSession::revision`** (§15
D616). `OndinApp::artboards` was a full-document walk answering a question about four nodes, asked
once per selected root per call, so a twenty-layer move spent 6.07 ms of a 16.7 ms frame before
anything was drawn. `OndinApp::with_frames` fills `FrameIndex` — the frames, their world boxes and a
walk counter — whenever the revision has moved. **The rule that keeps it correct is that nothing may
add, remove or move an artboard without a commit**: `revision` is bumped by `commit_inner`, which
undo and redo go through, and by `adopt_document`, and by nothing else. A gesture in flight
deliberately does not bump it — these are the *committed* world bounds, which is what the drop rule
has always been defined against.

**Alt scales about the box's own centre.** `tools::resized_box` and `tools::resize_group` take a
`symmetric` flag beside `keep_ratio`: normally the opposite edge stays put and the extent is the
distance from it, while with Alt the **centre** stays put and both edges move out together, so the
extent is twice the distance from the middle. It was briefly the node's transform origin instead, and
that generalisation had to be reversed after it was used — §15 D60 has why a fixed pivot and a handle
that tracks the pointer cannot both be honoured. So `resized_box` and `resize_factors` carry no
`pivot` parameter and `resize_to_handle`, `resize_group` and `resize_selection` compute none;
`a_moved_pivot_does_not_change_an_alt_resize` pins that across four pivot placements. Shift and Alt
compose — proportional about the centre. One subtlety is load-bearing and was a bug on the way in:
under `symmetric` the origin is centred on **both** axes,
including one the handle does not own. On an axis whose extent is unchanged that is a no-op (the
centre is half the extent, so it comes out at 0 exactly as the anchored rule gives) — but it is *not*
a no-op once `keep_ratio` has driven that axis from the other one, which is the Alt+Shift case on a
side handle, and leaving it at 0 centred the dragged axis while pinning the top edge of the axis
following it. `alt_resizes_about_the_centre` and
`alt_and_shift_resize_proportionally_about_the_centre` pin both halves. ⚠️ **And the subtlety was
written into only one of the two copies until 2026-09-08** (§15 D559): `resized_box`'s `edge` closure
answers the centre *before* it looks at the anchor, where `resize_factors`' `pin` asked the anchor
first and so pinned the minimum on the axis the ratio lock had just driven — one gesture giving
`(20,10)–(80,40)` for a `Rect` and `(20,0)–(80,30)` for a `Path`.
`alt_and_shift_on_a_side_handle_centre_the_followed_axis_for_a_path_too` is the third test, and the
one that drives the other copy. 🚨 **A second, larger divergence between the same two copies survived
until 2026-09-10** (§15 D753): `resize_factors` keeps the sign of the scale factor and so flips a
shape dragged past its anchor, and `resized_box` took `(at - held).abs()` and flipped nothing at all.
**Two copies of one rule diverge twice before anybody looks**, and this second one was invisible to
every existing test because the *box* is identical either way.

**The transform origin is draggable, and the toggle that arms it is a mode of working.**
`OndinApp::show_pivot` is app-wide and sticky rather than per node: rigging a shape to swing from one
corner is something a designer sets out to do, and whoever turns it on is about to place several, so
resetting it with the selection would mean re-arming it for each. It rides on the Transform panel's
header as a `ui::HeadAction` toggle (§9.2), dimmed with a tooltip for a multi-selection rather than
vanishing, since a set has no pivot to share and a control that disappears cannot say why. Escape
turns it off, slotted after `cancel_gesture` and before the `entered_group` unwind — outside anything
in flight, inside the selection state that survives it — and puts the handle away without undoing any
pivot already placed. `canvas::draw_pivot` has three states: **editable** while the toggle is on with
one layer selected; **read-only** on the layer under the pointer whose pivot has been *placed*, which
is the affordance that lets a shape spinning about its corner say why rather than being fought for ten
minutes; and absent otherwise. **That read-only state is hover-only, and only on a layer that is
neither selected nor mid-gesture** (and only under the Select tool). It began as any layer whose pivot
was placed, which parked the marker on the layer you were working on for as long as you worked on it.
It answers one question — why does this thing rotate oddly — and that question is asked *about* a
layer rather than while editing one: the gesture check covers moving, and the selection check covers
the layer already in hand, which has the Transform panel's toggle if the handle is wanted back.
*An affordance you cannot stop reading is clutter, so it belongs on the transient state (hover) rather
than on the persistent one (selection).* **The two live states are two Phosphor glyphs, not one glyph
in two tints**: `canvas::Marker::Editable` draws `icon::CROSSHAIR` and `Marker::ReadOnly` the lighter
`CROSSHAIR_SIMPLE`, both in `color::SELECT` at `PIVOT_GLYPH_PX` (22) with **nothing behind them**. The
shape is what carries "you can move this" against "someone moved this", so it survives being small,
sitting over busy artwork, and being read by someone who has not learnt which tint means which — and
`CROSSHAIR_SIMPLE` is also the Transform panel's toggle, so the read-only marker is literally the
picture on the button that would make it live. The hand-drawn ring, centre dot and four ticks it
replaced grounded that ring in `color::CARD` once the pivot was placed, which put a near-black disc in
the middle of the shape. `pivot_marker_tests::the_two_marker_weights_differ_and_both_fit_the_grab_radius`
holds the two apart and against `PIVOT_PICK_PX`, since a marker wider than its own grab radius is a
control you can see and cannot press, and `the_marker_paints_no_ground_behind_itself` counts the shapes:
one glyph, nothing else. A drag snaps to the nine points of the box (corners,
side middles, centre) within 6 screen px — ⚠️ **and the comparison happens in the node's *local* space,
so that threshold is divided by the zoom and by the node's own basis, one column norm per axis** (§15
D695): `|column 0|` of the world transform for local x and `|column 1|` for local y, because a group
carries scale and skew is a shipped gesture, so a single scalar cannot be right for both axes — and
the mean of the two is the quantity §5.6 refuses for a guide, the same wrong choice made twice in one
session in files that share no code. It read *"by the zoom and by nothing else"* until 2026-09-09,
which put the marker 24 screen units from a corner inside a 4× group.
There is a badge naming the position while it is placed, and
**the centre snaps to `None`**, so dragging the marker back to the middle genuinely undoes the change:
the field leaves the file (§5.11), the read-only affordance disappears, and `flip` goes back to the
union centreline. That last rule is `geometry::pivot_placed_at`'s rather than the snap's, so the
numeric fields below share it exactly (§15 D247); a degenerate axis is centred by itself there, which
is what lets a line drawn flat be dragged back to nothing at all. `Drag::Pivot { id }` carries no
`RenderOverrides` preview and needs none — the marker
is chrome drawn from the live pointer, the way a marquee is — and commits one `SetPivot` on release,
while `EditorSession::preview_pivot` resolves it against the box a live gesture is showing, because the
pivot itself is never overridden but the box it may be a fraction of is. One priority is deliberate:
the marker outranks the resize handles in `begin_select_drag` while the toggle is on, because a pivot
parked on a corner would otherwise be impossible to grab back.

**The origin has two numbers as well as a handle, they are percentages of the layer's own box, and
they are on the canvas** (`canvas::origin_fields`, §15 D247 and D252). They hang **under the layer's
bounding box in the size badge's slot**, replacing that badge while the header's crosshair is armed
over one layer: both are a readout under the selection, there is room for one, and W × H is not what
anyone is reading while placing an origin. `badge_placement` is shared by the two, so the swap cannot
move. **A shape being *drawn* takes the slot ahead of both** (§15 D292) — during a create drag the box
under the hand is plainly what is being measured. Since §15 D294 arming a creation tool clears the
selection, so the displaced readout is usually nothing at all; the arm still stands, because a
selection made *after* the tool was armed (`Ctrl+A`, the layers panel) would otherwise put a second
pill on the canvas quoting a layer nobody is looking at. They were a row in the Transform card for a day and came out again — the card is the busiest in
the panel and a second `X`/`Y` pair in it is one pair too many (D252).

A percentage rather than the local units W and H are in, because the stored `Pivot` is a fraction for
an authored box and an absolute point for an emergent one, and a field reading out whichever was
stored would change meaning with the kind under it: the display is a fraction for everything and
`pivot_for` goes on choosing the storage, the same division X/Y already draw. It is also the
vocabulary the marker speaks — its snap set is exactly 0, 50 and 100 on each axis, so *nought is the
left edge, fifty the centre, a hundred the right*, which is what makes an edge or a corner typeable
without arithmetic — and **a dragged marker lands on a whole one**, through these same two functions,
so the handle and the fields cannot produce different classes of value for one placement (§15 D253).
That rounding follows the nine-point snap rather than replacing it: the snap is in screen pixels and is
what makes a corner easy to hit at any zoom, and 0 / 50 / 100 survive it untouched. Unclamped,
because the marker is: a pivot may sit outside the box it is measured
against. An axis with no extent is **dimmed with a sentence saying why**, per axis rather than per
box, so a flat line keeps the field that still means something — and the fields are offered for a lone
line at all, where the size badge suppresses itself, because a percentage along a line is meaningful
where its `W × H` is not. Both at 50 clears the origin, which is the fields' own way of un-saying "not
moved" — a state the model can say and, before them, only the context menu's *Reset origin* could ask
for. `EditorSession::pivot_preview` is what makes them scrubbable: the overrides cannot carry a pivot,
so without it the readout would re-read the committed node every frame and the number would never move
(§15 D245).

**These are the first live egui widgets the canvas hosts** — everything else on it is painter plus
hand-rolled hit testing. `ui::badge_field` is the size badge's pill with `value_field`'s plumbing
inside it: the same `Scrub`, the same `expr::eval` parser, and the same second-claimant trick that
makes the label scrub as well as the digits. They are **upright** where the badge turns with the shape,
since an egui widget cannot be rotated; they take the badge's position and not its angle. They live in
an `egui::Area` of their own, and *that* is what keeps a press on a field from also starting a marquee
— measured, not assumed: any `Area` shields the layer beneath whatever its `Order` and whatever its
content senses, while the same rect interacted in the canvas's own `Ui` does not
(`canvas::overlay_claim`). **That shielding is wholesale**, which is a cost as well as the feature:
`wheel_input` names the fields' layer through `origin_fields_layer` and takes the wheel back, or
scrolling and zooming would die with the pointer parked over a pill (§15 D254). The middle-button pan
is the same collision and is still open there.

**What reads the pivot is every gesture that needs a fixed point to turn a whole transform about.**
`Handles::center`
became `Handles::pivot` — the node's own transform origin for a single selection, the union centre for
several — and that is what `Drag::Rotate` turns about; the
inspector's skew field rebuilds about it, its rotation field *composes* about it (§15 D206) and its two
quarter-turn buttons turn about it; and
`build::flip` — so both mirror buttons as well — mirrors a single layer about it **when one has
actually been placed**, and about the union centreline otherwise, for the reason D55 gives. **The two
gestures it deliberately does not generalise are the canvas skew and the Alt-resize**, each of which
already has a fixed point that is part of its own bargain — the side facing the dragged one for a
skew, the opposite edge for a resize — and substituting the pivot makes the gesture worse for the
shapes nobody has moved a pivot on. §15 D55 has the skew half of that boundary and D60 the resize
half, which was built before it was known to be impossible.

**W and H show for a `Path`, a `Boolean` and a `Group` too, and writing one is a synthesized handle
drag.** None of the three has an authored `size` — their extent is whatever their contents add up to — so
`inspector_single`'s `size0` falls back to `preview_local_box`, the same box the canvas handles are drawn
on; refusing to show the number was the panel disagreeing with the canvas about whether the shape has a
width (§15 D98, and D242 for the group, which was left out of that arm and so had no numeric resize at
all). An **empty** group is the one `None`: `local_box` unions children and has none, so the row is
absent rather than showing 0 × 0 over a field that could not write. The *write* picks between two
meanings: an authored `size` is replaced, which is one
operation and exactly what it always was, and anything else goes through `tools::resize_box_to`, which
puts a pointer at the corner the new box wants and routes it through `tools::resize_layer` — the path a
bottom-right drag already takes (§5.6). That is the point rather than an economy: a `Path`'s width has no
field to assign, so the handle's arithmetic is the only definition "make it 200 wide" has, and sharing it
is what stops a typed number and a dragged handle meaning two different things. It asks for geometry only
and neither modifier — a typed W must not multiply stroke widths (§5.6), and the proportion lock is
applied to the target size *before* the call, so `keep_ratio` would apply it twice. The write takes
neither the box nor the transform from the preview, so a scrub does not compound — the rule `resize_tx`
states for its own box. A `Line` shows no W/H, deliberately: its box is the meaningless one D99
took off the canvas. **What it shows instead, in W's slot, is an `L`** (§15 D229) — the number its
suppressed size badge would have wanted — and it writes through `tools::move_line_end`, the endpoint
handle's own verb, for the reason W/H writes through `resize_layer`. It **anchors the start**, because
X/Y report that point and Rotation reads the start→end vector, so growing from the far end would move
the numbers in two other fields.

**That same arithmetic has a third door, on `Ctrl`+arrows** (§15 D346, `shortcuts.md` §11). The chord
steps the selection's **box** by the nudge step — `→` wider, `←` narrower, `↓` taller, `↑` shorter, one
point and ten with `Shift`, out of the same `input::NudgeStep` the bare arrows read (§15 D330) — and
`OndinApp::size_step` implements neither half of the arithmetic itself: one selected layer goes through
`tools::resize_box_to`, the local box, so a rotated shape grows along its **own** axes, and several go
through `tools::resize_selection` over the world union, which is the split the panel already makes
between its single-layer card and its multi one. It is **held by its top-left corner**, the corner X and
Y report, so a held key grows the shape away from a fixed point rather than walking it — which is why it
does not `reveal_selection` (below), and why **one table in the keymap serves both actions**: a nudge
moves the box in the direction of the arrow, and a resize holding the top-left moves the opposite edge,
so the arrow names the edge that moves either way. `normal_mode` resolves the four signed pairs once and
picks the verb from the modifier rather than keeping two tables that happen to agree. The 1pt floor is
per axis and is the panel's own; it is there to stop the *ask* going negative rather than to stop an
extent reaching zero, since a negative target reflects the layer through its anchor — a handle dragged
past what it is anchored to being a flip, and the flip being the sign of the scale factor (§5.6). One
press moves one axis unless the selection's proportions are locked — every member of it, on either arm
— in which case both move and the arrow says which drives (below). A guide is a coordinate rather than a box, so a guide selection is inert, and
a burst of taps coalesces under its own undo verb, `resize-layers`, so a nudge and a resize can never
merge into one step.

**The Transform panel has a proportion lock**, the regenerated design's 28×28 `link-simple` button
after W and H. **W is exactly as wide as X and H absorbs the difference**, so the two rows share one
edge down the middle of the card: splitting the W/H/lock row evenly would put W's right edge a
button's-worth left of X's, and the eye reads that misalignment long before it reads the labels, while
H being the odd one out is invisible because nothing above it lines up with anything.
Locked, editing either field scales the other by the aspect taken **before** either is
touched, so both directions measure against the shape as it is rather than against a value the other
field has already changed. It lives on the node (`Node::proportions_locked`, §5.3) and is saved —
unlike the per-corner radius set beside it (§5.3), which is a **disclosure** about which fields are
showing and stays in `OndinApp` view state where losing it costs nothing. This one is a
**constraint** the user has put on the layer, because it changes what a gesture does rather than
which fields are visible, and a constraint that evaporates on reopen is a bug (§15 D41). The button
reads `DisplayNode::proportions_locked()` and commits `SetProportionsLocked` straight through
`session.commit` rather than the `edit_valve` (§9.3): it is a toggle, not a scrubbed value, so there
is no stream of intermediate states to coalesce. One departure from the design, which draws the solid
chain in the resting state: the button shows a **broken** chain when unlocked and a whole one when
locked. The tint alone would say the same thing, but only to someone who already knows which state is
which, and this is a control that has to be read at a glance while a number is being dragged.

**Its scope is the handles and the keyboard as well as the fields — the multi card's included.**
`canvas::keep_ratio` is the lock **XOR** Shift, so
a locked layer resizes proportionally from any handle as though Shift were held permanently, and
Shift on a locked layer *releases* the constraint — the only way left to ask for a free resize, and
the only reading under which the modifier still has something to say. Snapping is not folded into that
XOR, and is no longer Shift's to switch off at all (§15 D47): every resize snaps whichever way the
ratio is being read, and the aspect constraint is applied to the already-snapped pointer. The
consequence is worth stating plainly, because it is visible — a Shift-resize lands its dragged corner
*near* the feature it caught rather than exactly on it. The constraint wins over the snap. Over a
multi-selection the lock reads as **all** rather than any, so one locked member cannot constrain a box
the rest never asked to have constrained (§15 D50). **That reading is one function**,
`tools::proportions_locked`, and every door onto a *set* asks it: the handles through `keep_ratio`, the
multi W and H fields, `Ctrl`+arrows over one layer or several, and the multi card's chain button (§15
D347). It is asked the **whole selection** rather than `build::outermost`'s reduction of it, since the
question is what the user picked, and an empty selection is not locked — otherwise a vacuous `all` would
read as "every member is". **A locked selection pressed with `Ctrl`+arrows scales both axes** (§15
D346), the arrow naming which axis drives — but that pairing is the *fields'* literally: `tools::paired_size`,
the one expression all three numeric doors compute before the resize, rather than the handles' `Resize`
flag, which takes the larger of two factors and so would refuse to shrink a box only one of whose axes
is being driven.

**Directly under W and H, while the Scale tool is held, is a Scale field — one percentage in W's slot,
with `0.5x` and `2x` filling the rest of the row** (§15 D311, D313). It is the Scale tool's verb
rather than a second spelling of W: every W/H path in the panel passes `Resize::geometry`, where a 1px
border stays 1px and 16pt type stays 16pt, while this one passes
`tools::Scaling::Photographic` and takes strokes, corner radii and font size with it — which is what the
canvas does under an armed Scale tool (above) and what no number in the app could ask for before.
**The row exists only while that tool is armed** (§15 D312), which is the panel's way of saying which
verb is live: a field that changed meaning with the tool would be a hidden mode, where a field that
only *appears* with the tool announces itself. Being the card's first genuinely **optional** row, it is
also the reason every row from it downwards is drawn through `inspector::transform_row` and identified
by *name* rather than by where it sits (§15 D314): egui numbers a widget by its position among its
parent's children, so a row that comes and goes renumbers everything beneath it, and a half-typed
`DragValue` lives in `Context::data` under that number. No second **number** sits beside it, for the
reason a `Line`'s `L` has its row to itself (§15 D229): there is no second dimension to put there,
non-uniform scaling being exactly what W and H are. **No scale is
stored** — a resize writes geometry, so a doubled rect has an authored size of 200 and nothing to
decompose — so the field is a verb with a live readout, applying its percentage against the
**committed** box every frame and returning to 100 once the valve closes, by which time the box is the
new size — and returning to 100 again when the row *goes away*, since a percentage typed but never
committed has nothing else to clear it (§15 D314). It writes through `inspector::scale_tx`, which resizes the selection's union from
`Handle::BottomRight` so the top-left is held: the corner X and Y report, and the corner W and H resize
from — and through the **ordinary** edit valve (§9.3). It took a valve of its own for a few hours,
because a transaction relative to the box it is about to write cannot survive a commit per keystroke;
the same fault turned out to be in the shared valve for every field in the app, so this row went back
to the shared one (§15 D312, D316) — ⚠️ **which is one valve for this field and not one valve in the
app**: there are three hand-rolled ones, D316's fix reached only the shared one, and the other two
carried the same fault for two hundred entries (§9.3, §15 D519, D523). **And while the canvas handles are scaling under an armed Scale tool, the field
reads out the drag** — `canvas::live_scale_pct` compares the previewed union against the committed one,
one number from two factors by the geometric mean, and it is purely an indicator: the field commits
nothing, because its valve fires on the *field's* own engagement and that never begins (§15 D315). The two
multiples are the same verb with the typing done, `ui::label_button` at `FieldButton::Off` straight to
`commit_edit`, and **neither is ever the selected one**: a scale is applied and gone, so there is
no state a highlighted cell could be reporting. They are **halve and double** for that same reason — a
relative control has no absolute rest position to return to, so its shortcuts are the two ways out of
where it already is. The row read `1x`, `2x`, `3x` for a few hours, where `1x` did nothing at all
(§15 D312, D313).

**Rotation and skew share one row, and the four discrete transforms have a row of their own.** They
are the same kind of number about the same box, so they sit inline at X and Y's widths, which is what
frees the row below for four equal buttons — a quarter turn counter-clockwise, a quarter turn
clockwise, flip horizontal, flip vertical (`ui::field_button_sized`, splitting the card evenly rather
than leaving 28px squares and a gap). The design's layout, and it reads as "angles here, jumps
there". Skew's range is ±89° — it reads `tools::MAX_SKEW` itself now
rather than a hard-coded 89, so the field, the canvas gesture and the multi-selection skew field all
clamp at one number — and it borrows the `ANGLE` glyph from the star's inner-ratio field: a lean *is*
an angle, the two never appear in one panel, and the alternative was guessing at a codepoint the
icon font may not carry. Both fields read their value out of
`build::Basis::of` rather than `atan2(b, a)` — the rotation field only at rest, a gesture in flight
showing its own latched number (§15 D206) — and **only the skew field rebuilds** — it replaces `skew`
alone and keeps `angle` and `mirror` together, so the pair that has to agree is never split. A rebuild
**multiplies the residual scale back on**. That residual is not always identity even though a node's own
transform never carries
scale (§5.6): the basis shown here is the *world* one, and a sheared parent with a turned child
multiplies out to a basis with scale in it. Dropping it would resize the layer every time its angle
was nudged. **Rotation composes instead** — `inspector::turned_about`, the same
`rotate_about · old_world` the canvas ring and the quarter turns already use — because rebuilding is what
made it spin a mirrored layer half a turn per frame past ±90° (§15 D206), and composition needs no
residual because it takes nothing apart. Both fields turn the layer about its **pivot** (§5.3) rather
than about its local origin,
which is what makes typing 30° and dragging to 30° put the shape in the same place; §15 D55 has the
inconsistency that was, and why the skew rebuild is exact.

**A `Line` is the one kind whose rotation field is not its basis angle.** A line is drawn by dragging and
the direction goes into its *endpoint* (§5.3 stores the far point; the near one is the origin), so a
diagonal line's basis is the identity and the field read 0° for a line plainly running at 45°. It shows
the world-space angle from start to end instead — taken in **world** space because that is exact under any
basis a line can accumulate, a mirror included, where composing the endpoint's own angle with the basis
angle would not be. The *write* changed shape to match: it applies the **delta** — `typed` minus the
number the field was showing, turned about the pivot — rather than assigning the typed value. For every
other kind the two are
identical, since the field shows the basis angle; for a line the field shows a number the basis does not
hold, so "turn it by the difference" is the only reading that reaches the same place for both. The
identity edit stays exact either way, which is what makes writing the transform from the field every
frame safe. Nothing else about the field changed — rotating a line through it worked before this and
works the same way now. **What the difference is measured *from* is the part that later needed a latch**:
re-reading it per frame is what made a mirrored layer flash, and §15 D206 has why.

**No angle field ever reads `-0°`.** `inspector::shown_degrees` normalises every angle readout, the
multi panel's two included. Angles come back through `build::Basis`, an RQ decomposition, so an
unrotated node's is `atan2(±0, 1)` — a *signed* zero — and a mirrored or sheared one lands a few ulps
either side of it; all of them format as `-0`, which reads as a value somebody set. Worse, a rotation
of `-0.0` builds a matrix whose `b` is `-0.0`, so the sign survives every round trip and the field
reads `-0°` until the layer is turned and turned back. The **magnitude** is snapped and not just the
sign, because `-1e-17` prints identically and arrives by the same route, and the threshold (1e-9°) is
far below anything a half-degree drag or a typed number can produce. Note for whoever reads
`angle_tests`: it asserts `is_sign_positive` *and* the formatted string, because `-0.0 == 0.0` is
**true** — which is exactly why this survived a comparison.

**The quarter turns go through `tools::rotate_node`, not the angle field**, about the pivot read from
the committed tree — the same frame `rotate_node` reads the world transform from, or the layer lands a
fraction off the point it turned about. Adding 90 to the number above looks equivalent and is wrong
twice: `Basis` reports a *mirrored* layer's angle in its own frame, so writing the sum back turns it
the other way, and a *sheared* layer's two axes are not square, so there is no one number to add to.
Composing a rotation onto the world matrix is right for every matrix and is the same call the canvas
drag makes, so the two cannot disagree. The mirror buttons go through `build::flip` for the same
reason. **Both cards draw this row through one function** — `inspector::quarters_row`, taking a
`TurnScope` exactly as the paint panels take a `PaintScope` — and it was written twice until §15
D737, with the paragraph you are reading sitting beside the single-layer copy only.

**A multi-selection gets the whole inspector, not a count and two buttons.** `inspector_multi` used
to show "N layers selected", Group/Ungroup and Align, so everything else about several layers had to
be done one at a time even though the canvas already handled the set completely (above). It now
carries a Transform panel, an Appearance panel, Fill and Stroke, **Group Colors** and **Export** —
every panel
backed by §5.7a's bulk builders, so the app, MCP writes and the command line cannot disagree about
what "set the fill of these" means. §15 D53 has the reasoning, of which the load-bearing part is that
**"Mixed" is a panel rather than a label**. A selection with **frames** in it also gets *Frame
templates* and *Layout grid*, second and third, directly under the identity card and in the same order
as on a single frame — the two frame panels that are not a single layer's (§15 D389, D390, below).

**A frame gets two cards of its own, *Frame templates* and *Layout grid*, and the ordinary Fill and
Stroke panels for its paint** (§5.3b, §15 D385, D387). The two sit **second and third,
above Align and Transform** — under the identity and mask cards, because they say what kind of page
this is and what it is divided into, and everything below them is about a layer among layers.
**There is no third card for its ground.** A frame is `PaintScope::Node` like any other layer and gets
the shared panels — the `+`, the per-row eye, the reorder grip, the ✕, the mixed-selection row, the
whole list (§15 D400). It had a one-row card of its own until 2026-09-01, headed *Frame background*
until §15 D397 renamed it *Fill*, and each of that card's controls was a smaller version of something
the shared panel already did properly. ⚠️ **The one thing given up is a word**: an unfilled frame said
*Transparent*, which is truer of a frame than the shared *No fill* — but an empty shape is exactly as
transparent as an empty frame, so the distinction was never about frames, and one empty state that
reads the same on every layer is worth more than a truer word on one of them.
The grid card is one block per grid — an axis switch
(`columns`/`rows`, the dashboard's own two glyphs), an eye, an ✕, then the grid's **colour** on a Fill
row, then `N`/`G` and `M`/`W`, then a four-cell alignment strip whose glyphs are the Align panel's and
change with the axis, so *Left* over columns is *Top* over rows. ⚠️ **The fields an
alignment does not read are dimmed rather than hidden** — the value is being kept through the switch,
and a control that vanishes reads as a control the app does not have. The `+` adds *columns* to a
frame that has none and *rows* to one that already has columns, which is the commoner second grid —
and gives it the first colour in `layout::GRID_COLORS` the frame is not already using, on the same
argument one step over: the reason to add a second grid is to read it against the first (§15 D388).
**It also opens the card**, which rests closed while there is no grid to show and closes again when
the last one is deleted (`sync_paint_collapse`, Fill and Stroke's rule and a fourth synced-selection
field, since that edge is consumed by whoever asks first); a `+` that adds a row you cannot see is a
button that does nothing, and an empty card whose whole body is the words *No layout grid* is chrome
saying nothing (§15 D389).
⚠️ **A hidden grid's controls are `disable`d rather than merely faded**, which is a deliberate
departure from the Fill, Stroke and Effects rows: everything that *describes* the grid goes dead, and
the eye and the ✕ — the two controls that decide whether there is a grid at all — stay live. The eye
is an ordinary `FieldButton::Off` in both states with the glyph carrying the state (`EYE` /
`EYE_SLASH`), never a lit one, since the lit face would be marking the case that is true of every
grid by default. Rows sit at `ui::CARD_ROW_GAP` like every other panel's, and two grids twice that
apart, which is what the stroke list already puts between one stroke's block and the next (§15 D386).
⚠️ **The eye is not the outermost gate any more, and nothing in the card says so** (§15 D755):
*View ▸ Show layout grid* sits above it, so with that switch off an open eye here draws nothing. The
card was not changed by D755 and reads the switch nowhere — which follows from the switch being
workspace state and this panel being the document's, the two never writing to each other.

**Both frame cards find their own subject, where every other panel here is handed one** (§15 D389,
D390). They act on the selected **frames** — `frame_subjects`, one rule for the two of them — filtered
out of the selection rather than all-or-nothing, so a rectangle caught on the way round three frames
still leaves the three frames, and they draw nothing at all where the selection holds no frame, which
is what lets one call each serve both this and `inspector_multi`. Export is written the same way and
for the same reason. Over several frames the grid card takes Export's three states. **No frame has a
grid** → it rests closed, says *No layout grid*
when opened, and the `+` writes one grid to all of them. **They hold the same list** → the card shows
it, and changing, deleting or adding reaches every frame in one transaction and one undo step.
**Any frame differs** → the card is shown **open** — a message nobody can see explains nothing — says
*Mixed layout grids. Add to override.*, draws no rows, and the `+` replaces every frame's list with
the single grid it seeds rather than appending to each, which is the dead end §15 D274 argued out for
exports. ⚠️ **That the rows are drawn only where the frames agree is load-bearing**, not merely tidy:
it is what makes the first frame in document order a safe anchor for `PaintSlot::Grid(i)`, whose write
then goes out to every subject. **The detached picker is bound by the same fact and was not** (§15
D553): it now closes when `shared_grids` over `frame_subjects` answers `None`, where before it floated
over the anchor's colour and wrote through a row nobody could see. The list every frame agrees on
comes from the **committed** document, there being no override tree a grid can live in.

**Frame templates are a panel of pictures, not a dropdown** (§15 D385, D387). Five groups —
Phone/Tablet/Desktop/Print/Social — inside a scroll box capped at 184pt, each a two-across grid of
cells that draw the template at its own proportions in a fixed 20×28 slot (floored at 5pt a side, or a
banner is a hairline) with its name and its box beside it. A cell is painted by hand rather than
assembled from `ui::button_face`, and the difference is one state: a resting cell has **no ground at
all** where every field button has `color::FIELD`, because eighteen grounds in a scroll box is a wall
of buttons and what this is is a list. The lit and hovered inks are `button_face`'s own, so a lit cell
and a lit button are the same mark. It **reads** as well as writes — the size every selected frame
agrees on is the lit cell, and frames that match nothing, or that do not agree, light nothing, which is
the half that makes it a control rather than a menu. That size comes from the **committed** document,
so a frame being dragged by a handle does not light a template mid-gesture. ⚠️ The match is exact and
orientation-sensitive: a phone on its side lights nothing, because matching either order would name a
preset that applying would then silently rotate — and,
unordered, *Full HD* and *Story* are the same box. ⚠️ **Two entries may not share a box**, since
`preset_named` answers with the first match and the loser is a cell that can never be lit; the
design's own list carried such a pair and only one of the two is in the table. Print sizes are
**points at 72/inch** (A4 = 595×842), the unit the W/H fields already show. Picking one writes
`GeometryPatch::Size` — the same patch those two fields write, so a template is one undo step beside
them rather than a second way of saying how big a frame is — and a click on the cell that is already
lit writes nothing at all.

⚠️ **Over a multi-selection the panel is the *only* way to set several frames' own boxes, and it is not
a duplicate of the Transform card's W and H** (§15 D390). Those report the **union** and go through
`tools::resize_selection`, which scales the set as a rigid body and takes every frame's contents with
it, so typing 393 into W over four phone frames squashes the arrangement into a 393-wide box; a
template writes `GeometryPatch::Size` to each frame and leaves its children alone, which is what "make
these four artboards iPhones" means. Both are right about the thing they measure, and one of them is
the thing a designer laying out a flow is asking for. Every frame gets the patch, in one transaction
and one undo step. ⚠️ **Unlike the grid card, a disagreement here needs no message**: a template list
is a set of *alternatives*, so "none of the above" is a state it already shows by lighting nothing,
where a grid list is content and an empty one is indistinguishable from a mixed one unless the card
says which it is. Two states here against three there.

**The Effects card is the layer's stack, one row per effect, with a popover behind each row** (§5.3a,
§15 D333, D337). A row is the kind's glyph, its name, **one headline number** and an ✕, with the eye
outside the field as a paint row has it — `40%` for a shadow (its colour's alpha, which *is* its
opacity), the radius for a blur, and how many of the four channels are off-neutral for Filters. The
`+` in the header adds a drop shadow and brings up its numbers.

**Model order, first at the top, where the Fill card draws its list upside down.** The two are not
the same kind of list: paints are stacked in *space* and the renderer walks the list forward, so the
top row has to be the paint you see on top; effects are a **pipeline**, each taking what the one
before it produced (§6.4), so the list reads top-down like the sentence it is.

**The popover is the design's card with its title replaced by a kind combo.** A title is the one
thing about a popover already known from the row that opened it, and the combo says the same word
while making the row's kind changeable — which a fill row has had all along through the picker's
tabs. Retyping **carries across what the two kinds share** (`EffectKind::retyped`): two shadows share
every field, a shadow and a blur share the blur radius, `Filters` shares nothing. It sits in the lane
every inspector popover shares — clear of the cards, to their left — and dismisses through
`panels::dismissed_by_click`, which it is the fifth caller of rather than a fifth copy of. ⚠️ **It
was not in R4's clear until 2026-09-08** (§15 D533), so it survived a right-click and stood over the
canvas the context menu was aimed at — and because it reads `Escape` itself, one press then closed
the menu and the popover together.

**A shadow's colour is a Fill row: a chip, a hex and a percentage**, on `PaintSlot::Effect(i)` — the
fifth slot naming something that is not a fill, so the swatch, the hex field and the detached picker
are the app's own rather than a second colour panel. The percentage **is** the alpha; there is no
second field for the two to disagree about (§15 D333).

**A `Filters` row is the image card's adjustment row** (§15 D343): `ui::value_field_metered`, a bar
across the field's ground growing from the middle, plus a per-channel reset — the same control the
seven image adjustments use, so the two surfaces read alike. The three factor ranges are `0…200%`
**symmetric about their neutral**, which is what makes the meter honest (an asymmetric range would
make one side three times as sensitive as the other) and what makes it literally `factor − 1.0`. The
*units* stay factors at 100% neutral rather than `ImageAdjust`'s signed offsets from zero — D333 chose
them and stated the difference, and this adopts the control without undoing that.

**The card opens itself on a layer with effects and shuts on one without**, on Fill and Stroke's
rule, through a third `*_synced_selection` field — `paint_subject_changed` consumes its edge, so a
second caller in the same frame never learns the subject moved.

**Over a multi-selection it takes the Export panel's shape, not Fill's** (§15 D340): one agreed stack
or a disagreement, since an effect list has no honest per-property "mixed". Agreed, the rows draw and
every edit reaches all of them as one undo step; disagreeing, the card says *"These layers have
different effects"* and the `+` **replaces** every layer's stack — the opposite of Fill's inert `+`
(D53), because an effect card has no other way out of that state. `PaintSlot::Effect(i)` writes to
every selected layer, which is sound because the card's subject *is* the selection in both cases.
⚠️ **But it reads each subject's own list rather than cloning the anchor's**, and that premise is why:
the second door is the **detached picker**, which outlives the card, so a widening that stops the rows
being drawn can leave a picker floating over a selection whose stacks disagree — and a clone then
replaces another layer's whole stack with the anchor's. The widened write can only ever change one
entry's colour, whatever the card and the picker disagree about (§15 D635; the code cites `D476`,
which has no entry, and D553 carries the same argument at the `Grid` slot).

**Reordering the stack is a decided non-goal for v1** (§15 D340, `roadmap.md` §0), struck with a
measurement behind it: order changes a pixel only between `Filters` and `LayerBlur`, and between two
shadows on the same side. Nothing about the feature is open. A stack authored here draws on the canvas and in both exports (§15 D339); it did not on the
canvas for one day, and the card carried a line saying so.

**The Export panel is the layer's list of files, and the button that produces them** (§7, §15 D274).
One row per `ExportSpec`, on the design's `74px 1fr 28px 28px` grid: a scale dropdown, a format
dropdown, a settings button and an ✕. The scale **dims rather than disappears for SVG**, which
has no pixels for a multiplier to multiply — the two wrong answers being a control that vanishes and
moves everything beside it as the format changes, and one that silently resets a setting. Under each row, a faint line carries the **pixel size that row will produce** — the answer to "why is
my icon 47 pixels", and a line rather than a fifth cell because the number is five characters or
eleven depending on the scale. **The row and its line are one unit at 3, and one unit sits 6 from
the next** — `paint_unit`'s arrangement and its trap with it: `item_spacing` is zero inside and both
gaps are allocated, because egui spends the spacing in effect when a widget is *placed*, so a pitch
set for the two lines is also spent after the last of them (§15 D195). **A row that draws no size
line spends that line's gap here instead** — 6 + 3, written out from this list's own two numbers
rather than borrowed from `CARD_ROW_GAP`, which it happens to equal. That is every row over a
multi-selection and a single layer's SVG row: 6 is tight *because* a unit is a row plus its caption
and needs the contrast to read as one thing, so with no caption there is nothing left to group and
six points between two bare 28pt controls is crowding (§15 D274). The **last** row allocates nothing
either way, which is what leaves the button below the list at the card's ordinary pitch. **The rows
are a region of
their own with the pitch at zero**, because 6 is *below* `CARD_ROW_GAP` and a scope can add to a
spacing but not subtract from one. Not that function's numbers, though — it doubles the card's pitch
to the 18 two stroke entries sit at, which is sized for an entry of two controls where this is a
control and its caption; what has to read here is not "these are two entries" but "this caption goes
with the row above", and that is carried by the *relationship* between the two gaps rather than by
either distance (§15 D274). The line also zeroes
`interact_size.y` for itself: `Ui::horizontal` treats the theme's 24 as a **minimum row height**, so
a line of 13pt ink otherwise paints in a 24pt slot and adds five points to the gap at each end while
both gaps stay correct in the source (§15 D274).
**The card is closed on a layer that exports nothing and the header's `+` opens it**, which is Fill
and Stroke's rule (`sync_paint_collapse`) — it needs a synced-selection field of its own, because
`paint_subject_changed` consumes the edge and two callers in one frame lose it for one of them.
The settings are a **popover beside the panel**, the shell every other card here uses — 272 wide,
`menu_frame`'s padding, `popover_anchor`'s lane, `ui::POPOVER_SECTION_GAP` (§15 D275), and
`panels::dismissed_by_click`'s six terms
whole. It holds five labelled sections — prefix, suffix, JPEG quality, background, and the two
switches —
which is why it is not rows in the card: at that size an inline block pushes the export button and
every row below it down the column, which is `stroke_menu_popup`'s own reasoning.
⚠️ **The background section's chip goes muted over a multi-selection rather than painting one member's
frame, which is the size line's rule about a colour** (§15 D657). *Frame's own* resolves per layer, so
two rects in two frames — one white, one black — had the chip paint **white** and the export produce
one of each, under a tooltip reading *"the nearest frame's background"*, singular; it takes the same
one-subject value the size line does and says nothing where there is no single answer, with a plural
tooltip so a muted chip does not read as the setting having failed. **Only the *Frame's own* arm is
muted**: `Solid` and `Transparent` are properties of the spec and are exactly as true of thirty layers
as of one, so blanking them would be a second wrong answer in the other direction. The panel's own
menu is a second popover holding what belongs to no row — presets, copy/paste of a whole list, the
folder rule, and re-export-on-save. **The two are mutually exclusive**, unlike the inspector's other
popovers: they hang from one card a few points apart, so both open is one covering the other.
**Both are in the lane and therefore in all three of the sets that lane has** —
`OndinApp::a_popover_is_open`, so the detached picker is pushed clear of them; R4's clear, so a
right-click dismisses them; and `OndinApp::a_popover_owns_escape`, so `Escape` closes them without
paying out a rung of the ladder underneath (§15 D801). ⚠️ **These two read no key at all until
2026-09-19**, so `Escape` left them standing and dropped a rung behind them; one `key_pressed(Escape)`
block at the foot of `export_buttons` clears both flags, the two being mutually exclusive anyway.
⚠️ **They were in neither of the first two until 2026-09-08** (§15 D533): each is anchored at `POPOVER_W`, which is
the width the lane's own clearance is computed from, so a picker opened after one of them landed
underneath it with 236 of its 240 points inside the popover's span.
**Over a multi-selection the header's `+` stays live where Fill's goes inert**, and over a selection
whose layers export *differently* it **overrides rather than appends**: one click replaces every
subject's list with the single export it seeds, in one undoable transaction, so the selection agrees
afterwards and there are rows to edit. Appending to each layer's own list is well defined and is a
dead end — the layers still disagree, so the card repeats *Mixed exports. Add to override.* with one
more file per layer behind it and nothing reachable from inside the card that resolves the state; the
destruction that appending avoided is what Undo is for (§15 D274). The `+`'s tooltip is three-way for the
same reason, so the destructive click says what it is before it happens. **What it seeds climbs —
1×, 2×, 3×, then 4× for ever** (`ladder_scale`, a function of how many rows the list already holds
and of nothing else), with the format inherited from the last existing row and PNG when there is
nothing to inherit from, a disagreeing selection included. The first row is 1× because it is the
first, not because 1× happened to be unclaimed, which is what the rule this replaced actually
measured (§15 D274). The cap is not a fallback: past 3× the list stops being a density ladder, and
climbing further would be the panel inventing sizes rather than following one. Every rung is one of
`ExportScale::COMMON`'s own multipliers, so a seeded row reads back off the combo it sits in; a
repeat past the cap is safe on disk (§7's ` (2)` de-collision). A **Preview** section sits at the foot of the same
card, collapsed by
default — opening it is what turns on the one thing in the inspector that renders and encodes the
artwork, and it does so once per edit, keyed on `EditorSession::revision`. **JPEG quality is the one
scrubbable export setting, and it goes through neither shared committer** — it holds its own
in-flight value in `export_quality_scrub` (§15 D274). `commit_run` commits every frame, which makes
the drag uncancellable, since `cancel_gesture` undoes a scrub by dropping a preview; `edit_valve`
*is* that preview, and `RenderOverrides` absorbs a `SetExports` as a no-op, so the number would not
move under the hand at all. The decision is `quality_step`, a free function, because it has been
wrong once in each direction.

**In the multi Transform panel, position and size describe the union box while rotation and skew
describe the layers.** That is not an inconsistency — it is the only reading each has. A selection
*has* one position and one size, the box the canvas handles already resize, so X/Y/W/H move and scale
that box and every member follows. A selection does not have one rotation, so those two fields are a
property editor over the set: the shared value, or the word `Mixed`, which is what every mixed value in
the inspector says (§15 D130).
**Dragging rotation or skew nudges relatively** — every layer moves by the same amount and the
differences between them survive, which
is the only thing worth having over a set that disagrees — while **typing sets absolutely**, landing
every layer on the number, which is how a `Mixed` set is brought into line. Both act about **each
layer's own origin**, so the layers spin where they stand; sweeping the whole arrangement about the
union centre stays the canvas rotate ring's job (above) and is deliberately not reachable from a
number, because a field reading "30°" cannot also mean "swing everything a third of a turn about a
point off to the left". Skew clamps to `tools::MAX_SKEW`, the canvas gesture's own limit.
**Scale is on the union side of that split** (§15 D311), and is the clearest case for it: a set has one
box and one size, so scaling it about the union's top-left has an obvious reading — the arrangement
scales as one thing and the gaps go with it — where "turn the set by 30°" has none.

**Its rows are the single-layer panel's rows, not a rearrangement of them** (§15 D134): X/Y, then W/H
with the chain button in the slot it occupies on one layer, then the Scale percentage under them when
the Scale tool is armed (§15 D312) — and, as in the single-layer card, every row from that one down is
identified by name through `inspector::transform_row` rather than by position (§15 D314) — then
rotation paired with skew, then the four
discrete transforms — a quarter turn each way and the two mirrors. It used to put the mirrors *beside*
rotation and leave skew alone underneath, with no quarter turns, deferring them until somebody decided
what a quarter turn should sweep over a set. They have an answer and it is the one the angle field beside
them already gives: `inspector::rotate_selection_quarter` turns each layer about **its own** origin in
one transaction, so the layers spin in place and the arrangement is untouched — which also means the
buttons are **live over a mixed rotation**, a relative edit needing no shared value to start from. The
row itself is the single-layer card's, drawn through `inspector::quarters_row` with the scope threaded
as data (§15 D737); only the tooltips and that one call differ. The
mirrors are the deliberate asymmetry, and it is the model's rather than this panel's: `build::flip`
mirrors the set about the union's centreline, so the layers swap sides as one arrangement instead of each
turning over in place. **The chain button is live** (§15 D347): it shows D50's all-or-nothing reading —
whole chain when every member is locked, broken otherwise — and a press drives the whole set to
`!all_locked` in one transaction rather than toggling each, since flipping a mixed selection member by
member leaves it mixed, which is the one outcome no press of it can be asking for. It was present and
inert until 2026-08-25, on the premise that a selection has no shared lock to show; the W and H fields
beside it now pair on that lock, and reporting a state without offering the toggle would be a door with
no handle on the inside — a typed number having no Shift to release the ratio with. The header's pivot
toggle **is** still dimmed and inert (`ui::FieldButton::Disabled`), for a reason that only sounds like
the same one: a selection has no shared transform origin, and the union centre it would rotate about has
nowhere to be stored. W takes X's width and H what is left, so the edge
down the middle of the card lands where the single-layer panel puts it. The six
fields skip building their transaction unless the control is actually mid-edit, which the
single-layer panel does not bother with and this one must: a W or H edit runs
`tools::resize_selection`, which recurses into the geometry of every descendant, and six of them are
laid out every frame whether or not the pointer is near them.
⚠️ **That test is a cost saver and was never a correctness guard, which is how two defects lived
under it** (§15 D519, D520). `inspector::interacting` contains `lost_focus()`, so it is true on the
one frame a bare click through a field leaves it — and on that frame X, Y, W and H called
`build::move_by_world` and `tools::resize_selection`, which emit one op per member unconditionally,
so the click committed N writes that each set a layer to what it already was. The four arms return an
empty transaction now, as the two angle arms beside them always have; W and H compare **after**
`tools::paired_size`, a locked pair being able to turn a zero on one axis into a real change on the
other. What stops the *commit* is the valve's engagement latch, which never arms for a field that was
only focused — and D428's `changes_nothing` stops it a third time at `commit_inner`. So a bare click
through one of these fields is suppressed by **three** independent doors, and a test of the click
alone pins none of them: it stays green with the latch removed, green with the guard removed, and
green with **both** removed at once, which is measured rather than reasoned (§15 D520 has the double
flip). Each of the two doors this panel owns has its own test; the click-through test is a symptom
guard over all three and evidence about none.

**The multi Appearance panel is opacity and — when the selection holds any rect — corner radius**,
each showing the word `Mixed` when the members disagree (§15 D130) and both **absolute**. "20% more opaque" is not
something anyone asks a slider for and would run past 100% on the first drag. Opacity is set on the
outermost members only and the radius on the whole subtree, for §5.7a's reason. The row ends in the
single-layer panel's **per-corner button, present and inert**, and the two fields use the single-layer
arithmetic that leaves room for it — without which both were wider than their single-layer twins and
every number moved on the way from one layer to two (§15 D134). ⚠️ **"Disagree" is a tolerance rather
than `==`**, `build::OPACITY_AGREEMENT` and `RADIUS_AGREEMENT` (§5.7a), read by
`inspector::shared_opacity_shown` and `shared_radius_shown` — the two readouts that actually ship, and
untested until §15 D607.

**The Fill and Stroke panels are one implementation, not two.** They take a `PaintScope` —
`Node(NodeId)` or `Selection` — because a single shape and a whole selection want the same panel, a
list of paints with rows to add, edit and remove, and differ only in who the list is written to. So a
selection gets add-and-remove for free and there is no second set of multi-selection paint panels to
drift from the first. Over a selection the list shown is `build::shared_fills` / `shared_strokes`,
which answer with a `PaintShown` — the `List` every target agrees on, or `Mixed`. Adding from an empty
panel gives every target that one fill. Writes for a shared list go through
`build::set_fills_all` / `set_strokes_all`, which give every target *exactly* the list, so what the
panel shows is true of all of them. Both are hidden outright when nothing in scope can take paint
(`build::any_paint_in`) — one question for both since a frame stopped answering it differently from
the stroke side, which is what `any_strokeable_in` was for (§15 D400). Rows ride
`PaintSlot::Selection(PaintTarget, usize)` — the index names one row of the shared list — node-less
like `Canvas` and `Guide` before them and borrowing the root as their slot anchor (§9.2), so the
swatch, hex field, alpha and picker are the ones every other paint row uses.

**A selection whose targets disagree draws one stand-in row** — where it used to draw the ordinary
empty state, which was the one thing that was not true of them (§15 D53). **Any** disagreement, one
unpainted layer among painted ones included; the empty state is now only for a selection where nothing
is painted at all (§5.7a). It is the same
`paint_row` every other paint gets, told only which of its two values it may not state, and its values
are decided **property by property** (`build::shared_over_fills` / `shared_over_strokes`): what the
paints agree on is shown as itself and only the rest reads as mixed, so two layers differing only in
how many fills they have still show the colour they share. Both those reads reach the row through
`OndinApp::shown_over_fills` / `shown_over_strokes`, which ask `build`'s question of `display_node`
rather than of the committed tree — the same split as `build::shared_corner_radius` /
`shared_radius_shown`, and what makes a
*drag* on this row work at all (§15 D53). **Those two are one walk and two names for it** —
`shown_over`, taking the list as an accessor — so the *"one unpainted layer included"* fold above
(`Spread::bare`) has a single home rather than two copies that happen to agree; the names stay
because each is where the argument about **which list** lives (§15 D738, D400, D144). ⚠️ **The split is in the *tree* and was never meant to be in
the question** (§15 D607): where the two copies came to disagree about the question itself — an `==`
in core against a tolerance in the panel — the tolerance is core's constant now.

**What the row *says* and what its controls *operate from* are separate**, and they have to be:
`inspector::Spread<T>` answers the first with `agreed()` and the second with `base()`, the first paint in
scope. So the chip shows the mixed dash and the hex says "Mixed" while the picker opens on a **real
colour out of the selection** and follows every click, and the stroke weight scrubs from a real number
even where no weight is agreed at all. `shown_brushes` is the one entry point the chip, the hex and the
picker read, and `Spread::map` takes the alpha off that same walk so the two cannot disagree about what
they found. One consequence: `base()` can be a **gradient**, so a mixed row takes the hex field whatever
kind its base brush is — printing "Linear" would be a claim about a set that is not all linear, where
"Mixed" is true of either (§15 D53 has the flicker and the dead picker this split fixed).

**And what the controls operate *from* may not be written back until the user has moved it** (§15
D465). The opacity field's "Mixed" is a `custom_formatter` painted over `base()`'s real alpha, so a
click that focused the field and an `Enter` that left it committed that one paint's number onto every
other — nothing downstream could refuse it, since over a disagreeing set the write genuinely changes
something. A hazy field writes only where its value differs from what it was seeded with. The hex
field beside it needs no such guard **for the word**, and never did, because *its* "Mixed" is the
buffer's own text and `parse_hex` rejects it: a word drawn by a formatter is not a value the code can
refuse. ⚠️ **It needed the same guard for the opposite state** (§15 D517). Over an *agreeing* row it
committed on every `lost_focus()` with nothing compared, so a bare click quantised the colour to the
8 bits `hex_of` prints — anything the picker's HSV plane produced is off that lattice — and spent an
undo step doing it, `lost_focus()` being true on two consecutive frames and this field committing
straight to `commit_edit` rather than through `edit_valve` (§9.3), so D316's latch never reached it.
It compares the **bytes** now, `parse_hex(&text)` against `parse_hex(&hex_of(current))`, which is the
hazy rule's own shape arrived at from the other side; the mixed case still writes unconditionally,
there being no one colour to compare against over a set that disagrees.
⚠️ **The rule is not about the word *Mixed*, and the third instance is a field that never prints
it** (§15 D534). The **single-layer** Appearance panel's corner-radius field shows
`largest(corners)` when the four disagree — a plain number, so that a drag starts from the shape's
own scale — and handed that seed to `edit_valve` on a bare click, flattening three corners nobody
touched. Same guard, `shared.is_some() || r != seed`. So the family is **every field seeded from one
member of a disagreeing set**, single-layer panels included; what to ask of a numeric control is
where its value came from, not what it says.

Every control that can hold the word says **"Mixed"** — the hex, the opacity %, the stroke position and
weight — and only the 16px chip cannot, so that is the one dash on the row (`ui::Swatch::Mixed`; §15 D130
has the rule and why it is the word). Every
control on the row edits *one property* of every paint in scope through
`build::edit_fills_all` / `edit_strokes_all`, so the chip and the picker set the whole brush, the hex
sets RGB and keeps each paint's own alpha, and the % sets alpha and keeps each paint's own colour or
gradient. ⚠️ **Two controls one surface away were outside that rule until 2026-09-08** (§15 D540).
The picker's own hex field and its document-swatch grid also own a *colour* while the field beside
them owns the *number*, and both read the alpha off the stand-in brush and sent the whole brush
through the slot — so typing a hex over two layers at 100% and 40% brought both back at 100%. They
reach into each paint through `edit_paints_all` now. **The picker's plane and strips deliberately do
not**: a gradient chosen there is one the user asked every layer to have, and neither has a separate
opacity field beside it to own the number. What marks the family is the *control*, not the slot. Its eye reads whether **any** paint in scope is on rather than all of them, because with some
hidden and some not there is ink on the canvas and an eye already closed would describe a state the
artwork is not in. **The header's `+` stays and goes inert** (`ui::HeadAction::inert`, dimmed with the
reason in its tooltip): there is no list to add to, and both readings of an append are wrong —
appending to each target's own list changes nothing the panel can show, and replacing their lists is
the destruction this state exists to avoid — but a header control that comes and goes as the selection
changes is exactly what §15 D134 forbids, so it says so in place instead. The
row's `x` is therefore the only destructive control on
it, and deliberately so, since clearing every target is the way back to the empty state and a live `+`.
Group Colors below is still the half that keeps the layers different. The stand-in rides
`PaintSlot::SelectionAll(PaintTarget)` — every paint of every target at once, node-less like the rest
(§9.2) — and that slot stops existing the moment a write brings the targets into agreement, so
`write_slot` and `valve_slot` call `retarget_mixed_paint` to move the picker and the hex buffer onto
`Selection(target, 0)`. Without it the picker finds nothing to edit and shuts in the user's hand on the
first click, which is `retarget_group_color`'s failure reached from the other side.

**`stroke_properties`
comes along with the scope**: width, join, cap, dash, mitre limit and alignment work over a selection
with no extra machinery, because the scope carries a whole `Vec<Stroke>`. Three ask a sharper question,
and ask it the same way. Alignment is offered only when **every** target has a closed outline, since
one open path among them would be drawing centred while the field claimed otherwise; the **sides**
control only when every target is a rect, since one ellipse among them would be drawing its whole
outline while the field claimed an edge; and **join** only when every target has a corner to shape,
since Miter, Round and Bevel are the same drawing on an ellipse or a line
(`geometry::stroke_align_applies` / `stroke_sides_apply` / `stroke_join_applies`, §5.3).
`inspector::stroke_rule(scope, applies)` is that question spelled once and asked three times, differing
in nothing but the predicate — three copies of its selection arm was three places for it to drift.

**A mixed stroke unit has a second row of its own** (`mixed_stroke_properties`), laid out **exactly** as
the per-stroke row is — the same `inspector::paint_unit` places both, which is what stops them drifting
a second time (§15 D196) — because a stroke has more than a colour to agree about: position and weight, then
the two buttons the per-stroke row ends in. **The position dropdown itself is one function for both
rows** (`inspector::align_combo`, its width `align_combo_width`), which is the second thing holding
them in step and was ~50 lines re-typed until §15 D739. The
position dropdown shows "Mixed" as its selected text but **never lists it as an option** — it is a
report, not a value, so offering it would be offering a no-op — and lights no cell while the strokes
disagree, for `ui::segment_mixed`'s reason. Both readings fall out of one `Option<StrokeAlign>`: the
disagreement is `None`, so *"nothing is lit"* is `shown == Some(a)` being false for every `a` rather
than a second flag beside a value. The weight says "Mixed" too, and is **absolute**, starting
from 0 when they disagree, `inspector_multi_appearance`'s rule for exactly this shape of field; it writes
through
`set_stroke_weight` so a stroke carrying per-side widths is flattened onto the new master value rather
than left drawing something the field does not say. The dash/cap/join popup and the per-side selector
are **present and inert** (`ui::FieldButton::Disabled`), each saying in its tooltip that it wants one
stroke rather than a selection's worth: neither has a mixed reading worth showing — a dash pattern is a
list of numbers and a `Custom` side set is four more — and both are keyed by list index with no index
here to key them by, which is an argument for switching them off and not for taking them away. Dropping
them widened the two fields beside them, so clicking a second layer slid every number in the row
sideways (§15 D134). The
way to the rest is to bring the strokes into line first, or to edit one layer.

**A paint row is a list row: it carries a grip and an eye as well as its colour.** Which paint applies
first is a real question — two translucent fills stack differently either way round, and so do an
inside and an outside stroke (§6.3) — so the order is editable by dragging the grip, and the eye
toggles `Fill::visible` / `Stroke::visible` (eye / eye-slash, the row at `HIDDEN_OPACITY` while
hidden — **60%, not the design's 70%**, set by eye against the real panel once there were rows to
compare: at 70% a hidden row was near enough a live one that a list of three took a moment to read,
and the swatch keeps its full strength either way, below, so the extra 10% costs nothing that
matters). Both belong
to a *list*: `RowCtx::grip` is `Option<(PaintList, usize)>` and holding one is what earns the pair,
which is why the canvas ground, a guide's colour and a decoration pass `None` — none of them is one of
an ordered stack — and so does a Group Colors row, which is a census entry rather
than a place in an order. A frame's ground was the one *node* paint on that list and is not one any
more: it is fill 0 of a real list, so it carries both (§15 D400). **A list of one gets both anyway.** `RowCtx::reorderable` is the separate
question of whether the grip actually drags, and `ui::grip(ui, enabled, row_h)` answers it by not
sensing at all and dropping the "Drag to reorder" tooltip that would otherwise be
a lie — while **drawing the identical glyph**. A grip that dimmed or vanished on a one-row list would
make the row jump about as paints are added and removed, and would spend a visual distinction on a
state where nothing is being withheld: there is simply nowhere to move. The eye is unconditional for a
plainer reason: hiding the only fill is an ordinary thing. **The grab band is the whole left end of the
field** — `row_h` tall and reaching back through the field's own `ui::FIELD_PAD_X` inset to its
hairline — because six dots 11×20 is a small thing to catch and everything left of them is empty
ground. It stops at the glyph's right edge and does **not** take the 9pt gap before the colour chip:
that gap is the chip's approach, and swallowing it would trade a grip that is hard to grab for a swatch
that is hard to click, which is the worse half of the bargain (§15 D63). **The swatch is deliberately painted at
full opacity inside the dimmed scope**, in a nested `set_opacity(1.0)`: `Ui::multiply_opacity` fades
everything drawn under it, and `ui::swatch` rounds its corners by painting the leftover slivers in the
*ground* colour (`mask_corners`), so a faded mask goes translucent, the chip shows through it and the
square corners partly reappear — the "four visible notches" artifact `mask_corners` exists to prevent,
arriving by a new route and reading as a tessellation bug (§15 D57).
`a_dimmed_row_fades_everything_but_the_swatch` pins it as an A/B, because "the mask is opaque" would
also pass if the dim were doing nothing at all.

**A stroke is a multi-row unit and reorders as one.** The panel used to be one paint list over a single
row of properties that edited `strokes[0]`, which made a second stroke a colour with nobody's width;
each stroke now owns a colour row and, beneath it, position + weight + an options button + a sides
button (`1.2fr 1fr 28px 28px` — it was `1.35fr 1fr 28px` against one button, and the second one took
the difference), with dash, cap, join and the mitre limit in a popup behind the options button because
they are the properties nobody touches. Its sides rows come below that again when they are showing, so
a stroke is two, three or five rows tall. **`inspector::paint_unit` owns the pitch of that unit for both
the per-stroke loop and the mixed branch**: `item_spacing.y` is zero inside it and both gaps are
allocated, so the two rows sit one `ui::CARD_ROW_GAP` apart — an image fill's two lines exactly — and
one stroke sits **two** of them from the next, its own trailing gap plus the card's, which is what makes
the pair read as a group. The last entry gets no trailing gap, so the card's bottom margin is every
other card's. **The sides rows sit inside that zero**, so `stroke_sides_row` states `ui::CARD_ROW_GAP`
for itself exactly as `paint_row` does rather than inheriting nothing — one pitch inside a card, which
also makes an expanded stroke taller than it was before the unit existed (§15 D196). ⚠️ **Stating it on
a scope is not enough, and it was all that was there.** A scope's `item_spacing` goes between *its own*
items; what comes before the first of them is the parent's, and the parent's is that zero. So the sides
combo sat flush against the align/width line above it, and the two rows of per-side widths — which are
drawn *outside* that scope, in the same `paint_unit` closure — sat flush against the combo and against
each other. Three joins, one scope's worth of pitch, and the fix is two explicit `add_space` calls plus
a second scope: reported as "the per-side controls have no vertical spacing" (§15 D386). That is
also why a drop cannot be resolved by dividing by a row pitch: `paint::Slots` records the span each
display slot was **actually laid out** at and answers which gap a pointer is in — a span that now
includes the trailing gap for every entry but the last, which shifts the drop bands by half of one. The rest of the gesture is `paint::PaintDrag` (the carried index, where it
lands, and the slots from the frame before, dropped when the anchor node stops being what the panel is
showing), `paint::display_order`, `paint::landing` and `paint::reordered` — spelled once because two
lists need it and removing the carried item shifts
everything after it down. `paint::reordered_index` and `paint::removed_index` are that same off-by-one
read the other way round — where did the paint at this index *go* — and exist for the index-keyed chrome
rather than for the list (below). `PaintList` moved from `inspector.rs` to `paint.rs` to sit with them (§9.2).
Writes go through `write_fill_list`, which carries whole `Fill`s: the brush-only `write_fills` it
replaced could not round-trip visibility or order, and the panel was the only caller either ever had.
It and its stroke twin are one generic `write_paint_list` since §15 D637 — the two were eleven lines
apart in four tokens, and the argument above is *stronger* on the stroke side, which has `width`,
`sides`, `dashes`, `align`, `cap` and `join` for a brush list to lose as well.
None of those reorder pieces is about paint but the module it lives in: they are list-generic. That is
a fact about the code and no longer a plan — **the layers tree will not be taking the same treatment**,
and §15 D306 has the three reasons, chief among them that a gap between rows can express an index but
never which list it is in nor a drop *inside* a container.

**The reorder is live: the rows change places under the pointer.** `OndinApp::paint_order` runs
*before* the rows are drawn and returns the model indices to draw them in, so the list on screen during
the gesture is already the result of dropping — there is no insertion line, and so nothing that can be
hidden behind the row carrying it. `inspector::carried_unit` still lifts the carried entry into an
`Order::Tooltip` layer and translates that layer's shapes — egui's own `dnd_drag_source` recipe — so
the visuals move and the layout does not, which is what makes the gap the entry leaves *be* where it
lands. For a stroke the travelling unit is every one of its rows, and the options popup closes when a
drag starts. §15 D61 has the three things a live reorder needs — slot geometry stable enough to reuse from
the frame before, a landing that is a pure function of the pointer, and widget ids that follow the
paint rather than the slot — and D59 why the untouched layout is load-bearing rather than cosmetic, and
what it costs the grip's `Response`.

**The weight scrubs in whole units and types in any number** — `ui::Scrub::whole(0.5)`, the rule §9.2
now states once for every scrubbable field, replacing the `width.round()` this one and the four per-side
widths each carried at their own call site (§15 D75). A weight is almost always an integer, and scrubbing
one through 1.7000000000000002 puts a value nobody asked for into the saved file — but a hairline is a
real thing to want and the field is the only way to ask for one.
`ui::MAX_STROKE_WIDTH` (10 000) is the ceiling on it, on the four per-side widths and on the dash
lengths and spacings — a cap on the *field* and not on the model, since past a few thousand units the
number has stopped describing a stroke (§15 D73).

**The weight is the master, and editing it re-broadcasts.** It and a `Custom` set of per-side widths
describe the same quantity, so when they disagree one of them has to win, and it is this one:
`inspector::set_stroke_weight` writes the new weight to all four sides rather than leaving a number the
shape draws nowhere. This is the field that says how heavy the stroke is, the per-side row is an override
*of* it, and "set a weight, then customise" is the order the two are used in. A side sitting at 0 is
flattened with the rest — "no stroke here" is a per-side statement and "everything is this heavy now" is
exactly the instruction that overrides it, where sparing the zeroes would make this a partial
re-broadcast and so a third rule nobody asked for. The named single sides carry no widths of their own,
so there is nothing to re-broadcast and the variant is left alone. A free function rather than a closure
at the field, so the rule can be pinned:
`inspector::polish_tests::editing_the_weight_re_broadcasts_it_to_every_side`.

The position dropdown beside it takes its height
through `interact_size.y` / `button_padding.y`, since `ComboBox::width` is the only dimension a combo
