accepts — and it wants the full 28 rather than a
`field_row`'s content box, for the reason §15 D45 now records. Every scrubbable number on a stroke —
the weight, the four per-side widths, the dash lengths, the mitre angle — goes through
`inspector::stroke_valve` and so through the edit valve (§9.3), because a drag has to preview every
frame and what the release commits has to be the transaction it previewed; `strokes_tx` is the one
place the write fans out to a node or to every target in the selection, and it returns an **empty**
transaction when the list already says this, since the valve commits on `lost_focus` too and seven
fields tabbed through would otherwise be seven undo steps.

**The sides selector is rows in the card, not a popover** — deliberately unlike the dash/cap/join menu
directly above it, and the two reasons are one reason from either side. It carries *values* (the four
per-side widths), so it has to be readable beside the weight it overrides; and two strokes with sides
showing are two sets of rows one above the other, where two `Area`s would occlude each other. Being
drawn inside the unit the grip carries also means it travels with a reordering drag for free. The row
is **shown when it is open and at no other time** — `sides_apply && stroke_sides_open.contains(&index)`
— and the button **opens and closes it without ever touching the stroke**. It briefly did both, on the
reasoning that a control carrying a value the user set must not be hideable; with only two button states
that forces a choice between a lit button that cannot close its own row and a collapse that resets the
stroke to `All`, and `ui::FieldButton::Set` is the third state that avoids both (§15 D72). So
`OndinApp::stroke_sides_open` is no longer *pure* chrome — losing it collapses a row with a value in it,
which the button's accent border still declares. "All sides" is in the dropdown as well — the design
named five entries and left the button to imply the sixth, and the way back to the closed outline should
not be "guess that the toggle above undoes it". `inspector::forget_stroke_chrome` drops the
three index-keyed pieces of chrome together — the options popup, the open sides rows and the dash text
buffer — and is now for a **change of subject** only. It can close a panel and it cannot lose a
*setting*, which is what makes it safe to call bluntly. **A reorder and a removal renumber the list
rather than replacing it, so the chrome is renumbered with them**:
`inspector::remap_paint_indices(anchor, list, map)` carries the popup, the sides rows, the dash buffer,
the detached picker and the hex buffer over `paint::reordered_index` / `paint::removed_index`, and each
follows the paint it was opened on. A new subject is the one case with nowhere to follow *to* — index 1
of another layer's list is not a renumbering of anything — which is what the blunt call is left for
(§15 D132).

**The dash/cap/join popover is four states, not three segmented controls** (272px at 11px padding — `app::POPOVER_W`, up
from 210): which numbers a pattern needs depends on what kind of pattern it is — a dot needs one, a
dash two, a custom list a list — so it shows the fields of the mode it is in and nothing else, with cap
and join common to all four because they describe the ends and corners of ink however the ink is broken
up. The mode comes from `Stroke::dash_style()` and nothing else (§5.3), and `pattern_for` carries the
numbers across a switch so Dotted → Dashed → Dotted comes back where it started; only a mode with
nothing to inherit falls back to multiples of the stroke width, which is the scale a pattern is legible
at. Cap is a **named combo — "Straight / Rounded / Extended"** — rather than the segmented line samples
it was: the difference between a butt and a square cap is one width of ink at each end, which no
thumbnail at this size can show, and `Butt`/`Round`/`Square` are a rasterizer's words rather than a
designer's (`cap_label`, beside `join_label` and `align_label`). `dash_sample` and `cap_sample` are
deleted with them. The custom list is a comma-separated text field, **buffered and applied on defocus**
like the paint rows' hex field and for the same reason — typing `5, 10` passes through `5`, which is a real and different
pattern — and an unparseable list, an all-zero one or a single number leaves the model alone rather
than clearing it, because a typo must not silently turn the stroke solid. ⚠️ **It also writes only
when the text differs from what the field would *print* for the value it holds** (§15 D565). It used
to write on any parseable defocus, including the string it had printed itself, and the round trip is
lossy — `dash_list_text` drops a fractional part within `1e-9` of zero, so an SVG `stroke-dasharray`
of `5.0000000001` was silently rewritten to `5` by opening the popover and closing it. Comparing the
*parsed* lists cannot catch that, since they genuinely differ; comparing the strings asks the only
question that means anything, and the *undo-step* half of the same complaint is
`Transaction::changes_nothing`'s (§15 D428), which absorbs a retyping that differs only in spacing. The mitre angle appears only
under Miter, where it is the only join with a spike to limit — **and only where a join means anything at
all**, because it means something only under both. `Miter` is the *default* join, so an ellipse whose
stroke had never been touched satisfied the value test and showed the field: dimmed with the row above
it, but present, and a dimmed field reads as a control that could be used rather than one that cannot
exist. It is gated on `joins && join == Miter` now; the row above it stays and its tooltip still says
why. The **Join row dims outright where the
kind has no corner to shape** — `Ui::disable`, which blocks the interaction and fades the painter in one
call, because `segmented` paints its cells straight onto `ui.painter()` and a flag threaded through it
would have dimmed nothing. And the popover **stays open when a cap is chosen**: the combo's list is its
own `Area` below it, so the dismiss asks whether the click landed on a layer floating above the page
rather than whether it landed inside the popover's own rect (§15 D74).

**Group Colors lists every distinct solid colour in scope as its own editable row**, and
editing one recolours every use of that colour — every fill and every stroke — in one
transaction. **Scope is the selection, except that a single selected container contributes its
children rather than itself** (`group_color_scope`, §15 D401): a container is the box the question is
asked about, so a selected frame's own fills are the Fill card's business and this card reports what
is inside it. ⚠️ **One function because four readers take it** — the listing, the two edits and
`group_color_shown` — since narrowing the listing alone gives a row that says `1 match` and recolours
two layers. Each row rides `PaintSlot::GroupColor([u8; 4])`, keyed by the **committed** colour,
which is what keeps its transaction well defined for the whole of a drag; the moment the edit
commits, that key names a colour the document no longer holds, so the row and the picker are retargeted
onto the colour it became. Without that the picker finds nothing to edit on the next frame
and closes itself in the user's hand. **Both slot verbs do it, through the one helper**
(`inspector::retarget_after`, §15 D580): this said *`valve_slot`* alone until 2026-09-08 and the code
agreed with it, which made a **click** on the hue strip over one of these rows shut the picker where a
*drag* on the same strip did not — `pointer_slot` routes the click to `write_slot` and the drag to
`valve_slot`, so a retarget in one of the two covers one door of two. `group_color_shown` reads the **committed** document to find
where the colour lives and the override to see what it has become, so the swatch follows a live drag
while the key stays fixed. Both new slots are orphaned by the *selection* emptying rather than by any
one node leaving it, which is what lets layers be added to the set while the picker is up.

**A Group Colors row ends in a layer count and a reticle that selects them**, where a fill or stroke
row ends in an opacity and a remove cross. Neither of those has a meaning on a census entry: there is
no single paint to fade — the row stands for every fill and every stroke carrying the colour, a
frame's own ground among them as a fill like any other (§15 D400), each with its own alpha — and
nothing for "remove a colour that is present in the artwork" to do. So
`RowCtx` gained `census: Option<usize>` and `RowOut` gained `select: bool`, and the count is
`ColorUse::nodes.len()` while `uses` still counts paint slots. **The two numbers differ, and that is
the point**: a shape whose fill and stroke are the same colour is two uses and one layer, and the
number beside the button and the selection the button makes come from the same field so they cannot
disagree (§15 D71 has what the button does to the selection, and why).
🚨 **They can disagree in exactly one way now, deliberately, and the message is what carries it**
(§15 D748). The reticle is the fourth door that selects a *set the user described*, so it goes
through `OndinApp::may_select_in_bulk` and **leaves locked layers out** — *"Selected 2 of 3 layers
with this colour — 1 locked"*. The **count is not narrowed**: it is still `ColorUse::nodes`, the
layers carrying the colour, which is a fact about the document rather than a claim about what a click
will take, and making the two agree that way would answer *"where is this colour"* with a lie. (Nor
is it `uses` — the paragraph above is untouched.) All-locked changes nothing at all, not even the
selection.

**The panel lists gradients too, under the solids, and they edit exactly as the colours do.**
`build::gradients_in` (§5.7a) is the second half of the census, and every part of a row works for a ramp:
the count and the reticle answer "is this in here, and where", and the chip opens the picker. What differs
is the key. A colour row rides the value (`GroupColor([u8; 4])`); a gradient will not fit in a `Copy + Eq`
slot, so its row rides `PaintSlot::GroupGradient(build::PaintAt)` — the **first place** the census found
it, which is stable only because the census walk orders its roots (§5.7a, §15 D646: while it did not,
the same gradient in the same document keyed a different slot depending on the order the layers were
clicked) — and the edit is still by value: `slot_transaction` reads the brush back from that place in the
**committed** document and `build::repaint` changes every use of it. Committed rather than previewed,
because mid-drag the preview already holds the new gradient, so a `from` read through it would be the brush
the drag is replacing *with*. The picker's kind tabs still work here — a gradient row can be turned into a
solid, and whatever it becomes, the row's key still names the place (§15 D135, which also has why a
location key needs no retargeting where a value key does). **Under the solids rather than interleaved**,
because both lists are most-used first and merging them would order a gradient against a colour by a count
that means the same thing but reads differently.

**A group is organisation; a frame is a thing, and the inspector splits them on exactly that.** A
single selected **Group** gets the Fill and Stroke panels in `PaintScope::Selection` — the same
panels over the same targets a multi-selection gets — because a group has no paint of its own and
selecting it is the same act as selecting its contents as far as colour goes. A single selected
**Frame** keeps its own single-node inspector — `PaintScope::Node`, its Fill and Stroke panels written
to the frame itself (§15 D397, D400) — and gains only Group
Colors: its paint is its own, a second panel called Fill meaning "everything inside" beside it
is two different fills in one inspector, and Group Colors is the only way to reach the contents
without picking them apart. Both containers get Group Colors for that last reason. ⚠️ **The code did
not implement that sentence until 2026-09-01** — the census walked the subtree *from* the frame, so
the frame's own paint was in its own census, which was invisible while a frame's ground was one swatch
in one card and plain the moment D400 put the same swatch in the card directly above (§15 D401).

#### The Type panel and the typography popup (`panels/typography.rs`)

**The panel is what a designer reaches for every minute; the popup is strictly overflow.** The card
carries the family, the variant, the size, line height, letter spacing, and both alignments — four
rows. Everything else lives behind one sliders button in three tabs.

**No control appears in both places.** A duplicated control has to show "mixed" twice, which is two
chances to disagree, and it makes "which of these is the real setting" answerable only by trying it.
That is also why **horizontal *and* vertical alignment are inline and neither is in the Box or
Paragraph tab**: they are the controls a hand goes to without thinking, and moving either into a
popover would put a daily control two clicks away to make room for ones consulted monthly.

**The alignment row sits on the column grid of the paired field rows above it**, not on a module of its
own: the four-cell track is exactly `half`, so its right edge lands on the first field's; the three-cell
track takes what is left after the popover button, so it starts on the second field's left edge and the
button ends on the margin. Two passes got this wrong in opposite directions — first the vertical set
pinned at 22 a cell against a horizontal set taking the remainder (20 against 37), then both pinned at
the design's 28, which made the cells equal and put the tracks *off* the grid by 2 and 3 points.

Those two goals do not both fit — four cells across a half-card and three across the rest is not an
equal division at any card width — and **the grid wins**, because the row is read against the two rows
of paired fields directly above it: a 2pt step in a column edge is visible where a 1pt difference
between the two tracks' cell widths is not. What survives of the module is a tolerance, and the test
holds the row to both: the column edges exactly, the cells within a point of the 28pt button.

**The tabs are scopes, labelled with the scope word** — Character, Paragraph, Box, opening on
Character — because the label is what tells the user what a change will hit when the selection is
partial. There were four, and the fourth was `Font`: the axes, the `opsz` mode, the OpenType feature
list and the language, split off on the grounds that they are *generated from the family* rather than
fixed. That is a fact about how they are built and not about what they do — every one of them is
character-scoped — so the strip named three scopes and one implementation detail, and someone looking
for the weight axis had two character tabs to choose between. Folded back in, and the generated
sections sit at the *bottom* of the Character tab so that changing family does not move the controls
above them. Three cells of an inner 250px is also what retired the abbreviations (`Char`/`Para`/`Block`)
and the line of hint text that had to sit under them explaining what they meant.

**The Character tab reads top to bottom as fixed-then-generated**: Case, Decoration, Baseline & word
spacing, then Optical size, Language, Axes, OpenType.

⚠️ **A control whose list offers names shows a name when it is closed**, which sounds like nothing and
was false for *Language* until 2026-09-09 (§15 D704): `LANGUAGES` is a `(tag, name)` table, the open
list used the name and the closed field used the stored locale verbatim, so picking *German* left a
field reading `de`. **A locale the table does not offer falls back to the tag and not to *None***,
because a document can carry one — an imported `xml:lang`, or a file written against a longer list —
and that is a real setting, not an absent one. The tag is a wire value and this is the only place the
panel ever showed one.

**The OpenType list is curated, and what it leaves out is why it is readable.** A face's `GSUB`/`GPOS`
offers `aalt`, `ccmp`, `locl`, `mark`, `mkmk`, `numr` and `dnom` beside its stylistic sets, and every one
of those is required, applied per script by the shaper, or applied as a corollary of another feature — a
switch for one does not offer a choice, it offers a way to mis-shape text. The registry says so itself,
per tag, in its *UI suggestion* text, so that is the authority the panel's `REGISTRY` carries rather
than a judgement of ours; *Show all features* is the way to the rest — and *Show fewer features* is
offered unconditionally while the list is expanded, a mode nobody can leave being worse than a control
nobody needs (§15 D193) — and nothing in the model changes either way, since `CharAttr::Features` still
carries any tag. ⚠️ **The collapsed offer counts the rows a click would actually add**, which means
**both** filters and not just the curation (§15 D691): the list above it is also narrowed by the search
field, so a count taken before that field is drawn offered *"Show all features (n more)"* against a
needle that excluded every one of the n, and the click added nothing. One search predicate, written
once and asked by the row loop and by the count. Each row is named — the registry's friendly name, or the font's own for the two ranges
a font may define — and says what it does on hover, where the four-letter tag also now lives (§15 D157).
**What the list can show at all is bounded by the file**, and a web font's file is a subset: the same
family offers a fraction of the features an installed copy does (§15 D192).

**One row in that list is not a switch.** A `cvXX` the font declares more than one named value for is a
1..n choice by the registry's own definition, so it keeps its name on a row of the same size and left
edge as its neighbours and draws a full-width dropdown under it — set closer to its own name than to
the rows either side, so two lines read as one row — with *Off* as the first item rather than
a switch beside it, since `FeatureSetting::value` is one number for both questions (§15 D157).

**One decoration, not two, though the model holds both.** `TextStyle` carries an underline and a
strikethrough independently and the renderer draws whichever are set; the control is a three-cell track
— none, underline, strikethrough — and picking one clears the other. A line under *and* through the
same run is a mistake far more often than a request, and the pair cost two toggles, two collapsible
blocks of four controls each, and a reader who had to check both to know what was on. The tuning
(thickness, offset, style, colour) is carried across when the choice changes, so switching is a change
of which line rather than a reset of how it is drawn.

**The one control that is not carried across is skip-ink**, because it is the one the other kind cannot
use: the toggle shares the line-style row and is drawn for an underline only, absent rather than dimmed
on a strikethrough, with the dropdown taking the freed width back (§15 D357, §5.4). Its state *is*
carried in the model — the flag rides in the same `Decoration` the tuning does — so a run switched back
from strikethrough to underline resumes the setting it had. It is lit in its default state, against this
chrome's habit, because what the button reports is what the line is doing.

**A decoration's colour is a paint slot** — `PaintSlot::TextDecoration(DecorationSide)` — so the
swatch opens the detached picker exactly as every other swatch in the app does, over a row of the same
shape the paint lists use (chip, editable hex, opacity, reset). It is one of the six node-less slots
(§9.2) and rides one for their reason: the swatch, the picker and the hex field are all written against
a slot, so a decoration riding one gets the whole colour panel instead of a parallel copy of it.

**It is one of the two slots whose write is not a `Transaction`**, the other being the text's own colour
(§15 D154). A character attribute goes into a live editing session's own spans while one owns the range
(§9.3), so all three slot verbs divert these — the shared predicate is `PaintSlot::char_scoped` and the
single route is `write_char_slot`, which ends in `apply_char_attrs` / `char_valve` where the scope question
is already answered once. `slot_transaction` returns an empty transaction for them rather than
`unreachable!`: the cost of being wrong about a diversion is a panic in the user's hands.

The third verb, `preview_slot`, used to *decline* instead of diverting — which is why a decoration's
colour alone did not follow the pointer on the press frame. That was D129's gap and it closed when the
second character-scoped slot arrived and the three branches became one (D154); it still declines for a
live selection, where the route is the editor's spans rather than a render override.

Absence still means "the text's own", and the row draws that state with the *resolved* paint rather than
a placeholder grey — a grey chip would be a claim about a colour the panel does not know. The paint, not
a colour: `TypeSubject::text_paint` is the node's first visible fill whole, because that is what the
renderer gives an uncoloured decoration, so a gradient-filled node shows its **ramp** in the chip
(`text_ramp`) where flattening it to black claimed a flat underline the canvas was not drawing (§15
D150). `text_color` is the one-colour collapse the hex and the picker still need, and it is the first
stop. **Opening the picker adopts that colour first**, because the picker edits `Decoration::color` and
an inheriting decoration has nothing for it to point at; adopting the value already on screen means the
click changes what is *editable* and not what is drawn — and for a gradient that is the first stop too,
which is `write_char_slot`'s own collapse, so the row promises what the click produces.

**Reset slots are always drawn, dimmed when there is nothing to put back.** An axis row and the
decoration colour row both end in a 26×26 square that restores the font's own value. Drawing it only
when it applied — with the space still allocated, so the field beside it would not change width — left
an empty square at the end of the row, and an empty square at the end of a row reads as the row
stopping short, which is how it was reported. `FieldButton`'s third state does the work instead: the
ground and the glyph say "nothing to undo" while the geometry never moves.

**What makes a reset live is `TypeSubject::ragged`, not the value the control is showing** — and the
distinction is subtle enough to have been a bug. `mixed` is about what a control may *say*, and over a
whole node it is false by design however ragged the spans are, because a whole-node write flattens them:
`shown()` is displaying the value the next write will produce and is not lying. A reset asks a different
question — *is there anything here to put back* — and answering it from `shown()` reads one byte (byte 0
with the layer merely selected, the caret's left-hand byte in a session — `resolve_at`, §15 D589) and
calls it the node. Reported as a red underline colour whose reset button was dimmed and inert: the colour was
in a span that did not reach byte 0. The write was correct all along, which is why the test covers both
halves separately.

**The card scrolls when it has to.** With a variable font, a decoration showing its four controls and
`opsz` on Manual, the Character tab measures a little over 700pt — which is what folding the Font tab
in bought, and is taller than the popup's anchor leaves on a laptop. The body sits in a `ScrollArea`
capped at the window height less its margins, and the tab strip stays *outside* it: the strip is how
you leave a tab, and a tab you have scrolled to the bottom of is exactly where you need it. Invisible
whenever the card fits, which is every other tab and most fonts. **The `ScrollArea` is given an
explicit `max_rect`** rather than the room the `Area` has, or its height ratchets downwards and never
recovers — §15 D106.

**The popup's click-away dismissal now forgives three things**, and each misses in its own way: the
button that opened it (D82), an overlay above it for its own combo lists (D74), and the colour picker
*below* it in layer order, which a decoration's swatch opens. Without the third, the first click in
that picker closed the popup, which orphaned and closed the picker — the control was unusable in one
click. The picker is recognised by layer **identity** (`picker::layer_id`), not by rect: it draws after
the inspector, so its rect for this frame does not exist when the test runs.

**And a click that ends or cancels a gesture is not a click-away.** A scrub started in the popover is
finished — or right-click-cancelled — with the pointer wherever it has been dragged to, which is usually
out over the canvas, and that release read as a click on the page. Restricting the test to the primary
button was the first attempt and was not enough: the *cancel* is the right-click while the left button is
still held, and the release that follows is a primary event. So the fourth term asks about the gesture
(`dragged_id().is_some() || gesture_cancelled` — the latter is cleared at the *end* of the frame the
release arrives in, so it is still true when the test runs) rather than about which button ended it. The
stroke popover keeps the primary-button rule for the same underlying reason. **The one exemption from it
is gone with the menu it belonged to**: the inspector's three-dots *Guides* menu kept `any_click`, on the
grounds that it was a dropdown with nothing to scrub, and its two actions are icon buttons in the body of
the guide card now (§9.4's guide cards) — so every inspector popover reads the primary button and there
is nothing left to keep in step.

**"Clip content" is a `switch_row`, not an `egui::checkbox`.** It was the one boolean in the inspector
that egui styled rather than us — a tick in a square at egui's own metrics, beside rows of 28pt fields —
and it is now the same control the OpenType list is built from. A switch also reports its state through
two things at once, the knob's travel and the track's colour, where a tick reports through one.

**A section is separated from the next by 15, not the design's 10.** The mock draws each tab as its own
card of three or four sections; the real Character tab has seven, and at 10 against an in-section gap of
5 the ratio is 2:1 — not enough to group by, so the card read as one long list of controls. 3:1 groups.

**Where a character write goes is decided by one field**, `TypeSubject::range`:

- **A live editing session with a selection** — the range is that selection, every character control
  can read *mixed*, and the write goes into the session's own spans (`TextEdit::style_selection`),
  which previews itself and commits once when the session ends (§9.3: one editing session is one undo
  step). ⚠️ **A list-valued attribute needs the second door**, `TextEdit::style_selection_per_run`
  (§15 D752): `CharAttr::Features` and `CharAttr::Variations` each carry a whole list, so changing one
  tag means reading a list, editing it and writing it back — and `style_selection` writes one value
  over everything, which for a list is a **flatten**. The per-run form takes a closure over each run's
  own value; the boundaries are `Spans::runs_of`'s and the merge is the caller's. No drag valve there: the session *is* the preview, and a second one would be two previews of
  one edit. The canvas is fed from the editor by `canvas::preview_session` — the `SetText` every
  session-scoped *panel* write ends with, and one function rather than a copy per write site, since a
  copy that forgot one of `SetText`'s three fields would silently drop whichever the caller was not
  thinking about. (`text_mode_input`'s own keystroke preview still builds that transaction inline,
  behind its `changed` gate.) Two things follow for the *cancel* path, and both had to be built: the write lands in the
  editor rather than in a render override, so a right-click has no preview to drop and
  `app::InFlight::session_scrub` (§15 D785) is the only record of what the value was, wound back through
  `canvas::restyle_session_with` (§15 D168); and the session's own preview is exempt from every clear,
  a commit's and a cancel's alike, through `EditorSession::clear_gesture_preview` (§15 D109).
- **Anything else** — the range is the whole node, and the write sets the node's *default* **and drops
  that attribute's overrides**. Both halves, always: setting the default alone is how "make it all
  24pt" leaves a 16pt run behind.

**What a character control *shows* is decided by a second field, and it is not `range.start`**
(`TypeSubject::resolve_at`, §15 D589). Where the range disagrees with itself, `shown` resolves the
attribute at one byte — and resolving at `range.start` means **byte 0** for a bare caret, whose range
is the whole node by the rule above, while `mixed` is structurally `false` there and so says nothing.
The field named the value at the start of the text and the next keystroke produced something else:
measured on `"hello world"` with a 40pt run over the first five bytes and a node default of 16, the
caret at the end read 40 and typed 16. **A bare caret resolves at the byte to its *left***, because
that is what an insertion inherits — `Spans::edited` sends a span whose `end == at` and a span whose
`start == at` both to `at + inserted`, so typing joins the run that *ends* at the caret and never the
one that begins there — and at byte 0 there is no such run, so the answer is the node's defaults.
⚠️ **This is the readout only.** The write is the bullet above and is unchanged: a bare-caret
character write still sets the default and drops the overrides.

**A paragraph write has the same two targets and does not answer the question the same way**, which is
why the seven spannable paragraph controls read `TypeSubject::para_range` rather than `range`. The range
is the selection **snapped outward to hard breaks** (`text::paragraph_bounds`); **a bare caret is
partial here**, where for a character attribute it is not, because a caret has no characters to restyle
but is unambiguously inside one paragraph; and **any open session is partial, a select-all included**,
so the node's paragraph *defaults* are reachable only with the layer selected and no session running.
That last rule was built the other way first and reversed — §15 D164 has the hazard it walked into, and
the same one is still live in the character scope above. The rest of the Paragraph tab, and all of the
Box tab, has one target either way: `Alignment`, `Justify` and the base direction are one value per
`Layout` (§15 D77), and the two sections that edit them say so on hover (`WHOLE_LAYER`), because a
control that quietly ignores the selection reads as broken rather than as limited. Only one of the two is
always there: "Last line" is drawn only under `Justify`, so on any other alignment "Text direction" is
the section carrying that hover on its own.

**"Spacing & indent" is five controls in three rows**: the spacing and the first-line indent, the
26×26 hanging pair under them, then the two block indents `indent_start`/`indent_end`. The pair shows
mixed as **neither square lit** — there is no third square and a dash cannot be drawn on a glyph, so
"not one of the two" is what says the selection holds both, and a press then makes it uniform as a drag
on a mixed field does. The block indents are prefixed with `icon::ARROW_LINE_LEFT`/`ARROW_LINE_RIGHT`
rather than a third and fourth text glyph, so the two kinds of indent do not read as four states of one
control; which side each arrow's bar sits on *is* the margin its number is measured from (§15 D164).

Mixed is spelled **"Mixed"** — in a field's digits as much as in a text control — and drawn as a dash
only where the control has no room for the word: `ui::segment_mixed` in a segmented track, which raises
no cell and paints the dash in the middle, and `ui::Swatch::Mixed` on a 16px chip. Not blank, which reads
as a broken control, and not one of the several values, which reads as a claim the next drag would then
make true for all of them. **That is the app's rule and not just this panel's**, and the threshold is
size rather than value type — §15 D130 has how it came to be that way round.

⚠️ **This panel's *numeric fields* do not keep it, and the paragraph above named the two dashes as
though nothing else disagreed** (§15 D636; the sentence read *"this panel does not keep it"* until
§15 D752 gave the panel a control that does — `ui::switch_row_mixed` spells the word, in this same
card, so the departure is the numeric fields' and not the panel's).
`typography::mixed_text` replaces a `DragValue`'s digits with the dash at five call sites
— the Size field, the list *Level* field, `length_char_field`'s three character lengths,
`length_field`'s five paragraph ones, and since 2026-09-09 the variable-axis field — and the line
height field carries its own copy of the same formatter, while the inspector's numeric fields spell
the word. Whether a 74pt field behind a two-letter prefix is *"too small to hold five letters"* is
the size question D130 leaves to be asked; it has not been asked, and D636 widened the population by
one without answering it. **The rule stands as written until it is.**

**Three states on one field, twice.** Line height's suffix cycles `auto → % → px`, and a decoration's
thickness and offset cycle `Font → px → %` — because in both cases the third state is a *value* ("the
font decides") rather than a collapsed control, so it belongs beside the units rather than in a fourth
widget. `ui::Suffix` is the unit itself: its own dimmed, clickable widget rather than
`DragValue::suffix`, which renders the unit inside the number's text run in one colour — the same
reason `ui::Prefix` exists at the other end (D75).

⚠️ **Leaving that third state seeds what the font was deciding, and the thickness field seeded zero
until 2026-09-08** (§15 D570). Line height's `auto` seeds the shaped first line's own height (§15
D162); a decoration's thickness had no metric to seed from, so its `Font` face wrote `Px(0.0)` — and a
zero-height band is not a thin line, `render::scene::decoration_path` and `core::text::crossings` each
opening by refusing one, so one click on the chip erased the underline and left `0.00 px` on screen
with no number to guess back. `TextLayout::decoration_sizes` is that metric now, the first run's own
`(underline, strikethrough)` straight off `run.metrics()`, pre-clamp and pre-override. **The offset
field still seeds zero and that is deliberate**: its face metric is on the same call but carries
parley's sign where this field's is the opposite (§15 D151), and a band on the baseline is visible and
recoverable where no band at all is not. ⚠️ **The two cycles run the other way round from each other**,
so a fix carried across from line height without reading them produces the right number in the wrong
unit — at 20pt `Em(1.37)` is a 27px underline.

⚠️ **A `Length` field's px range is *derived* from its `%` range at the current font size, and nothing
in this panel states a px cap** (`typography::px_range_for`, §15 D425). `px = pct/100 × font_size` is
exactly what `ondin_core::Length::in_unit` computes, so a value legal at one end converts to a value
legal at the other **by construction** — which is the only arrangement under which clicking the unit
chip cannot change the number it converts. Before it there was one px cap in the file,
`MAX_LINE_HEIGHT_PX`, named for line height and used as the bound of all *nine* `Length` fields
including six that measure nothing like one: decoration thickness `Px(50)` at 16pt came back as 32px,
and letter spacing `Px(-100)` came back as −8px. If a px cap is ever wanted that is *not* the `%` cap
in the other unit, it is a second quantity and wants naming as one.

⚠️ **The *floor* is the caller's, not the shared function's** (§15 D546). `optional_length_field`
serves a decoration's thickness and its offset and had one symmetric range for both — chosen for the
offset, the signed one — so a thickness of `−5 px` was accepted, shown and saved. It takes a `signed`
flag now, and the model floors the thickness too (§5.4), because the panel is the door a hand-edited
file does not use. *A range shared by two fields is a claim that the two fields are the same kind of
quantity.*

⚠️ **Every `Length` field reports on a frame the value changed and again on the frame the drag ends,
and `optional_length_field` did not until 2026-09-15** (§15 D765). It reported on **every** frame it
held a value, idle ones included. The release half is the one that cannot be dropped — it is the
frame `edit_valve` commits on, and the one frame a changed-only field has nothing to say, since
`value_field` has already settled the number on every dragged frame (§15 D109). 🚨 **The doc arguing
the divergence cited `OndinApp::char_length`, a method that has never existed** — the function is
`length_char_field` — **and its link reference redirected the name to the `OndinApp` type, so
`cargo doc` resolved it**; *a citation that resolves to the wrong item is worse than one that
dangles.* ⚠️ **The two `char_valve` callers are not a third answer**: that function takes a
`CharAttr` rather than an `Option` and its own comment records D109 being caused by a guard in
exactly that position, so it is a different contract. **Four copies of this control, not three** —
`type_line_height_field` is the fourth, and unifying them is declined: about twelve parameters over
functions that genuinely differ, `type_line_height_field`'s `auto` face showing a *resolved px
value* where the others show a placeholder. ⚠️ **The three character `Length` fields also had no
hover text at all**, on `length_field`'s own argument for having one — *"the field is labelled by a
14pt glyph and nothing else"* — with two of them side by side in one row behind two icons. They have
one now.

**A clickable unit is a control inside the field, and is drawn as one.** It paints an 18pt rounded chip
that lights on hover and darkens under the press, sized to its own text where that is wider (`auto`,
`Font`), and it **hangs 4pt past the content box into the field's own padding** so its edge finishes 5pt
inside the hairline where the digits finish 9 — the design's `margin-right:-4px`. That gap is the whole
difference between a unit that belongs to the field and a label parked near it. Its own id and its own
rect: the field keeps the rest of the row, so there is one focus target for typing and two hover states
for the eye. It used to be a bare galley with a pointing-hand cursor — a thing you could click with no
sign that you could.

**Hover brightens the unit; it does not draw a ground behind it.** There was a chip, and the chip was
what made the two labels look unequal: `%` and `px` do not fill a galley box the same way — one has a
descender and the other does not, so measured against a field centre of 14.0 the first inks a centre of
14.5 and the second 16.5 — and a box drawn tightly around either put its ink visibly off the box's own
middle, which is the thing the eye then reads as needing to be centred. Removing the ground removes the
reference, which is also why the one-point optical lift it briefly carried is gone. The hit box stays
four points wider than the text on each side: two characters of 11pt type is a small thing to aim at, and
there is nothing else in that corner of the field to hit. **No pointing hand** — the chrome never sets
one, and the brightening text is the affordance.

**The unit's galley is laid out in `Color32::PLACEHOLDER`, and that is what makes the hover visible at
all.** `Painter::galley`'s colour argument is a *fallback*: the tessellator substitutes it only where a
section left that sentinel. Built with `.color(…)` baked in, a galley ignores it — so the hover state was
computed, handed over and silently dropped, and the ink never moved. Omitting the colour is not the fix
either: `into_galley` fills an unset colour with the style's own `text_color`, which came out
full-strength white at rest. `hovering_the_unit_changes_the_colour_it_is_actually_drawn_in` asserts the
sentinel *and* that the fallback differs between the two states, because either half alone passes while
the control is broken — the first version of that probe read `fallback_color` back and reported success.

**The unit's strip is allocated, not merely painted into**, and that is load-bearing rather than
tidiness: `field_frame` shrink-wraps its content, so a strip that was subtracted from the number's width
and then drawn over left the frame that much narrower than the size its caller asked for — a 130pt field
painting 110, its unit astride the border, and a row of two of them stopping 42pt short of the card.
One bug, three reported symptoms. §15 D105.

**Every gap inside a value field is measured by hand** — the prefix strip via `add_space`, the unit's
via its own width — so `item_spacing.x` is zeroed in the row. Left at the theme's, egui inserted one of
its own before the newly-allocated unit strip and the frame came out exactly that much too wide.

**The Box tab's *Sizing* strip is a second door's worth of behaviour, so its body is a method.**
`OndinApp::set_text_sizing(id, cell)` is what the segmented control calls and what the context menu's
three checkable rows call (`context-menus.md` §5.6, §15 D261) — §8's rule that a row and the control it
duplicates must be the same verb, which only holds while there is one verb to be. Three things live in
it that a second call site would otherwise have had to remember: the switch **adopts the shaped size**,
so changing mode does not move the text; it ends in `text_session_restyled`, so a live editor re-shapes
rather than drawing to the old width; and it measures the **preview** layout rather than the committed
one, because during a session the size to adopt is the one on screen and the committed size would snap
the box back to what it measured before the last keystroke. The menu reads its tick off the **display**
node for that same reason, so the state a row reports and the state the verb adopts are the same side of
the preview. A scale may still not change *which* of the three a layer is in (§5.6) — that is the user's
answer to "who decides this box" and only these two doors author it.

**Wrapping is a Box question, so the three wrap controls live in the Box tab**, as three stacked
segmented tracks rather than three dropdowns: every option is one or two words and there are eight
altogether, so a dropdown would hide seven of them behind a click each and say nothing about the
alternatives. **Word break and Long words dim under `NoWrap`** — that mode reaches parley as
`TextWrapMode(NoWrap)` and suppresses line breaking outright, so both are rules about breaks that
cannot happen. Dimmed and *not reset*, the same rule `stroke_rule` follows for Join, so a stored
`word_break` survives a trip through `NoWrap` and back; and the gate stops there, because hard breaks
still break under `NoWrap` and the paragraph spacing and indent controls must go on working.
`wrap_gate_tests` pins all three clauses — the two dead controls, the stored value surviving, and the
Wrap strip itself still answering a click, which is the control without which the other assertions
pass against a section nobody drew (§15 D804). A whole
row of dimmed cells reads as "this does not apply" where a dimmed dropdown just reads as broken.

**`ui::slider` is hand-painted, like `segmented` and `switch`.** The design specifies a 3pt rail, an 11pt
knob, the filled half in `ACCENT_600` and the knob in `ACCENT_100` with a soft shadow under it, and
`egui::Slider` derives all four from `Spacing` and `Visuals` in ways that cannot be reached without
restyling every slider in the process — it drew a chunky rail with a handle barely thicker than it, which
beside these fields read as a different control from a different app. Painting it also drops the text
box, the arrows and the drag handles, none of which the axis rows want: they carry their own numeric
field. The knob's centre travels `half..width − half` so it cannot hang off the rail, and the rail is
drawn full width underneath — a knob whose *edge* touched the end would read as a value short of the
maximum. It is **absolute**, unlike a `value_field`: a slider jumps to where it is pressed, because it
has a rail to point at.
⚠️ **`SLIDER_H` is the row and not the ink, and the shadow leaves it by exactly one point** (§15
D673). The shadow is a `half`-radius disc drawn one point lower, so a slider paints `SLIDER_H + 1`
into the `SLIDER_H` it allocates — measured at ppp 1.0 over a 120pt slider, row `120 × 11` and ink
`120 × 12`. The bleed is kept, a shadow outside the box being what a shadow is, and it lands in the
caller's row gap; what could not stand was the constant's own doc calling the knob the tallest thing
in the row. `a_sliders_shadow_leaves_the_row_by_exactly_one_point`
is the gate on how far, and asserts the other three sides are tight. ⚠️ **`SLIDER_H` is `pub` and
`slider` reserves it on its callers' behalf, which is not the same as *"what every caller
reserves"*** (§15 D766): **no production code outside `ui.rs` reads it**, and the stronger sentence
is the one somebody packs a row against.
⚠️ **`panels::picker::slider_track` was said to answer the same question the other way, and it
answers a different question** (§15 D766, ruling §15 D673). It allocates `TRACK_H + 6.0` and that
`+ 6.0` bounds its knob **vertically** — 7.0 of reach against a 7.5 half-row — while letting it hang
**7pt off each horizontal end, unclamped**; `ui::slider` bleeds 1pt below and **clamps travel** so
its knob cannot leave the rail. **They bound different axes**, so *"its knob is given room where
`ui::slider`'s overhangs"* — the sentence this replaces — is true of one axis and silent about the
one where the answers are reversed, and there was no *which is right* to rule on. ⚠️ **Nor were the
two constants ever one quantity**: `picker`'s is the **rail's** thickness, which is why it is
`TRACK_H` now, where this one is the **knob diameter** with `SLIDER_RAIL_H` under it — unifying the
values would have thickened the picker's two gradient strips, re-cornered them and left the knob
exactly where it was. The horizontal overhang fits because the card's `PAD` is 11, a fact about the
*card*; `the_alpha_knob_stays_inside_the_cards_padding_at_both_ends` is what says so, nothing in
`picker.rs` having asserted a slider dimension before it.

**`ui::switch_row` is the toggle list's row**, and the switch in it is *painted* rather than allocated:
a 26×16 switch at the end of a wide row is a small thing to hit, and a clickable switch inside a
clickable row is the trap `icon_button_padded` describes — the inner claimant wins the hit test
wherever it lies, so the row would be live everywhere except on the control. One claimant, the row. The
knob's travel and the track's colour both change, because either alone is a state that has to be
inspected rather than seen, which is the failure mode of a checkbox in a scrolling list; and the label
takes two tiers of contrast so a column of a dozen rows can be read as a column. The hover ground is
painted **wider than the row** rather than the row taking an inset, because the label has to line up
with the eyebrow above it and the segmented tracks around it — it borrows the card's padding, which is
empty either way. The label's size and its two tiers of ink are `ui::SWITCH_ROW_LABEL_PT` and
`ui::switch_row_ink` rather than literals inside the row, because the feature list's n-way `cvXX` row
paints its own name into the same column (§15 D157), and two literals is how the two come to differ by
half a point — which only ever shows up on screen.
**A row over a selection whose runs disagree says "Mixed" where the switch would be**
(`ui::switch_row_mixed`, §15 D752) — the word rather than a third knob position, which is D130's rule
and also the maintainer's picture of it: *"a three way switch would be visually weird (thumb in the
middle?)"*. It is the same `switch_row_inner` behind an `on: Option<bool>`, so the hover ground, the
row height, the ink tiers and the right margin cannot come apart between the two spellings; the word
is right-aligned to the margin the switch occupies, and the label takes the *off* tier, a range that
disagrees not being a range the feature is on for. ⚠️ **The row stays live and the tooltip says what
a click will do** — dim is a readout and not a disablement, clicking is how a mixed range is
resolved, and a row that shows no position has to mean something predictable from the row alone
(it turns the feature **on**).

#### The font picker (`fonts/preview.rs`, `panels/typography.rs`)

**Every row is set in the family it names.** Choosing a typeface is done by eye, so a column of names
all in the UI font is a list you have to click through to read. This is the one part of the picker
that is about the *drawing* rather than the speed — and it pays for the speed too, because drawing a
row asks for that family's regular upright, which is exactly the file applying the family needs.
Previewing is prefetching; by the time the user clicks, the bytes are already registered.

**A row's name is rasterized through `vello_cpu`, not through egui's fonts.** `Context::add_font`
looks like the obvious route and is a trap: it sets `fonts = None`, so egui rebuilds every font,
drops every cached galley and re-uploads the whole atlas — a stutter per row, or per batch at best,
plus a second copy of every font's bytes beside parley's. Instead `text::family_preview` shapes the
name and `render::rasterize_glyph_run` draws it into one small cached texture per family. Nothing
touches egui's atlas, and the preview goes through the *document's* shaping path, so the row shows
what the canvas will draw. The strips are white coverage **tinted at draw time**, so one image serves
the normal, hovered and selected colours and follows the theme rather than being baked against it.

**The preview declines rather than falling back.** An unregistered family shapes perfectly well —
parley substitutes Inter — so the tempting implementation draws a row reading "Bungee Shade" set in
Inter, about a typeface the user is choosing by eye. `family_preview` returns `None` unless the run
came from that family's own blob and no glyph is `.notdef`; the third case that catches is a symbol
font, whose Latin name would otherwise be a row of empty boxes. The caller then draws the name in the
UI font, which is honest about not knowing.

**A fourth reason to decline is the strip's own size, and the two axes are bounded differently on
purpose** (`preview::strip_px`, §15 D586). A **width** over `MAX_STRIP_PT` is *clipped* — the useful
part of a family name is its beginning — while a **height** over `MAX_STRIP_H_PT` is **refused**,
because a strip is one line and half of one is not a shorter name. ⚠️ **The height had no bound at
all until 2026-09-08**, and the input that reaches it is a font declaring a small `unitsPerEm` against
maximal `ascender`/`descender`: the spec allows 16, both metrics are `i16`, so a line-box ratio of
~2,048 is representable and 15 pt × 2,048 × ppp 2 is about 61,000 px — where `rasterize_glyph_run`'s
`as u16` wrapped and epaint asserted on the mismatch, on the UI thread, for one row. `MAX_STRIP_H_PT`
is six times `PREVIEW_PT`, five times the widest real ratio (Inter measures 1.21), so the bound is set
by what a *row* can sensibly show rather than by what would overflow — and well below the wrap the
same arithmetic is a 128 MB allocation that `FRAME_BUDGET` cannot catch, the progress guarantee
rasterizing a frame's first strip before it consults the budget at all. The decision is a free
function so a test can drive it, no font in the tree having such metrics (§15 D269's shape).

**And a pulsing dot at the row's right edge says the face is still on its way** (§15 D353). The
fallback above is honest and unreadable on its own: plenty of families resemble the UI font, and a
row whose download *failed* looks exactly like one still waiting. The dot is drawn on
`FontService::is_loading`, and its room (`LOADING_DOT_SLOT`) is reserved on **every** row, lit or
not — taking it only while loading reflows the name at the moment its face arrives, so a list
settling after a scroll twitches once per row. A pulse rather than a spinner because twenty can be
on screen during a scroll, a raised cosine so every dot starts at the trough (the clock is
wall-clock, not per-row, so a shape starting anywhere else has each row scroll in at a different
brightness), never fully dark or the list strobes, and `paint_loading_dot` asks for its own repaint
because this eframe is reactive and the animation would otherwise freeze between inputs.

**The list is virtualized, and that is not an optimization.** System fonts plus the Google catalog is
~1900 families; a widget per family cost about a second of layout, id hashing and glyph
rasterization every time the list opened, for the twenty rows a scroll area then showed.
`ScrollArea::show_rows` needs a fixed row height, which is why `FAMILY_ROW_H` is a constant and the
rows are drawn by hand rather than with `selectable_label`. The filter's match list is memoized
against the needle **and** the family list's revision, since the list grows under an open picker as
the catalog and the system scan land. Each of those arrivals wakes the UI thread itself (§5.4a); the
rows still in flight when a scroll stops otherwise keep the fallback font until the mouse moves
(§15 D110).

**This is the one popup in the app you are meant to click *into*, so it does not close on a click
inside itself.** egui's `ComboBox` default counts a click anywhere as a dismissal, which meant the
search field the list exists to be filtered by closed the list (§15 D194). This combo alone asks for
`CloseOnClickOutside` and then closes itself explicitly where a family row is picked, since with that
behaviour nothing else does; every other combo in the app is a plain list of rows and keeps the
default.

**Applying a family clears the layer's variable-axis settings and its OpenType features**, because
both are named by tag and a tag means something different in the next typeface — `wdth 75` on a family
with no width axis is silently nothing, and `ss01` is a different alternate everywhere — so carrying
them over is how a font swap comes out looking wrong in a way nothing on screen explains. **That is
right for a family *change* and destructive on a *re-pick***, and until 2026-09-07 clicking the row the
list already draws as selected cleared every axis and every feature and left an undo step behind
(§15 D467). `family_row` reports `clicked()` for any row and gates nothing — `selected` decides only
the ground it paints, the rows being drawn by hand for `show_rows` — so the decision is the call site's
and is spelled once, in `family_actually_changed`. **A re-pick over a *mixed* selection is still an
edit**: the family the row shows is one member's — the *Mixed* convention (§15 D130) — so picking it
is what makes the selection agree, and the clearing is right for every layer it moves.

**`%` is letter spacing's default unit and px is paragraph spacing's**, and the split is deliberate.
Tracking has to scale with size or a type token cannot carry it; paragraph spacing belongs to the
layout's spacing scale, so a 24px gap should stay 24px when the type is tuned.

**A gesture dragged into the canvas edge scrolls the view** (`canvas::autopan`). Moving a layer
somewhere off screen, marqueeing more than fits, drawing a shape bigger than the viewport or pulling a
guide across the document all used to run out of room, with no way through but to abandon the gesture,
scroll, and start again. Inside a 32pt band the view travels toward the pointer at up to 900 pt/s,
**quadratically** — the band is the only speed control there is, so the slow end has to be the long end
or nothing can be placed. Three things make it work, and each is a separate mistake if missed:

- **It runs before the input handlers.** Every gesture recomputes its world point from the live pointer
  each frame, so panning first means the drag advances *because the world under a still hand moved* —
  no gesture code knows auto-pan exists. Panning afterwards would scroll the view while the preview was
  computed against the previous camera, and the two would disagree by a frame's scroll.
- **It requests a repaint.** eframe here is reactive: hold the hand still at the edge and there are no
  pointer events, so without this the view scrolls only while the mouse is *also* moving, which is
  precisely when it is not needed.
- **The camera moves toward the pointer, not away.** `pan_pixels` takes the delta the *content* moves
  by, so passing the reach through unnegated makes the canvas flee whatever is being dragged at it.

`Drag::autopans` states the exemption as a **rule and not as a list of names** (§15 D760): `Pan`, whose
hand is already moving the view so the band's speed would add to it and run away; **every gesture that
turns about a fixed pivot**, which can always be finished where it started — its reachable set is a
circle about a centre already inside the box, bounded by the circumradius, and it does not grow with
pointer travel; and **`Guide`, because its band and its home are the same place.** ⚠️ **It read *"the
three exemptions"* and named `Rotate` alone until 2026-09-15, and the code had the same shape**:
`Drag::PointRotate` — the node tool's rotation of a point selection — auto-panned for months, 42.23px
measured, on precisely the argument written here for exempting `Rotate`, while its own doc cited
`Drag::Rotate` and established two of the three clauses. A count in this sentence is what let the
fourth turning gesture arrive outside it, so there is no count in it now. The ruler
bars are `rulers::THICKNESS` = 20pt against a 32pt band, so a gesture that starts on a bar — which every
new guide does — is inside the band before it begins, and the only way *out* of the bar is through the
remaining 12pt of it. Clicking a ruler therefore scrolled the view for as long as the button was held and
then left nothing behind, a press that never leaves the bar creating no guide. Suppressing the bar alone
was tried first and came back as "much less than before, but still happens" — it made the strip the second
cause instead of the first, which is what excluding the whole `Drag` kind answers.

**What that gives up is dragging a guide beyond the visible area in one gesture, and the Guide panel's
position field is the better answer to it anyway**: a number is a surer way to put a guide somewhere you
cannot see than a view that scrolls while you aim. Placing a guide is aiming at *artwork*, so scrolling
the artwork underneath was working against the gesture even where it fired legitimately.
`OndinApp::ruler_at` — the method the free `rulers::ruler_at` had always claimed to have and did not —
stays, with `guide_input` and `guide_at` as its callers: they were asking its two-part question by hand
(`rulers_on() && ruler_at(..).is_some()`), which stays right until one of them forgets the first half and
claims a press for a bar nobody can see (§15 D35's class of mismatch).

**Cancelling puts the view back.** `autopan_total` accumulates what the auto-scroll moved the camera by,
in world units, and `cancel_gesture` subtracts it — "leave no trace" has to include the view, or a
right-click leaves the user looking at blank page with the layer they were dragging somewhere off
screen. A running total rather than a camera snapshot, so a zoom or a wheel-pan made *during* the drag
is left alone: it was asked for, and only this feature's own scrolling is undone. **It is one drag's
total, so it is cleared at both ends of one drag**: `normal_mode_input` zeroes it on `drag_started()`
*and* on `drag_stopped()`, above the tool routing so the node, pen and image-edit families are still on
the path when it runs, and `finish_drag` keeps its own idempotent reset for the sentence that goes with
it — a completed gesture keeps the view where it scrolled to, the layer being there now. Without the
release half, a drag that *landed* leaves its scrolling in the accumulator for the next unrelated
cancel to spend (§15 D579).

**The same problem without a pointer: `reveal_selection`.** A held arrow key or a scrubbed X field walks
a layer off the screen with nothing at the canvas edge to notice, so the nudge action and the inspector's
X and Y scroll it back — by the *minimum* that shows it, and only once it has actually left. Centring on
every nudge would jump the view on a 1px tap. W, H, rotation, skew and the `Ctrl`+arrow size step
(§15 D346) deliberately do not: they change
what a layer *is* rather than where it is, and a box growing past the edge is a thing whose near side you
can still see. `reveal_axis` is the arithmetic, and its interesting case is a selection larger than the
viewport: that scrolls **not at all** when it overhangs both edges — it already fills the view, and
pulling one edge in would push the other out for the next nudge to undo.

**The layers tree scrolls on the same curve** (`ui::edge_scroll_speed`, shared with the canvas): a row
dragged into a 22pt band at either end of the tree scrolls it, so a reparent into something scrolled out
of sight is possible at all. Slower than the canvas (420 pt/s), because the target is one 20px row rather
than a region. `scroll_with_delta_animation` with `ScrollAnimation::none()`, since the pointer is the
clock and egui's default easing keeps gliding after the hand stops — overshooting the row being aimed at.
⚠️ **It lives in `app::layers_panel` and there is exactly one of it** (§15 D576). `layers_tree` had a
second, running every frame on the same band, and `scroll_with_delta_animation` *accumulates*: the pair
came to 960 pt/s at 60 Hz and 1500 at 120, only one of the two being `dt`-scaled, and the animation
being last-write-wins meant the second put back the easing the first had passed `none()` to remove.
Both doc comments claimed to be the only implementation. **A second autoscroller is not a second
opinion, it is a summand** — worth knowing before adding one anywhere a band is already read.

**Snap candidates re-cull as the view moves, deliberately.** `snapping()` reads the live viewport, so a
target can appear or vanish mid-gesture with nothing but the scroll causing it. The alternative —
snapshotting candidates when the gesture starts — means scrolling to a layer and then being unable to
snap to the thing now filling the screen. *Snap to what you can see* is the rule everywhere else in the
tool, and this keeps it under a moving view.

#### Booleans (`core::boolean`, `NodeKind::Boolean`, the identity card's second row)

**Non-destructive, like Figma's.** `NodeKind::Boolean { op }` is a container: its children keep their
transforms and geometry, stay selectable and editable, and the combined outline is *derived* — cached in
`Resolved` beside the shaped text layouts, invalidated children-first, because a boolean may contain a
boolean and moving one operand changes the shape of every boolean above it. It is the second thing that
layer derives rather than reads, and the parallel is exact rather than convenient: a boolean's outline is
no more a function of its own kind than a text layout is, so `geometry::local_path` cannot produce it and
returns `None` for it on purpose.

**Everything that needs "this shape's own path" therefore goes through a wrapper.**
`Resolved::local_path` is the canvas's and `svg::outline` the exporter's; each answers a boolean from the
derived outline and everything else from `geometry::local_path`. Both symptoms of asking the bare function
were silent — an aligned stroke exported *centred* because its clip was built from `None`, and a
fit-to-corners dash pattern measured an outline it never received (§15 D93). ⚠️ **The canvas half of
that sentence was an intention rather than a description until 2026-09-08** (§15 D563):
`Resolved::local_path`'s only caller was `Resolved::mask_path`, and the canvas's hover and key-layer
ring asked the bare function — so a boolean's ring was drawn as every operand's outline, three times
too wide on the finding's fixture, and no gate could say so, `dead_code` never firing on a `pub` item
in core. It has two callers now, `mask_path` and `canvas::stroke_outlines`, and the `match` beneath
the second carries a `Boolean` arm for the boolean whose outline is legitimately empty or abandoned
(§15 D239), which would otherwise fall through to the container arm and be drawn as its operands
again.

**Stroke alignment is granted to a boolean by kind, not by measurement.**
`geometry::stroke_align_applies` needs a closed outline to have an inside, and measuring one goes through
`local_path` — so a boolean read "not closed", the one answer its outline is never: `boolean::from_flo`
closes every subpath and normalizes each one's winding against its nesting depth, which is precisely what
makes an inside well defined even where the shape has holes. Measured, it cost the alignment dropdown on a
boolean's Stroke panel *and* made both the canvas and the SVG draw an inside or outside stroke centred
while `Resolved` had already sized the node through `stroke_expansion` as though the ink were where the
model said.

**kurbo has no path booleans** (its tracking issue is open), so the arithmetic is `flo_curves`, which
keeps curves as curves. The polygon-clipping alternatives are far faster and flatten everything first —
a union of two circles would leave a thousand-segment polyline in the save file, the SVG, and anything
edited afterwards. **Geometry is scaled by a constant factor on the way into flo_curves and back out
again** — `boolean::c` multiplies and `boolean::k` divides, and they are the only two coordinate
conversions, so they are the whole seam — because flo_curves compiles in absolute tolerances that no
argument reaches: its `GraphPath` merges two points closer than a `CLOSE_DISTANCE` of 0.01 into one,
which unscaled is a hundredth of a *world* unit, so an `Intersect` result thinner than that had its two
short ends erased and came back as a bow-tie with exactly half the area (§15 D794). The accuracy handed
to flo_curves is read in that scaled space. **Both figures are constants, not parameters**: an accuracy
that varied with the zoom or with the size of the shape would make the geometry a boolean *produces*
depend on the camera, and the same two shapes would combine to two different paths, each written into
the document and kept. `Exclude` is composed, since flo_curves has no XOR.

**Two conventions have to be reconciled, and both bit.** flo_curves works **even-odd** and Ondin fills
**non-zero**: a hole comes back as a second subpath wound the *same* way as the outline around it, which
non-zero paints solid. `boolean::from_flo` forces each subpath's direction to alternate with its nesting
depth, so a result means the same thing under either rule — which is also what makes it safe to hand to
SVG. **Nesting is counted from a representative interior point, and a subpath whose one cannot be found
is kept rather than dropped** (§15 D457): `representative_point` takes the bounding-box centre where
that is inside, and otherwise runs a **scan line** — a horizontal ray intersected with every segment,
the crossings sorted, the midpoint of the first span `contains` confirms — which is exact for a closed
curve of any thickness, where the 8×8 grid it replaced missed anything thinner than an eighth of its own
box and so *deleted* a crescent's only subpath. Losing the winding correction is a hole that fills
solid; losing the geometry is a shape that is not there. And `Exclude` is **not**
`sub(add(a,b), intersect(a,b))`: the intersection's boundary is made entirely
of pieces of the operands' own edges, so that subtraction hands the traversal the same graph as `a ∪ b`
and gets the two operands straight back. It is `path_full_intersect`'s two exterior paths instead — `a \ b`
and `b \ a` from one cut, disjoint by construction (§15 D91).

**The four operations and the order they read in.** Children are stored bottom-first, so operand order
*is* layer order: `Subtract` is the bottom child less everything above it, which is what the layer list
already shows. `build::boolean` refuses fewer than two operands, refuses text — a text node has no
outline until its glyphs are converted, a feature that does not exist — and **gives the result the bottom
operand's paint**, without which the boolean evaluates correctly and then draws nothing, reading as an
operation that deleted the artwork. Figma outlines the glyphs for you; refusing is the honest answer,
because the alternative is a text node swallowed into a shape it contributes nothing to. **Outlining a
stroke is absent for the same reason**: turning ink into a filled path — glyphs or strokes — is its own
feature with its own model behind it, not a gap in this one (§15 D126).

**The key layer chooses the bottom operand, and only for `Subtract`.** `build::boolean` takes a
`key: Option<NodeId>` fifth argument: the designated member moves to index 0 and the rest keep their
relative z-order, so a three-operand subtract still cuts in the order the layer list showed.
**`build::mask` takes the same argument and does the same thing to the order** (§15 D286) — the chosen
layer to index 0 of the new group, everything else keeping its relative z-order, and a `key` from some
other selection ignored rather than refused. A mask clips what is drawn *above* it, so "the mask" and
"the bottom of the stack" are one position, which is why designating one is a reorder here too. Since the
container inherits the bottom operand's paint, the key decides the paint too. The other three operations
fold commutatively — Exclude included, which is the correction §15 D113 records — so reordering their
operands would rewrite the tree and change the inherited paint while leaving the shape identical, and
the key is simply inert for them. ⚠️ **`Subtract` is also the only one that is not *associative*, and
that is a second property rather than the same one said twice** (§15 D614): `boolean::fold_operands`
folds `Union` and `Intersect` as a **balanced tree** — adjacent pairs, then pairs of pairs — and
keeps the left fold for `Subtract`, where `((a−b)−c)−d` and `(a−b)−(c−d)` are different shapes
because everything `d` takes out of `c` comes back. Commutativity licenses reordering the operands;
only associativity licenses rebracketing the fold. **Once the container exists the key is not stored anywhere**:
operand order *is* child order, so re-designating inside a boolean is an `Operation::Reorder` to index 0
(`canvas::designate_key`), visible in the layer list, undoable, and unable to disagree with the order the
user can see and drag.

**And the layers tree says which one it is** (§15 D244). `layers::subtract_base` marks `children[0]` of a
`Subtract` — the bottom row, the tree drawing topmost-first — with a faint `stack-simple` glyph in the
same right-hand slot an artboard's size badge uses, which the eye and lock take over on hover; the two
share a `RowBadge` and a colour, and `BADGE_ICON` is the measured size that puts the pictogram on the
word's ink height. Only `Subtract`: the other
three fold commutatively, so a mark on any of their operands would be claiming a significance the
arithmetic cannot see. It is derived from the tree on every frame rather than stored, which is what makes
dragging the operand up one row *stop* it being the base — the failure this design exists to avoid is a
marker that disagrees with the order the user can see.

**That slot now has three claimants and the mask wins it** (§15 D285). A mask's row wears
`ph-circle-half` ahead of both the frame's size badge and the `Subtract` base mark, because it is the
one of the three that changes what you *see*: a mask draws nothing, so its row is the only place in
the app that says the layer is still there. The other two annotate a layer already on the canvas. No
row can want two of them — a frame cannot be a mask (`NodeKind::can_mask`), and a boolean's operands
are consumed by the operation rather than painted, so a mask among them would clip nothing.

**Switching the operation is a `GeometryPatch`**, not a rebuild: the children and the paint stay, undo
returns the previous operation rather than dissolving the container, and re-picking the current value is
an empty transaction so it adds no undo step. Being a geometry patch also means it travels the ordinary
preview→commit valve, which is what a hovering dropdown would need.

**The control is disabled, never hidden, with one layer selected.** A control that vanishes leaves the
user wondering whether the app has the feature; one that is visibly unavailable says "not for this
selection". Its enabled/disabled test *is* `build::boolean`'s — a throwaway dry run — so the dropdown is
live exactly when using it would succeed, rather than re-deriving the rule and disagreeing with it. With
a boolean selected it reads that boolean's operation and switches it. `Ctrl+Alt+U/S/I/X` are the same
four commands (§15 D207 for what adding the first `Ctrl+Alt` chords exposed about the rest of the keymap,
and **D204** for the fourth of them, which cut the selection instead of reaching this operation at all).

**The operands never reach the canvas** (`scene::paint_node` stops at a boolean).
They are inputs consumed by the operation; their geometry and paint stay in the document, which is what
makes the container releasable, and none of it is drawn. That also answers what "combining into one
attribute panel" means: the boolean's own fill and stroke govern the whole result, and an operand's
appearance is inert until it is released. *This was missed at first and made the feature look broken
rather than subtly wrong — see §15 D88.* The panel has to **offer** those two, and for a while it did not:
`inspector_single` kept a third hand-written copy of the paintable-kinds list, so a selected boolean showed
no Fill and no Stroke panel at all and there was no way to colour the shape it had just made. It asks
`NodeKind::takes_paint()` now (§15 D92).

**A gesture re-derives the outline in the preview**, not on release: `RenderOverrides` carries its own
boolean cache, filled once per preview build (deepest boolean first) from the gesture's pending state.
**Deepest is each boolean's own depth from the *root***, not the distance walked from the seed that
found it (§15 D461): a seed-relative count is not comparable *between* seeds, and it also had the order
exactly backwards, so a boolean nested inside a boolean previewed against its child's pre-drag outline
and snapped into place on release. The
recursion is shared with `Resolved` — `boolean::evaluate_node` against a `boolean::Operands`, five
lookups the caller supplies — so the committed and previewed answers cannot disagree about what a boolean
means.

**There are three views now, and the third is why `Operands` walks lookups rather than a `Document`.**
`Resolved` reads the committed tree and its own cache, `RenderOverrides` reads a gesture's pending state,
and a **ghost** reads a captured subtree the document has never seen — which is what `children_of` and
`visible_of` were added for, and why neither `evaluate_node` nor `operand_of` takes a `&Document` any more.
The committed half is spelled once as `Resolved::operand_path(doc, id)` — "what this subtree contributes as
an operand, in its parent's space", the question flatten asks of an arbitrary selection — over a
`with_committed_view` callback, which is a callback because the `Operands` fields are `&dyn Fn`s and so are
locals that cannot be handed back.

**The copy an Alt-drag carries previews the boolean, not its operands.** `render::GhostNode` has a
`path: Option<BezPath>`, evaluated **once when the ghost subtree is built** (`build_ghost`, children-first,
threading a map so a boolean inside a boolean is read rather than evaluated twice) and never in the scene
walk — the field exists precisely to keep path arithmetic out of the frame, the bargain a ghost's shaped
text already makes. `scene::paint_ghost` also **stops at a `Boolean`** exactly as `paint_node` does;
without that it went on to draw the operands over a result that was not there, so a subtracted bite looked
whole and un-cut while it was being dragged and appeared at the instant of release (§15 D94).

**A ghost can also *be* an operand, and the preview counts it.** Alt-dragging a copy of a layer that is
inside a boolean parents the copy to the boolean itself (`canvas::ClonedSubtree` lands a copy beside its
source), so on release it joins the operation — and a preview that ignored it showed the pre-drag outline
and jumped at the drop. `RenderOverrides::reevaluate_booleans` seeds its walk from **two** places for that
reason: a *moved* node reshapes every boolean above it, so the seed is its parent's chain, while a *ghost*
reshapes the boolean it is parented **to**, so the seed is that parent itself. The lookups grew the matching
branches — `operand_children` appends the ghosts parented to a node to its committed children,
`operand_visible` answers a ghost's own flag, and `nested` falls back to a ghost's `GhostNode::path` before
the committed cache. It **appends** the ghost, and the reason that used to be right twice over has been
overtaken on both counts: ghosts no longer draw after their parent's real children (§6.2), and a copy
staying among its siblings now names an index rather than appending (§15 D42). What keeps it sound is the
*operation* rather than the order: `boolean::evaluate` is a left fold in which only the **first** operand
is order-sensitive — Subtract's tail is a union and the other three are commutative — and a copy lands at
its source's index *plus one*, so it can never take slot 0. *Recheck that if anything is ever able to
insert an operand at index 0: `a_ghost_operand_widens_the_boolean_it_is_dropped_into` appends, so nothing
yet compares a preview against a commit that puts an operand mid-list.* The consequence below is worth
stating plainly, because it narrows a rule stated above: a preview
**can** add artwork a boolean consumes, even though it still cannot reparent, reorder or delete — so
`children_of` is no longer "the document's answer and only the document's" (§15 D94).

**All five lookups matter, and the kind is the one that is easy to forget.** A resize expresses itself
as new *geometry* as well as a new transform, so an evaluator that overrides only transforms moves a
boolean's operands without resizing them: the shape shuffles about under the pointer and snaps to the
right size on release (§15 D90). `Operands::kind_of` is what closes that, and `RenderOverrides` answers it
with `current_kind`, which already existed for the text previews.

**Everything that measures a boolean measures its *result*.** `query::local_box` reads the cached
outline ahead of the child union it uses for a group, and `session::preview_local_box` reads the
*previewed* outline first — so the selection outline, the dimensions badge, the resize handles and the
transform fields all describe the visible shape rather than the operands feeding it. A subtraction
otherwise reported a box reaching out to wherever the subtracted shape ended, and a resize then scaled
against a rectangle the artwork does not have, which is what made a boolean feel like a multi-selection
being transformed layer by layer instead of a block (§15 D89).

**The layer name follows the operation, unless it is the user's.** A boolean is created named after its
