operation, so switching Union → Intersect renames it — but only when the current name is still one of the
four labels, **with or without a number after it** (`naming::is_boolean_label`, §5.7b): every boolean is
numbered — the first is "Union 1" — and an exact-match test left every one of them reading "Union 1" over an
intersection. The number comes across rather than being re-derived, so flipping the operation back and
forth does not walk it. Anything else has been typed by hand and is never overwritten — "Badge 2" is
numbered but is not a name we ever wrote, so it stays theirs (§15 D127).

**Selecting one works like a group.** A boolean is in the spatial index and hit-tested against its
derived outline (`query::hit_test`, which reads the cache because `contains_local` cannot build it), and
`group_chain` treats it as a group so a click on the artwork selects the container rather than an operand
nothing drew. Double-click still steps inside, which is how an operand gets edited.

**The layers row draws the operation's own glyph** (`layers::op_glyph`, sitting beside `node_icon` and
shared with the inspector's dropdown so one operation is never two different pictures). It used to draw the
path icon for all four and lean on the *name* to tell them apart, which works until the layer is renamed —
and a boolean gets renamed like anything else. The icon is the half of the row that cannot be edited away.

**And that row takes a drop like a group's.** `layers::layer_row`'s `is_container` counts `Boolean`
alongside `Group` and `Artboard`, so the middle of the row means "inside it" and gets the outline that
says so (§9.2). Its children *are* its operands, which makes dropping a shape onto it the way a third
operand is added, and `build::can_parent` has always allowed it. Left out, the row offered only
"between its siblings", and the one way in was to aim at the gap between two operands with the row
expanded — legal, and with no highlight to say the drop was going inside.

**Grouping inside a boolean re-parenthesises the operation, and that is a feature.** Entering a boolean,
selecting two operands and pressing `Ctrl+G` really does group them; `boolean::operand_of` gives a `Group`
the *union* of its contents, so `a ⊻ b ⊻ c` becomes `a ⊻ (b ∪ c)` — a different shape, measured rather than
asserted (§15 D95). Figma allows it for the same reason.

**SVG flattens, at the boundary and nowhere else.** There is no boolean container in SVG, so the
exporter writes the derived outline and deliberately *not* the operands — emitting those too would draw
the shapes the boolean was meant to consume. Everything else in that writer that needs the shape's path —
the alignment clip, the resolved dash pattern — reads it through `svg::outline` for the reason above.

**Release is `build::ungroup`, and its body needed nothing added.** The operands were never destroyed —
that is what non-destructive means — so dissolving the container is the identical splice a group needs, with
the transform folded into each child so nothing moves. `Ctrl+Shift+G` and the identity row's Ungroup
action both reach it. The one asymmetry is paint, deliberately: the boolean's own fill and stroke governed
the result and go away with it, while each operand's own paint — inert while it was consumed — comes back
into view. `build::boolean` giving the container the *bottom* operand's paint is what makes that round trip
land somewhere recognisable (`releasing_a_boolean_gives_its_operands_back_in_place`).

**Flatten is the destructive counterpart** (`build::flatten`), and it admits exactly two selections. **One
boolean** is replaced in place by a `Path` carrying its derived outline, keeping its transform, z-slot,
paint, name *and* opacity/visibility, because it is the same layer. **Two or more layers** become their
union in the parent's space, as a new `Path` at the topmost member's slot taking the bottom member's paint —
`boolean`'s own rule, so unite-then-flatten and flatten agree. Groups in the selection contribute their
contents unioned and nested booleans their results, because `Resolved::operand_path` is what is asked of
each member, and `build::carried_paint` is shared by all three arms. A **single non-boolean is refused**
rather than converted, and since 2026-08-19 that is a *decision* with the conversion built beside it
rather than a gap (§15 D230): turning a rect into a path is a **different verb**, `build::outline`,
reached from the context menu's *Outline shape*. Keeping the two apart is the point — *Flatten* means
"throw the operands away and keep the answer", and a *Flatten* that quietly outlined a lone rect would
be the row a user reached for doing something the word does not say. The two rows are never offered
together, by construction: one excludes a set, `Shape | Path` excludes a boolean.
Text, `Artboard` and `Root` are refused for `boolean`'s reasons, and a selection that *is* admissible has
**two** refusals left, because the user's next move differs (§15 D736). `OpError::EmptyGeometry` is a
boolean whose operands cancel out — the kind was right and the *geometry* was empty, which the user fixes by
moving a shape rather than by selecting differently. `OpError::BooleanAbandoned` is one whose arithmetic was
**given up on**, D239's `catch_unwind` having caught an unwind out of flo_curves, and moving a shape cannot
help that. Both reach the door as `evaluate`'s `None`, and the two arms separate them by different means:
`flatten_union` calls `evaluate` itself, so it brackets `boolean::failures` across the call; `flatten_boolean`
never calls it at all — it reads a cache filled on an earlier pass — so it asks D298's
`Resolved::boolean_failed` mark instead. The destruction is one `DeleteNode` over a node that still has
children, so one undo restores all of it; `flattening_a_boolean_keeps_its_outline_and_discards_the_operands`
pins that, because "the inverse captures the subtree" is load-bearing here rather than incidental.

**`build::outline` is the other verb, and it is *Flatten*'s sibling rather than a mode of it**
(§15 D230). One shape becomes the `Path` its own outline traces: a rect, an ellipse, a polygon, a star,
a line, or a `Path` whose per-anchor radii are still in the model and get **baked into the geometry**.
It needs no `Resolved` at all — `geometry::local_path` is a pure function of the node's kind — which is
the whole difference in cost between the two operations. `build::can_outline` is the predicate, and it
is a question about *state* on exactly one kind: `round_corners` returns a path untouched when **no
radius is `> 0`**, so a path with nothing to bake answers no and the menu row is **present and dimmed**
rather than absent. ⚠️ **That is not the same test as *every radius is `<= 0`*, and the difference is
`NaN`** (§15 D640): both of `round_corners`' guards were spelled the second way, which a `NaN` passes,
and what it reached made the corner the *largest* fillet the clamp allows rather than none. `can_outline`
had the right predicate all along, so for as long as that lasted the row was dimmed for having nothing
to bake while the canvas drew the shape rounded to its inscribed circle. A `Group` is refused because its outline is the union of its contents, which is
what `flatten` gives a set — a different verb — and `Boolean`, `Artboard`, `Text` and `Root` are
refused for the reasons above.

**`build::outline_text` is the third verb, and text's refusal above is exactly why it is a third**
(§15 D260). A `Text` layer becomes the `Path` its **glyphs** trace — the context menu's *Convert to
path*, Affinity's *Convert Text to Curves*. Every other kind's outline is a pure function of its own
geometry; a text node's is a **shaped** thing, so this one takes a `Resolved` where `outline` needs
none — the same difference in cost that separates `flatten` from `outline`, arriving at a third door
for the same reason. The outlining itself is not new and is not here: `ondin_core::text::outline`
(§5.4, §6.3, §15 D145) builds the path from the cached layout, and the glyph coordinates it produces
are **already node-local** — the same ones the render walk hands a backend — so the conversion has
nothing to transform on the way out. `build::can_outline_text` is the predicate and it **asks
`text::outline`** rather than counting glyphs: a node whose every character is a space has glyphs and
no contours, so a cheap proxy would leave the row live and the verb would then answer `EmptyGeometry`
after the click. Empty content is refused rather than converted for the same reason a `Path` holding
nothing is not worth making — it draws nothing and can never be picked again. Building the outlines
costs about a microsecond a glyph, which is why the menu takes its answer **once at open**
(`ContextMenu::text_outlineable`) rather than per frame, and why the render walk gates the same
construction on there being a visible stroke to use it.
**The three share one body**, `build::replace_with_path`, because "what survives being redrawn" is a list
and a list written twice drifts (§15 D87, D92). That sharing is what found the pivot: the body's own
comment claims the layer survives, and a **moved pivot** was being dropped — silently resetting the
rotation centre of a layer the user had placed one on. It is carried now. **So is the mask flag**, for
the same reason and with a louder symptom: the new path is the same shape in the same slot, so it clips
the same run, and dropping it would release the mask as a side effect of *Outline shape* — which reads
as the artwork above snapping back to full size with nothing on screen saying why (§15 D282).
`build::flatten_union` deliberately does not carry it: that verb makes a genuinely new layer out of
several and inherits only paint. **And so is the fill rule**, which is the one carry that changes what is
*drawn* rather than preserving a property beside the drawing: `Node::fill_rule` *derives* even-odd from
the operation for an `Exclude` (§15 D239), and this body's whole job is to throw the operation away — so
until 2026-08-31 a flattened exclusion handed back the same concatenated subpaths under the default
non-zero rule, which is its **union**, every hole filled in. What is carried is the *effective* rule, one
line for two cases: the derived one, and the stored one an outlined compound `Path` would otherwise lose
the same way. *Lock* and the **proportion
lock** are still dropped deliberately, the second because this operation's whole purpose is to stop the
layer having an authored box for that constraint to be about (§15 D41). **Neither conversion has a
chord** (`shortcuts.md`, *Deliberately unbound*): a one-way structural conversion is not worth a
keystroke, and `Ctrl+E` must not come to cover either by having the only key.

**Its home is the fifth row of the same dropdown, under a hairline.** It is the one entry that is not a
state the control can come back showing — what it leaves selected is a `Path`, so the closed control goes
straight back to disabled — and the rule plus a different family of glyph (`arrows-merge`, not a fifth set
diagram) is what says "an action, not an operation". The three 28×28 slots beside the dropdown are the
design's own, and now hold Mask, Group and Ungroup (below). `Ctrl+E` is the keyboard route (Figma's chord;
plain `E` is still the ellipse tool, and `input.rs`'s `plain` gate is what keeps them apart), and
`inspector::flatten_selection` gates on the **dropdown's own predicate**, so the keyboard path reports
"Select a boolean, or two or more layers, to flatten" rather than the builder's "operation not valid for this
node kind". `inspector::popup_rule` draws the hairline: `ui::rule` transposed, snapped through the shared
`ui::hairline_in_column` — it was a *copy* of that arithmetic until 2026-09-07 and carried its parity bug
(§15 D479) — and
sized from `available_width` so it always spans the ground it is drawn on rather than overhanging the card
on the frame the popup opens. Its clear space is stated as two absolute gaps — `ABOVE` 5pt and `BELOW`
4pt — with the layout's own `item_spacing.y` **subtracted back out**, because a vertical layout inserts
that spacing before every item and so no box small enough could get the gap under 6: `add_space` moves
the cursor without inserting spacing and takes a negative amount, which makes the pull-back exact and
keeps it right if the spacing is ever retuned.

**The menu asks for its own height** (`ComboBox::height(BOOL_MENU_H)`, 220). egui's default is
`Spacing::combo_height` at 200, which the five rows, the separator and the menu's own margins came close
enough to that the list could put itself in a scroll area — and a menu of five fixed entries has nothing
below to scroll *to*, so the bar is pure cost. 220 leaves headroom over the 166 the content measures, so
a retuned row height cannot quietly reintroduce it.

**The row is four controls, and three of them are the design's own.** Beside the dropdown sit Mask,
Group and Ungroup as 28×28 icon buttons, with `ACTION_GLYPH` at 16 in the box — the ratio the card's
own eye and lock already use (16 in 22), so the two rows read as one control set. **Mask
(`ph-circle-half`) is live since 2026-08-21, and it is the only one of the three that is a *state*
rather than an event** (§15 D285): Group and Ungroup happen and are over, where a mask is something a
layer *is*, so the button lights `active` while the layer it points at is one and clicking it again
releases it. `Inspector::mask_action` is the one question behind both halves — `Make { members, key }`
or `Release(id)` — so what the button *looks* like and what it *does* cannot disagree. **Making it
goes through `build::mask`**, which wraps two or more layers in a group (§15 D286); a lone layer is
flagged where it stands. Which layer becomes the mask is **`build::mask_target`'s** answer and nothing
else's — the key if one is designated among the members, else the bottom-most member that is **not a
picture**, else the bottom-most (§5.5a, §15 D287). The control asks that function only to decide
whether it can be live; the builder asks it again rather than being told, so the two cannot disagree
about which layer they are talking about. **The builder gets the last word** besides: `mask_action`
dry-runs `build::mask` on a throwaway `IdSource`, the way the boolean dropdown does, so a refusal
`build::group` owns — a selection with a frame in it — dims the control instead of failing after the
click. **Release is read from either end**:
one selected layer that is a mask, or one
selected container holding one — the second arm being what makes the operation undoable from the
selection the first arm leaves behind, at the cost that a selected mask-group answers *Release* and so
cannot be made a mask of *its* siblings from here (§15 D286). It requires **one parent** across the selection, two layers in
different groups having no stacking order a mask could mean, and it returns a `Result` because each
refusal has a different thing to fix and the row's tooltips are what say which — one of them being the
button **stricter than the operation**: a layer inside a `Boolean` is a maskable *kind*, so
`op_set_mask` would accept it and the flag would clip nothing, operands not being artwork (§5.3).
⚠️ **Stricter than `op_set_mask`, and *not* stricter than the builder** — measured 2026-09-09 (§15
D625) by disabling that refusal, which does not reach `Ok`: the dry run above still declines, in
`build::group`'s words. So the boolean guard is redundant for correctness and load-bearing for the
**message**, which is what the `Result` exists for, and a test asserting `is_err()` cannot tell it
from a dead guard.
The keyboard reaches the same verb on **`Ctrl+Alt+M`** (`shortcuts.md`, §15 D286), and so does the
context menu's *Use as mask*. Group and Ungroup (`ph-selection-plus`,
`ph-selection-slash`) call the same `group_selected_from_panel` / `ungroup_selected_from_panel` as
before; only the presentation and the gating are new. They used to be a pair of default-styled text
buttons above the count in `inspector_multi`, the one visibly unstyled control pair left in the
inspector. All three codepoints were **confirmed by an atlas dump** rather than trusted from
`Phosphor.codepoints.txt`: the font's `post` table is **version 3.0**, which carries no glyph names,
so a wrong codepoint lays out perfectly and renders nothing at all. ⚠️ **This read *"the font has no
`post` table"* until 2026-09-10** (§15 D751, and D754 for the measurement and the other six copies of
it), which is wrong about the file and right about the
consequence — a reader who went and looked would have found the tag and concluded the whole sentence
was mistaken. The dump is still the only check.

**A Mask card sits directly under the identity card, while the selection is a mask *or a container
holding one*** (`inspector::inspector_mask`, §15 D288). One full-width dropdown, one question: *Shape*
or *Alpha*. It is present-or-absent rather than always-there-and-inert because a card that is usually
dead is noise a disabled *button* is worth paying for and a whole card is not — the layers row is what
says a mask exists at all, and this says what kind. **Following the group is the point**: `build::mask`
leaves the *group* selected, so a card that asked only "is this layer a mask" vanished at the instant
the operation finished, while the identity row's button one card above went on reporting that the same
selection was masked.

`inspector::mask_card_targets` is the rule and is a **free function**, because the rule is a function of
the document and the selection and a test of it should not have to stand a panel up (§15 D303, which
retired the older reason that an `OndinApp` could not be built at all): the selected layer if it is
a mask, otherwise its **direct** mask children. Its own flag wins, so a group that is both describes
itself rather than something a level down. **Direct children only is what makes nesting safe** — a mask
group inside another group leaves the outer one alone, because the outer's children include a *group*
and a group is not a mask, so no selection ever silently rewrites a mode several levels down. The
target is a **list**, since a group can hold two runs: they report *Mixed* on the
`mixed_stroke_properties` convention and a pick writes to every target that would change, in one
transaction. **There is no "mask group" flag** — being one is derived from the children every time it
is asked, D113's rule and D244's precedent, so dragging the mask out stops the group being one with
nothing to go stale. A third mode would be a third entry in the same dropdown with nothing else moving.

**Ungroup asks what the selection contains, Group what shape it is** (`inspector::group_actions`).
Ungroup is live exactly when something selected is a `Group` or a `Boolean`, which is what
`app::ungroup_selection` then acts on — the control and the action ask the same question, so it
cannot be live and then do nothing. ⚠️ **Both buttons call that verb rather than re-implementing it,
and until 2026-09-08 neither did** (§15 D562): the panel's own ungroup left the selection empty
instead of selecting the freed layers, said nothing on success, swallowed the builder's `Err` so a
refusal was silent, and committed once per container against the rule below. **One press is one transaction however many containers it
dissolves** (§15 D521): `app::ungroup_selection` committed inside the loop until 2026-09-07, so two
groups cost two undo steps and one `Ctrl+Z` brought one of them back; it builds through
`build::ungroup_all` now, which is where the ordering lives (§5.7a). Group is `build::group`'s own answer, dry-run on a throwaway
`IdSource` the way `booleanable_selection` tests the dropdown, with **one rule on top: a selection
that is already exactly one container is refused**. The builder would take it and mint a group
containing one group — legal, and never what anyone meant; two containers, or a container and a
layer, are a real grouping and stay live. The three cases the design asks for fall out of that pair
rather than being enumerated: ordinary layers group and cannot ungroup, a lone group or boolean
ungroups and cannot group, and a container plus anything else does both. The lone-container refusal
reads as a redundant guard in front of a builder that would say yes; it is not one, and nothing
would catch its removal — the row's gating has no test behind it. **Writable now and unwritten**: this
said an `OndinApp` could not be constructed, which stopped being true on 2026-08-22 (§15 D303), so
"nothing would catch it" is a queue rather than a fact.

**What is still owed here, so none of the above reads as finished.** Booleans *are* tested at the **pixel**
level, and this said otherwise until 2026-08-19: `ondin-export/tests/boolean.rs` renders a subtracted hole
and an excluded overlap and asserts each is `alpha == 0`, which is the `--png` version this asked for, and
they are not one test twice — a hole is a reversed nested subpath and an exclusion is the absence of any
subpath, so they fail to the two different halves of D91. **Performance is measured, and it found a panic
rather than a cost** (§15 D239). Every operand edit re-runs the arithmetic for the whole boolean, once more per preview
build, and now once per ghost subtree build (once per gesture, not per frame) — and for `Union`, `Subtract`
and `Intersect` that is free enough to leave alone, under 4 ms at sixty-four overlapping operands, so the
per-operand caching once floated for it is not to be built.
⚠️ **That measurement was taken on an overlapping ring and does not describe the disjoint case,
which is the one masks are made of** (§15 D614). A ring's union collapses to a handful of subpaths
however many operands go in; N *disjoint* rects — a group of icons used as a shape mask — leave the
accumulator one subpath per operand, so the old left fold was Θ(N²): **103 ms at 256 operands**, and
paid **per repaint** through `scene::mask_geometry` and **per pointer move** through
`resolve::mask_path`, neither of which caches. Folded as a balanced tree it is 6.4 ms at 256 and N
log N thereafter, which is why the cache is still not to be built — but the reason is now the fold's
shape rather than the ring's. `Exclude` is the outlier (19.9 ms at twenty,
1.1 s at sixty-four), and worse, some operand sets make flo_curves **panic** out of
`GraphPath::exterior_paths` on an intransitive comparator. **No operation is exempt from that**, which is why
the unwind is caught at the one seam they all pass through: `boolean::evaluate` answers `None` and the
boolean draws nothing, so a wrong shape is not a lost document. The upstream defect is untouched, and the
guard is inert under `panic = "abort"` — which nothing sets, and the root `Cargo.toml` says beside its
profiles why not. **That absence is enforced rather than asked for** (§15 D445): a
`#[cfg(panic = "abort")] compile_error!` sits beside the guard, so the setting fails the build with the
reason attached. ⚠️ The manifest note had argued for a fortnight that such a gate was impossible, on
two claims that were both false — the cfg is stable and testable, and the guard's own synthetic panic
aborts its test binary under the setting. **And the same `None` that made the guard safe is what made the failure invisible**, so
the seam also counts: `boolean::failures()` is a thread-local tally read *either side* of a call, because
an intersection that came out empty answers `None` too and drawing nothing is correct for that one.
`Resolved` brackets each `evaluate_node` with it and keeps the answer per node
(`Resolved::boolean_failed`); the layers row wears the same warning colour §5.5a gives a picture that
cannot be drawn, and a commit that trips the defect says so in the status bar. A count rather than a flag,
because a group operand is unioned by an inner `evaluate` that catches its own unwind — only a number that
goes up composes across the nesting (§15 D298).

**And it draws §5.5a's placeholder, over the operands' union** — the same grey ground, rim and cross, off
the same `missing_placeholder`, because it is the same fact about a layer and a second placeholder
vocabulary for a second cause would be two things to learn about one symptom (§15 D299). The box is
`query::boolean_placeholder`: `local_box`'s child-union fallback with the failure test in front of it, and
the *only* extent the node has left, since its own outline is what failed and unioning the operands means
re-running the arithmetic that gave up. The scene walk, the hit test, `Resolved::recompute_bounds` and the
SVG writer all ask that one function, so the drawing, the click target and the culling box cannot part
company — and giving the node **world bounds** is half the change rather than a detail: a boolean with no
cached outline had none, so it was absent from the R-tree and could be selected from the layers tree and
not from the canvas, exactly as `is_indexed`'s own comment records for the case before it. The placeholder
is committed-only: a preview that is re-evaluating a boolean always leaves an entry, so
`RenderOverrides::boolean_path` being `None` is what "no gesture owns this node" is spelled as, and a box
lagging a drag is not drawn at all. **Text still cannot be an
operand**, deliberately — and that arm is exactly the one a **mask** grows instead, `Resolved::mask_path`
taking a text node's glyph outlines where `boolean::operand_of` refuses it (§5.9, §15 D282).
**Outline-stroke does not exist.**

**A layer on its way out of a frame draws outside that frame's clip**
(`RenderOverrides::escape_clip`, §15 D86). An artboard clips its children, and a child being dragged past
that edge is still a child until the gesture commits — so it drew cut off at the frame's boundary, with
only the selection box outside to say where it really was, and snapped into view at the instant of
release. The Alt-drag copy gets the same treatment (`escape_clip_ghosts`), since a ghost hangs off the
original's parent and was clipped by exactly the same edge.

**It is set exactly when the release would reparent**, through the same `move_destination` /
`frame_covering` the drop uses — a frame keeps a layer while it covers more than half of it. That is what
makes the drawing worth trusting: still clipped means dropping it stays in the frame, drawing in full
means dropping it takes it out. A threshold invented for the renderer would make the picture a guess about
its own gesture.

**Z-order is untouched.** The escaping child is drawn where its siblings expect it, so the parent's clip
layer is closed and reopened *around* it rather than the child being deferred to the end of the walk.
Which shape covers which is information the user is steering by, and a dragged layer that jumped to the
front would lose it (Figma does not do that either). One consequence, and it is why the walk tracks
whether the layer is open rather than assuming: a frame below full opacity composites in two pieces while
a child is leaving, so two of its children overlapping *across* that boundary blend against each other
rather than within one group. It needs a semi-transparent clipping frame, overlapping children and a drag
to see; the alternative is a layer visibly cut in half.

Driven from the **gesture**, never derived from the overrides: "has a transform override" is a different
question, and a resize gives a child one too — a box growing past its frame's edge is meant to stay
clipped, so deriving it would trade this pop-on-release for the mirror image of it.

**The box a create tool is dragging out is chrome as well**: a `color::SELECT` outline at 1.5px,
over the renderer's ghost of the shape itself, so the gesture always says where the layer will land
and says it in the app's own hue rather than as artwork — the same statement the marquee makes. Not
the Line tool, whose drag runs corner to corner, so a box around it would describe a shape it is not
making. **Both its ends come from `canvas::create_box`, the same function the transaction uses**,
rather than from the raw pointer it used to read: an outline taken straight from the pointer honoured
neither Shift nor the pixel grid, so a Shift-drawn square committed square with a *rectangle* drawn
around it (§15 D51). *Both* ends, because under Alt the near one is not the press point either
(§15 D289) — an outline still pinned there while the shape grew both ways would be the same broken
promise one axis further along.

**And the size pill hangs under that box, exactly as it hangs under a selection** (§15 D292).
`canvas::paint_size_pill` is one painter and `canvas::size_label` one rounding, shared by the drag and
the selection, because the release turns one into the other in a single frame: two pills differing by a
point of padding or a decimal would read as a twitch at the moment the number is being watched hardest.
The box both the outline and the pill quote comes from `create_outline_box`, so a gesture cannot draw
one box and report another — the Line tool answers `None` there and gets neither, which is the same
rule that keeps the badge off a lone selected line.
`the_size_pill_hangs_clear_of_the_bottom_handles_grab_radius` paints through the shared function and
asserts the pill clears `HANDLE_PICK_PX`, which is the constraint the gap exists for and the number the
neighbouring `badge_frame` test never reads.

**The copy an Alt-drag carries is a ghost of the artwork, and the chrome follows it.** While Alt is
held during a move the original stays exactly where it is and the *copy* travels, as in Figma. The
copy is previewed as itself — a `render::GhostNode` subtree, so a group or a frame previews with its
children and its clip (§6.2) — and the selection outline, the handles and the size badge are all
drawn offset onto it by `canvas::alt_clone_offset`, because the copy is the thing under the pointer
and the thing that will be selected on release. The `SELECT_DIM` outline is still drawn on each
layer's committed box, but its meaning has changed with the gesture: it marks **the original that is
staying**, not a copy nobody can see. It appears and disappears with the key, which is what makes the
modifier discoverable in the middle of a drag. §15 D40 has the whole gesture, including why it used to
be the other way round.

**The pixel grid is the faintest layer of chrome there is.** `grid.rs` draws a one-world-unit lattice
— one unit is one pixel (§6.2) — *over* the artwork, so a shape's edge can be read against a pixel
boundary, and *under* every other overlay, because none of them should have to compete with it. That
also settles the bottom of the overlay stack, which had never been stated: the grid first, then each
frame's name tag, then everything that answers a gesture, and the ruler bars with their guides over
all of it.

It appears at `grid::VISIBLE_AT_ZOOM` = 8.0 — **800% as the zoom readout spells it**, since
`camera.zoom` is device pixels per world unit and the readout is that same number as a percentage, so
the threshold is the one the user sees. Below roughly that, one-pixel cells sit closer together than
the hairlines drawn between them and the lattice reads as a grey wash rather than as a grid. ⚠️ **This
said both halves were pinned by `the_grid_threshold_is_the_zoom_readout_at_800_percent` and
`a_cell_is_wide_enough_to_read_at_the_threshold`, and neither of those ever called into the grid**
(§15 D504): one re-derives the readout arithmetic from the constant and the other is
`assert!(8.0 >= 8.0)`, so narrowing `>=` to `>` — the grid not appearing at exactly 800% — stayed
green. What pins the behaviour is
`the_grid_is_on_at_the_threshold_and_off_below_it_and_off_when_switched_off`, which brackets 7.99 /
8.0 / 8.01 and asserts the switch at each. The threshold is also what bounds the line count
**by construction** rather than by a cap: cells at least 8 device px apart cannot number more than the
canvas's pixel width over eight. **The ink is a neutral mid-grey at low alpha**, deliberately not a
tint of the chrome's near-white. This is the one overlay drawn over artwork of *any* lightness — the
canvas ground is document state and may be white (§15 D28), and a frame's own background usually is —
so a light hairline would vanish exactly where a pixel grid is most wanted, inside a white frame, and
a ground-derived ink would only ever solve one of the two directions. The ruler bars are excluded from
it: they are chrome of their own, and a lattice under their ticks would make both unreadable —
asserted since 2026-09-07 by `the_lattice_does_not_run_under_the_ruler_bars`, which measures the
leftmost vertical against the bar's thickness **with the rulers-off case as its control**, deleting
the inset leaving the line count roughly unchanged (§15 D504).

**Every line lands on the device grid through `rulers::snap_across_axis`** — the guides' own snap, and
it matters more here than anywhere else in the app because every line is the thinnest thing the screen
can draw, and one that straddles two pixels comes out as a two-pixel smear (§9.1). ⚠️ **It was
hand-inlined until 2026-09-07** as `round() / ppp + half` with the half unconditional (§15 D484), which
agreed at every scale *only* because the grid's line is `1.0 / ppp` points — exactly one device pixel,
so the copy only ever reached the odd branch. A 2pt grid line would have made it silently wrong, and
nothing in `grid.rs` stated the dependency. `a_pixel_grid_line_covers_whole_pixels_at_either_width`
asserts whole-pixel coverage at one *and* two device pixels, which is what makes it an assertion about
the call rather than about the callee.

Showing the grid and snapping to it are separately switchable, on purpose: "where are the pixel
boundaries" only has a useful answer when they are far enough apart to see, while "should my geometry
be whole" is true at every zoom or none.

**The top bar's right cluster carries two dropdowns**, between undo/redo and the zoom readout: **View**
(an eye and a caret) and **Snap** (a magnet and a caret), each a 160pt column of `ui::MENU_ITEM_H`
checkable rows — 24 since 2026-08-20, the same constant the context menus allocate against (§15 D262).
`ui::menu_check` is that row, drawn in the `ui::menu_frame` every floating dropdown shares.
Its 13pt accent tick keeps its column whether or not it is showing, so labels stay in one line down
the menu instead of shuffling left as things are switched off, and "off" is a dimmer label as well as
a missing tick — which is what lets the state be read at a glance rather than row by row. View holds
*Show rulers*, *Show guides*, *Lock guides*, *Show grid*, *Show layout grid*, *Show layers*, *Show
toolbar* and *Present
mode*; Snap holds *Snap to shapes*, *Snap to guides*, *Snap to grid* and *Snap to baselines*. The last
is fourth deliberately: it is the only one of the four with no accelerator and the only one that is not
Illustrator's, so it reads as the addition it is rather than displacing a row whose position someone
already knows (§15 D355). **Both menus render their rows
from `input::ViewSwitch`** — the same enum a chord names — so a row's label, its order and the state it
drives all come out of one place and cannot drift from the keyboard's reading of the same switch
(§15 D208). All of them are **view state**, following
`show_rulers`'s precedent rather than `canvas_background`'s (§15 D28), because none of them has
persisted geometric meaning; ten of the eleven switches default on, and present mode is off and not a
peer of the others anyway. The exception is **Lock guides**, which is off because locking guides
nobody has placed yet is a mode with nothing in it. The two guide rows sit straight after the rulers
they are pulled out of — rulers, guides, lock, grid — which is Illustrator's order.
**Show layout grid is fifth, immediately after Show grid** (§15 D755), because the two are different
objects — the pixel lattice against a frame's own column and row bands — and the question *"which
grid did I just hide"* is answered by reading one row against the other. It is **unbound**, on
*Snap to baselines*' reasoning (§15 D355): a chord is spent to match a convention and there is none
here to match, so `ViewSwitch::accel` answers `None` for two of the twelve.

**Rightmost in that cluster is the Settings button** — Phosphor's upright `sliders`, 28pt, ten points
clear of everything to its left because everything to its left is *this document's* and this is the
app's. It opens `settings.rs`'s modal, which is where preferences that belong to no panel live: the
arrow-key nudge step, *Show tree guides* and *Collapse groups on open* under one **Layers** eyebrow,
and the web-font switch with the cache row beside it (§5.4a, §15 D330, §15 D331). `Ctrl+,` is the same door (`shortcuts.md` §8) and can only *open* one, because
`input::resolve` is not called at all while a modal is up. It is deliberately **not** a fourth
`TopMenu` value — a modal is not a dropdown, and `Option<settings::Settings>` has to hold the form's
staged contents anyway. Preferences that a panel *is* a door onto stay on that panel: *Slashes in
names make folders* and *Re-export on save* are export habits and remain in the export popover,
written on the spot, where this modal stages everything and writes on *Save changes*.

**There is no *Share*.** An accent-outlined button sat at the right end of the cluster until
2026-08-24 and is gone: this is a local file editor with nothing to share, so it was a promise nothing
behind it could keep. The Settings button took its place in the corner.

The three dropdowns are mutually exclusive **by construction**: `app::TopMenu` holds one value
(`None | View | Snap | Zoom`), replacing the old `zoom_menu: bool`, and the design models it the same
way — its `openMenu` prop is an enum over exactly those. Three independent flags would admit two menus
overlapping with nothing ever closing the one behind. `OndinApp::dropdown` spells the *closing* half
once as well — a click outside, and Escape — because that is the half that gets forgotten, and a menu
that only closes by re-clicking its own head is one that sits over the canvas while the user works
around it. `OndinApp::context_menu` is the same one-slot shape a level out, and opening a context
menu empties this field along with the three floating popovers (above).

**Present mode hides every piece of chrome at once** — top bar, layers pane, tool rail, inspector,
picker and the rulers — leaving the artwork **and the canvas working normally**. 🚨 **That
enumeration is exhaustive and is the whole of the ruling** (§15 D750): guides, layout grids, the
selection box, the handles, the size badge, the hover outline and the frame name tags all stay, being
things you edit *with* rather than parts of the app around them, and the mode exists for editing a
large design with the panels out of the way or on a laptop screen the panels eat half of. The ruler
**bars** go because they are window furniture at the edge of the frame. *A reader tempted to fold
`present` into some overlay's predicate should read D750 first* — two such guards existed, each
arguing at length that present mode *"hides every other overlay"*, and neither was true even of the
code. It is *not* a fourth view switch beside the others: it
**overrides** the ones it reads for as long as it is on and leaves them untouched, so leaving it
restores the workspace the user had rather than a default one. ⚠️ **It reads three of the other seven
View rows** — rulers, layers and toolbar — and never touched *Show grid*, *Show layout grid* or *Lock guides* at all. ⚠️ **The canvas menu says so since §15 D758**: that menu opens in present mode now
(D756), and its *Show rulers* row is **dimmed** there — *"Present mode hides the rulers"* — while the
other four View rows stay live. **One row and not the group**, which is this paragraph's asymmetry
reaching a control: a repair that dimmed the group would be wrong about four of them, and a test that
only looked at *Show rulers* would pass it. Escape is the way out, and it is handled **first**
in `OndinApp::escape`, ahead of everything else that key unwinds, because it is the only state whose
own way out is hidden by the state itself; the menu row that turns it on closes the menu along with
the chrome it lives in. ⚠️ **One thing outside that ladder takes the key ahead of it, and since §15
D756 it can happen**: a context menu opens in present mode now, R3 answers Escape at the top of the
frame and returns without calling `escape`, so the first press closes the menu and the second leaves
the mode — the right order, and it costs no code. §1 carries it as scope, and §15 D37 has why it is a View row at all when the
design's menu has no such thing.

**The rulers are two 20pt bars; the guides pulled out of them are document state.** The bars
themselves are view state (`OndinApp::show_rulers`, on by default, `Shift`+`R` through the one
mode-aware keymap — it cannot collide with the Rect tool, whose single-key block is gated on Shift
being up — and *View ▸ Show rulers*). Every reader asks `OndinApp::rulers_on()` rather than that flag,
since present mode hides the bars too and their absence has to mean the same thing to the hit test as
to the paint, or the app claims a press for a bar nobody can see — D35's class of bug again.
⚠️ **A guide drag is the one reader that asks it *once*, at the press, and carries the answer**
(`GuideDrag::rulers_shown`, §15 D555): both halves of that predicate are live chords, and the
gesture's discard test was the only term feeding its commit, so `Shift+R` or `Ctrl+\` pressed with
the button still down turned the **cancel** gesture into a **create** one — a guide committed at
whatever coordinate the vanished bar sat over, selected and dirty, while the rest of the drag drew
nothing and the cursor went on promising a live guide. It is `left_ruler`'s rule at the other half of
the same question: that field latches the pointer's position against the bars, this one latches the
bars' existence — and **both** of that function's terms read the latch, the one deciding the commit
and the one deciding the announcement, which took two passes and is the discard cursor's paragraph
below. The
guides are not view state: they are saved with the file (§5.5), because a guide down the middle
of a layout is part of how that layout was built. **A guide is drawn as egui chrome, not as scene
content**, and all three things that makes true are wanted: it stays one hairline wide at every
zoom, it sits above the artwork including a frame that clips, and it is invisible to `ondin export`,
which renders the document rather than the editor. None of the three would hold if it were a node.

**Whether the guides are shown and whether they are locked are two more view switches**, `Ctrl+;` and
`Ctrl+Alt+;` (`shortcuts.md` §6), and each has its own predicate for the same reason `rulers_on()` has
one: `guides_on()` is `show_guides` and nothing else, and `guides_pickable()` is that and
`!lock_guides`. 🚨 **It read `show_guides && !present` until 2026-09-10 and the `!present` is gone**
(§15 D750) — present mode hides the app's chrome and leaves the canvas alone, so a designer working
with the panels out of the way keeps the guides they are aligning to. What the predicate still buys
is the other half of D136's bug, which is what made the fold look right: the guide *loop* was never
gated at all, so it drew guides over the artwork whichever switch was off, and every reader going
through one predicate is what fixed that. ⚠️ **`rulers_on()` keeps its `!self.present`** — the bars
are the other kind of thing — and **a guide is still draggable in present mode**, what the mode costs
being the *creation* of one, which is a drag off a bar that is not there; the Guide panel's position
field is the way in. `guide_lines()` returns nothing when the guides are off as well: *Show
guides* and *Snap to guides* are separate switches, but a shape jumping to a line that is not on
screen reads as a bug rather than as a snap. **Lock is a global toggle, not a per-guide property** —
Illustrator's and Photoshop's model, on this same chord; Figma and Sketch have no guide lock at all —
and that is what makes "locked = not selectable outright" safe, since the toggle that locked them is
the toggle that unlocks them and nothing has to stay reachable through a locked guide. It falls out of
**one early return** in `guide_at`, which the five things that *act* on a guide — hover, the cursor, the
press, the drag and the discard — all already go through. The measure overlay deliberately does not: it
goes through `guide_under`, the same search with no lock check, because **what may be measured is what
may be snapped to, not what may be picked up** (§15 D202). ⚠️ **Two verbs reach a guide through the
*selection* rather than through `guide_at`, and needed a gate of their own** (§15 D541): the arrow-key
nudge and `Delete`. Hiding the guides does not clear the selection and **may not** — `measurable_guide`
relies on a selected guide being able to be invisible — so `rulers::nudge_guides` and
`inspector::remove_selected_guides` each ask `guides_on()` for themselves, the second saying so in the
status line rather than swallowing the press. Without it, four presses of `↓` moved a line drawing zero
shapes and `Delete` destroyed it, under either switch and by identical numbers. It is the settings
modal's rule — *armed invisible state is worse than a refused chord* — arriving at the one surface an
enumeration scoped to the pointer could not see. Explicitly *not* the inspector header's lock button: a per-guide lock puts the
control that unlocks a guide on the card you reach by selecting it, so locking the last guide hides
the way back. New guides can still be dragged out of the ruler while locked and land locked — the
switch exists to stop existing placements being nudged, not to block the feature — but **the release
must not select one**, because a selected-but-unselectable guide would draw 2px blue and never be
pickable again; `set_guides_locked` drops any guides it is holding on locking for the same reason. It
drops the **guide** half only, through `Selection::clear_guides`, and that narrowness is the
interesting part rather than an implementation detail: the exclusivity invariant makes "there is only
ever one of the two to drop" read as though clearing everything were harmless, and it is not — with
*layers* selected there are no guides to drop, so a full clear achieved nothing except deselecting the
user's work. Pulling a
guide out of the ruler while the guides are *hidden* switches *Show guides* back on, and does so **on
the press** rather than the release, so the line is visible while it is being placed; the lock is
deliberately not treated that way, since locked guides are still on screen doing their job.

**Each ruler highlights the selection.** A tinted band spans the selection's world extent on that
bar's axis — the top bar the x range, the left bar the y range — with the band's two end coordinates
called out in `ACCENT_200` over the ordinary tick numbers. It answers a question the ticks alone
cannot: not "where is this" but "how wide is it", read off the ruler without going to the inspector.
A tinted ground (`ACCENT_900`) rather than an outline, because it has to read as a *region of the
ruler* rather than as another object drawn on it, and in the accent's darkest tier so the ticks and
numbers over it stay the brightest things in the bar. It is read through the preview layer, so it
tracks a live drag or resize rather than arriving a frame late, and a tick number that would sit
under one of the band's own numbers is dropped in favour of it (`EXTENT_LABEL_CLEAR`) — two numbers
overprinted are worse than either alone. **The band's two numbers take the same fallback the tick
numbers do** — plain form, then a thousands form (`1080` → `1.1k`), then nothing — because on the
left bar the constraint is not the end of the ruler but the 17pt a label has to read *across*, and
those are two different questions that were for a while one `if`: a 1920×1080 frame's band read `0`
and then nothing at all while the lattice beside it printed `1k` (§15 D547). Like the tick labels
they are clipped to their own bar, so unlike a guide's position chip (§15 D34) they cannot grow to
fit and a shorter number is the only alternative to no number. The band is clamped to the bar rather
than skipped when the selection runs off the viewport, because a band stopping at the edge says "it
continues" where nothing at all would say "no selection", but it vanishes entirely once none of it is
on screen rather than showing a sliver pinned at the edge claiming the selection ends there.
`extent_band` is a free function precisely so that arithmetic can be tested
(`the_selection_band_spans_its_axis_and_clips_to_the_bar`) — the band's geometry is a function of the
selection's box and the bar, and a test of it should not have to stand the app up (§15 D303, which
retired the older reason that an `OndinApp` could not be built at all).

**With a single frame selected the rulers count from that frame's own origin**, so `0` sits on its
leading edge and the band then reads `0` to the frame's width — exactly the `W` the inspector is
showing. The tick lattice is anchored to that origin rather than merely relabelled, so `0` lands on
the frame's edge instead of a step away from it. Only a lone frame, though: Figma also re-origins
for a shape *inside* a frame and this deliberately does not, because the inspector reads X/Y in
world space (D5) and the two would then disagree about where the same shape is. §15 D36 has the
argument, and the rough edge on a rotated frame. **The origin is not draggable and never will be**, for
the same reason — §15 D137.

*Two different things in this crate are called a guide, and they are not the same.* `rulers.rs` has
these — persistent lines the user places, saved with the document. `snap.rs::Guide` is a transient
line drawn for one frame to explain a snap that is happening, and it is neither saved nor
selectable. `snap.rs` both snaps *to* the first and draws the second, and its module docs open by
saying so, because that is the end of the collision where someone will meet it.

**A gesture snaps to ruler guides as well as to node bounds.** The dragged box's edges and centres
are compared against both, and the guides arrive as `snap::GuideLines { x, y }` — plain coordinates
split by the axis each guide pins, not `ondin_core::Guide`s, so `snap.rs` goes on knowing nothing
about the document. `OndinApp::guide_lines` builds it through `shown_guide`, so a guide being
dragged snaps against where it *looks like it is* rather than where the document still says it is.
**A frame-scoped guide is projected there, and only where projecting means something.** That is why
frame-local guides and coordinate-only snapping cost `snap.rs` no change at all: the projection
happens at the collection site rather than in the comparison. `rulers::upright(world)` — angle and
skew both ≈ 0, mirrors allowed — is the predicate, and a guide in a rotated frame has no single world
x or y to report, so it contributes nothing and **draws but does not attract**. A quarter turn is
deliberately not treated as upright either: a horizontal guide in a 90° frame pins a world *x*, which
`GuideLines`'s axis split cannot express, so the honest answer is the same one. One predicate, and it
also decides whether the dotted extension is drawn (below) and whether the measure overlay can quote
the guide at all (`rulers::measure_guide`, below), so "does it snap", "does it extend" and "can it be
measured to" cannot drift apart.
Every guide is considered, with no culling: a document has a handful of guides where it has
thousands of nodes, so the view test `snap::targets` needs would cost more than the comparison it
saves. Two rules on top of that. **A ruler guide wins a tie with a node** — someone placed the guide
on purpose and to line work up against, while a node edge at the same coordinate is a coincidence,
and preferring the guide is also what stops a snap flickering between the two as a node moves under
it. And **snapping to a guide draws no snap line**: the guide is already a line across the whole
canvas in its own colour, so a second one laid exactly along it would say nothing and muddy the one
already there. The private `Matched { Node(Rect), RulerGuide, Baseline(f64), Spacing(..) }` enum exists
for that second rule alone — it decides what is drawn, never where the box lands.

**A gesture snaps to text baselines too, and that is its own switch** (§15 D355). `Snapping::baselines`
is a bare `Vec<f64>` of world ys — `canvas::baseline_lines` reads `TextLayout::baselines` off the
cached layout of every visible text node in view that is not part of the gesture, and transforms it,
so the whole source costs one point per line and nothing is re-shaped; `SNAP_TARGET_LIMIT` caps it,
as it caps the shape targets. **"Not part of the gesture" means the whole subtree, not the node
named**, the rule `snapped_resize` states and `snap::targets` had all along: this asked
`moving.contains(&id)` alone until 2026-09-07, so dragging a group offered the baselines of the text
*inside* it, read off the committed tree and therefore standing still — the group stuck for the first
six units and then jumped (§15 D468). `snap::is_inside_any` is the one spelling of the ancestry half,
asked by both sources. **A y-only source rather than more `guides.y`**, though the shape is
identical, because the two part company downstream: a ruler guide is *already a drawn line* and so a
match on one draws no mark, whereas a baseline is invisible unless its own node is selected — and the
node being snapped to is by definition not the one being dragged — so `Matched::Baseline` **does** draw
its mark, spanning the moving box alone, there being no target rect to reach towards. It carries the
matched coordinate rather than re-deriving it the way `Node` does through `nearest_of`: a rect has
three features per axis and the winner has to be recovered, where a baseline *is* the coordinate.
**Its own menu toggle rather than a refinement of *Snap to shapes***, because every line of every text
node in view is a candidate — an order of magnitude more magnetism than the other three together on a
page of copy — and someone who wants edges and centres without it needs a way to say so. On by
default, and deliberately **unbound**: the other three chords are Illustrator's and there is no
convention to match for this one. **A rotated or skewed text node contributes nothing**, on the same
reasoning as a guide in a rotated frame: a slanted baseline has no single world y, and offering the
transformed one would snap a box to a number that lies on the baseline at exactly one point. **A
half-turn is admitted**, though, and that is what the off-diagonal test is chosen for rather than an
accident of it: at 180° the baselines really are still horizontal, where `rulers::upright`'s
decomposition would refuse them. It is
still *drawn* (above), which is the better way round for a gap — the honest fix is a slanted snap
target, which nothing in `snap.rs` can express.
`a_rotated_or_hidden_text_node_offers_no_baselines_but_a_half_turn_does` pins the refusal, the
half-turn and the hidden-node skip, `the_moving_node_is_excluded_from_its_own_baselines` pins the
exclusion without which a text node snaps to itself and cannot be moved, and
`a_moving_group_does_not_snap_to_the_baseline_of_the_text_inside_it` pins the ancestry half and that
`snapping` hands the gesture the same answer — none of the first three passes a non-empty `moving` at
all, which is why the ancestry half could be missing under a suite that read as covering it. **A ruler guide the user placed still wins a dead heat
against a baseline they did not**, and so does a node edge; `a_ruler_guide_takes_a_tie_against_a_baseline`
pins all three cases, and §15 D355 records which mechanism is actually load-bearing there and which
merely looks it.

**A move also snaps to *equal gaps*, and that is the one snap whose explanation carries numbers.**
`snap::spacing_candidates` offers two per axis: put the moving box **halfway between its two
neighbours** — the delta that equalizes the gaps is half their difference — or **match the rhythm** past
the end of a run, where the gap between the last two members is what the next gap wants to be, so a row
spaces itself as it is built rather than only once it is finished and distributed. Only boxes that
**share a band** with the moving one are considered, strictly: two shapes whose vertical extents miss
each other are not in a row and the horizontal "gap" between them is a number about nothing, and the
same test is what keeps the candidate set the size of a row rather than of the viewport. Nothing is
offered against a neighbour the box *overlaps* on the axis, there being no gap to equalize and a sign
that would flip under the pointer, and nothing below `snap::MIN_GAP` (0.5), a gap that small being two
boxes touching — which alignment already handles. It is **move only**: `snap_point` is untouched,
because a resize would have to decide whether to equalize by moving the dragged edge or the anchored
one, and the anchored edge is the thing a resize may not touch (`a_resize_handle_gets_no_spacing`
asserts that rather than leaving it an omission). A disabled *Snap to shapes* leaves `targets` empty, so
spacing switches off with the alignment candidates and needs no fourth toggle.

**What a snap drew arrives as `snap::Marks { guides, gaps }`.** Two lists because the two say different
kinds of thing: a `Guide` is an alignment, a bare line whose number would be zero, where a gap is only
worth drawing *with* its number. The gaps are `measure::Measure`s and go through
`canvas::draw_measure` — the Alt-hover measure's own function — so a red labelled distance means one
thing everywhere, whether the app is *reporting* a gap or has just *created* one. `From<Vec<Guide>>`
converts for the four non-move snap functions, none of which can produce a gap, and the overlay builds
`Marks` in **every**
arm of its match on `Drag` rather than in the move arm alone, so there is no second match beside it
asking the same question of the same gesture. §15 D200 has the precedence, why the gaps are built from
the neighbours after the delta lands rather than at candidate time, and the fixture trap in testing any
of it.

**Shift locks the axis of a move, and the lock is enforced inside the snap.** `snap::move_axes` says
which world axes the drag may travel along — both, or with the key held the one it has gone furthest
along — and `snap::constrain` zeroes the rest before the snap ever sees the delta. `snap_rect` then
takes that same `(bool, bool)` pair `snap_point` has always taken, gating node candidates, ruler-guide
candidates *and* the pixel-grid fallback per axis, so a locked axis comes back with an adjustment of
exactly zero and no line. Constraining **inside** the snap rather than zeroing its result afterwards is
the load-bearing part: a snap on the locked axis would slide the layer off the line the user is
holding it to, and it would draw a guide taking credit for an adjustment that was then thrown away.
The dominant axis is re-read from the live delta **every frame** rather than fixed when the key went
down, so a drag that starts sideways and swings downward follows the hand, and the tie goes to x —
which is what makes the first frame of every Shift-drag, where the delta is still zero, horizontal
rather than undefined; undefined there is a layer that refuses to move until the pointer happens to
break the tie. `shift_locks_the_axis_the_drag_is_mostly_travelling_along` and
`a_locked_axis_neither_snaps_nor_explains_itself` pin the two halves, and §15 D47 has why Shift means
this and not what it used to.

**A resize snaps too, and it snaps the pointer rather than the box.** `snap::snap_point` is the
resize counterpart of `snap_rect`, and it has to be a separate function rather than a reuse: a move
translates the whole box, so every edge is a candidate and any of them may pull it, whereas a resize
moves one corner or edge and **must leave the opposite one exactly where it is** — snapping the box
would drag the anchored side along, which is the one thing a resize may not do. So it snaps the
*pointer* instead: `resize_to_handle` puts the dragged handle exactly where the pointer is, so a
snapped pointer is a snapped edge and nothing else moves. Node features and ruler guides both, with
the same tolerance as a move and the same rule about lines — drawn for a node match, not for a guide.
`Shift` does not switch it off; the key's only meaning on a resize is `keep_ratio` (§15 D47).

The subtle part is `OndinApp::resize_axes`: which **world** axes the handle travels along. Taken from
`Handle::outward` mapped through the node's world transform, not from `Handle::outward` alone,
because on a node rotated 45° the "right" side moves along both world axes and snapping only x would
hold it back from a horizontal guide it is plainly crossing; the axes the handle does *not* travel
along must be left untouched, or the anchored edge moves. The threshold is 0.3, well inside 1/√2, so
a 45° edge claims both axes rather than neither — pinned by
`a_resize_handle_snaps_only_on_the_axes_it_moves` and
`a_resize_handle_snaps_to_shapes_and_explains_only_those`. **A multi-selection is the same reading with
its own frame in place of a node's world transform** — `canvas::selection_frame`, the transform its
handles are drawn with — rather than the `Affine::IDENTITY` short-circuit it used to take, which was
right only while a set's box could only be upright and wrong from the moment a turn or a lean outlived
its gesture (§15 D326, D478); at rest that frame *is* the identity, so this is the world reading it
always was, and `a_turned_sets_snap_axes_are_its_own` pins the pair. The lines explaining a live gesture are
recomputed in `draw_canvas` for Move and Resize alike rather than stashed on `Drag`: they are a pure
function of the pointer and the document, so a stored copy could only go stale.

**And a dragged guide snaps onto shapes.** `snap::snap_guide` catches node edges and centres on the
guide's own axis. It earns its place through a workflow rather than through symmetry, and the
workflow is what explains the whole feature: block a layout out with plain rectangles, drop guides
onto their edges, delete the rectangles. Without it the guides in that sequence are placed by eye and
the rectangles were pointless. Nodes only, deliberately — **not** other guides: two guides at the
same coordinate are a mistake rather than a goal, and making them attract each other would make that
mistake easier to commit. Nothing is excluded from the target set either, in contrast with
`snap::targets`, which drops **the gesture's own subtree and nothing else** (§15 D43) — a guide is not
a node, so it has no self to skip and nothing travelling with it, and the whole visible page is fair
game. The snap is off at the
press and on from the first move, because a guide that jumped to a nearby edge the instant it was
picked up would look like a misplaced click. `Shift` does nothing here at all, deliberately: it used to
suppress the snap, and a guide has one axis and so nothing to constrain instead (§15 D48).
`a_dragged_guide_catches_shape_edges_and_centres` pins the edges and the centres.

**Pixel rounding is the fallback under every snap, never a competitor to one.** `snap::pixel_delta`
is consulted only for an axis nothing else claimed: an alignment or guide match on an axis wins
outright and rounding is not asked, because a shape lined up with another shape's edge at 100.5
belongs at 100.5, and rounding it to 100 afterwards would break the alignment that was just found. So
the precedence above — a ruler guide beats a node, and beats a baseline — extends downward into a full
ladder: **node/guide/baseline match > pixel grid > nothing**, with an equal-gap match competing on distance at the top
rung and losing ties to the alignments (above, and §15 D200). That is what keeps geometry whole without
the designer thinking about it. An axis a Shift-locked move has forbidden is outside the ladder altogether and is
not offered the grid either, so a layer held to a line does not creep onto whole pixels perpendicular
to it, however fractional it was to begin with.

It reaches four kinds of gesture. A move rounds the box's *leading* edge — the node's position, the number the
inspector's X field holds — so the width is untouched. A resize rounds the dragged edge only and never
an anchored axis, for the same reason `snap_point` exists at all — and that one function serves five
gestures, a line endpoint, a pen anchor and a point or segment drag alongside the handle, all of them
governed by the same *Snap to grid* switch (§15 D440). A dragged guide rounds, because a
guide half a pixel off passes that error on to everything aligned against it. And **shape creation**
rounds both ends of the drag, through `canvas::pixel_point`: a shape born 433.7 wide has to be
corrected by hand afterwards, so creation is where "pixel perfect" is actually won or lost. Creation
takes the grid and deliberately *not* alignment snapping — a drag that draws a box is aiming at a
*size*, and having the far corner jump to a neighbour's edge mid-draw changes the size being watched.
`an_unclaimed_axis_falls_to_the_pixel_grid`, `an_alignment_match_is_not_then_rounded_away`,
`a_resize_rounds_the_dragged_edge_only` and `a_guide_that_catches_nothing_lands_on_a_whole_pixel` pin
the four, and `each_snap_source_can_be_switched_off_independently` pins the shapes, guides and grid
toggles **over a move, which is the only path it drives** — `a_dragged_point_falls_to_the_grid_only_when_the_grid_is_on`
is the grid half of it over `snap_point`, added when that gesture turned out not to be asking (§15
D440) — and **not the baselines one**, whose switch is asserted on the overlay half only
(`a_selected_text_node_draws_one_hairline_per_baseline`) and nowhere on the source half. Shift does not
suppress the grid on a creation drag any more — the grid is the Snap menu's to switch off (§15 D47).

**Shift while drawing constrains the extents instead.** `canvas::create_corner` gives the far corner of
a shape being dragged out the same extent on both axes while the key is held, so a rect comes out
square, an ellipse circular and a polygon regular. The **larger** extent wins, so the shape grows to
enclose the pointer rather than shrinking to whichever axis the hand travelled less along, and each
axis keeps its own sign, so the constraint works in all four directions from the press. The order is
load-bearing: the corner is **rounded to the grid and then squared**, never the other way round.
`begin_create` already puts `start` on the grid, so squaring a rounded extent gives two equal whole
numbers, where squaring first and rounding second rounds each axis independently and can leave a
"square" a pixel off. `squared_corner` is a free function for the same reason `frame_covering` is —
the arithmetic can then be checked without a live gesture — and
`a_constrained_draw_is_square_in_every_direction` pins all four diagonals, the single-axis drag a plain
`min` would have collapsed to a zero-extent sliver, and the no-drag case a careless `copysign` turns
into `NaN`. `create_corner` dispatches on the **gesture's own** `shape`, the one `Drag::Create` carries,
and not on `self.tool`, so the constraint cannot change under a drag already in flight.

**A line gets a direction instead of equal extents.** Equal extents on a line means exactly 45°, which
would make a Shift-drawn *horizontal* line impossible, so `canvas::axial_corner` pulls the far end onto
the nearest **eighth of a turn** — the two axes and the four diagonals. Eighths rather than
`ROTATE_SNAP`'s 15°, because the two gestures want different granularities: rotating an existing shape
is a fine adjustment and wants many stops, whereas drawing a constrained line is asking for one of the
few directions a designer actually names, and finer steps only make the axes harder to hit. **The
direction is held as an integer step, not as an angle**, which is the load-bearing part — for a multiple
of 45° the unit vector rounds to one of the eight `(0, ±1)`, `(±1, 0)`, `(±1, ±1)`, so rounding the
*length* to a whole number is enough to land the endpoint on the pixel grid without leaving the angle.
Going through `cos`/`sin` and rounding the resulting endpoint per axis instead would put a 45° line on
the grid at the cost of it no longer being at 45°, which is the one thing the constraint exists to
promise (§15 D47). The length itself is the pointer's **projection** onto that direction, the same way
an axis-locked move drops the component it may not travel (`snap::constrain`), so the endpoint tracks
how far along the line the hand has gone rather than swinging out to the full drag distance.
`a_constrained_line_lands_on_an_exact_eighth_of_a_turn` asserts both requirements together across all
eight directions — whole `dx` and `dy` *and* equal-or-one-zero — since the grid and the angle are
exactly where they could conflict, plus the degenerate no-drag case. `axial_corner` has a second
caller now — the endpoint handles a selected line gets (above), measuring from the end that is *not*
moving — so a line is straightened by exactly the rule it was drawn straight by. **The Pen tool gets
nothing**, and
that exclusion is permanent rather than a gap: it places anchors one click at a time, so there is no
extent for a modifier to constrain.

**Alt while drawing moves the press point to the *centre* of what comes out** (§15 D289). Without it a
create drag reads corner to corner; with it `canvas::create_box` mirrors the near end through the
press, so the shape grows both ways at once and the point the hand put down is the point it is centred
on. That is the gesture an ellipse in particular wants, where the thing the eye is placing is the
centre and the corner it is nominally drawn from is a fiction — Figma, Illustrator and Photoshop all
read Alt this way, and it is the same sentence Alt already speaks on a resize handle (`tools::Resize`'s
`symmetric`): *hold the middle still*. A line takes the same arm; its two ends are not a box, but they
are the same two points, and "grow out from where I clicked" is if anything more obviously right for a
line. **The order is load-bearing again, and the other way round from the grid's**: `create_box`
constrains *first* and mirrors second. The constraint is then measured from the press, so squaring
gives equal extents from the centre and doubling them leaves a square; mirroring first and squaring
after also yields a square, but one measured across a box the pointer is only half of, and it lands
centred somewhere the hand never pointed at — a 30 × 20 drag from `(100, 100)` comes out centred at
`(100, 110)`. The grid survives either way, since `start` is on it and so therefore is `2·start −
corner`. `centred_ends` is a free function for the reason `squared_corner` is, and
`alt_grows_the_drawn_box_out_from_the_press_point` and
`alt_and_shift_centre_the_square_on_the_press_rather_than_near_it` pin the two claims — both on the
*centre* rather than on the size, which is what tells the right answer from the two wrong ones that
have the same extent.

**Every creation tool's click goes through one table**, `Tool::click_makes() -> Option<ClickCreate>`,
an exhaustive `match` over `Tool` with no wildcard (§15 D295). What a click has to decide when the
gesture gives it no box is where the *size* comes from, and there are three answers: a constant
(`DefaultBox` — Rect, Ellipse, Polygon, Star), the file (`FittedImage` — Image), or what gets typed
(`TextNode` — Text). Frame and Line answer `None` deliberately, and everything else is not a creation
tool. `canvas::normal_mode_input` has **one** creation-click arm dispatching on it. It was three
separate `if`s and one of the three was simply absent — the Image tool had no click arm at all, so a
loaded cursor could only be discharged by dragging a box, while the completeness of the set was
asserted in a doc comment that nothing could contradict. A `match` with no wildcard is that same claim
as a build error.

**A click with a shape tool makes one at a default size** (§15 D291). `ClickCreate::DefaultBox`
— Rect, Ellipse, Polygon and Star — answers a plain click with a `tools::CLICK_CREATE_SIZE` square at
the pointer, so the four tools stop being drag-only: a 100 × 100 rect, a 100-diameter circle, and a
triangle and a five-pointed star in the same box, each with its tool's own defaults because the
transaction is built by the same `create_tx`. Before this the click did **nothing at all**, and not by
a decision: egui reports a still press as `clicked()` and never as a drag, so `Drag::Create` never
started and `MIN_CREATE_PX`'s "discard a stray click" arm was never even reached — that constant only
ever discarded the out-and-back drag. **The click synthesizes the gesture rather than duplicating it**:
`click_create` runs `begin_create` (which picks the parent frame, mints the id and seeds the side
count), takes two points from `click_box`, and hands them to `commit_create` — the tail the drag's
release now shares, so "text opens for typing, an image spends itself, a shape goes back to Select"
is written once. **Alt centres the box on the click and does not resize it**, which is the one place
Alt reads differently from a drag: a drag's Alt doubles the extent because the extent is what the hand
is authoring, and a click authors none. Shift has nothing to say, the default box being square already.
**Frame and Line are held back deliberately** — a default-sized frame is a guess about a layout, and a
line has no box, so the box arm would hand it a diagonal nobody asked for. `tools.rs`'s
`every_tool_answers_a_click_with_exactly_what_it_should` lists all fourteen tools rather than
spot-checking, since the list is exactly what prose got wrong, and pins the containment with it:
anything that answers a click drags a box too, or it would be a creation tool with only one way to be
given a size.

**A click with the Image tool places the picture at its own size** (`ClickCreate::FittedImage`, §15
D295) — intrinsic, aspect kept, shrunk only if it exceeds the frame or the viewport
(`tools::fitted_image_size`, D177), and centred on the pointer rather than hung from it, because a
loaded cursor is holding the picture rather than its top-left corner. A *drag* takes
`create_image_in_box` instead and is obeyed exactly, aspect included: a drawn box is an instruction,
and the fit rule exists for the gesture that gives no size. The two gestures differ in how the layer is
measured and in nothing else.

**A create drag also reads two keys of its own** (`canvas::reshape_create`, `shortcuts.md` §9): `Space`
held repositions the shape that is not committed yet, and `↑`/`↓` add and remove a polygon's or star's
sides while it is being drawn — Figma's and Illustrator's respectively, and the two most-missed gestures
when they are absent. Both are read in the gesture's own loop rather than resolved into an `Action`,
which is the same division the pen's `Enter` and a text session's `Tab` already follow: a key that
reaches the *document* wants the keymap, a key that only means something inside a gesture already in
flight belongs to that gesture. Space moves `start` by the pointer **delta** and not to its position,
because the key is picked up and put down mid-drag and the far corner is already tracking the pointer;
the side count lives on `Drag::Create` as a live field seeded from the tool's default, so it survives
into the commit rebuild. The arrows' other claimant is the keymap's nudge, so `dispatch` drops
`Action::Nudge` for as long as a create drag is up — otherwise drawing a heptagon walks the previously
selected layer four steps across the artboard — and `Action::SizeStep` with it, for the sharper version
of the same reason: a shape whose size the pointer is drawing must not also be taking one from the
keyboard (§15 D346). The cursor's armed-pan check excludes a live create
drag, so Space mid-draw does not promise a pan it will not give. `tools::step_sides` holds the
arithmetic and its clamp to `geometry::MIN_SIDES..=MAX_SIDES` so they can be tested away from a gesture.

**An armed pan outranks every tool, and a *click* while it is armed is the same statement as the drag**
(§15 D293). `panning_armed` — Space held, the Hand tool, or a middle-button drag — already guards
`guide_input`, the pen, the node tool, image editing and the drag arm, each spelling it out for itself.
The three **click** arms now read one binding, `let clicked = resp.clicked() && !panning_armed`, rather
than repeating the condition: written per arm it was carried by one of the three, so Space+click
planted a caret with the Text tool and changed or cleared the selection with Select — a pan that
happened not to travel, arriving at the tool as an edit. *A guard written once per arm should be read
as a guard that is already missing from one of them.*

**Every source arrives as one value.** `snap::Snapping { targets, guides, baselines, pixel, zoom }` is
built in one place — `OndinApp::snapping` — and every snap function takes it whole. A struct rather
than a parameter each, because they are one decision, "what may snapping consult", and threading them
separately is how a call site ends up honouring some and quietly forgetting one. **A source
that is switched off arrives empty, not flagged**: an empty candidate list cannot win, so the toggle
is enforced by construction at that one site instead of being re-checked at every comparison. `pixel`
is the exception and has to be a flag, because the lattice is everywhere and there is no list of it to
leave empty. `zoom` is deliberately not `Default`-able — a zero zoom would make the screen-space
tolerance effectively infinite and snap everything to everything. And **the Snap menu is the only way
to switch snapping off**: no gesture and no modifier is a switch for it, and the menu's own
everything-off state goes through the ordinary path with empty sources rather than through a
special case — which is why `snap::Snapping::none` is `#[cfg(test)]` and not production API (§15 D47).
A count of the toggles is deliberately not written into that sentence: it said "three" until baselines
made it four (§15 D355), and the rule it states was never about how many there are.

One gesture, one transaction, as everywhere else (invariant 5). Dragging off a ruler creates a
guide; dragging a guide moves it; dropping one back on *its own* ruler deletes it — and a
brand-new one released there is simply never created, so history never hears about the gesture at
all. **Where the pointer is when the drag ends decides the scope**: inside a frame's boundary scopes
the guide to it, outside leaves it global, and a guide can be dragged from either mode to the other in
one gesture. Frames nest, so it is the innermost frame under the pointer — the rule `create_artboard`
already uses, with one difference that matters: `rulers::frame_at_world` tests containment through the
frame's *inverse* world transform, so a **rotated** frame's true rectangle is what counts and a drop
in the corner of its AABB stays global. The commit is one `SetGuideScope` and never a position edit
beside a scope edit, for §5.7's reason. The press both selects the guide and picks it up, as a layer's
handles do, `Delete`/`Backspace`
removes, and a press that never moved commits nothing, because an undo step for a guide that is
exactly where it was is a step the user has to press through to reach a real one — where "moved"
