counts the *scope* too, since dragging a guide into a frame without shifting its line is still a
change. **That whole table is `finish_guide_drag`'s six arms, and it had no test caller at all until
2026-09-07** (§15 D474): `the_guide_commit_table_answers_each_of_its_arms` now releases the drag and
asserts against the document and the undo depth, and it is what says an Alt-dragged copy dropped back
on the ruler leaves the original alone. ⚠️ **The no-op rule above is enforced twice now**, and the
guard here is no longer the load-bearing copy — a `SetGuideScope` that writes back the owner and
position already stored is dropped at `EditorSession::commit_inner` (§15 D428), so what the local
`moved` test buys is the operation not being built. **Shift+click adds a guide to the selection** and deliberately does not start a move: several
guides do not share an axis, so there is nothing one drag of them could mean. `Ctrl+A` still selects
**layers** whatever is selected, decided rather than overlooked — "select every guide" is not what
that chord means anywhere else — and `Selection::set` clears the guide half accordingly. **Arrow keys
nudge every selected guide** along the one axis each of them has: `OndinApp::nudge` routes to
`nudge_guides`, which gives each guide only the arrow component on its own axis, so Up on a mixed-axis
selection moves the horizontals and leaves the verticals alone — inert
rather than an error, since beeping about Left when Up and Down both work would be noise. One press,
one transaction, one undo step over the whole set, and `Shift` still gives the coarse step; Remove and
the picker's write are one transaction over the set for the same reason. ⚠️ **And a *burst* of presses
is one undo step too, since 2026-09-07** (§15 D482): the nudge commits through `commit_run` under its
own verb, `nudge-guides`, so it can never coalesce into a layer nudge. It was a plain `commit` until
then — which the sentence above did not cover, being written about the set rather than about the repeat
— and a two-second hold of `↓` put about 45 entries on the undo stack where the same keystroke on a
layer put one. The obstruction was core's rather than the app's: `Shape` was built from
`Operation::overwrites`, which answers `None` for a guide (§5.8). The
priority on the canvas is: an armed pan, then **any selection chrome**, then the ruler bar — which claims a press from
**every** tool, since dragging a rectangle out of the ruler was never what anyone meant — then the
guide lines, which answer the Select tool only, because they lie over artwork a pen or shape tool is
aimed at. A gesture already in flight keeps the pointer regardless, so a marquee dragged up over the
ruler is still a marquee.

⚠️ **"Any selection chrome" is `OndinApp::chrome_claims`, and that middle rung read "a selection
handle" until 2026-09-07** (§15 D486). It asked `Handles::armed`, which knows the corner handles, the
side bands and the rotate ring and nothing else, where `canvas::begin_select_drag`'s press ladder has
**four** rungs above the artwork — the pivot marker, a line's endpoints, the rail handle, then the box
handles — so three of the four were invisible to it and a guide lying across one of them took the press
the cursor had just promised. For a lone `Line` it was false at *every* pixel, `selection_handles`
returning `None` for one. `chrome_claims` walks the same four and answers a bool; it takes the point as
a parameter because the two callers legitimately ask about different ones — the hover position here,
`press_origin` there (§15 D29). **A parallel ladder rather than a lifted one**, so the two can drift,
and `a_guide_does_not_steal_a_press_the_chrome_claims` is what binds them: it sweeps a strip of points
and asserts the gate and the ladder agree at every one. A fifth rung in `begin_select_drag` owes
`chrome_claims` a term.

**Everything above is decided on the press, from `press_origin`, not at drag-start** — the ruler
bar's claim included. Getting that wrong is what made a guide nearly impossible to pick up at all;
§15 D35 has the failure and why it is the same class of bug as D29. The grab band is
`GUIDE_PICK_PT`, 6pt, deliberately the same as `canvas::EDGE_PICK_PX`: a guide and the invisible
strip along a selection box's edge are the same affordance — a line you drag sideways — so one
should be no harder to hit than the other. **Drawing and picking are built from one resolved
`GuideLine`**, and the distance is to that **segment** rather than to an infinite line, so a scoped
guide is grabbable exactly where it is drawn and the empty canvas beside a short one is not a 6pt band
claiming to be a guide. The dotted continuation is not a target either, which is consistent: it only
appears once the guide is already hovered or selected.

**Guides join the clipboard.** `OndinApp::guide_clipboard: Option<Vec<Guide>>` sits beside the layer
`clipboard`, and the two are kept mutually exclusive **by hand** — every copy clears the other — which is
deliberately the shape `Selection` uses for its own two halves (§9.3) and for the same reason: a selection
is layers *or* guides, so a copy is one or the other and there is no state where holding both means
anything. **`property_clipboard` is a third slot and is deliberately *not* in that arrangement**
(§15 D257): it answers a different chord with a different verb, so holding an appearance *and* a set
of layers at once means exactly what it says, and clearing one from the other would make copying a
layer silently forget an appearance the user is halfway through applying. Whole `Guide`s rather than
captured subtrees, because a guide has no children, transform or
paint, so the struct *is* the template. `app::pasted_guide(from, id, owner, step)` is the one placement rule,
shared by paste and duplicate so the two cannot drift: fresh id, axis and colour carried across, position
stepped by `GUIDE_PASTE_OFFSET` — `PASTE_OFFSET.x`, so a guide and a layer step by the same amount — and a
free function, so the placement is testable without an `OndinApp` (§15 D35). ⚠️ **The step is a
parameter and not the constant, so that paste-in-place can ask for none** (§15 D248): *in place* has
to mean the same thing to a guide as to a layer, or one chord is two features. Every other caller
passes `GUIDE_PASTE_OFFSET`. (This sentence read `pasted_guide(from, id, owner)` until 2026-09-09 and
had been an argument short since D248 added the fourth.) **The scope comes across
rather than being re-derived from the pointer**: a guide down the middle of a card belongs to that card. A
frame deleted between the copy and the paste is the one case that cannot be honoured, and those guides
fall back to the canvas rather than being dropped, so a paste never silently loses one — the number is
carried over unchanged, so a frame-local offset becomes a world coordinate, which is the honest
consequence of there being nothing left to measure it against, and the message says how many were
re-scoped. ⚠️ **Both counts in that message come off the ops the paste built, never off the
selection** (§15 D680), and the reason is the lock two paragraphs down: `select_pasted_guides`
returns early while guides are locked, so a count read after it said *"Pasted 0 guide(s) — 2 whose
frame is gone are now on the canvas"*. `duplicate_guides` had it right all along, which is what makes
this a disagreement between two doors on one rule rather than an oversight. **The copy also puts the axis and the number on the *system* clipboard, and that is not
decoration**: `egui_winit` only emits `Event::Paste` when the OS clipboard holds something, and that event
is the only form `Ctrl`+`V` reaches the app in, so a copy that left it alone would be a copy that could
not be pasted. `Ctrl`+`X` needed its guard widened to ask about guides at all: it tested the *layer*
selection only, so with a guide selected Cut returned while Copy worked — a gap the user can see, since
one of two adjacent keys silently doing nothing reads as broken rather than as unimplemented.

**`Ctrl`+`D` on a guide goes through neither the clipboard nor a `CloneChain`.** Not the clipboard,
because duplicate is its own verb and borrowing it would make `Ctrl`+`D` silently overwrite what
`Ctrl`+`C` put there; no chain, because the copy becomes the selection, so repeating `Ctrl`+`D` walks
along in even steps by itself and lays out a row of guides without measuring anything — which is the case
the chain exists to serve for layers (below). It shares the placement rule and nothing else. **`Alt`+drag
copies a guide** the way it copies a layer: `GuideDrag::copying`, a live modifier read every frame (§15
D40), needing none of `canvas::AltClone`'s machinery — no subtree to capture, no ids minted up front —
because nothing is created until the release. Only an existing guide can be copied; on a new one Alt would
change nothing. Two places had to learn it and both are what a later edit would undo: the draw loop stops
skipping the dragged guide, since the original really does stay put and drawing it is the point, and
`shown_guide` stops applying the drag override to it — otherwise the "original" follows the pointer too
and the copy is invisible, one line moving where two were promised. A copy released over the ruler is
discarded like any other line in flight, and the original is untouched (§15 D140). Every one of these
leaves the new guide **unselected while the guides are locked** — paste and duplicate through
`select_pasted_guides`, the Alt-copy's release inline beside the fresh guide's — which is the lock's
selected-but-unselectable trap (above) reaching two more call sites.

**A guide has three states and only the selected one changes the ink.** Resting is 1px in the guide's
own colour; hover is that same 1px line *plus* the position chip and the dotted extension, with no
darken and no extra weight — the chip is the affordance, and Figma's darken-on-hover would have been
defeated by a per-guide colour anyway; selected is 2px in `color::SELECT`, the same blue as every
hover outline and bounding box in the app (§15 D13), with the chip. **The blue overrides a recoloured
guide for as long as it is picked**, which reverses an earlier decision and is intended; §15 D139 has
the reversal and the bug it caused.

**A frame-scoped guide shows a dotted continuation beyond its frame**, on hover and while selected
(Figma's). It is the guide's own line carried on, taking exactly the `(width, colour)` that state gave
the solid part from the same two locals, so it cannot drift from the line it belongs to. Global guides
have none — they already span the canvas — and nor does a guide in a rotated frame, because a dashed
line promising an alignment that cannot happen is worse than no line (the `upright` predicate above).
**Two clipping tests are live at once and they are different tests**: the solid segment is bounded by
the owner *frame*, the dotted one by the viewport.

**The rulers track the pointer**, as Photoshop, Illustrator and Figma all do: a full-thickness mark
on both bars, from the `hover_pos` already threaded in for the guide hover test. Full thickness rather
than a longer tick because it has to be findable while it *moves*, and with no number beside it — the
bar's own ticks say where it is. Suppressed while a **guide** drag is in flight, and only then: that
gesture already puts a chip in the same bar carrying the number, so a second moving mark would say it
twice in the one moment the bar is busiest. Every other drag keeps it, which is most of what the mark
is for.

**A guide dragged back onto its own ruler gets a cursor that says it will be thrown away**:
`Bitmap::Discard`, rasterized from Phosphor `trash-simple`, with `CursorIcon::NoDrop` as the stock
fallback — the nearest thing the platform has, though it says the wrong thing on its own, since the
drop is accepted and *destructive*. It branches off `GuideDrag::announces_discard()` —
`discarding && left_ruler`, one conjunction in one place — so the cursor cannot disagree with the fade,
and **neither of them fires on a guide that has not yet been off the bars once**: *not yet
placed* and *about to be deleted* are different states, and §15 D140 has the bug that made the difference
plain. `discarding` alone still drives the commit. `ruler_cursor` returns
`(CursorIcon, Option<Bitmap>)` for it.

⚠️ **Both halves of that conjunction are latched against the bars as they were at the press**, and it
took two passes to get there (§15 D555). `discarding` was latched first and *"off the bars once"* was
left asked live, so taking the bars away mid-drag made `left_ruler` true without the pointer having
left one and the fade and the bin appeared over a new guide that did not exist yet — the very state
D140 added the field to prevent, reached by the other door, with nothing committing differently.
`update_guide_drag` now spells both terms against `GuideDrag::rulers_shown` and the free `ruler_at`
rather than the `rulers_on()`-folding method, which makes each a pure geometry test against the
layout the press saw: the bars' *region* does not move, so neither question depends on whether the
bar is currently painted.

**A selected guide gets the same three cards a layer does, and they take a set.** A **Guide** identity
card (ruler icon, fixed name — there is nothing to rename — with no eye and no lock, the same shape as
the canvas card and for the same reason, reading *Guide* or *N Guides*), a **Transform** panel holding
one full-width position field per **axis** present in the selection, since a guide constrains one axis
and floats free on the other, and an **Appearance** panel with the
colour and a reset that is dead while it is already the default. The reset writes `color: None`
rather than a copy of today's default, so the guide goes back to *following* it. **That card and the
canvas ground's are one implementation** — `inspector::colour_panel` over a `ColourCard`, the row
itself `single_paint_row` — and they were written twice until §15 D740, with the explanation of why
the row asks for `set_min_width` surviving on the canvas copy alone. Each caller still builds its own
reset transaction, a `SetGuideColor { color: None }` per recoloured guide against one
`SetCanvasBackground`, so the two very different answers stay where they can be read against what the
button says. A mixed-axis
selection is therefore two fields rather than one confused one — the field is labelled by the
coordinate the guide *places* (§5.5), so two axes have two different things to say — and each reads
`Mixed` or a shared number on its own, reusing `Mixed` as a numeric formatter exactly as two paint
rows report a colour and an opacity independently; the colour row shows `Swatch::Mixed` where the
selected guides disagree. **For a frame-scoped guide that field holds the offset from its frame rather
than a world coordinate — the single documented exception to §9.3's world-space rule**, which states it
with its two reasons; the ruler chip quotes the same number, so the two readouts of the guide agree. *Remove* and *Remove all Guides* are **28×28 icon buttons in the body of the
card**, as the identity row's mask/group/ungroup are, each as one transaction so clearing a page of
guides is one undo step. They were a three-dots menu until 2026-08-03, which predated that pattern and
was its last survivor; removing it took `self.guide_menu`, the popup's dismissal rules and the one
exemption from the drag-aware click-away rule with it (see above).

**An occupied frame is picked by its name, not by its background.** Every frame carries its name on
the canvas, above its own top-left corner and outside the box so the tag never covers artwork — 5px
in from the left edge, 5px between the bottom of the text and the top edge, 11pt, in `text::MUTED`
or `color::SELECT` when that frame is selected, drawn under every other overlay bar the pixel grid.
That tag exists
because a frame with anything in it is no longer directly clickable: `canvas::pick_leaf` skips it so
its background passes the press through to the marquee (§5.10, §15 D22). An **empty** frame is still
clickable anywhere, and a frame that is *already* the selection stays draggable from anywhere inside
it (`selected_frame_at`), so picking one by its name and then reaching for the middle of it does not
rubber-band the selection away.

**So the tag is a pick, and every door that resolves a pointer to a layer owes it** —
`canvas::pick_at_pointer`, the tag then `pick_leaf`, which the select-click arm and the context-menu
door both call. The menu door asked `pick_leaf` alone until 2026-09-07 and therefore had **no way at
all** of reaching an occupied frame, a right-click on the tag opening the empty-canvas menu instead
(§15 D469). `begin_select_drag` is the third door and still adds `selected_frame_at` on top, which is
the sentence above and is a widening the other two do not have.

⚠️ **And where two tags coincide, the one a click picks is the one the user can read** (§15 D554).
`OndinApp::artboards` is depth-first in child order — paint order — so every reader of it takes the
**last** match, and `canvas::frame_label_at` took the first until 2026-09-08. A page frame with a
full-bleed header flush in its top-left corner puts both tags on exactly the same pixels, every tag
sitting 5px in from its own frame's left edge; `draw_frame_labels` paints the inner one last, so
*Header* is the only word legible there and the click selected `Page` — with `hover_target`, which
resolves through the same function, having outlined the wrong frame before the click took it.
Siblings do it too: a long name on the left reaches over its neighbour's tag.

**Frame membership follows the artwork.** Dragging a layer more than half out of its frame moves it
onto the canvas, belonging to no frame; dragging it more than half into one attaches it. A frame is
a glorified group, so this is the same rule read in both directions — see §15 D20 for the area
test, the limits on which layers hop, and why it commits as one transaction with the move.

Creation reads the same way. `canvas::draw_target` gives a new layer the topmost frame that actually
**contains** the press and the document root when no frame does, so a shape, a text node or a path
started in open space is standalone rather than adopted by a frame it is nowhere near (§15 D25).
Frames themselves always land at the root, wherever they are drawn, because they may not nest.

**`Ctrl`+`D` remembers.** A duplicate lands in place; move it and duplicate again and the new copy
repeats that movement, as does every press after it — `CloneChain` holds the last clone, where it
was placed, and the step being repeated. Duplicating anything else starts a new run at zero, which
is what keeps it predictable. `Ctrl`+`V` offsets by 20 in each axis so a paste is visibly a paste.

**Every copy lands one step above the thing it came from**, not on top of the whole parent: duplicate,
paste and Alt-drag all agree on that now (§15 D40 for the Alt-drag, D42 for the preview that has to
match it). A copy belongs over its original and *under*
whatever was already above it — appending sent it to the front of the layer hierarchy instead. Paste
can name that slot because a captured subtree keeps the **original's** ids until `insert_subtrees`
remaps them, so the node it came from is still there to look up; when it is not — cut, deleted, or the
paste is going to a different parent — there is no "just above it" to name and appending is the only
answer left, which is the same fallback Alt-drag takes when the copy has crossed into another frame.
Several copies out of the *same* parent each take their own original's slot, which needs
`insert_subtrees` to advance each index past only the earlier inserts that landed at or below it rather
than past all of them — a flat count is right only while the indices ascend, and they do not when the
selection is walked top-down (§15 D100). ⚠️ **Alt-drag did not go through `insert_subtrees` and kept the
count this sentence forbids, until 2026-09-07** (§15 D512): it builds its own `InsertSubtree`, because
the destination parent and the transform both come from where the pointer is, and it restated the
numbering instead of borrowing it. A selection is in **pick order**, so shift-clicking a stack front to
back put both copies at the front of the parent with the lower one on top — the very layout the
paragraph above says was fixed, reachable by nothing but the click order and reported by nothing on
screen. It keeps the indices now, the same accumulator under both doors. **The name comes along too**: a typed name is kept and a
numbered one increments, per destination parent and across every copy in the one transaction
(`build::CopyNames`, §5.7b).

**A copy carries the pictures it needs**, because a captured subtree does not. `OndinApp::clipboard` is
an `Option<Clip>` holding the subtrees *and* the image-table entries their fills key into — one struct
rather than two slots, so the halves cannot drift — collected by `build::image_ids_in` in
`copy_selection` at **copy** time, which is `clipboard_from`'s moment and for its kind of reason (§15
D251): it is the last instant the document holding those bytes is certainly the one on screen. On the way in, `insert_all` prepends
`build::missing_image_ops` to the transaction, so only what the target lacks is added and the ops sit
**before** the layers that use them — `tools::place_image`'s ordering rule, since undo reverses a
transaction and the entry must come out after its layers. The clipboard deliberately survives an open
(`reset_transient_state` clears `alt_clone`, whose ids cannot outlive their document, and leaves this
alone), so pasting a picture into a different document is a supported gesture rather than an accident;
⚠️ **that function is a hand-written list with nothing checking it** — the Appearance panel's
`per_corner_radius` disclosure set holds ids of the same class and was cleared *nowhere* in the
workspace until 2026-09-07, growing for the life of the process across every document opened (§15
D447). Nothing wrong was ever drawn from it, a `NodeId`'s random per-session actor making a stale id
dangle rather than collide, which is exactly why nobody found it by looking at the screen;
before the entries travelled it arrived as the missing-image placeholder (§15 D280). Duplicate passes
no entries at all, being unable to leave the document it reads from.
⚠️ **`go_to_dashboard`'s clear list is the second one of the same class and it had the same kind of
hole** (§15 D526): it clears `picker`, `context_menu`, `open_menu` and `rename_entry` and did not clear
`confirming_close`, so walking to the library under the *Unsaved changes* card left the flag stuck
`true` on a screen that does not draw the card — the question unanswerable, and the card returning over
a clean document on the way back in.
⚠️ **`cancel_gesture`'s own list is the third and its omission was the one with a *deadline* behind
it** (§15 D535): eleven fields named by hand — `drag`, `guide_previews`, `layer_drag`, `paint_drag`,
`alt_clone`, `autopan_total`, `session_scrub`, `settings_scrub`, `grid_scrub`, `grid_paint`,
`chrome_hold` — and not `opacity_entry`, so `Escape` over a pending opacity digit dropped the preview
and `fold_opacity_entry` committed it six hundred milliseconds later anyway. **Three hand-written
lists of editor state to drop, three omissions, and nothing checks any of them** — worth suspecting
wherever a new piece of transient state is added, because the only thing that finds one of these is a
person reading the list against the struct.
🚨 **The fourth omission is in the same function and in the *other* list** (§15 D588). `cancel_gesture`
is a gate and then a clear, and the gate **was** a hand-written list too — `has_gesture_preview`,
`session_scrub`, `settings_scrub`, `grid_scrub`, `grid_paint`, `export_quality_scrub`,
`guide_position_drag` — while `paint_drag` appeared only in the clear. So the clear was correct and
unreachable: a paint-row reorder with nothing else in flight returned at the gate. The one term that
covered it was `ctx.dragged_id()`, which is the blinking one D168 warns about, so it worked for a
slow right-click and failed for a fast one — and did not recover, egui not re-arming the drag while
the primary stays down, so one fast click made the reorder uncancellable and the release committed
it. **Reading a clear list against the struct is not enough; it has to be read against the gate
above it**, because the two go out of step in the direction nothing on screen shows.
⚠️ **The gate is no longer one of the hand-written lists, and the clear still is** (§15 **D785**,
`[A2-L7-02]`'s narrow half). The seven values a gesture holds — `session_scrub`, `settings_scrub`,
`paint_drag`, `export_quality_scrub`, `grid_scrub`, `grid_paint`, `guide_position_drag` — live in
`app::InFlight`, and `InFlight::any` is `*self != Self::default()`, a `PartialEq` against `Default`
and therefore **exhaustive by construction**: an eighth value is covered the day it is added, with
nothing to remember. `drag` and `layer_drag` are still named beside it, because the function *acts* on
those two where everything in `InFlight` is read back by its own owner on `gesture_cancelled` — **the
line is "a value a gesture is holding", not "a gesture"**. 🚨 **Clearing is deliberately not folded
into the type**: `grid_scrub` and `grid_paint` are dropped by the cancel, and the rest are read back
through `gesture_cancelled`, which is how a field that has to *restore* something gets the chance —
`session_scrub` being the only record of what the spans were. **A blanket `*self = Self::default()`
reads as the obvious completion of that change and would take it away.**
🚨 **The fifth is not an omission at all — the gate's own first term was the wrong predicate** (§15
D609). `has_gesture_preview` asked `!preview_holds_session`, so a field scrub engaged *over* a live
text session, which is both things at once, answered **false** and the cancel fell through to
`ctx.dragged_id()` once more. **A hand-written list can be complete and still wrong, when one of its
terms cannot describe a state that is reachable** — and no single `bool` distinguishes all four
combinations of "a session" and "a gesture", which is why the repair was two fields rather than a
third value on one.

**Selection is group-first** (Figma semantics). A click selects the outermost `Group` above whatever
the hit test found — that is the point of grouping, and it is what makes a group draggable as a
unit. `Ctrl` reaches straight through to the leaf however deep it sits; `Ctrl`+`Alt` picks the
immediate child of the outermost group, one level in rather than all the way. Over a selection
handle band the key means a skew instead — handle bands are dispatched before deep-select, which is
what left `Ctrl` free for that gesture (above). **Both also enter the
group**, exactly as double-clicking it does — reaching inside with a modifier is the same statement
as stepping in, and without it the next plain click jumps back out to the whole group and leaves the
one before it looking undone. While `OndinApp::entered_group` is set, `group_chain` stops there, so
clicks pick its contents instead of re-selecting it; a click on anything outside it clears the scope
in the same gesture that selects elsewhere, and so does a click on empty canvas (D22). Nothing about
the document changes, which is why there is no affordance for it — what the click selects says
plainly enough where you are. Load-bearing: `pick_for_click` opens the scope *after* asking
`pick_preview` what to select, because the preview must still see the scope as it was — the modifier
decides what is picked and, separately, that isolation follows.

**The canvas never selects a locked layer, by any gesture** (§15 D321, D746). A click refuses it
(`query::hit_test`), and so does a rubber band: `canvas::apply_marquee` picks frame *contents* rather
than the frames, plus the loose layers that belong to no frame, and the list it walks —
`OndinApp::marquee_candidates` — is filtered by `OndinApp::may_select_in_bulk`, which is
`query::is_effectively_locked` and nothing else. The same reading `hit_test` has always used, so a
layer inside a locked group is no more band-selectable than it is clickable; the band asked the
node's **own** flag until 2026-08-23, which made it the way to pick up something a click refused, and
the predicate sat in `apply_marquee` rather than in the shared helper until 2026-09-10, which is how
`Ctrl+A` came to disagree with it. ⚠️ The *visibility* half is still `apply_marquee`'s own and still
the node's flag, deliberately: a layer inside a hidden group can be marquee-selected where a click on
it cannot. What was decided is the lock, and a hidden-but-unlocked layer is fully editable anyway
(`context-menus.md` §5.9), so widening this would be a second decision.
⚠️ **The layers panel is the exception and it is the ruling's own** (§15 D746, D71, D323): clicking a
row selects a locked layer, `layers::select_from_row` reading no lock at all, and once it is selected
the inspector's rules apply unchanged — a lock stops a layer being dragged about, not recoloured.
🚨 **The rule is not about the canvas, which is why the predicate is called `may_select_in_bulk` and
why there are four doors rather than three** (§15 D748). What the four have in common is that the
user described a **set** — everything, everything under the band, everything using this colour —
rather than pointing at a layer; a layers-panel row points at one. So the fourth is a *panel*:
`inspector::select_by_color`, the Group Colors reticle (§9.2), which included locked layers on
purpose until the maintainer ruled and now reports *"Selected 2 of 3 layers with this colour — 1
locked"*. **The surface is not what separates them** — a predicate named for one would have argued
that door out of the rule, which is close to what happened.

**`Ctrl+A` is a third door and it agrees with the other two about the lock** (`OndinApp::select_all`,
§15 D709, D746). It takes the same candidates — `marquee_candidates`, whose two halves are the
paragraph above — so a locked layer is left alone and a **hidden** one is selected like any other,
the two halves of one question answering differently on purpose. **With the candidate range empty the
chord selects the frames themselves** (`root_artboards`), which is the one state in which it picks a
frame at all — a document of nothing but empty frames would otherwise answer `Ctrl+A` with nothing —
and those frames are filtered too. 🚨 **The emptiness is asked of the range *before* the lock filter**
(`marquee_range`), because the filtered list cannot tell "these frames are empty" from "everything in
them is locked", and answering the second like the first selects the frames and lets `Delete` take
the locked children down with their parents. ⚠️ All three of those decisions were untested until
2026-09-09 and the lock was unruled until 2026-09-10: adding a `visible && !is_effectively_locked`
filter to the candidate set left the whole suite green, so any implementation of the chord passed.
`app::select_all_tests` is a test each now, plus one for `Ctrl+A` then `Delete`. **The lock is
enforced at *selection* time and nowhere else**: `delete_selection`, `nudge`, the restacks and the
aligns read it nowhere, so a door that puts a locked id in the selection has already armed all of
them, which is why the repair went to the door rather than in front of each verb.

**A double-click goes one level in, and the group step goes first** (`canvas::double_click_pick`,
§15 D287). Descend while there is a group left to descend into; only with none left does the click
mean "open this layer's contents" — text into a caret, a picture into image editing, a path into its
points. The kind arms used to be asked *before* the group step, on the reasoning that an image-filled
shape is a leaf and so had no group step to steal: true of a leaf on the artboard, false of the same
leaf inside a group, which is where the step was being stolen. `entered_group` is what remembers how
far in you are, so the third double-click on a picture nested one group deep is the one that crops.
It changed text and paths as well as pictures — they had the identical fault and nobody had reported
it — and "one level means one" is the rule that fixes all three at once.

**`Alt`+`Shift`+click designates the key layer** — the member align aligns to, the base operand of a
boolean (§15 D113), and, since 2026-08-21, **which layer of a selection becomes the mask** (§15 D286). Not `Ctrl`+`Shift`, which is the natural composition of deep-select and extend and
stays free for it. On a layer that is not selected yet it adds it first, since a key needs something to
be key *of*; inside an existing boolean it is a reorder to index 0 instead. The chord starts **no drag
on the artwork**, because Alt alone means drag-a-copy and that copy commits on any release that moved
(D40) — so a designation that slipped past egui's drag threshold would otherwise leave a duplicate
behind. **On the box's own chrome it starts the drag as normal**, and the refusal sits inside
`begin_select_drag` below the pivot, line-end and handle arms rather than gating the call, for the
reason those arms are not what the chord is aimed at: a designation is a click *on a layer*, so no slip
off a handle can designate anything and none of those gestures duplicates. Gating the call instead —
which is what this did until 2026-08-22 — made `Alt`+`Shift` on a corner inert, i.e. left no way to ask
for a resize that is both proportional and about the centre although either half worked alone, and it
read as a dead spot rather than as a refusal because `select_cursor` answers from `Handles::armed`,
which never saw the chord (§15 D289).

**`Alt` on a resting pointer quotes distances.** Hold it with something selected and hover another
layer — or a ruler guide — and the overlay draws one thin red line per distance between the two,
ticked at each end with the number on a pill at its middle (`measure.rs`, `canvas::draw_measures`).
Per axis, and the two axes never consult each other about *what* to say: apart on an axis gives the
gap between the two facing edges, overlapping gives the distance between the near edges and between
the far ones. So a layer beside another quotes the gap plus whatever its edges are offset by, a layer
inside a frame its four insets, and a layer diagonally away one number per axis — and those two
**meet**, forming an L from one box's corner to the other's, because the horizontal sits on the
selection's near edge and the vertical on the target's. **Flush counts as apart**, so two touching
boxes report a gap of zero, which is then dropped as any measure that would be labelled `0` is: that
case is a snap's normal outcome and so the one that had to be right. A **ruler guide** under the
pointer wins over the layer under it — the precedence the press already has, `guide_input` claiming it
from every tool — and is measured on one axis only, being infinite along its own, with a guide
*across* the selection quoting both sides. The target is `canvas::hover_target`, the same call the
hover outline resolves through, so `Ctrl`+`Alt` cannot ring one layer and measure to another; the
whole overlay is gated on `canvas::hover_chrome_live`, the three-term "is resting-pointer chrome live
this frame" question the hover outline and the key trace ask as well. It quotes **world bounding
boxes**, so a rotated layer is measured by the upright box around it, which is the box snapping
already compares. §15 D198 has the rest — the label's refusal to round and the third chrome hue it
introduced — and the same `Measure` is what an equal-gap snap draws (above, §15 D200).

**Four pairings, from two branches**: a selected layer to a hovered layer, a selected layer to a
hovered ruler guide, a selected **guide** to a hovered layer, and a selected guide to a hovered
**guide**. The third is the one no other tool has, and it is the pairing a guide's selection most
obviously raises — a guide exists to line work up
against, so "how far is that from this" is the question, and before it the only way to ask was to select
the layer instead and hover back. `measure::to_guide` answers both mixed pairings, its first parameter
named `box_` rather than `selection` precisely because which of the two was clicked first is not its
business; one function means the two directions cannot disagree about a number they both quote. The
branch is an **`else`, not a precedence rule**, and `Selection`'s exclusivity invariant (§9.3) is what
makes that sound: every way of selecting a guide clears the layers and every way of selecting a layer
clears the guides, so the two can never both apply. Every selected guide measures, not just one — a
vertical and a horizontal together read as a cross through the hovered layer. `rulers::measurable_guide`
is `measure_guide`'s by-id half, where both directions meet, and it re-asks `guides_on()` rather than
inheriting the check: *View ▸ Hide guides* does not clear the guide selection, so without it the overlay
would measure from a line nobody can see (§15 D201). **A hidden guide is therefore not measured to and a
*locked* one is** — the hover path goes through `guide_under`, which asks nothing about the lock, because
what may be measured is what may be snapped to rather than what may be picked up (§15 D202). The cursor
over that same locked guide still does not change, `guide_cursor` going through `guide_at`, so the chrome
says "no grab on offer" while the overlay says "but here is the distance" — the two true statements about
a locked, visible guide.

**Guide to guide is the one pairing whose line has no position the geometry can prefer.** Every other
measure derives its perpendicular coordinate from what the two subjects share; two parallel guides are
both infinite and share nothing, so `measure::between_guides` takes an `at` and the caller chooses it.
`draw_measures` chooses the **middle of the canvas** — `canvas_inner(rect).center()` through `to_world`,
so the line clears the ruler bars, the same inset the drop-target overlay takes — and **not** the pointer,
which is the obvious candidate and the worst one available: hovering a vertical guide pins the pointer's
x within a few points of it, leaving y the coordinate the hand is free to sweep and *is* sweeping along
the line, so the label would slide about while the number never changed (§15 D203). Perpendicular guides
come back with nothing, two lines that cross having no distance to quote, and so do two guides at the
same coordinate — which is also what makes hovering a guide that is *itself* selected draw nothing.
`Axis::across()` owns the flip from "the axis a guide pins" to "the axis a line quoting it runs along",
spelled once because both guide functions need it.

**The layers panel selects the way a file manager does: `Shift` takes a range, `Ctrl`/`Cmd` toggles
one row.** The range runs along the rows *as displayed*, so a collapsed subtree is not in it and
neither is anything a name filter has hidden; the anchor is the last row clicked without `Shift` and
a `Shift`-click does not move it, so a range can be stretched and pulled back from one end. This is
not the canvas's `Shift`, which still adds and removes one layer at a time — §15 D54 has why the two
surfaces differ on purpose, and why neither of them is D47's `Shift`. The rest of the panel follows
the same intent: a drag carries the whole selection (reduced through `build::outermost`) and **follows
the indent**, so taking a layer to the bottom of its group and moving left carries it out of the group
and into the parent (§9.4, §15 D345) — and resting that drag on a collapsed group for a second opens
it, so a branch that is not on screen can be ordered within rather than only dropped onto. A
double-click renames in place as one undo step with `Escape` to discard, the tree un-collapses and
scrolls to a selection made on the canvas, dragging near the top or bottom edge auto-scrolls, and one
header button collapses everything or expands everything depending on what it finds. **`Ctrl+R`, `F2`
and the context menu's *Rename* row open that same rename field** rather than a second one —
`renaming_layer` is the whole of the state, and now the whole of what a door does: **the field asks for
the caret itself, on the frame it first draws** (§15 D216, D332). Two of the doors cannot draw it in the
frame that opened it — the double-click reads a `renaming` flag latched earlier in the row, and the
context menu is drawn *after* the layers panel — and ⚠️ **a focus request naming a widget the frame does
not draw is not the deferral it looks like**: egui keeps a freshly requested focus past its own
dead-man's switch on purpose, then builds the AccessKit update from the nodes the pass registered, so
`accesskit_consumer` panics on the focused id it cannot find. `read_response(id).is_none()` is the
one-shot — "this field did not exist last pass" — and it is the only spelling that is neither that panic
nor the trap of re-requesting whenever the field lacks focus, which fires on the very frame `Enter` or
`Escape` takes it away. The chord shows the layers panel if it was hidden, since a rename armed against a panel
nobody can see would swallow the next keystrokes with nothing on screen to explain it, and it refuses a
multi-selection, there being no one row to lay the field over.

**The pen draws curves.** Press plants an anchor and dragging before release pulls handles out of it,
turning a corner into a smooth point; the two handles mirror each other by default, and **`Alt` while
dragging breaks the pair**, leaving the incoming one where it was so the segment arrives straight and
leaves on a curve. The modifier is read live every frame rather than latched at the press, so pressing
and releasing it mid-drag re-mirrors — the same live-modifier rule `sync_alt_clone` follows for a
duplicate drag (§15 D40). An anchor therefore carries *two* handle vectors (`preview::PenAnchor { at,
out, back }`) and is a corner only when both are zero. A segment is emitted as a line when **the two
handles it uses** are both zero (`PenAnchor::straight_to`) and as a cubic otherwise, so a path clicked
out with corners is still a polyline in the file rather than curves with collinear control points —
and so is the straight half of a path that curves elsewhere (§15 D117). The canvas rubber band is
drawn from `tools::pen_outline` — the same function the commit uses — so it cannot promise a curve
the commit will not produce, and it is stroked in the ink and width the commit will use
(`PEN_STROKE_COLOR`/`PEN_STROKE_WIDTH`, black at 2 units) rather than as a chrome hairline: on a
curve, what the line will *look* like is most of what you are judging while you draw it. Only the
anchors and their control handles stay in the selection colour, because those are chrome.

**Backspace takes back the last anchor mid-draw** (`canvas::pen_backspace`), and cancels the path when
the first one goes. Undo cannot do this job — nothing is committed until the path is finished, so a
mis-clicked anchor is not in the history at all — and it has to be intercepted in `app::dispatch` as
`Action::Delete if self.pen.is_some()`, since Backspace and Delete both already resolve to
`Action::Delete` and keyboard actions are dispatched *before* `pen_input` runs. Pressing the first
anchor again still closes the path, within `PEN_PICK_PX` (7 screen pt) — one named distance for "close
enough to a pen anchor or a handle", so the gestures still to come do not each invent their own. §15
D114 has the reasoning for all three, and the two model decisions the pen's creation half closes.

**Closing has an affordance, and it is a snap.** Inside that same radius the pending segment stops dead
*on* the first anchor instead of trailing past it and the anchor takes a ring, so the tolerance
announces itself rather than being found by clicking and missing (`tools::pen_close_snap`, asked by both
`canvas::pen_press` and the overlay so the look and the behaviour cannot differ). The press that closes
then **swallows the rest of itself** — `gesture_cancelled`, because `finish_pen` has switched to Select
and the release would otherwise land as an ordinary click on the artwork. §15 D116 has both.

**A stored path can be read back into anchors, and the pen resumes one.** `tools::pen_anchors` is the
inverse of `pen_outline` — a `BezPath` into `Vec<PenSubpath>`, each a run of anchors plus whether it
closes — and it copes with paths the pen never wrote: quads are elevated to the cubic with the same
curve, several subpaths come back as several, and the duplicate point a `ClosePath` leaves behind is
folded onto the first anchor instead of accumulating one per round trip. `tools::pen_path` writes a
whole list back, `map_subpaths` moves one through a transform, and `rewrite_path` commits it as one
`SetGeometry`/`GeometryPatch::Path` **without touching the node's transform**, which is the one way it
differs from `create_path`.

⚠️ **The round trip moves in a third way, and it is the one that *adds*** (§15 D583). `pen_outline`
draws the closing segment **and** emits `ClosePath`, so a closed subpath whose last point is not
already the first — `M0,0 L80,0 L80,60 Z`, which is what `svg_in` builds for a `<polygon>` and what
`BezPath::from_svg` gives for any `d` ending in `Z` — comes back carrying a `LineTo(0,0)` the stored
path never had. So `pen_path(&pen_anchors(&p, &[]))` is `p` only for paths the pen itself wrote, and
**`rewrite_path`'s no-op guard therefore compares canonical forms**: both sides go through
`pen_anchors` → `pen_path`/`pen_radii` for the comparison, and nothing about what is stored changes,
which is what keeps this out of invariant 9's migration territory. Compared raw, a bare *click* into
the corner-radius field committed a `SetGeometry` and grew the saved outline a segment the user never
drew; `pen_radii`'s trailing-zero trim was the same miss on the other half, a stored `[0, 0, 0]` never
being `[]`. Nothing is lost by canonicalising: the two forms differ only in a segment of zero length
and in radii already zero, so a *"changed nothing"* answer is never a dropped edit.

On that, pressing an open path's endpoint with the pen picks it up and carries on drawing it
(`canvas::pen_resume`, `pen_resume_target`). The grab is `PEN_PICK_PX`, the same radius closing uses,
and it is ringed on hover exactly as the close target is — the same promise deserves the same
vocabulary. The pen only appends, so resuming at the *start* of a subpath reverses a working copy and
`finish_pen` turns it back, which means extending the start **prepends** rather than flipping the
path's direction, and lets a resume that changed nothing be recognised as one and skipped rather than
becoming an empty undo step. §15 D117 has the four decisions.

**The node tool (`A`) edits a path's points.** It is a tool rather than a mode, which is the case the
"when a mode earns its keep" principle was written for: it is on the rail, named, has a letter, and puts
its own chrome on the canvas. Its subject is the layer selection when that is a single `Path`, so
`A` with one picked, a click with the tool armed, and the **double-click** that does both at once are
three ways in with no fourth piece of state behind them. Double-click is the same gesture that steps into
a group and opens a text node — one level *in*, and what that level is depends on what you are on.

Anchors draw as markers over the path — square for a corner, round for a smooth point — and the
selection box is suppressed while they are up (`canvas::chrome_hidden`, which also covers a pen gesture),
because a resize box round a path whose points are being dragged offers two contradictory gestures over
the same pixels. Clicking an anchor selects it, `Shift` adds, a drag from empty canvas marquees over
them, and dragging one moves every selected anchor by the same delta. Its handles are dragged from the
dots on their stalks, or pulled **out** of the anchor with `Ctrl`+drag; either way `Alt` breaks the pair
as the pen's own drag does. `Delete` removes the selected points and heals the path. `Enter` steps in and
back out again, where `Escape` unwinds a rung at a time. Every grab is `PEN_PICK_PX` through
`canvas::node_grab`, which offers only handles that are actually **drawn**. Dragging a handle back onto
its anchor within that same radius **retracts** it, which is how a smooth point becomes a corner again.

**A rewind of the document drops the point selection and any live pen run** (§15 D568). `PointSet`
holds `(subpath, anchor)` **indices**, so an undo that renumbers the anchors leaves a set that is still
in range and no longer names what the user clicked; every structural edit in the tool clears or re-sets
it, and undo and redo were the two doors with nothing. Truncation is not the guard here — the failing
case leaves every index valid — so `OndinApp::document_rewound` clears, and it runs only where
`EditorSession::undo` reports that the document actually moved, which is what keeps `Ctrl+Z` at the
bottom of the stack from deselecting anything. `PenState` goes with it for a stronger reason:
`PenEdit::subpaths` is a **snapshot** of the node's subpaths taken at the resume and `finish_pen` writes
the whole list back, so a pen run spanning an undo would put back the geometry the undo removed.

**The pen is reachable from inside the edit.** `P` arms `app::pen_bias` rather than switching tool, so the
path, its selection and its points survive; the pointer target then picks the verb (`canvas::pen_verb`) —
an open end of the edited path continues it, its ink inserts an anchor, and bare canvas begins a **new
subpath in the same node**. A handle, a middle anchor and the point box keep the meanings they have, and
another layer under the pointer still switches subject. The pen's own cursor appears exactly where a verb
is armed, from the same query the press runs, and Escape disarms the bias one rung above the points. The
bias reaches only the edited node (`canvas::pen_scope`), which is what confines a join to one path; the pen
tool's own cross-layer join is unchanged. Because a new run in the same node makes winding a question — we
fill non-zero, so the same way round fills solid and the opposite way cuts a hole — `Shift`+`D`
(`canvas::reverse_subpaths`) turns the runs the selected points are on the other way round, or every run
when nothing is selected, and it works on a selected path outside point editing too, exactly as the corner
radius does. §15 D125. **A locked path refuses on both doors**: the first inherits `edited_path`'s check,
and the fallback arm asks `query::is_effectively_locked` itself, which it did not until 2026-09-07
(§15 D514).

The inspector changes subject with the tool (`inspector_points`): an **Edit Path** identity card with
every action dead, Transform reduced to X/Y of the selected points, Appearance to opacity, Fill and
Stroke unchanged and still the whole path's. The align row's eight buttons act on points instead of
layers, needing two points to align and three to distribute, **and so does the spacing row beneath
them** — `tools::space_points`, needing two, holding the first on the axis because a set of points has
no key to designate (§15 D243). The **arrow keys** nudge points rather than the layer.

**A path's corners round.** `NodeKind::Path` carries a radius per anchor, resolved into geometry by
`geometry::local_path` the way a `Rect`'s four already are — never baked, so the value scrubs both ways.
The Appearance field writes to the selected corner points, or to every corner of a path selected without
the node tool. Every corner rounds, whatever its neighbours do; a radius on a smooth anchor draws nothing, because
there is no turn there to cut. §15 D119. §15 D118; the corner radius that panel still
owes is D119, which is a model change rather than an inspector one.

**An image fill has a row of its own** (§15 D180). `panels::paint::PaintKind` carries an `Image`
variant, deliberately absent from `PaintKind::ALL` — that array is the picker's tab strip, and the
other three convert to one another where an image does not: you pick one from a file dialog, not from
a colour wheel. The row keeps the chip, so the labels down the list stay on one x, and the chip now
draws the picture's thumbnail — `ui::Swatch::Picture`, over the checkerboard like every other paint
and **at the brush's own `ImageSampler::alpha`**, so a fill faded to 30% draws a chip faded to 30%
(§15 D784); it drew untinted until 2026-09-15, which is §15 D564's *one document drawn two ways in one
frame* and had been true since the variant existed. The alpha rides on the variant rather than being
folded into the texture, because the texture is **shared** — `thumbs` keys its atlas by picture, and
two layers can carry one photograph at two opacities — and the tint is allowed to be a uniform
multiplier and nothing else, so it is white scaled by the alpha, which leaves every hue where it was.
It still falls back to the grey ramp it drew before while a thumbnail is missing or deferred
(§15 D189) — and the hex field is a plain "Image"
label. `picker_body` returns early
for an image rather than drawing a hue wheel over a photograph.

**Clicking either of them steps into image editing** (§15 D305), which is the fourth door onto the
mode and the shape the gradient arm beside it already had: a colour row's swatch opens the thing
that edits that colour, so a picture's opens the thing that edits that picture. Both carried a
`clicked()` that went nowhere until 2026-08-23 — the chip's was explicitly suppressed for a picture
and the label was an `egui::Label` with no `Sense` at all — which is the state this paragraph used
to describe as "clicking it opens nothing". Both now say *Edit this picture — crop it, move it,
scale it* and both route through `OndinApp::begin_image_edit`, the one function all four doors call.
**Which row is the door is `inspector::row_edits_the_mode_s_picture`, and it asks
`tools::croppable_fill` rather than this row's own brush**: on a layer with two image fills the mode
takes the first *visible* one, so the second row's click is inert rather than entering the mode with
the handles on somebody else's photograph. **A locked layer closes the door too** (§15 D320), a locked
*group* included (§15 D321) — the `door` predicate asks `query::is_effectively_locked`, the same question
`begin_image_edit` will ask when the click arrives, and both tooltips gain a third state naming the lock,
since a row that promises "edit this picture" and does nothing is worse than one that promises nothing. Only the door
closes: the picker still opens from a locked layer's colour rows, a lock stopping a layer being dragged
about rather than recoloured.

**The row has one line, and everything a picture wants is in image editing's card** (§15 D268). It
carried three controls that have all moved there: a four-cell **Fill / Fit / Crop / Tile** strip on a
second line, and two popover buttons beside it. Every one of them decides something about a picture
you are working *on* rather than one you have merely selected — the strip least defensibly, since
choosing *Crop* there deliberately changed nothing on screen and then left the bounding box resizing
rather than cropping, which is the report D268 answers. The mode write still goes through
`write_slot` and `paint::with_fit` wherever it is drawn, so a fill, a stroke, an artboard background
and a whole selection all write the same way and the crop survives the switch.

**Everything else a picture wants is a control rather than a gesture, so it is one card with two
tabs** (§15 D182, D190, D268). `inspector::image_edit_card` draws a `POPOVER_W` `Area` at
`popover_anchor`, taken from the **paint row's** own rectangle rather than from a button's, so it
hangs level with the picture it describes in the lane the other popovers share
(`picker_lane_right`, which asks `edited_image` rather than a field). It follows `stroke_menu_popup`
in everything but its life: `Foreground`, `menu_frame`, `POPOVER_W`.

**It has no button and no way to close it, and both absences are the design.** The card appears when
a picture is double-clicked and goes when `Enter` or `Escape` leaves the mode — which is what
answers D118 rather than dodging it: an open 272pt card beside the row is a louder statement that a
mode is running than a rail button lit whether or not it has a subject. So the six-term click-away
rule every other popover here runs is **absent rather than reimplemented** — nothing outside the card
can dismiss it, so there is no dismissal to get right — and `Escape` is not a term either, having a
meaning one rung up. It is also why `OndinApp` keeps only `image_tab: ImageCard` where it used to
keep `Option<(NodeId, PaintSlot, ImageCard)>`: *is a card open, on which layer, on which paint* are
all `canvas::edited_image`'s to answer now, so nothing clears this on a selection change, remaps it
through a paint reorder or drops it when a row is dragged, because a stale value cannot exist. What
is left is a preference — which tab you were last on — kept across entries deliberately.

**The tab strip is the header.** A two-cell `ui::segmented` at full width, carrying
`ImageCard::title` for its labels, so neither arm draws an eyebrow repeating the tab it is inside.
The card's controls are 26 (`CELL`) and `ui::segmented` pads two either side, so both tracks — this
one and the mode strip inside Settings — are asked for `TRACK_CELL`, four **less**. That subtraction
is the trap the image row sprang in both directions before the card existed (§15 D180, D190), and
`the_image_cards_tracks_and_fields_are_one_height` is what keeps it the right way round, asserting
against a bare `CELL` painting 30 rather than against nothing.

**Settings opens with the four framing modes**, which since D268 are an *override* rather than the
way into cropping: Crop is what the handles and the pan do, and picking Fill, Fit or Tile re-frames
the picture inside the box the crop left and takes the ghosted original away with it. The rectangle
survives untouched, so coming back to Crop brings both back.
The two sections `images.md` planned as headings inside one card are now its two tabs
(**Settings**, **Adjustments**, §15 D186, D190, D268). The **Asset** eyebrow went
with that split — left standing over one entry — and **came back on 2026-08-19** over three of five
(§15 D225); it stands over **two of five** since 2026-08-23, *Export original…* having been removed
from this card and from the context menu together (§15 D305). Settings has the room, so the third
card D190 held in reserve is still in reserve, for the two entries that wait on a **linked** source
(*Embed*/*Link*, *Relink…*). *Replace…* picks one file, embeds it and
**keeps the framing**, which is what makes it the repair for a picture that has gone missing rather
than a fresh placement; ***Replace and reset*** is the same verb with the four framing fields put back
to their defaults and the **adjustments kept**, those being the other card's business and per-pixel
rather than geometric. Both decline for a selection slot exactly where *original size* does — the
`context-menus.md` §5.7 row that verb now is, D181's reason being about the slot rather than about
the door — and both are
deferred to after the `Area` closure returns because the file dialog is modal.
***Export original…* was here and is gone.** It wrote `ImageEntry`'s stored bytes back out through
`ImageFormat::extension` — the encoded original, byte-identical to the file that went in, asking
nothing of the crop, since rendering what is on screen is `ondin export`. Removed on 2026-08-23 from
both of its doors at once (§15 D305): the capability is real and the reach is not, "export this
picture" meaning the layer at a size and a format, which is what the Export panel is (§15 D274). Two
rules went with it and are recorded rather than deleted. It was the row **a locked layer kept live
for a reason about locking itself** — a lock protects a layer from being changed and reading its
bytes back out changes nothing — where *Edit image*, the other live row, was live only because the
mode's other doors did not check the lock either (§15 D268), which is a match with a gap rather than
agreement and stopped being true on 2026-08-23 (§15 D320); that distinction now survives with no
instance at all, which is the reason to read it here rather than derive it again. And it **dimmed in three states rather than two** — fine, *linked*, or an id the
table does not hold — through `tools::original_refusal`, which returned the sentence rather than a
flag because a `bool` had told a document missing a picture that it was linked, naming a feature the
app cannot author (§15 D280, D261's rule about two doors onto one verb). That predicate went with
the rows; its reasoning is kept as comments where it stood, because it is the spec to rebuild from
the day linking is authored, and its removal put `ImageEntry::is_linked` back to zero callers.
Both replaces
leave the card standing behind the modal dialog, which they could not while there was a click-away
rule for a modal window to starve; staying is also right, since a replace keeps the framing and the
card comes back describing the new picture in the same terms. In Settings: a **Mirror**
eyebrow over two `ui::label_button`s reading *Horizontal* and *Vertical*, which are actions and never light up
(§5.5a) and which carry **words where the Transform panel's flips carry glyphs**, because on a
symmetric shape the two operations are the same picture and only the label can tell them apart (§15
D182) — there is no quarter turn here, that being the Transform panel's job; a tile-scale
**a row of two half-width fields, *Scale* (`icon::RESIZE`) and *Tile* (`icon::GRID_FOUR`)**, both in
percent of the source's own pixels
(`1.0` is one unit per source pixel), each read by one mode and **dimmed rather than hidden** for the
other three — glyphs rather than words because two well-separated pictures carry it where seven
tone-adjustment glyphs could not, with the name at the head of each tooltip (§15 D271) — the values are real and merely unread, and a pair that came and went as the strip above
it was clicked would read as a glitch. *Scale* is the zoom the crop gesture deliberately cannot do
(§15 D271): a handle drag moves the window with the picture nailed down and a pan slides the picture
under a fixed window, so how big the picture is has no gesture and is a number instead. Its floor is
`ImageRef::cover_scale` — under `Crop` the rectangle maps onto the frame exactly, so there is no
letterboxing a smaller picture could sit in, and zooming out stops where the crop reaches the source.
That is not "scale up only": cover is well under 100% on a layer smaller than its picture. **Its ceiling
is `floor.max(10_000.0)` for the same reason** (§15 D462): `cover_scale` is frame world units over
picture *pixels* and is uncapped, so a 16×16 icon on a 1920×1080 rectangle covers at 12 000% — and a
floor above the flat 10 000% this used to read left the field asking for an empty interval, which
`f64::clamp` answers with a panic on the UI thread. Where cover is past the constant, cover *is* the
honest ceiling; this is the one numeric field in the inspector whose bound comes from the document.
Writing
goes through `image::crop_scaled`, a uniform scale about the window's centre, so it can neither
introduce a stretch nor remove one the layer's own resize put there; the readout is seeded from
`cover_crop` where the mode is not Crop, so the dimmed number is the one entering Crop would give.
**It scrubs in hundredths where its neighbour takes whole units** (§15 D273): a crop scale is
*multiplicative*, so what the eye reads is `Δs / s` and a whole-point step lurches three times as far
at the floor as at 300% — a tile scale has no centre for a step to swing a distant corner around, and
keeps the coarser one;
and *Reset crop*, which restores `whole_crop()`'s sentinel and not a computed cover rectangle.
**There is no *Original size* here since 2026-08-23**, and the sentence that used to describe it is
why it left: it was the one entry in this card that is not a paint edit — it resizes the **node**,
through the same two spellings the W/H fields choose between, to `ImageRef::oriented_size` — and a
verb aimed at the layer is one a hand wants *after* playing with a picture, when the mode is no
longer open. It is `context-menus.md` §5.7's row alone now (§15 D305), which also settles a
disagreement the two doors had: the menu row dims on a locked layer and this one, gated only on
"the picture has a size", committed the geometry write anyway — D261's failure in the sharpest
shape it has taken, since the write was **geometry** rather than a crop.
There is no *Edit crop…*
beside them any more either: it was a fourth door into the crop tool, dimmed unless this row happened
to be the fill that tool would act on, and the card only exists while that fill is being edited — so
the row would offer what the user is already doing (§15 D268). All three actions in Settings — *Reset
crop* and the two replaces — go
through `inspector::menu_action`, which is what lets a **dimmed** row still say why it is unavailable:
a widget inside a disabled `Ui` reports no hover and a `ui.scope`'s response is never hovered either,
so the row is shadowed by an explicit `Sense::empty()` claimant over the same rect (§15 D182, D688 —
it is hovered for being **last**, not for sensing anything, and `Sense::hover()` was the same value).
In Adjustments: seven rows built from `Adjustment::ALL`, so the panel cannot list six of them or call
one something the snapshot calls something else, **at the card's own `IMAGE_CARD_GAP` and not a pitch
of their own** — they sat at 4 and read as a table rather than as seven controls, and the fix is the
absence of an override rather than a bigger number, so the claim stays "the same as the rest of the
card" (§15 D269). ⚠️ **And the card's own number is the panel's now** — `IMAGE_CARD_GAP` was 10,
picked for the card rather than read off the column it sits in, so image editing stacked its rows a
point looser than Transform two cards above it; it is `ui::CARD_ROW_GAP` (§15 D386). Each row is a
`ui::value_field_metered` whose **prefix is the
word** — no icon set has seven tone-adjustment glyphs anyone can tell apart — scrubbing percent under
the hand where the file keeps `-1..=1`, and written through `valve_slot` so a scrub is one undo step
(§9.3). The meter is a wash of the accent across the field's own ink **growing from the field's
middle**, negative filling left and positive right, each half's travel being half the ink so that ±1
reaches an edge and each pair of corners rounding only where the bar meets that end: these seven are
offsets from a neutral zero rather than quantities, so a bar drawing −40 and +40 alike would
contradict the digits beside it rather than compress them (§15 D190, which recorded the opposite until
the reversal). **That middle is marked by a 1pt tick in the same wash** (`ui::METER_TICK_W`, painted
from `ui::meter_wash()` as the bar is, so the two cannot drift apart), the full height of the ink and
so stopping short of the border, and **always drawn rather than only at rest**: a row at zero drawing
nothing at all reads as an empty box instead of as a control at its neutral value, and a tick that
went away as soon as the row had a value would remove the origin exactly when the bar gives it
something to be read against (§15 D190). The number itself is **right-aligned** here where every
other field puts it beside the
prefix, because a number in the middle of a field the bar is crossing reads as a label *on* the bar,
and a prefix that is a word rather than a glyph would land it somewhere different in all seven rows.
The sign is still carried exactly by `inspector::signed_number`'s `+12` / `-8`.
A reset per slider is **dimmed rather than absent** at rest, because a control that came and
went would move the six rows under it every time a value crossed zero, and it re-checks the state
after `.clicked()` as the undo and redo buttons do; *Reset adjustments* is the group's own
`menu_action` (§15 D186).
**Image editing (`Tool::ImageEdit`) makes the layer's box a window onto its picture** (§15 D268).

**It replaced the crop tool, and the reversal is the point.** D181 argued that a crop must be a
*tool* — a rail slot, a letter, chrome — because D118's rule is that a mode entered only by
double-click is the failure to avoid. That was answered on the machine by the thing it did not
predict: a tool armed from the rail has no subject, and a **mode strip offering *Crop* beside a
bounding box that resized rather than cropped** is two controls disagreeing about one word. So the
rail button and `C` are gone, and what answers D118 instead is that the mode cannot be entered
without a picture to enter, and that entering it puts a card on the panel and an outline round the
whole photograph. It announces itself by being impossible to be in by accident, which a rail button
is precisely not. It stays a `Tool` variant rather than a field of its own, because the input
routing, the cursor, `chrome_hidden`, the `Escape` ladder and `Enter`'s toggle are all keyed off
`self.tool`, and a parallel `editing_image` would be a second answer to "what is the canvas doing".

Its subject is derived, not stored: `canvas::edited_image` is the one place that answers which fill,
from the tool plus a single selection whose first **visible** image fill is the one acted on
(`tools::croppable_fill`, one line onto `Paint::image_fill` since §15 D287), so no field records it —
`edited_path`'s rule exactly. **Four ways in**: the **double-click** on a picture, `Enter` on a
selected one — the same one-level-in gesture as a group's children, a text node's characters and a
path's points, with `Enter` toggling back out where `Escape` unwinds a rung at a time — the *Edit
image* row at the head of `context-menus.md` §5.7 since 2026-08-22, and, since 2026-08-23, a **click
on a fill row's swatch or its *Image* label** in the inspector (§15 D305). The double-click arm sits
**behind the group step**
(above): on a picture inside a group the first double-click selects the picture and the second crops
it, which is what makes "select it without editing it" a gesture that exists at all (§15 D287). The
menu row is the repair D118 asks for and the one this mode went without for two days: *Edit crop…*
had gone with the tool, and the question was re-asked and reversed (§15 D268). **All four say the
same sentence because they call the same function** — `OndinApp::begin_image_edit(id)`, which selects
the layer, takes the tool and prints the status line; the first three carried a copy of it with a
note that a constant would want all of them at once, and the fourth is what earned it (§15 D305).
All four ask
`tools::croppable_fill` rather than a rule of their own, so none of them can offer a picture the mode
would then refuse — the panel door through `inspector::row_edits_the_mode_s_picture`, which compares
that answer against the row's own slot so that the second image fill of a layer with two is inert
rather than opening the mode onto the other photograph. **And a lock refuses all four, in that one
function** (§15 D320): `begin_image_edit` returns early on a locked node with *"This layer is locked —
unlock it to edit the picture"*, before it selects anything or takes the tool. **A crop is a resize** —
`crop_resize_tx` writes through `tools::resize_layer`, the write *Original size* has always been dimmed
for — so the lock reaches it exactly as it reaches its neighbour in `context-menus.md` §5.7's head.
**Refusing at the four doors is not enough, and `edited_image` carries the same guard** (§15 D463):
arming is not the only way to be *in* the mode, since the layers panel can lock the row while image
editing is already armed, and can move the selection onto a *different*, locked picture without
`choose_tool` being re-entered — neither route passes `begin_image_edit`, and the crop gesture reads
`edited_image`. So the refusal sits on the funnel as well as at the doors, which is `edited_path`'s
argument one paragraph down in almost the same words. The
*Edit image* row dims **because** the mode refuses and never instead of it: a menu refusing where the
chord allows is §15 D261's failure, so the mode changes first and the row follows. It asks
`query::is_effectively_locked`, so **a locked group closes the door on the picture inside it** — the own
flag for one day, and effective since the day after (§15 D321).

**Text and points refuse the same way, in the same shape** (§15 D321). `canvas::begin_edit_text` and
`enter_action`'s `Path` arm each return early with a sentence of their own, which closes the *worse*
direction of the same fault: *Edit text* and *Edit points* have always dimmed on a locked layer while
`Enter` opened the mode on it, so the menu refused where the chord allowed. The points guard is the one
**not** in a shared funnel — nothing in `tools/` reads the lock, so a locked path's anchors are draggable
the moment the tool is armed, which makes arming it the thing to refuse. **And `Enter` is not the only
way to arm it**: `A` and the rail's node button reach `choose_tool(Tool::Node)` with no lock check, and
`canvas::edited_path` takes its subject from the layer selection, which a locked layer can join from the
panel. So the refusal sits in `edited_path` — a locked path is not a subject — rather than in the tool
switch, that being the one query every reader of the point-editing state passes through and a lock check
in the general switch being a rule about one kind in the code that knows about none. The tool still
arms; it finds nothing, exactly as pressing `A` over a rectangle already does. **A verb with a second
door owes the same check on that door** (§15 D514): `canvas::reverse_subpaths` asks `edited_path` first
and so inherits this guard, but its fallback onto a single selected path — the latitude described
above — asked only the *kind*, so `Shift+D` reversed a locked path that was merely selected. It asks
`query::is_effectively_locked` in that arm now, rather than folding a lock into the kind test.

**Outside the mode, resizing a picture resizes it. Inside it, the handles crop.** That sentence is
the whole change. A handle drag moves one edge of the layer's box with the picture nailed down in
world space, so the box reveals less or more of it; a drag on the picture slides it under a box that
is nailed down. Between them they reach every crop there is, and **neither can scale the
photograph** — deliberately, since scaling is what resizing the layer does outside the mode. The
old tool had both verbs on one drag, which is the other half of why "I chose Crop and it resized"
was the report it was. Side handles are therefore live where the crop tool had none: a handle owns
whatever axes it owns, and with a *moving* box there is no stretching degree of freedom to protect
against.

The arithmetic is three pieces, each testable on its own. `ImageRef::picture_box` reads the whole
photograph's rectangle off the very transform the backends paint with, so the outline drawn round it
cannot land anywhere but where the picture is; `tools::crop_resized` moves the grabbed edge, bounded
by that rectangle — the outline is a real limit, because there is nothing beyond the photograph to
open a window onto — and **holds the handle on its own side of the box**, where a resize handle may
cross over and mirror the layer, since a mirrored window would flip a photograph the mode promises
not to move; and `image::crop_reframed` re-reads the old mapping at the new box's corners, which is
the one answer that leaves the picture still. Because the crop and the frame stay in exact
proportion, the gesture can neither stretch nor squash. `crop_resize_tx` then aims
`tools::resize_layer` at the corner `crop_resized` returned, so the box written and the box the crop
was computed against are the same box, and emits **one transaction** carrying the geometry and the
`SetFills` together: either alone is a bug you can see. Both drags capture their starting values at
the press and re-derive from them every frame, preview through `session.set_preview` and commit; the
mode is forced to `Crop` on the way, because that is what either drag means whichever of the four
the fill was in. ⚠️ **And both are gated on travel before they commit, which they were not until
2026-09-08** (§15 D528): forcing the mode is a real write, so a press and a release with no movement —
dismissing the mode, or checking where you are — flipped a `Fill` picture to `Crop` and left an undo
step, invisibly, since a `Fill` picture's seed crop already *is* `cover_crop`. Each drag carries a
`grab_world` from the press and the commit asks `gesture_travelled` (§9.3); the **preview** is
deliberately ungated, or `image_ghost_live`'s promise that the offcut appears on the first travelled
frame would slip by a gesture. An untravelled release clears the preview through
`clear_gesture_preview`, or the click would go on showing the flip it did not make. `a_crop_drag_leaves_the_photograph_exactly_where_it_was` asserts the composition at
the symptom — the brush transform in world space, unchanged across the drag.

**The offcut is drawn, and it is real ink.** While the mode is open and the fill is in `Crop`,
`canvas::image_ghost` builds a `RenderOverrides` **chrome ghost**: a `Rect` at `picture_box`, filled
with the same picture uncropped — orientation and the seven adjustments along with it, because the
offcut is the same photograph — at `GHOST_ALPHA` times the layer's own opacity, at the layer's own
index so it draws *under* it. The real fill covers the middle at full strength and what shows around
it is what the crop is giving up, which is the drawing Figma's crop makes. `whole_crop` on that
rectangle is the identity by construction, the mapping `picture_box` was read off being its inverse,
so the ghost cannot land anywhere but exactly around the window whatever the orientation.

**The chrome ghost is a `Ghost` but not a preview**, and `RenderOverrides` keeps it in a field of its
own for that reason: `is_empty` is how the app asks "is a gesture in flight"
(`Session::has_gesture_preview`), and a mode that answered yes for as long as it was open would have
`cancel_gesture` unwinding a drag nobody started on every right-click. `ghosts_of` chains it, so the
z-ordered draw and the cull that must not return before reaching a ghost both cover it for free. It
is **re-installed every frame from one place**, the top of `draw_canvas`, which is downstream of
every way the state can have changed and is what lets it survive a commit — a `set_preview` replaces
the overrides wholesale, and the alternative is the second call at every call site that
`preview_guide` pays for.

The selection box is suppressed while the mode is up (`chrome_hidden`) and `canvas::draw_crop_box`
draws the window **dashed** — 3pt at 6/6 (`CROP_DASH_PX`, `CROP_GAP_PX`, `CROP_STROKE_PX`), coarser
and heavier than the guide extension's 1pt 3/3 it started as, because the dash is the whole of what
distinguishes this box from the selection's and a hairline with gaps in it is not enough of a
difference — with the selection's own hollow handles on
its corners, plus the picture's solid outline when the ghost is live. Both read through `shown_crop`,
so they track a drag instead of sitting at the committed rectangle until release. The dash is what
tells the two rectangles apart: provisional, a line you are still moving, against the solid edge of a
